Chapter 1 Introduction to Cost and Management Accounting

Question 1. Discuss the impact of Information Technology in Cost Accounting.

[6 Marks | 8 Minutes] (MTP Sep ‘23, RTP May’22)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 1. The impact of IT in cost accounting may include the followings: (i) After the introduction of ERPs, different functional activities get integrated and as a consequence a single entry into the accounting system provides custom made reports for every purpose and saves an organization from preparing different sets of documents. Reconciliation process of results of both cost and financial accounting systems become simpler and less sophisticated.

(ii) A move towards paperless environment can be seen where documents like Bill of Material, Material Requisition Note, Goods Received Note, labour utilization report etc. are no longer required to be prepared in multiple copies, the related department can get e copy from the system.

(iii) Information Technology with the help of internet (including intranet and extranet) helps in resource procurement and mobilization. For example, production department can get materials from the stores without issuing material requisition note physically. Similarly, purchase orders can be initiated to the suppliers with the help of extranet. This enables an entity to shift towards Just-in-Time (JIT) approach of inventory management and production.

(iv) Cost information for a cost center or cost object is ascertained with accuracy in timely manner. Each cost center and cost object is codified and all related costs are assigned to the cost object or cost center. This process automates the cost accumulation and ascertainment process. The cost information can be customized as per the requirement. For example, when an entity manufacture or provide services, it can know information job -wise, batch-wise, process-wise, cost center wise etc.

(v) Uniformity in preparation of report, budgets and standards can be achieved with the help of IT. ERP software plays an important role in bringing uniformity irrespective of location, currency, language and regulations.

(vi) Cost and revenue variance reports are generated in real time basis which enables the management to take control measures immediately.

(vii) IT enables an entity to monitor and analyse each process of manufacturing or service activity closely to eliminate non value added activities. The above are examples of few areas where Cost Accounting is done with the help of IT.

(1+1+1+1+1+0.5+0.5) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Keyword Focus – Highlight IT tools (ERP, extranet, automation) and their direct impact on costing (JIT,

variance analysis).

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 2

2. Examples Over Theory – Instead of "IT saves time," write "e-MRN eliminates physical copies, reducing

processing time by 30%."

3. Structured Bullets – List 6-7 crisp points (ICAI prefers brevity).
4. Time-Saver – Pre-memorize 2-3 unique examples (e.g., codified cost centers, batch-wise tracking).

Examiner Observations Students often make the following mistakes while answering this question:

1. Generic Statements – Many students write vague points like "IT improves efficiency" without linking it to cost

accounting specifics (e.g., ERP integration, real-time variance analysis).

2. Lack of Examples – Examiners expect practical applications (e.g., JIT inventory via extranet, automated cost

accumulation). Students miss these and write theoretical definitions.

3. Repetition – Points like "reduces paperwork" and "improves accuracy" are repeated without expanding on

how (e.g., e-copies replacing physical MRN/GRN).

4. Ignoring Customization – Few mention how IT allows tailored reports (job-wise, batch-wise costing), a key

ICAI expectation.

5. No Real-Time Focus – Overlooking the critical advantage of real-time variance reporting for quick decision-

making.

6. Structure Issues – Bullet points are preferred, but students write paragraphs, losing clarity and marks

Question 2. DISCUSS the essential features of a good cost accounting system?

[6 Marks | 6 Minutes\](Study material) [Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 2. ESSENTIALS OF A GOOD COST ACCOUNTING SYSTEM The essential features, which a good Cost Accounting System should possess, are as follows: (a) Informative and simple: Cost accounting system should be tailor-made, practical, simple and capable of meeting the requirements of a business concern. The system of costing should not sacrifice the utility by introducing inaccurate and unnecessary details.

(b) Accurate and authentic: The data to be used by the cost accounting system should be accurate and authenticated; otherwise it may distort the output of the system and a wrong decision may be taken.

(c) Uniformity and consistency: There should be uniformity and consistency in classification, treatment and reporting of cost data and related information. This is required for benchmarking and comparability of the results of the system for both horizontal and vertical analysis.

(d) Integrated and inclusive: The cost accounting system should be integrated with other systems like financial accounting, taxation, statistics and operational research etc. to have a complete overview and clarity in results.

(e) Flexible and adaptive: The cost accounting system should be flexible enough to make necessary amendment and modifications in the system to incorporate changes in technological, reporting, regulatory and other requirements.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 3

(f) Trust on the system: Management should have trust on the system and its output. For this, an active role of management is required for the development of such a system that reflects a strong conviction in using information for decision making. (1+1+1+1+1+1)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Keyword First: Start with bolded headings (e.g., Accuracy, Flexibility) to save time.
2. Example-Based: For each feature, add a 1-line practical instance (e.g., "Flexibility helps in adopting ABC

costing if production methods change").

3. Avoid Over-Explaining: Stick to 3-4 lines per feature; examiners prioritize clarity over length.

Pre-Defined Structure: Memorize a 4-point framework (Introduction, Features, Example, Conclusion) to streamline writing.

Examiner Observations Students often make the following mistakes while answering this question:

1. Theoretical Repetition Without Depth – Many students merely list the features (e.g., "informative,"

"accurate") without explaining why they are essential or how they impact decision-making. Examiners expect practical relevance, not just definitions.

2. Missing Real-World Linkage – A common error is failing to connect features to business scenarios (e.g., how

"flexibility" helps in adapting to GST changes). ICAI prefers applied knowledge over rote memorization.

3. Ignoring Interconnectivity – Students treat each feature in isolation, but examiners look for integration (e.g.,

how "uniformity" aids in benchmarking across departments).

4. Overlooking "Trust on the System" – This is often under-explained. Students should emphasize management

buy-in (e.g., how cost data influences pricing strategies).

5. Excessive Jargon Without Clarity – Using terms like "horizontal and vertical analysis" without simple

explanations can lose marks.

6. Structure Issues – Bullet points are acceptable, but flow and coherence matter. Some students mix up

"integrated" with "adaptive," leading to redundancy.

Question 3. Discuss the four different methods of costing along with their applicability to concerned industry?

[6 Marks | 6 Minutes\](MTP March ‘18)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 3. Four different methods of costing along with their applicability to concerned industry have been discussed as below: (i) Job Costing: The objective under this method of costing is to ascertain the cost of each job order. A job card is prepared for each job to accumulate costs. The cost of the job is determined by adding all costs against the job it has incurred. This method of costing is used in printing press, foundries and general engineering workshops, advertising etc.

(ii) Batch Costing: This system of costing is used where small components/ parts of the same kind are required to be manufactured in large quantities. Here batch of similar products is treated as a job and cost of such a job is ascertained as discussed under (1), above. If in a cycle manufacturing unit, rims are produced in batches of 2,500 units each, then the cost will be determined in relation to a batch of 2,500 units.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 4

(iii) Contract Costing: If a job is very big and takes a long time for its completion, then method used for costing is known as Contract Costing. Here the cost of each contract is ascertained separately. It is suitable for firms engaged in the construct ion of bridges, roads, buildings etc.

(iv) Operating Costing: The method of Costing used in service rendering undertakings is known as operating costing. This method of costing is used in undertakings like transport, supply of water, telephone services, hospitals, nursing homes etc. (2+2+1+1)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Pre-Memorized Examples: Use atypical industries (e.g., "film production" for job costing) to stand out.
2. Flowchart Mindset: Visualize methods as: a. Job: Single unit → Printing press. b. Batch: Group of identical units → Bakery (cookie batches). c. Contract: Long-term → Road construction. d. Operating: Services → Cloud hosting (cost per server).

b. Avoid Definitions: Focus on why the method suits the industry (e.g., "batch costing reduces setup costs in apparel manufacturing"). c. Bullet Points: Save time with 1-line explanations per method.

Examiner Observations Students often make these mistakes while answering:

1. Vague Industry Linkage – Many just name the costing method (e.g., "Job Costing") but fail to specify unique

industries (e.g., "advertising agencies" for job costing). ICAI expects precise examples, not generic terms like "manufacturing."

2. Confusing Batch & Process Costing – Students mix batch costing (discrete batches) with process

costing (continuous production). A clear distinction is needed (e.g., "bicycle rims vs. petroleum refining").

3. Overlooking Operating Costing Nuances – Some write "transport" but miss sub-categories (e.g., "logistics vs.

passenger buses"). Examiners prefer granularity.

4. Ignoring Hybrid Systems – Modern industries (e.g., automobiles) use multiple methods (job + batch). Students

rarely discuss overlaps, losing application marks.

5. Definition-Heavy, Zero Insight – Merely defining "contract costing" without explaining progress

billing or escalation clauses (common in construction) shows lack of depth.

6. Structure Issues – Listing methods without logical flow (e.g., job → batch → contract → operating) appears

disjointed.

Question 4. DISCUSS the steps to be followed to exercise control over cost.

[6 Marks | 6 Minutes\](MTP Oct’20) [Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 4. To exercise control over cost, following steps are followed: (i) Determination of pre-determined standard or results: Standard cost or performance targets for a cost object or a cost centre is set before initiation of production or service activity. These are desired cost or result that need to be achieved.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 5

(ii) Measurement of actual performance: Actual cost or result of the cost object or cost centre is measured. Performance should be measured in the same manner in which the targets are set i.e. if the targets are set up operation-wise, and then the actual costs should also be collected and measured operation-wise to have a common basis for comparison.

(iii) Comparison of actual performance with set standard or target: The actual performance so measured is compared against the set standard and desired target. Any deviation (variance) between the two is noted and reported to the appropriate person or authority.

(iv) Analysis of variance and action: The variance in results so noted are further analysed to know the reasons for variance and appropriate action is taken to ensure compliance in future. If necessary, the standards are further amended to take developments into account. (1+2+2+1)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Flowchart Format: Draw a quick PDCA cycle (Plan-Do-Check-Act) to structure steps.
2. Pre-Learned Examples: Use automobile industry (e.g., Toyota’s Just-in-Time inventory control).
3. Bullet Points: Write 1-line explanations per step (e.g., "Standards: Budgeted material cost per unit = ₹50").
4. Highlight Keywords: Underline "variance analysis," "responsibility centers" for examiner attention.
5. Avoid Definitions: Focus on "how" (e.g., "Use variance reports to negotiate bulk discounts").

Examiner Observations Students often make these mistakes while answering:

1. Theoretical Explanation Without Practical Linkage – Many students list steps (e.g., "set standards") but fail to

explain how these steps apply in real business scenarios (e.g., "standard costing in automobile manufacturing"). ICAI expects applied knowledge, not just definitions.

2. Missing Variance Analysis Depth – A common error is briefly mentioning "variance analysis" without

detailing types of variances (e.g., material price variance, labor efficiency variance) or corrective actions (e.g., renegotiating supplier contracts).

3. Ignoring Feedback Loop – Students often skip the final step of revising standards (e.g., updating cost

benchmarks due to inflation). This step is crucial for continuous improvement.

4. Overlooking Responsibility Accounting – Few students link cost control to departmental accountability (e.g.,

production manager responsible for material usage variance). Examiners look for role-specific actions.

5. Repetitive Phrasing – Some students describe each step in similar words (e.g., "compare actual vs. standard"

without explaining tools like cost control charts).

6. No Industry-Specific Examples – Answers remain generic instead of using sector-based cases (e.g., "hospital

cost control via activity-based costing").

Important Note:- a) In this theoretical question on ‘Cost control and Cost reduction’, below average performance of the examinees was observed. b) The theory question required knowledge of the concepts of two terms Cost Control and Cost Reduction to identify differences between them. Most of the examinees answered partly correct. Performance of the examinees was below average.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Tabular Format: Use two columns (Cost Control vs. Reduction) for quick comparison.

Pre-Learned Examples: a. Control: Monthly fuel budget adherence in logistics. b. Reduction: Switching to EVs to cut fuel costs permanently. c. Keyword Emphasis: Bold "preventive," "corrective," "continuous" for clarity.

2. Avoid Definitions: Focus on functional contrasts (e.g., "Control detects variances; Reduction eliminates root

causes").

3. 30-Second Brainstorm: Jot down 3 industry examples before writing.

Examiner Observations Students often make these mistakes while answering:

1. Superficial Differentiation – Many just state "cost control maintains, cost reduction reduces" without

explaining how they function differently in practice (e.g., cost control uses budgets vs. cost reduction uses value engineering).

2. Missing Strategic Perspective – Few highlight that cost reduction is proactive (e.g., redesigning products to cut

material costs) while cost control is reactive (e.g., monitoring variances).

3. Ignoring Time Horizon – Students often skip clarifying that cost control is short-term (monthly budgets) while

cost reduction is long-term (process re-engineering).

4. No Real-World Examples – Answers lack industry-specific instances (e.g., cost control in retail (inventory

audits) vs. cost reduction in manufacturing (automation).

5. Overlapping Points – Some list differences like "past vs. future" but fail to tie them to decision-making (e.g.,

cost reduction drives innovation).

6. Neglecting Continuous Improvement – The "no end" aspect of cost reduction is rarely expanded (e.g., Kaizen

costing in Toyota).

Question 7. Explain Direct Expenses and how these are measured and their treatment in cost accounting.

[5 Marks | 7 Minutes\](PYP May ’19) [Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 7. Direct Expense: Expenses other than direct material cost and direct employee cost, which are incurred to manufacture a product or for provision of service and can be directly traced in an economically feasible manner to a cost object. The following costs are examples for direct expenses: (i) Royalty paid/ payable for production or provision of service; (ii) Hire charges paid for hiring specific equipment; (iii) Cost for product/ service specific design or drawing; (iv) Cost of product/ service specific software; (v) Other expenses which are directly related with the production of goods or provision of service. The above list of expenses is not exhaustive; any other expenses which are directly attributable to the production or service are also included as direct expenses.

Measurement of Direct Expenses The direct expenses are measured at invoice or agreed price net of rebate or discount but includes duties and taxes (for which input credit not available), commission and other directly attributable costs. In case of sub-contracting, where goods are get manufactured by job workers independent of the principal entity, are measured at agreed price. Where the principal supplies some materials to the job workers, the value of such materials and other incidental expenses are added with the job charges paid to the job workers.

Treatment of Direct Expenses Direct Expenses forms part the prime cost for the product or service to which it can be directly traceable and attributable. In case of lump-sum payment or one-time payment, the cost is amortized over the estimated production volume or benefit derived. If the expenses incurred are of insignificant amount. i.e. not material, it can be treated as part of overheads.

Important Note:- This theoretical question was related to ‘Direct Expenses’. Poor performance of the examinees was observed.

(2+2+1) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Use the "D-M-T" Framework: a. Define (What are direct expenses?). b. Measure (How to calculate? Net price + duties, subcontracting rules). c. Treat (Prime cost? Amortization? Overheads if immaterial?). d. Memorize Key Examples: Royalty, software, subcontracting. e. Highlight Exceptions: a. Amortization for lump sums (e.g., patent fees). f. Materiality rule (small expenses → overheads).

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to:

1. Vague Definition – Many fail to clearly define Direct Expenses as costs other than direct material and

labor but still directly traceable to a cost object.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 9

2. Incomplete Examples – Some list only generic expenses (e.g., "royalty") but miss specific cases like product-

specific software or subcontracting charges.

3. Measurement Errors – A common mistake is ignoring net of discounts/duties or misclassifying taxes (e.g.,

including GST if input credit is available).

4. Treatment Confusion – Students incorrectly state that all direct expenses go to prime cost without

mentioning amortization for lump-sum payments or insignificant expenses treated as overheads.

5. Subcontracting Misunderstanding – Few explain how job worker charges are measured (agreed price +

supplied materials).

6. Overlooking Materiality Concept – Many miss the exception where immaterial direct expenses are classified

as overheads.

Question 8. DISCUSS the different cost centres that on organization can have?

[8 Marks | 10 Minutes\](Study material) [Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 8. As the organization grows, its functions, organizational structure and other related functions also grow in terms of volume and complexity. To have a better control over the organization, management delegates its responsibility and authority to various departments or persons. These departments or persons are known as responsibility centres and are held responsible for performance in terms of expenditure, revenue, profitability and return on investment. Performance of these responsibility centres are measured against some set standards (input-output ratio, budgets etc.) and evaluated against organizational goal and performance targets.

(i) Cost Centres: The responsibility centre which is held accountable for incurrence of costs which are under its control. The performance of this responsibility centre is measured against pre-determined standards or budgets.

The cost centres are of two types: (a) Standard Cost Centre and (b) Discretionary Cost Centre

(a) Standard Cost Centre: Cost Centre where output is measurable and input required for the output can be specified. Based on a well-established study, an estimate of standard units of input to produce a unit of output is set. The actual cost for inputs is compared with the standard cost. Any deviation (variance) in cost is measured and analyzed into controllable and uncontrollable cost. The manager of the cost centre is expected to comply with the standard and held responsible for adverse cost variances. The input- output ratio for a standard cost centre is clearly identifiable. (b) Discretionary Cost Centre: The cost centre whose output cannot be measured in financial terms, thus input-output ratio cannot be defined. The cost of input is compared with allocated budget for the activity. Examples of discretionary cost centres are Research & Development department, Advertisement department where output of these department cannot be measured with certainty and co-related with cost incurred on inputs.

(ii) Revenue Centres: The responsibility centres which are accountable for generation of revenue for the entity. Sales Department for example, is responsible for achievement of sales target and revenue generation. Though, revenue centres do not have control on expenditures it incurs but sometimes expenditures related with selling activities like commission to sales person etc. are incurred by revenue centres.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 10

(iii) Profit Centres: These are the responsibility centres which have both responsibility of generation of revenue and incurrence of expenditures. Since, managers of profit centres are accountable for both costs as well as revenue, profitability is the basis for measurement of performance of these responsibility centres. Examples of profit centres are decentralised branches of an organisation.

(iv) Investment Centres: These are the responsibility centres which are not only responsible for profitability but also have the authority to make capital investment decisions. The performance of these responsibility centres are measured on the basis of Return on Investment (ROI) besides profit. Examples of investment centres are Maharatna, Navratna and Miniratna companies of Public Sector Undertakings of Central Government.

(2+1+1+1+1+1+1) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Use the "CRPI" Acronym: a. Cost Centres → Revenue → Profit → Investment.
2. Focus on Key Differentiators: a. Cost Centres: Control expenses only. b. Revenue Centres: Generate sales (no

cost control).

b. Profit Centres: Manage both cost & revenue. d. Investment Centres: ROI-driven.

3. Add Examples for Clarity: a. Discretionary cost centre → "Advertising department". b. Investment centre →

"ONGC (Navratna PSU)".

Examiner Observations Students often face challenges with this question due to:

1. Overgeneralization – Many fail to clearly distinguish between cost, revenue, profit, and investment centres,

treating them as interchangeable.

2. Incomplete Classification – Some only discuss cost centres but miss revenue, profit, and investment centres,

despite the question asking for "different cost centres" (implying all responsibility centres).

3. Standard vs. Discretionary Cost Centre Confusion – A frequent error is not explaining the key difference: a. Standard Cost Centre: Input-output measurable (e.g., production). b. Discretionary Cost Centre: Output not measurable (e.g., R&D).
4. Lack of Examples – Students mention types but skip real-world examples (e.g., "Navratna companies" for

investment centres).

5. Performance Measurement Gaps – Few clarify how each centre is evaluated: a. Cost centres → Budget vs. Actual. b. Revenue centres → Sales targets. c. Profit centres → Profitability. d. Investment centres → ROI.
6. Misplaced Emphasis – Some over-explain cost centres but under-explain profit/investment centres, losing

balance.

(0.5+0.5+1+1+1) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. EF-EX-MEA Framework: a. Definition first (30 seconds) b. Examples in bullet points (5 standard ones - 60 seconds) c. Measurement note (30 seconds)

Examiner Observations Students often make these errors when answering this question:

1. Definition Gaps - Many provide examples without first clearly defining direct expenses as costs other

than direct materials and labor that are directly traceable to a cost object.

2. Overlooking Key Characteristics - A significant number fail to emphasize the traceability and economic

feasibility aspects that distinguish direct expenses from overheads.

3. Example Quality Issues - Common mistakes include: a. Using vague examples like "production costs" instead of

specific ones like royalty payments b. Including borderline cases that could be indirect (e.g., general factory maintenance) c. Omitting important standard examples like job worker charges or product-specific software

4. Structural Problems - Many answers: a. Present examples in paragraph form rather than clear bullet points b. Mix direct and indirect expenses without proper distinction c. Fail to mention measurement aspects (invoice price, net of discounts)
5. Conceptual Confusion - Some students incorrectly: a. Include direct labor as a direct expense

b. Treat all production expenses as direct c. Overlook the materiality principle (small direct expenses may be treated as overhead)

Question 10. Narrate the objectives of cost accounting.

[6 Marks | 8 Minutes\](Nov ’23)[Medium | ICAI Fav ]

Answer 10. The main objectives of introduction of a Cost Accounting System in a manufacturing organization are as follows: (i) Ascertainment of cost: The main objective of a Cost Accounting system is to ascertain cost for cost objects. Costing may be post completion or continuous but the aim is to arrive at a complete and accurate cost figure to assist the users to compare, control and make various decisions.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 12

(ii) Determination of selling price: Cost Accounting System in a manufacturing organisation enables to determine desired selling price after adding expected profit margin with the cost of the goods manufactured.

(iii) Cost control and Cost reduction: Cost Accounting System equips the cost controller to adhere and control the cost estimate or cost budget and assist them to identify the areas of cost reduction.

(iv) Ascertainment of profit of each activity: Cost Accounting System helps to classify cost on the basis of activity to ascertain activity wise profitability.

(v) Assisting in managerial decision making: Cost Accounting System provides relevant cost information and assists managers to make various decisions. (2+1+1+1+1)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. P-C-D Framework: a. Primary (Ascertainment, Pricing) b. Control (Monitoring, Reduction) c. Decision (Profitability, Management)
2. Memory Triggers: a. CAP-D" - Cost, Ascertain, Price, Decide b. Remember 3 tiers with 2 objectives each
3. Presentation Tips: a. Use numbered points b. Bold technical terms c. Add one-line explanations
4. Time-Savers: a. Pre-memorize the 6 standard objectives b. Use bullet points instead of paragraphs c. Allocate 1 minute per objective

Examiner Observations Students frequently make these errors when answering this question:

1. Incomplete Coverage - Many students list only 3-4 objectives, missing key aspects like activity-wise

profitability or decision-making support.

2. Vague Phrasing - Common weak statements include: a. "Helps in cost control" (without explaining how) b. "Determines prices" (failing to mention profit margin addition) c. "Assists management" (not specifying decision-making)
3. Concept Confusion - Notable mix-ups between: a. Cost ascertainment vs. cost control b. Pricing determination vs. profitability analysis c. General accounting vs. cost accounting objectives
4. Structural Issues - Poor presentation with: a. Long paragraphs instead of numbered points b. Missing logical flow from basic to advanced objectives c. Omitting connecting phrases like "The system enables..."
5. Real-world Application Gap - Most answers lack practical examples showing how these objectives translate to

business scenarios.

6. Priority Misordering - Students often: a. Bury key objectives like cost ascertainment b. Over-emphasize secondary benefits c. Fail to highlight the decision-making primacy

Question 11. State the method of costing that would be most suitable for: (i) Oil Refinery (ii) Interior Decoration (iii) Airlines Company (iv) Advertising (v) Car Assembly.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](PYP Jan ‘21)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 11.

Method of Costing © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 13

S. No. Industry Method of Costing (i) Oil Refinery Process Costing (ii) Interior Decoration Job Costing (iii) Airlines Company Operation/ Service Costing (iv) Advertising Job Costing (v) Car Assembly Multiple Costing

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. P-C-D Framework: a. Primary (Ascertainment, Pricing) b. Control (Monitoring, Reduction) c. Decision (Profitability, Management)
2. Memory Triggers: a. "CAP-D" - Cost, Ascertain, Price, Decide b. Remember 3 tiers with 2 objectives each
3. Presentation Tips: a. Use numbered points b. Bold technical terms c. Add one-line explanations
4. Time-Savers: a. Pre-memorize the 6 standard objectives b. Use bullet points instead of paragraphs c. Allocate 1 minute per objective

Examiner Observations

1. Misclassification of Industries – Students often confuse:

a. Oil Refinery (Process Costing) with Batch Costing (thinking of batches of oil instead of continuous flow). b. Airlines (Operation/Service Costing) with Process Costing (assuming flight operations are like manufacturing processes). c. Car Assembly (Multiple Costing) with Job/Batch Costing (missing the combination of different costing methods).

2. Overlooking Hybrid Methods – Many students miss that Car Assembly uses Multiple Costing (combination of

Process + Job/Batch Costing), not just one method.

3. Service Sector Confusion – Advertising and Interior Decoration are both Job Costing, but some students

incorrectly assign Contract Costing (for large projects) or Batch Costing (assuming multiple ads are batched).

4. Vague Justifications – Some students list methods without explaining why they fit the industry (e.g., "Oil

Refinery = Process Costing" without mentioning continuous production).

5. Missing Unique Cases – Airlines is tricky because it’s a service industry but uses Operation Costing (cost per

flight hour/passenger-mile), not Job or Process Costing.

Question 12. LIST DOWN certain financial expenses and income included in Financial Accounts only.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](RTP Jan 2025)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 12. Items included in Financial Accounts only- (A) Purely Financial Expenses: (i) Interest on loans or bank mortgages (ii) Expenses and discounts on issue of shares, debentures etc. (iii) Other capital losses i.e., loss by fire not covered by insurance etc. (iv) Losses on the sales of fixed assets and investments (v) Income tax, donations, subscriptions (vi) Expenses of the company’s share transfer office, if any. © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 14

(B) Purely Financial Income (i) Interest received on bank deposits, loans and investments (ii) Dividends received (iii) Profits on the sale of fixed assets and investments (iv) Transfer fee received (v) Rent receivables.

(3+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. FIRE Framework: a. Financing (loans, shares) b. Investing (assets, investments) c. Regulatory (tax, donations) d. Extraordinary (fire losses)
2. Memory Triggers: a. For expenses: "LOST-C" (Loans, Offerings, Sales, Taxes, Capital) b. For income: "D-PART" (Dividends, Profits, Assets, Rent, Transfer)
3. Elimination Method: a. Ask: "Is this related to core operations?" b. If no → likely financial item
4. Time-Savers: a. Pre-memorize 5 standard expenses & 5 incomes b. Use two-column format for quick presentation

1. Incomplete Coverage - Many students list only 3-4 objectives, missing key aspects like activity-wise profitability

or decision-making support.

2. Vague Phrasing - Common weak statements include: a. "Helps in cost control" (without explaining how) b. "Determines prices" (failing to mention profit margin addition) c. "Assists management" (not specifying decision-making)
3. Concept Confusion - Notable mix-ups between: a. Cost ascertainment vs. cost control b. Pricing determination vs. profitability analysis c. General accounting vs. cost accounting objectives
4. Structural Issues - Poor presentation with: a. Long paragraphs instead of numbered points b. Missing logical flow from basic to advanced objectives c. Omitting connecting phrases like "The system enables..."
