Question 13. Discuss the prerequisite of installing cost accounting system.

[6 Marks | 8 Minutes\](MTP Aug ‘18)[Medium | ICAI Fav]

Answer 13. Before setting up a system of cost accounting the under mentioned factors should be studied: (i) Objective: The objective of costing system, for example whether it is being introduced for fixing prices or for insisting a system of cost control.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 15

(ii) Nature of Business or Industry: The Industry in which business is operating. Every business industry has its own peculiarity and objectives. According to its cost information requirement cost accounting methods are followed. For example, an oil refinery maintains process wise cost accounts to find out cost incurred on a particular process say in crude refinement process etc.

(iii) Organizational Hierarchy: Costing system should fulfil the information requirement s of different levels of management. Top management is concerned with the corporate strategy, strategic level management is concerned with marketing strategy, product diversification, product pricing etc. Operational level management needs the information on standard quantity to be consumed, report on idle time etc.

(iv) Knowing the product: Nature of product determines the type of costing system to be implemented. The product which has by -products requires costing system which account for by-products as well. In case of perishable or short self - life, marginal costing method is required to know the contribution and minimum price at which it can be sold.

(v) Knowing the production process: A good costing system can never be established without the complete knowledge of the production process. Cost apportionment can be done on the most appropriate and scientific basis if a cost accountant can identify degree of effort or resources consumed in a particular process. This also includes some basic technical know -how and process peculiarity.

(vi) Information synchronization: Establishment of a department or a system requires substantial amount of organizational resources. While drafting a costing system, information needs of various other departments should be taken into account. For example, in a typical business organization accounts department needs to submit monthly stock statement to its lender bank, quantity wise stock details at the time of filing returns to tax authorities etc.

(vii) Method of maintenance of cost records: The manner in which Cost and Financial accounts could be inter- locked into a single integral accounting system and how the results of separate sets of accounts i.e. cost and financial, could be reconciled by means of control accounts.

(viii) Statutory compliances and audit: Records are to be maintained to comply with statutory requirements and applicable cost accounting standards to be followed.

(ix) Information Attributes: Information generated from the Costing system should possess all the attributes of information i.e. complete, accurate, timeliness, relevant etc. to have an effective management information system (MIS).

(0.5+1+1+0.5+0.5+0.5+1+0.5+0.5) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Keyword-Based Framework: Use the acronym "PONSI" – Process/Product, Organization, Nature of

business, Statutory, Information attributes.

2. Flowchart Mindset: Visualize the cost accounting system as a pipeline—start with objectives, move to

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 16

technical needs (process/product), and end with compliance.

3. ICAI Keywords: Include terms like "Control Accounts," "CAS," "Section 148," and "MIS" to align with

examiner expectations.

4. Time Management: Spend 8-10 minutes max (for 6 marks). Allocate 1 minute per point + 2 minutes for

examples/compliance.

Examiner Observations Students often make the following mistakes while answering this question:

1. Generic Points Without Explanation – Many write broad headings (e.g., "Nature of Business") but fail to

elaborate with industry-specific examples (e.g., process costing in oil refineries).

2. Missing Practical Linkage – They list prerequisites but don’t connect them to real-world applications (e.g., how

perishable goods require marginal costing for pricing decisions).

3. Ignoring Compliance Aspects – Statutory requirements (like Cost Audit under Section 148 of Companies Act)

are overlooked despite being a key ICAI focus area.

4. Repetition of Financial Accounting – Some confuse cost accounting prerequisites with financial accounting

systems, missing unique needs like cost centers or activity-based costing.

5. Incomplete Synchronization Point – Few explain how cost data integrates with other departments (e.g.,

inventory reports for banks or tax filings).

6. Vague Information Attributes – Terms like "accurate" or "timely" are stated without context on how they

impact decision-making (e.g., real-time cost data for pricing strategies).

Question 14. EXPLAIN the difference between product cost and period cost.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](April ’19, Oct’22) [Easy | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 14. Product costs are those costs that are identified with the goods purchased or produced for resale. In a manufacturing organisation they are attached to the product and that are included in the inventory valuation for finished goods, or for incomplete goods. Product cost is also known as inventoriable cost. Under absorption costing method it includes direct material, direct labour, direct expenses, directly attributable costs (variable and non-variable) and other production (manufacturing) overheads. Under marginal costing method Product Costs includes all variable production costs and the all fixed costs are deducted from the contribution.

Periods costs are the costs, which are not assigned to the products but are charged as expense against revenue of the period in which they are incurred. General Administration, marketing, sales and distributor overheads are recognized as period costs.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Two-Column Format: Visually segregate "Product" (DM, DL, FOH) and "Period" (Admin, Selling) costs.
2. Keyword Triggers: Use "inventoriable," "capitalize," "P&L impact" to align with ICAI’s marking scheme.
3. Flowchart Shortcut: a. Product Cost: Manufacturing → Inventory → COGS when sold. b. Period Cost: Non-manufacturing → P&L in incurred period.
4. Time-Saver: Skip lengthy examples; instead, write: a. "E.g., factory rent = product cost (absorption); sales team salary = period cost. © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 17

Examiner Observations Students often make these errors while answering this question:

1. Confusing Absorption vs. Marginal Costing Treatment – Many incorrectly state that fixed production

overheads are always part of product costs (ignoring marginal costing, where they are period costs).

2. Vague Examples – Listing "marketing costs" as period costs is correct, but top-scorers specify advertising, sales

commissions, or rent for admin offices to show clarity.

3. Inventory Valuation Misunderstanding – Weak answers fail to highlight that product costs capitalize into

inventory (appearing in Balance Sheet) while period costs hit P&L immediately.

4. Overlap in Definitions – Some mix direct vs. indirect costs with product/period costs (e.g., calling "factory

supervisor salary" a period cost—it’s a product cost under absorption costing).

5. Missing Marginal Costing Angle – A frequent oversight is not contrasting how fixed manufacturing costs shift

from product cost (absorption) to period cost (marginal).

Question 15. Identify the methods of costing from the following statements: (i) Costs are directly charged to a group of products. (ii) Nature of the product is complex and method cannot be ascertained. (iii) Costs ascertained for a single product. (iv) All costs are directly charged to a specific job. (v) Costs are charged to operations and averaged over units produced.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](PYP May’22) [Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 15.

Method of costing followed Situation Method of costing (i) Costs are directly charged to a group of products. Batch costing (ii) Nature of the product is complex and method cannot be ascertained. Multiple costing (iii) Cost is ascertained for a single product. Unit/ Single/Output costing (iv) All costs are directly charged to a specific job. Job costing (v) Costs are charged to operations and averaged over units produced. Process costing

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Keyword Mapping – Match phrases like "group of products" → Batch Costing, "specific job" → Job Costing.
2. Eliminate Incorrect Options – For (v), "operations + averaged" = Process Costing (not Operating Costing).
3. Avoid Overthinking – (iii) is clearly Unit Costing; don’t confuse with Job Costing.
4. Focus on Definitions – Multiple Costing is rare but tested; remember it’s for complex products (e.g.,

airplanes).

Examiner Observations Students often make the following mistakes while attempting this question:

1. Confusing Batch Costing with Job Costing – Many students incorrectly label situation (i) as "Job Costing"

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 18

instead of "Batch Costing" because both involve grouping, but batch costing applies to identical products, while job costing is for unique orders.

2. Misinterpreting Multiple Costing – In situation (ii), students wrongly assume "Process Costing" or "Composite

Costing," but "Multiple Costing" is used when a product has complex components requiring different costing methods (e.g., automobiles).

3. Overcomplicating Unit Costing – Situation (iii) is straightforward, but some students write "Process Costing" or

"Job Costing" instead of "Unit/Single/Output Costing", which is used for homogeneous single products like bricks.

4. Ignoring Direct Charging in Job Costing – For situation (iv), students sometimes write "Contract Costing," but

the key here is "specific job", not a long-term project.

5. Mixing Process & Operation Costing – In situation (v), a few students incorrectly choose "Operating Costing"

(used for services) instead of "Process Costing", which averages costs over mass-produced units.

Question 16. DISCUSS the four different methods of costing along with their applicability to concerned industry?

[6 Marks | 7 Minutes\](Study material)[Medium | ICAI Fav]

Answer 16. Different industries follow different methods of costing because of the differences in the nature of their work. The various methods of costing are as follows: Methods Description Single or Output Under this method, the cost of a product is ascertained, the product being the only one Costing produced like bricks, coals, etc. Batch Costing This method is the extension of job costing. A batch may represent a number of small

orders passed through the factory in batch. Each batch here is treated as a unit of cost and thus separately costed. Here cost per unit is determined by dividing the cost of the batch by the number of units produced in the batch. Job Costing Under this method of costing, cost of each job is ascertained separately. It is suitable in all

cases where work is undertaken on receiving a customer’s order like a printing press, motor workshop, etc. Contract Costing Under this method, the cost of each contract is ascertained separately. It is suitable for

firms engaged in the construction of bridges, roads, buildings etc. Process Costing Under this method, the cost of completing each stage of work is ascertained, like cost of

making pulp and cost of making paper from pulp. In mechanical operations, the cost of each operation may be ascertained separately; the name given is operation costing. Operating Costing It is used in the case of concerns rendering services like transport, supply of water, retail

trade etc. Multiple Costing It is a combination of two or more methods of costing outlined above. Suppose a firm

manufactures bicycles including its components; the parts will be costed by the system of job or batch costing but the cost of assembling the bicycle will be computed by the single or output costing method. The whole system of costing is known as multiple costing.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 19

The following table summarises the various methods of costing applied in different industries:

Nature of Output Method Cost Examples of Industries A Series of Processes Process costing or For each process Sugar

Operation Costing Construction of building Contract Costing For each contract Real estate Similar units of a Single Product, Unit or output or Single For the entire Cold Drinks produced by Single Process Costing activity, but averaged

for the output Rendering of Services Operating Costing For all services Hospitals Customer Specifications: Job Costing For each order/ Advertising single Unit assignment/job Consisting of multiple varieties of Multiple Costing Combination of any Car Assembly activities and processes method

Industries also follows Activity Based Costing which is an accounting methodology that assigns costs to activities rather than products or services. ABC is a technique which involves identification of cost with each cost driving activity and making it as the basis for apportionment of costs over different cost objects/ jobs/ products/customers or services.

(3+3) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Keyword Mapping: a. "Single product" → Unit Costing (coal). b. "Customer’s order" → Job Costing (printing press). c. "Identical batches" → Batch Costing (medicines). d. "Long-term project" → Contract Costing (buildings).
2. Exclude Redundancies: Skip listing "Single/Unit/Output" as separate methods.
3. Prioritize Examples: Memorize 1–2 industry examples per method (e.g., Process → Sugar, Operating →

Hospitals).

4. ABC as Bonus: Mention Activity-Based Costing briefly if time permits (1 line).

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to:

1. Confusing Process & Operation Costing – Many incorrectly label "Operation Costing" as a separate method

rather than a subset of Process Costing (mechanical operations like car assembly).

2. Misapplying Batch Costing – Some students associate it with large-scale production (like Process Costing), but

it’s specifically for identical grouped orders (e.g., pharmaceuticals, bakery).

3. Overlooking Multiple Costing Complexity – Students define it as a standalone method rather than

a combination (e.g., bicycles using Job + Output Costing).

4. Mixing Job & Contract Costing – While both deal with specific orders, Contract Costing applies to long-term

projects (bridges) with stage-wise billing, unlike short-term Job Costing (print orders).

5. Ignoring Service Sector Nuances – "Operating Costing" is often missed for service industries (hospitals,

transport), with students wrongly applying Unit Costing.

6. Redundant Definitions – Repetition of "Single/Unit/Output Costing" as distinct methods, despite being

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 20

synonymous.

Question 17. Mention the cost units (physical measurements) for the following Industry/product: (i) Automobile (ii) Gas (iii) Brick works (iv) Power (v) Steel (vi) Transport (by road) (vii) Chemical (viii) Oil (ix) Brewing (x) Cement

[5 Marks | 5 Minutes\](PYP Nov 22)[Easy | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 17.

Industry or Product Cost Units Automobile Number Gas Cubic feet Brick works 1,000 bricks Power Kilo-watt hour (kWh) Steel Tonne Transport (by road) Passenger- kilometer or Tonne-kilometer Chemical Litre, gallon, kilogram, tonne etc. Oil Barrel, tonne, litre Brewing Barrel Cement Ton/ per bag etc.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Memorize Industry Standards: a. Gas = Cubic feet, Oil/Brewing = Barrel, Power = kWh.
2. Composite Units: a. Transport → "X kilometer" (passenger/tonne).
3. Bulk Quantities: a. Bricks → 1,000 units, not per piece.
4. Dual Units: a. Cement → Ton/bag, Chemicals → kg/liter/gallon.
5. Avoid Assumptions: a. Automobile → Number (not "per vehicle").

Examiner Observations Students frequently make these errors in this question:

1. Overlooking Standardized Units – For gas, some write "liters" instead of cubic feet, which is the industry

norm. Similarly, oil is measured in barrels (not just liters/tonnes).

2. Ignoring Composite Units – In transport, students mention only "kilometer" but miss "passenger-kilometer"

or "tonne-kilometer", which are critical for cost calculation.

3. Misapplying Bulk Measurements – Brickworks cost unit is per 1,000 bricks (not per brick), which many miss.
4. Confusing Weight vs. Volume – For chemicals, students often default to "kg" but miss liters/gallons (used for

liquid chemicals).

5. Inconsistent Units for Cement – Some write only "ton" or only "bag," but both are acceptable (ICAI

accepts "ton/per bag").

6. Overcomplicating Brewing – A few write "liters" instead of the industry-standard barrel.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 21

Question 18. Cost and Management Accounting information is used by different stakeholders. The users of the information can be broadly categorised into internal and external to the entity. GIVE two examples of internal users and three examples of external users and EXPLAIN how they are concerned with the Cost and Management Accounting information.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](MTP Jan 2025)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 18. Internal Users Internal users, who use the Cost and Management Accounting information may include the followings: (a) Policy Makers- The policy makers are those who formulate strategies (i) To achieve the goals (short & long term both) to fulfil the objectives of the organisation. (ii) To position the organisation into the competitive market environment. (iii) To design the organisational structure to get the policy and strategies implemented. Etc.

(b) Managers- The managers use the information (i) To know the cost of a cost object and cost centre (ii) To know the price for the product or service (iii) To measure and evaluate performance of responsibility centres (iv) To the know the profitability-product-wise, department-wise, customer-wise etc. (v) To evaluate the strategic options and to make decisions

(c) Operational level staff- The operational level staff like supervisors, foreman, and team leaders require information (i) To know the objectives and performance goals for them (ii) To know product and service specifications like volume, quality and process etc. (iii) To know the performance parameters against which their performance is measured and evaluated. (iv) To know divisional (responsibility centre) profitability etc.

(d) Employees- Employees are concerned with the information related with time and attendance, incentives for work, performance standards etc.

External Users External users, who use the Cost and Management Accounting information may include the followings: (a) Regulatory Authorities- Regulatory Authorities are concerned with cost accounting data and information for different purpose which includes tariff determination, providing subsidies, rate fixation etc. To do this the regulatory bodies require information on the basis of some standards and format in this regard.

(b) Auditors- The auditors while conducting audit of financial accounts or for some other special purpose audit like cost audit etc. require information related with costing and reports reviewed by management etc.

(c) Shareholders- Shareholders are concerned with information that effect their investment in the entity. Management communicates to the shareholders through periodic communique, annual reports etc. regarding new orders received, product expansion, market share for products etc.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 22

(d) Creditors and Lenders- Creditors and lenders are concerned with data and information which affects an entity’s ability to serve lenders or creditors. For example, any financial institutions which provides loan to an entity against book debts and inventories are more concerned with regular reporting on net debt position and stock balances.

(3+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Segregate Clearly – First list 2 internal (e.g., Managers, Employees) and 3 external (e.g., Regulators, Auditors,

Shareholders).

2. Use Action-Oriented Explanations – Instead of "managers need data," write:

a. Managers: a. Use for pricing, cost control, performance evaluation.

b. Regulators: Need for tariff setting, subsidy allocation.

3. Avoid Overlap – Ensure creditors and shareholders have distinct concerns (debt vs. profitability).
4. Prioritize Uncommon Stakeholders – Mention Operational Staff (internal) and Auditors (external) to stand

out.

5. Structured Format – Use bullet points for clarity and speed

Examiner Observations Students frequently make these errors when answering this question:

1. Confusing Internal vs. External Users – Many mix up internal (e.g., managers) with external users (e.g.,

shareholders), leading to incorrect categorization.

2. Vague Explanations – Instead of specifying how stakeholders use cost data (e.g., "managers use it for pricing

decisions"), students give generic statements like "they need information."

3. Overlooking Key Stakeholders – Some miss Regulatory Authorities (external) or Operational Staff (internal),

focusing only on obvious ones like shareholders and managers.

4. Repetitive Points – For external users, students list multiple financial stakeholders (e.g., creditors, lenders,

investors) without differentiating their specific concerns (e.g., creditors focus on debt position, shareholders on profitability).

5. Ignoring Practical Applications – For Auditors, students often say "they check accounts" but fail to

mention cost audit or compliance reporting.

6. Incomplete Examples – Some list only one internal user (e.g., managers) and two external users, missing the

required count (2 internal + 3 external).

Question 19. State the limitations of cost and management accounting.

[4 Marks | 5 Minutes\](MTP Oct ’18, RTP Nov’21) [Easy | ICAI Fav]

Answer 19. Like other branches of accounting, cost and management accounting is also having certain limitations. The limitations of cost and management accounting are as follows:

1. Expensive: It is expensive because analysis, allocation and absorption of overheads require considerable

amount of additional work, and hence additional money.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 23

2. Requirement of Reconciliation: The results shown by cost accounts differ from those shown by financial

accounts. Thus Preparation of reconciliation statements is necessary to verify their accuracy.

3. Duplication of Work: It involves duplication of work as organization has to maintain two sets of accounts i.e.

Financial Account and Cost Account.

4. Inefficiency: Costing system itself does not control costs but its usage does. (1+1+1+1) Approach & Time-Saving Tips
1. Memorize Core Limitations – Focus on ICAI’s key points: a. Expensive setup b. Reconciliation needed c. Duplication of work d. System doesn’t auto-control costs
2. Add 1-2 Extra Points for depth (if time permits): a. Lack of uniformity in methods b. Behavioral biases in data use
3. Use Cause-Effect Structure: a. "Duplication occurs because financial and cost accounts are maintained separately."
4. Avoid Fluff – Stick to 4-5 crisp points with 1-line explanations.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to:

1. Listing Too Few Limitations – Many students mention only 2-3 points (e.g., "expensive," "duplication of work")

but miss critical ones like "lack of uniformity" or "dependence on financial accounting."

2. Vague Explanations – Instead of elaborating on why a limitation exists (e.g., "reconciliation is needed due to

different accounting objectives"), students state generic phrases like "it causes problems."

3. Missing Key ICAI-Specified Limitations – The study material highlights "inefficiency in cost control" (system

doesn’t control costs automatically), but students overlook this.

4. Overemphasis on Cost Aspect – Some focus only on cost accounting limitations (e.g., overhead allocation) but

ignore management accounting limitations like "behavioral bias in data interpretation."

5. Repetition of Similar Points – Writing "expensive" and "additional resources" as separate limitations dilutes

the answer.

6. No Real-World Context – Failing to link limitations to practical scenarios (e.g., "small firms avoid it due to high

costs") reduces marks.

Question 20. DISCUSS the Standard and Discretionary Cost Centres.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](MTP Oct ‘23, Old & New SM)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 20. (i) Standards Cost Centre: Cost Centre where output is measurable and input required for the output can be specified. Based on a well-established study, an estimate of standard units of input to produce a unit of output is set. The actual cost for inputs is compared with the standard cost. Any deviation (variance) in cost is measured and analysed into controllable and uncontrollable cost. The manager of the cost centre is supposed to comply with the standard and held responsible for adverse cost variances. The input-output ratio for a standard cost centre is clearly identifiable.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 24

(ii) Discretionary Cost Centre: The cost center whose output cannot be measured in financial terms, thus input- output ratio cannot be defined. The cost of input is compared with allocated budget for the activity. Example of discretionary cost centers are Research & Development department, Advertisement department where output of these department cannot be measured with certainty and co-related with cost incurred on inputs.

(3+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Keyword-Based Definitions: a. Standard: "Measurable output," "input-output ratio," "variance analysis." b. Discretionary: "No financial output measurement," "budget comparison."
2. Examples Matter: a. Standard: Manufacturing units. b. Discretionary: R&D, Advertising.
3. Managerial Accountability: a. Explicitly state that Standard Cost Centre managers are responsible for

variances.

4. Avoid Redundancy: a. Don’t repeat "output not measurable" for Discretionary Centres; instead, clarify "not in

financial terms."

5. Structured Format: a. Use bullet points for clarity and speed.

Examiner Observations Students often make these errors when answering this question:

1. Confusing Definitions – Many mix up Standard and Discretionary Cost Centres, failing to clearly distinguish

that Standard Centres have measurable outputs, while Discretionary Centres do not.

2. Incomplete Examples – Some mention "R&D" for Discretionary Cost Centres but forget Advertising or HR

Departments, which are equally valid.

3. Missing Key Differentiators – Students overlook that Standard Cost Centres involve variance

analysis (comparing actual vs. standard costs), while Discretionary Centres rely on budget comparisons.

4. Overcomplicating Discretionary Centres – A few incorrectly state that output is "not measurable at all," but

ICAI specifies it’s "not measurable in financial terms."

5. No Managerial Responsibility Link – For Standard Cost Centres, many fail to mention that managers are held

accountable for variances.

6. Vague Language – Using phrases like "hard to measure" instead of precise ICAI terminology like "input-output

ratio cannot be defined" (for Discretionary Centres).

Question 21. How do you deal with the following in cost accounts? (i) Fringe benefits (ii) Bad debts.

[4 Marks | 6 Minutes\](MTP, Oct’21)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 21. (i) Fringe benefits: These are the additional payments or facilities provided to the workers apart from their salary and direct cost-allowances like house rent, dearness and city compensatory allowances. These benefits are given in the form of overtime, extra shift duty allowance, holiday pay, pension facilities etc. These indirect benefits stand to improve the morale, loyalty and stability of employees towards the organization. If the amount of fringe benefit is considerably large, it may be recovered as direct charge by means of a supplementary wage or labour rate; otherwise, these may be collected as part of production overheads.

(ii) Bad debts: There is no unanimity among different authors of Cost Accounting about the treatment of bad debts. One view is that ‘bad debts’ should be excluded from cost. According to this view bad debts are financial © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 25

losses and therefore, they should not be included in the cost of a particular job or product. According to another view it should form part of selling and distribution overheads, especially when they arise in the normal course of trading. Therefore, bad debts should be treated in cost accounting in the same way as any other selling and distribution cost. However extra ordinarily large bad debts should not be included in cost accounts.

(2+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. For Fringe Benefits: a. Direct charge if large (e.g., overtime via supplementary wage rate). b. Production overhead if small/indirect (e.g., pension facilities). c. Mention employee morale as a secondary point.
2. For Bad Debts: a. Exclude if abnormal/financial loss. b. Include in selling overhead if normal trade-related. c. Cite lack of unanimity among experts for depth.
3. Use ICAI Keywords: a. "Supplementary wage rate," "selling & distribution overhead," "financial loss."
4. Structured Format: a. Two clear headings (Fringe Benefits/Bad Debts) with bullet points.

Examiner Observations Students frequently make these errors when answering this question:

1. Misclassification of Fringe Benefits – Many incorrectly treat all fringe benefits as direct labor costs, failing to

distinguish between: a. Direct charge (for large, identifiable benefits like overtime)

b. Production overheads (for smaller, indirect benefits like holiday pay)

2. Overgeneralizing Bad Debts – Students often: a. Claim bad debts are always excluded from cost accounts (ignoring the "normal course of trading" exception). b. Fail to specify that abnormally large bad debts should not be included.
3. Lack of Clarity on Treatment – For fringe benefits, some miss the supplementary wage rate option. For bad

debts, many omit the selling & distribution overhead perspective.

4. No Reference to Cost Accounting Principles – Answers lack phrases like: a. "As per CAS/X" (for authority) b. "Financial loss vs. normal trading loss" (for bad debts)
5. Repetition Without Depth – Stating "fringe benefits improve morale" without explaining how they are

accounted for in costs.

Question 22. DISCUSS cost classification based on variability and controllability.

[6 Marks | 8 Minutes\](MTP March ‘18) (RTP May ’21 & May ’19, Old & New SM) [Medium | ICAI Fav ]

Answer 22. Cost classification based on variability (i) Fixed Costs – These are the costs which are incurred for a period, and which, within certain output and turnover limits, tend to be unaffected by fluctuations in the levels of activity (output or turnover). They do not tend to increase or decrease with the changes in output. For example, rent, insurance of factory building etc., remain the same for different levels of production.

(ii) Variable Costs – These costs tend to vary with the volume of activity. Any increase in the activity results in an increase in the variable cost and vice-versa. For example, cost of direct labour, etc.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 26

(iii) Semi-variable Costs – These costs contain both fixed and variable components and are thus partly affected by fluctuations in the level of activity. Examples of semi variable costs are telephone bills, gas and electricity etc.

Cost classification based on controllability: (i) Controllable Costs - Cost that can be controlled, typically by a cost, profit or investment centre manager is called controllable cost. Controllable costs incurred in a particular responsibility centre can be influenced by the action of the executive heading that responsibility centre. For example, direct costs comprising direct labour, direct material, direct expenses and some of the overheads are generally controllable by the shop level management.

(ii) Uncontrollable Costs - Costs which cannot be influenced by the action of a specified member of an undertaking are known as uncontrollable costs. For example, expenditure incurred by, say, the tool room is controllable by the foreman in-charge of that section but the share of the tool-room expenditure which is apportioned to a machine shop is not to be controlled by the machine shop foreman. (3+3)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Structure by Classification: a. Variability: Fixed (rent), Variable (direct materials), Semi-variable (electricity). b. Controllability: Controllable (direct labor), Uncontrollable (apportioned overheads).
2. Keyword Focus: a. Fixed: "Time-bound," "unchanged with output." b. Semi-variable: "Fixed base + variable component." c. Controllable: "Influenced by responsibility center."
3. Contextual Examples: a. Uncontrollable: Machine shop foreman can’t control tool-room allocations.
4. Avoid Redundancy: a. Don’t repeat "direct materials" for both variability and controllability.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to:

1. Confusing Semi-Variable Costs – Many incorrectly label all utility costs (e.g., electricity) as variable, ignoring

their fixed base charges.

2. Overlooking Controllability Context – Students state costs are "uncontrollable" without specifying by

whom (e.g., machine shop foreman vs. tool-room foreman).

3. Incomplete Examples – For fixed costs, generic terms like "rent" are used but miss depreciation or salaries of

permanent staff.

4. Misinterpreting Controllable Costs – Some assume all direct costs are controllable, but certain overheads

(e.g., allocated corporate costs) may not be.

5. Ignoring Timeframe – Fixed costs are time-bound (e.g., annual insurance), but students treat them as

perpetually unchanging.

6. Vague Definitions – Using "changes with production" for variable costs instead of "varies proportionally with

activity level."

Question 23. DESCRIBE Operation costing with two examples of industries where operation costing is applied.

[4 Marks | 5 Minutes\](RTP Nov ’20)[Medium | ICAI Fav]

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 27

Answer 23. This product costing system is used when an entity produces more than one variant of final product using different materials but with similar conversion activities. This means conversion activity is similar for all the product variants but materials differ significantly. Operation Costing method is also known as Hybrid product costing system as materials costs are accumulated by job order or batch wise but conversion costs i.e. labour and overheads costs are accumulated by department, and process costing methods are used to assign these costs to products. Moreover, under operation costing, conversion costs are applied to products using a predetermined application rate. This predetermined rate is based on budgeted conversion costs. The two examples of industries are Ready made garments and Jeweller making.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Keyword-Based Definition: a. Start with: "Hybrid system for products with different materials but similar

conversion processes."

b. Highlight: i. Materials → Job/batch-wise tracking. ii. Conversion costs → Departmental process costing. iii. Predetermined rate for overhead allocation.

2. Industry Examples: a. Ready-made garments: Same stitching process, different fabrics. b. Jewelry making: Same polishing/casting, different metals/gems.
3. Avoid Redundancy: a. Don’t explain job/process costing separately; focus on hybrid nature.
4. ICAI Keywords: a. "Hybrid product costing," "budgeted conversion costs," "material variation."

Examiner Observations Students often make these errors when answering this question:

1. Confusing Operation Costing with Process Costing – Many students incorrectly describe pure process costing (homogeneous products) instead of emphasizing hybrid costing (different materials but similar conversion activities).
2. Vague Industry Examples – Some provide generic examples like "manufacturing" instead of specific industries

like ready-made garments or jewelry making, which clearly demonstrate material variation with standardized processes.

3. Missing Key Terminology – Students fail to mention: a. "Hybrid costing system" (combining job + process

costing). b. "Predetermined conversion cost rate" (based on budgeted costs).

4. Incomplete Definition – Answers often skip: a. Material costs tracked by job/batch.

b. Conversion costs applied uniformly via departmental rates.

5. Overcomplicating the Concept – Some unnecessarily compare it with other methods (e.g., batch costing)

instead of sticking to ICAI’s definition.

Question 24. DEFINE Controllable Cost and Uncontrollable Cost.

[4 Marks | 5 Minutes\](RTP Nov ’18) (MTP March ’19, April ’23 & Sep ‘23) Or EXPLAIN the difference between controllable & uncontrollable costs?

(RTP May ’22)[Easy | ICAI Fav]

Answer 24. (i) Controllable Costs: - Cost that can be controlled, typically by a cost, profit or investment centre manager is called controllable cost. Controllable costs incurred in a particular responsibility centre can be influenced by the action of the executive heading that responsibility centre. For example, direct costs comprising

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 28

direct labour, direct material, direct expenses and some of the overheads are generally controllable by the shop level management.

(ii) Uncontrollable Costs - Costs which cannot be influenced by the action of a specified member of an undertaking are known as uncontrollable costs. For example, expenditure incurred by, say, the tool room is controllable by the foreman in-charge of that section but the share of the tool-room expenditure which is apportioned to a machine shop is not to be controlled by the machine shop foreman.

(2+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Keyword-Centric Definitions: a. Controllable: "Influenced by responsibility center managers" (e.g., direct

labor).

b. Uncontrollable: "Cannot be altered by assigned personnel" (e.g., allocated overheads).

2. Hierarchy-Based Examples: a. Use ICAI’s tool-room vs. machine shop example to show controllability shifts.
3. Avoid Absolutes: a. Clarify that controllability depends on managerial level (e.g., CEO controls costs a

foreman cannot).

4. Structured Format: a. Two clear headings with 1 definition + 1 example each.

Examiner Observations Students frequently make these errors when answering this question:

1. Vague Definitions – Many students define controllable costs as "costs that can be changed" without

specifying by whom (e.g., responsibility center managers).

2. Misattribution of Control – Some label all direct costs as controllable, ignoring that certain allocated costs

(e.g., corporate overheads) are uncontrollable at lower levels.

3. Overgeneralization – Students state "fixed costs are uncontrollable," which is incorrect (e.g., supervisor

salaries are fixed but controllable by department heads).

4. Weak Examples – For uncontrollable costs, generic terms like "rent" are used instead of ICAI-preferred

examples (e.g., apportioned tool-room costs).

5. Missing Context – Answers lack real-world scenarios (e.g., machine shop foreman vs. tool-room foreman) to

illustrate controllability limits.

6. No Link to Responsibility Accounting – Few mention that controllability is tied to organizational

hierarchy and authority levels.

Question 25. State the Method of Costing to be used in the following industries: (i) Real Estate (ii) Motor repairing workshop (iii) Chemical Industry (iv) Transport service (v) Assembly of bicycles (vi) Biscuits manufacturing Industry (vii) Power supply Companies (viii) Car manufacturing Industry (ix) Cement Industry (x) Printing Press

[5 Marks |6 Minutes\](PYP Nov ‘20) [Medium | ICAI Fav]

Answer 25. Method of costing used in different industries: S. No. Industries Method of Costing © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 29

(i) Real Estate Contract Costing (ii) Motor Repairing Workshop Job Costing (iii) Chemical Industry Process Costing (iv) Transport Service Service/Operating Costing (v) Assembly of Bicycles Unit/Single/Output/Multiple Costing (vi) Biscuits Manufacturing Industry Batch Costing (vii) Power Supply Companies Service/Operating Costing (viii) Car Manufacturing Industry Multiple Costing (ix) Cement Industry Unit/Single/Output Costing (x) Printing Press Job Costing

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Service Industries First: Identify transport/power as Operating Costing (unique to services).
2. Project-Based: Real estate = Contract Costing; printing = Job Costing.
3. Mass Production: a. Continuous flow (chemicals) = Process Costing b. Standard batches (biscuits) = Batch Costing
4. Complex Manufacturing: a. Cars/bicycles = Multiple Costing (combined methods)
5. Single Product: Cement = Unit Costing (avoids over complication).
6. Use Abbreviations: Write "Op. Costing" to save time.

Examiner Observations Students frequently make these errors in this question:

1. Confusing Batch vs Process Costing: Many incorrectly assign Process Costing to biscuit manufacturing (which

uses Batch Costing for standardized batches) and chemical industry (which genuinely uses Process Costing for continuous production).

2. Overlooking Hybrid Methods: For bicycle assembly and car manufacturing, students often select only Unit or

Job Costing, missing Multiple Costing which combines methods for complex production.

3. Service Industry Errors: Transport and power companies are sometimes assigned Job Costing instead of the

correct Operating Costing (which tracks service-specific units like passenger-km or kWh).

4. Real Estate Misclassification: Some students incorrectly use Job Costing instead of Contract Costing, not

recognizing the long-term, project-based nature of real estate.

5. Redundant Terminology: Using multiple terms like "Unit/Single/Output" for cement industry wastes time –

ICAI accepts any one of these.

6. Printing Press Oversight: While most get this right, some confuse it with Batch Costing when it's clearly Job

Costing (customer-specific orders).

Question 26. Briefly explain the ‘techniques of costing’.

[6 Marks | 8 Minutes\](PYP Dec ‘21)[Difficult | ICAI Twister | High Chance for Exams] Answer 26. Techniques Description Uniform Costing When a number of firms in an industry agree among themselves to follow the same system of

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 30

costing in detail, adopting common terminology for various items and processes they are said to follow a system of uniform costing. Advantages of such a system are: i. A comparison of the performance of each of the firms can be made with that of another, or with the average performance in the industry. ii. Under such a system, it is also possible to determine the cost of production of goods which is true for the industry as a whole. It is found useful when tax relief or protection is sought from the Government. Marginal Costing It is defined as the ascertainment of marginal cost by differentiating between fixed and

variable costs. It is used to ascertain effect of changes in volume or type of output on profit. Standard Costing It is the name given to the technique whereby standard costs are pre-determined and and Variance subsequently compared with the recorded actual costs. It is thus a technique of cost Analysis ascertainment and cost control. This technique may be used in conjunction with any method

of costing. However, it is especially suitable where the manufacturing method involves production of standardized goods of repetitive nature. Historical It is the ascertainment of costs after they have been incurred. This type of costing has limited Costing utility.

Post Costing: It means ascertainment of cost after production is completed. Continuous costing: Cost is ascertained as soon as the job is completed or even when the job is in progress. Absorption It is the practice of charging all costs, both variable and fixed to operations, processes or Costing products. This differs from marginal costing where fixed costs are excluded. Direct costing Direct costing is a specialized form of cost analysis that only uses variable costs to make

decisions. It does not consider fixed costs, which are assumed to be associated with the time periods in which they are incurred.

Important Note:- This theory question on technique of costing was not answered well. Examinees answered different methods of costing instead of techniques. Performance of the examinees was poor.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Keyword-Based Definitions : a. Marginal Costing: "Fixed vs. variable cost segregation + profit analysis". b. Standard Costing: "Predetermined vs. actual cost comparison + variance analysis". c. Prioritize Key Techniques: Focus on: a. Marginal, Standard, Absorption (most frequently tested). b. Briefly cover Uniform, Historical, Direct.
2. Use Bullet Points: For clarity and speed.
3. Add 1-Line Applications: a. E.g., "Uniform costing enables industry-wide tax negotiations".
4. Avoid Redundancy: Don’t repeat similar points for absorption/direct costing.

Examiner Observations Students frequently struggle with this question due to:

1. Confusing Techniques with Methods: Many incorrectly explain methods (like job/process costing) instead of techniques (like marginal/standard costing). This fundamental misunderstanding leads to complete answer failure.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 31

2. Incomplete Coverage: Students often mention only 2-3 techniques (typically marginal and standard costing) while missing others like uniform costing or historical costing.
3. Vague Definitions: Explanations lack precision, e.g., defining marginal costing as "variable cost analysis" without clarifying fixed vs. variable cost segregation or decision-making utility.
4. No Practical Applications: Few students link techniques to real-world use cases, e.g., uniform costing for industry benchmarking or standard costing for variance analysis.
5. Overlooking Historical Costing: Most ignore this technique entirely or mislabel it as "outdated" without explaining its post-costing nature.
6. Redundant Explanations: Some describe absorption and direct costing separately but fail to highlight their key difference (treatment of fixed costs).

Question 27. Define cost objects and give examples of any four cost objects.

[4 Marks | 5 Minutes\](PYP May ‘23) [Easy | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 27. Definition of cost objects: Cost object is anything for which a separate measurement of cost is required. Cost object may be a product, a service, a project, a customer, a brand category, an activity, a department or a programme etc. Examples of cost objects Product Smart phone, Tablet computer, SUV Car, Book etc. Service An airline flight from Delhi to Mumbai, Concurrent audit assignment, Utility bill payment facility

etc. Project Metro Rail project, Road projects etc. Activity Quality inspection of materials, Placing of orders etc. Process Refinement of crudes in oil refineries, melting of billets or ingots in

rolling mills etc. Department Production department, Finance & Accounts, Safety etc.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Memorize ICAI’s Definition Verbatim: a. "Anything for which separate cost measurement is required."
2. Use Diverse Categories: Pick 1 example each from: a. Products (SUV car) b. Services (Delhi-Mumbai flight) c. Projects (Metro rail) d. Departments (Production)
3. Avoid Redundancy: Don’t list multiple similar examples (e.g., car + bike).
4. Bullet Points for Clarity: a. Definition → 1 line b. Examples → 4 clear categories

Examiner Observations Students often make these errors when answering this question:

1. Vague Definitions – Many define cost objects as simply "items with costs" rather than specifying "anything requiring separate cost measurement" (ICAI’s exact phrasing).
2. Limited Examples – Students tend to give only product/service examples (e.g., cars, flights) but miss projects, activities, or departments, which are equally valid.
3. Overlapping Categories – Some confuse processes with activities (e.g., labeling "quality inspection" as a

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 32

process instead of an activity).

4. Too Broad/Narrow Examples – Examples like "manufacturing" (too broad) or "screws in a car" (too narrow) deviate from ICAI’s preferred mid-level examples (e.g., "SUV car," "metro rail project").
5. No Structured Format – Answers often lack clear separation between definition and examples, making them harder to evaluate.
6. Missing Key Cost Objects – Few mention customers or brand categories, which are explicitly listed in ICAI materials.

Question28. DISCUSS cost classification based on variability and controllability?

[8 Marks | 14 Minutes\](Study material)[Difficult | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer28. It means the grouping of costs according to their common characteristics. The important ways of classification of costs are: (1) By Nature or Element (2) By Functions (3) By Variability or Behaviour (4) By Controllability (5) By Normality (6) By Costs for Managerial Decision Making

(1) By Nature or Element Under this type of classification of cost, total cost of a cost object is classified on the basis of element of cost i.e., material, labour, other expenses and overheads. (i)Material: Material cost means cost of raw material required to make a product into finished goods. The materials can be directly attributable to a cost object or allocable on some reasonable basis where direct attribution is not possible. Materials which are present in the finished product (cost object) or can be economically identified in the product are termed as direct materials. For example, cloth in dress making; materials purchased for a specific job etc. However, in some cases a material may be direct but it is treated as indirect; because it is used in small quantities, it is not economically feasible to identify that quantity. Those materials which are used for purposes ancillary to the business are also treated as Indirect Materials. (ii) Labour: Wages paid to workers for converting the raw materials into finished goods, is called labour cost/ labour which can be economically identified or attributed wholly to a cost object is termed as direct labour. For example, employee engaged on the actual production of the product or in carrying out the necessary operations for converting the raw materials into finished product. (iii) Other Expenses: All expenses other than material or labour which are incurred for a particular cost object are termed as other Expenses. For example, hire charges for some special machinery, cost of defective work etc. (iv) Overheads: The aggregate of indirect material costs, indirect labour costs and indirect expenses is termed as Overheads. The main groups into which overheads may be subdivided are as follows:

- Production or Works Overheads: Indirect expenses which are incurred in the factory and for the running of

the factory. E.g.: rent, power etc.

- Administration Overheads: Indirect expenses related to management and administration of business. E.g.:

office rent, lighting, telephone etc.

- Selling Overheads: Indirect expenses incurred for marketing of a commodity. E.g.: Advertisement expenses,

commission to sales persons etc.

- Distribution Overheads: Indirect expenses incurred for dispatch of the goods E.g.: warehouse charges,

packing (secondary) and loading charges.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 33

(2) By Functions Under this classification, costs are divided according to the function for which they have been incurred. It includes the following: (i) Production/ Manufacturing Cost (ii) Administration Cost (iii) Selling Cost (iv) Distribution Cost (v) Research and Development cost etc.

(3) By Variability or Behaviour Based on this classification, costs are classified into three groups viz., fixed, variable and semi-variable.

(a) Fixed costs– These are the costs which are incurred for a period, and which, within certain output and turnover limits, tend to be unaffected by fluctuations in the levels of activity (output or turnover). They do not tend to increase or decrease with the changes in output. For example, rent, insurance of factory building etc., remain the same for different levels of production. (b) Variable Costs– These costs tend to vary with the volume of activity. Any increase in the activity results in an increase in the variable cost and vice versa. For example, cost of direct material, cost of direct labour, etc. (c) Semi-variable costs– These costs contain both fixed and variable components and are thus partly affected by fluctuations in the level of activity. Examples of semi variable costs are telephone bills, gas and electricity etc.

Methods of segregating Semi-variable costs into fixed and variable costs The segregation of semi-variable costs into fixed and variable costs can be carried out by using the following methods: (a) Graphical method (b) High-Low method (c) Analytical method (d) Comparison by period or level of activity method (e) Least squares method

(a) Graphical Method: Under this method, the following steps are followed: (i) A large number of observations regarding the total costs at different levels of output are plotted on a graph. (ii) The output is plotted on the X-axis and the total cost is plotted on the Y-axis. (iii) Then, by judgment, a line of “best-fit”, which passes through all or most of the points, is drawn. (iv) The point at which this line cuts the Y-axis indicates the total fixed cost component in the total cost. (v) If a line is drawn at this point parallel to the X-axis, this indicates the fixed cost. (vi) The variable cost, at any level of output, is derived by deducting this fixed cost element from the total cost. (b) High- Low Method: Under this method, difference between the total cost at highest and lowest volume is divided by the difference between the sales value at the highest and lowest volume. The quotient thus obtained gives us the rate of variable cost in relation to sales value. (c) Analytical Method: Under this method an experienced cost accountant tries to judge empirically what proportion of the semi-variable cost would be variable and what would be fixed. The degree of variability is ascertained for each item of semi-variable expenses. For example, some semi-variable expenses may vary to the extent of 20% while others may vary to the extent of 80%. Although it is very difficult to estimate the extent of variability of an expense, the method is easy to apply. (d) Comparison by period or level of activity method: Under this method, the variable overhead may be determined by comparing two levels of output with the amount of expenses at those levels.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 34

(e) Least Square Method: This is the best method to segregate semi-variable costs into its fixed and variable components. This is a statistical method and is based on finding out a line of best fit for a number of observations. The method uses the linear equation y = mx + c, where ‘m’ represents the variable element of cost per unit, ‘c’ represents the total fixed cost, ‘y’ represents the total cost, ‘x’ represents the volume of output. The total cost is thus split into its fixed and variable elements by solving this equation.

(4) By Controllability Costs here may be classified into controllable and uncontrollable costs. (a) Controllable Costs: - Cost that can be controlled, typically by a cost, profit or investment centre manager is called controllable cost. Controllable costs incurred in a particular responsibility canter can be influenced by the action of the manager heading that responsibility centre. For example, direct costs comprising direct labour, direct material, direct expenses and some of the overheads are generally controllable by the shop floor supervisor or the factory manager. (b) Uncontrollable Costs - Costs which cannot be influenced by the action of a specified member of an undertaking are known as uncontrollable costs. For example, expenditure incurred by say, the tool room is controllable by the foreman in-charge of that section but the share of the tool-room expenditure which is apportioned to a machine shop is not controlled by the machine shop foreman.

Distinction between Controllable Cost and Uncontrollable Cost: The distinction between controllable and uncontrollable costs is not very prominent and is sometimes left to individual judgment. In fact, no cost is uncontrollable; it is only in relation to a particular individual that we may specify a particular cost to be either controllable or uncontrollable. (4+4)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Structure First: a. Create clear headings for each classification type b. Use bullet points under each for key concepts
2. Prioritize Key Elements: a. Variability: Focus on definitions + examples of fixed/variable/semi-variable b. Controllability: Emphasize relative nature with examples c. Semi-variable segregation: List all 5 methods with 1-line descriptions
3. Use Standard Examples: a. Fixed: Rent, insurance b. Variable: Direct materials c. Semi-variable: Telephone bills d. Controllable: Direct labor by supervisor e. Uncontrollable: Allocated corporate costs
4. Highlight Formulas: a. y = mx + c for least squares b. High-low method calculation
5. Time Allocation: a. 2 minutes planning/structure b. 10 minutes writing c. 2 minutes review

Examiner Observations Students frequently make these errors when attempting this comprehensive question:

1. Confusing Classification Bases - Many mix up "variability" with "controllability" classifications, failing to

maintain clear separation between behavior-based (fixed/variable) and control-based classifications.

2. Incomplete Coverage - Students often focus only on fixed/variable costs while neglecting semi-variable costs

and methods to segregate them, which carries significant marks.

3. Misapplication of Methods - For semi-variable cost segregation, students: © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 35

a. Describe methods incorrectly (e.g., confusing high-low with least squares) b. Fail to mention key formulas (like y=mx+c for least squares) c. Overlook practical applications of each method

4. Overgeneralizing Controllability - Common mistakes include: a. Stating all direct costs are controllable (some allocated costs may not be) b. Ignoring the hierarchical nature of controllability c. Missing the tool-room vs machine shop example
5. Theoretical Without Practical - Answers often lack: a. Concrete examples for each classification b. Real-world applications of cost behavior c. Managerial implications of classifications
6. Formatting Issues - Many students present answers in unstructured paragraphs rather than clear, marked

classifications with sub-headings.

Question 29. Cost control emphasis is on past and present, while cost reduction emphasis is on present and future. DISCUSS some more differences between Cost control and Cost reduction.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes] (MTP May 2025)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 29.

Cost Control Cost Reduction

1. Cost control aims at maintaining the costs in 1. Cost reduction is concerned with reducing costs. It

accordance with the established standards. challenges all standards and endeavours to improvise

them continuously

2. Cost control seeks to attain lowest possible cost 2. Cost reduction recognises no condition as permanent,

under existing conditions. since a change will result in lower cost.

3. Cost control is a preventive function. 3. Cost reduction is a corrective function. It operates even when an efficient cost control system exists.
4. Cost control ends when targets are achieved. 4. Cost reduction has no visible end and is a continuous process.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Tabulate Differences: Use a two-column format (Cost Control vs Cost Reduction) for clarity.
2. Key Keywords: Focus on "standards," "timeframe," "continuity," and "corrective vs preventive".
3. Avoid Generalizations: Instead of "saves costs," specify how (e.g., "challenges existing benchmarks").
4. Prioritize ICAI’s Style: Use phrases like "no condition as permanent" (ICAI’s language).

Examiner Observations Students often make these mistakes while answering:

1. Mixing Definitions: Confusing cost control (maintaining standards) with cost reduction (challenging standards).
2. Overlapping Timeframes: Failing to clearly distinguish that cost control is past/present-oriented (corrective),

while cost reduction is present/future-oriented (proactive).

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 36

3. Static vs Dynamic Approach: Not emphasizing that cost control is preventive (follows set standards), whereas

cost reduction is continuous improvement (questions standards).

4. End Goal Misinterpretation: Stating cost control "ends" when targets are met, but missing that cost reduction

is perpetual.

5. Repetitive Points: Writing generic differences like "cost control saves money" without linking to standards,

flexibility, or corrective actions.

Question 30. Mention and explain types of responsibility centers.

[6 Marks | 7 Minutes\](PYP Nov ‘18)[Easy | ICAI Fav]

Answer 30. There are four types of responsibility centres: (i) Cost Centres: The responsibility centre which is held accountable for incurrence of costs which are under its control. The performance of this responsibility centre is measured against pre- determined standards or budgets. The cost centres are of two types: (a) Standard Cost Centre and (b) Discretionary Cost Centre

(ii) Revenue Centres: The responsibility centres which are accountable for generation of revenue for the entity. Sales Department for example, is the responsible for achievement of sales target and revenue generation. Though, revenue centres does not have control on the all expenditures it incurs but some time expenditures related with selling activities like commission to sales person etc. are incurred by revenue centres.

(iii) Profit Centres: These are the responsibility centres which have both responsibility of generation of revenue and incurrence of expenditures. Since, managers of profit centres are accountable for both costs as well as revenue, profitability is the basis for measurement of performance of these responsibility centres. Examples of profit centres are decentralised branches of an organisation.

(iv) Investment Centres: These are the responsibility centres which are not only responsible for profitability but also has the authority to make capital investment decisions. The performance of these responsibility centres is measured based on Return on Investment (ROI) besides profit. Important Note:- This was a theoretical question on responsibility centres. Below average performance was observed.

(2+2+1+1) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Memorize the 4 Types – Use acronym "CRPI" (Cost, Revenue, Profit, Investment).
2. Pre-Define Key Terms – ROI for investment centers, "control" for cost centers.
3. Add 1 Example Each – Ensures full marks (e.g., "Sales Dept. for revenue center").

Examiner Observations Students often make these mistakes:

1. Confusing Cost & Profit Centers – Many mix discretionary vs. standard cost centers or fail to specify that

profit centers control both revenue & costs.

2. Overlooking Investment Centers – A common error is missing ROI as a performance metric, instead just

stating "profitability." © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 37

3. Incomplete Revenue Centre Explanation – Some write only "sales department" without clarifying limited

expense control.

4. Theoretical Gaps – Weak answers lack examples (e.g., "R&D is a discretionary cost center") or misuse terms

like "budgeted costs" without context.

5. Structure Issues – Unorganized answers lose marks even if content is correct.

Question 31. DISCUSS short notes on (i) Discretionary Cost Centre and (ii) Investment Centre.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](RTP Nov 20 & May ‘18)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 31. (i) Discretionary Cost Centre: The cost centre whose output cannot be measured in financial terms, thus input-output ratio cannot be defined. The cost of input is compared with allocated budget for the activity. Example of discretionary cost centres are Research & Development department, Advertisement department where output of these department cannot be measured with certainty and co-related with cost incurred on inputs.

(ii) Investment Centres: These are the responsibility centres which are not only responsible for profitability but also has the authority to make capital investment decisions. The performance of these responsibility centres are measured on the basis of Return on Investment (ROI) besides profit. Examples of investment centres are Maharatna, Navratna and Miniratna companies of Public Sector Undertakings of Central Government.

(3+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Pre-Define Key Terms: a. Discretionary = No financial output. b. Investment Centre = ROI + Capital autonomy.
2. Use ICAI Keywords: "Budget comparison," "Maharatna PSUs."
3. Structured Format: a. Definition → Measurement → Example (ensures full coverage).
4. Time-Saver: Avoid over-explaining examples; 1-2 lines suffice.

Examiner Observations Common student mistakes:

1. Discretionary vs. Standard Cost Centers: Many fail to highlight the absence of measurable output (e.g., stating

"R&D spends money" without explaining why it’s discretionary).

2. ROI Misinterpretation: In investment centers, students often mention profit but skip ROI or confuse it with

Residual Income (RI).

3. Vague Examples: Generic terms like "manufacturing unit" for investment centers (should specify autonomy in

investments, e.g., PSUs).

4. Overemphasis on Profit: For investment centers, some only discuss profitability without linking to capital

decisions.

5. Structural Issues: Unbalanced explanations (e.g., 4 lines for Discretionary Cost Centre but 1 for Investment

Centre).

Question 32. DISCUSS the essential features of a good cost accounting system?

[6 Marks | 7 Minutes] (Study material) [Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 38

Answer 32. ESSENTIALS OF A GOOD COST ACCOUNTING SYSTEM The essential features, which a good Cost Accounting System should possess, are as follows: (a) Informative and simple: Cost accounting system should be tailor-made, practical, simple and capable of meeting the requirements of a business concern. The system of costing should not sacrifice the utility by introducing inaccurate and unnecessary details.

(b) Accurate and authentic: The data to be used by the cost accounting system should be accurate and authenticated; otherwise it m ay distort the output of the system and a wrong decision may be taken.

(c) Uniformity and consistency: There should be uniformity and consistency in classification, treatment and reporting of cost data and related information. This is required for benchmarking and comparability of the results of the system for both horizontal and vertical analysis.

(d) Integrated and inclusive: The cost accounting system should be integrated with other systems like financial accounting, taxation, statistics and operational research etc. to have a complete overview and clarity in results.

(e) Flexible and adaptive: The cost accounting system should be flexible enough to make necessary amendment and modifications in the system to incorporate changes in technological, reporting, regulatory and other requirements.

(f) Trust on the system: Management should have trust on the system and its output. For this, an active role of management is required for the development of such a system that reflects a strong conviction in using information for decision making. (1+1+1+1+1+1)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Use Mnemonics: "I-A-U-I-F-T" (Informative, Accurate, Uniform, Integrated, Flexible, Trust).
2. Pre-Define Keywords: a. Integrated = Sync with financial/tax systems. b. Flexible = Adapts to regulatory

changes.

3. Structured Format: a. Feature → 1-line definition → 1-line rationale (e.g., "Uniformity: Ensures comparability

across periods").

4. Time-Saver: Avoid lengthy examples; ICAI values clarity over elaboration.

Examiner Observations Students often make these mistakes:

1. Overgeneralization – Stating "should be good" without specifics like uniformity or integration.
2. Missing Practicality – Ignoring simplicity or flexibility, focusing only on accuracy.
3. Confusing Integration – Some equate integration with "automation" rather than linking to financial/tax

systems.

4. Neglecting Management Trust – A frequently skipped point, though critical for real-world applicability.
5. Repetitive Explanations – Describing accuracy and authenticity as separate ideas when they overlap.
6. No Examples – Failing to illustrate (e.g., "ERP systems for integration").

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 39

Question 33. Though Cost Accounting and Management Accounting are used synonymously, but there are a few differences. ENUMERATE any five differences.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](RTP Sep. 2025)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

quantitative aspect. (ii) Objective It records the cost of producing a It provides information to management

accounting, budgeting, taxation, planning etc. (iv) Recording of data It uses both past and present figures. It is focused with the projection of figures

for future. (v) Development Its development is related to industrial Its development is related to the need of

revolution. modern business world. (vi) Rules and It follows certain principles and It does not follow any specific rules and

Regulation procedures for recording costs of regulations.

different products.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Quick Brainstorming – Jot down key contrasts (e.g., nature, objective, scope, data type, rules).
2. Prioritize Unique Points – Focus on qualitative vs. quantitative, future vs. past data, and regulatory

adherence.

3. Tabular Format – Saves time and ensures clarity. Use headings like "Basis/Cost Accounting/Management

Accounting."

4. Avoid Over-Explaining – Stick to 1-line differences per point (ICAI values brevity).

Examiner Observations Students often make the following mistakes while answering this question:

1. Overlapping Definitions – Many students fail to clearly differentiate between the two and end up writing

similar points for both.

2. Ignoring Key Basis Points – Some miss critical distinctions like "Rules & Regulations" (Cost Accounting follows

principles, while Management Accounting does not).

3. Qualitative vs. Quantitative Aspect – A frequent error is not emphasizing that Management Accounting

includes qualitative (non-financial) data, unlike Cost Accounting.

4. Future vs. Past Data – Students mix up the time orientation—Cost Accounting uses past/present data, while

Management Accounting is future-focused.

5. Scope Misinterpretation – Many incorrectly state that Cost Accounting has a wider scope, whereas

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 40

Management Accounting covers financial accounting, budgeting, and strategic planning.

6. Redundant Points – Repetition of ideas (e.g., only listing "planning" under Management Accounting without

explaining coordination or decision-making).

Question 34. Discuss the essential features of a good cost accounting system.

Answer 34. The essential features, which a good cost accounting system should possess, are as follows: (a) Informative and simple: Cost accounting system should be tailor-made, practical, simple and capable of meeting the requirements of a business concern. The system of costing should not sacrifice the utility by introducing inaccurate and unnecess ary details.

(b) Accurate and authentic: The data to be used by the cost accounting system should be accurate and authenticated; otherwise it may distort the output of the system and a wrong decision may be taken.

(c) Uniformity and consistency: There should be uniformity and consistency in classification, treatment and reporting of cost data and related information. This is required for benchmarking and comparability of the results of the system for both horizontal and vertical analysis.

(d) Integrated and inclusive: The cost accounting system should be integrated with other systems like financial accounting, taxation, statistics and operational research etc. to have a complete overview and clarity in results.

(e) Flexible and adaptive: The cost accounting system should be flexible enough to make necessary amendment and modifications in the system to incorporate changes in technological, reporting, regulatory and other requirements.

textbook rigidity. 4.Neglecting Integration – Failing to highlight how the system must sync with financial accounting, taxation, and operations for holistic decision-making. 5.Underemphasizing Trust – Overlooking that management’s conviction in the system is crucial for its success (a subtle but critical ICAI expectation). 6.Generic Language – Using fluff like "should be good" instead of specifics like "uniformity in benchmarking" or "adaptive to technological changes."

Question 35. STATE the method of costing for the following industries: (i) Sugar manufacturing (ii) Bridge Construction (iii) Advertising (iv) Car Assembly

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Industry-Specific Logic – Match the production nature to the method: a. Continuous output (sugar) → Process costing. b. Unique projects (bridges, ads) → Contract/job costing. c. Hybrid production (cars) → Multiple costing.
2. Elimination Technique – Rule out illogical options (e.g., sugar can’t be job costing).

1. Confusing Process & Batch Costing – Some incorrectly assign batch costing to sugar manufacturing (which is

3. Overlooking Car Assembly – Many students skip this or wrongly cite unit costing (correct

method: multiple/operating costing, as it combines job + process elements).

Question 36.Specify the types of Responsibility centres under the following situations: (i) Purchase of bonds, stocks, or real estate property. (ii) Ticket counter in a Railway station. 2. Elimination Method: a. If a unit can’t control costs → Revenue center. b. If it uses capital investments → Investment center.
3. ICAI Keywords: a. "Purchase of bonds/stocks" → Investment (capital focus). b. "Decentralized branches" → Profit (autonomy in operations).

2. Misclassifying Decentralized Branches – Some assume they are cost/revenue centers, ignoring their profit

accountability.

3. Overgeneralizing Sales Department – A common error is calling it a "profit center" (correct: revenue center as

it doesn’t control costs).

4. Ignoring Context Clues – E.g., ticket counters only generate revenue (no cost control), but students force-fit
