Question37. Explain: Opportunity cost.

[2 Marks | 3 Minutes] (PYP May ’18)[Easy | ICAI Fav]

Answer37. Opportunity Cost - This cost refers to the value of sacrifice made or benefit of opportunity foregone in accepting an alternative course of action. For example, a firm financing its expansion plan by withdrawing money from its bank deposits. In such a case the loss of interest on the bank deposit is the opportunity cost for carrying out the expansion plan. © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 43

Examiner Observations Students often falter in answering this question due to:

1. Definition Without Context – Many write textbook definitions ("next best alternative forgone") but fail to link

it to decision-making, losing marks for lack of application.

2. Overcomplicating Examples – Using hypothetical scenarios (e.g., "choosing between MBA and job") instead

of business-relevant examples (e.g., capital allocation).

3. Ignoring Quantitative Aspect – Not specifying measurable sacrifice (e.g., "loss of bank interest" is better than

vague "loss of income").

4. Confusing with Sunk Cost – Some incorrectly associate opportunity cost with irrecoverable past costs,

diluting the concept.

5. Repetition – Restating the same idea in different words (e.g., "sacrifice" and "foregone benefit" as separate

points).

Question 38. DESCRIBE the factors which are to be considered before installing a system of cost accounting?

[7 Marks | 10 Minutes\](Study material) [Difficult | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 38. As in the case of every other form of activity, it should be considered whether it would be profitable to have a Cost Accounting System. Management of an organisation needs complete and accurate information to make decisions. A well-established costing system should provide all relevant information as and when required by management as well as various stakeholders. Before setting up a system of cost accounting the factors mentioned below should be studied: (a) Objective: The objective of setting up the costing system, for example whether it is being introduced for fixing prices or for establishing a system of cost control.

(b) Nature of Business or Industry: The industry in which the business is operating. Every business or industry has its own uniqueness and objectives. According to its cost information requirement, cost accounting methods are followed. For example, an oil refinery maintains process wise cost accounts to find out the cost incurred on a particular process, say in crude refinement process etc.

(c) Organisational Hierarchy: Costing system should fulfil the information requirements of different levels of management. Top management is concerned with the corporate strategy, strategic level management is concerned with marketing strategy, product diversification, product pricing etc. Operational level management needs the information on standard quantity to be consumed, report on idle time etc.

(d) Knowing the product: Nature of the product determines the type of costing system to be implemented. The product which has by-products requires costing system which accounts for by-products as well. In case of perishable or short self- life products, marginal costing is appropriate to know the contribution and minimum price at which products could be sold.

(e) Knowing the production process: A good costing system can never be established without the complete knowledge of the production process. Cost apportionment can be done on the most appropriate and scientific

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 44

basis if a cost accountant can identify degree of effort or resources consumed in a particular process. This also includes some basic technical know-how and process peculiarity.

(f) Information synchronisation: Establishment of a department or a system requires substantial amount of organisational resources. While drafting a costing system, information needs of various other departments should be taken into account. For example, in a typical business organisation accounts department needs to submit monthly stock statement to its lender bank, quantity wise stock details at the time of filing returns to tax authorities etc.

(g) Method of maintenance of cost records: The organization must determine beforehand the manner in which Cost and Financial Accounts could be inter-locked into a single integral accounting system and how the results of separate sets of accounts i.e. cost and financial, could be reconciled by means of control accounts.

(h) Statutory compliances and audit: Records are to be maintained to comply with statutory requirements and applicable cost accounting standards should be followed.

(i) Information Attributes: Information generated from the Costing system should possess all the attributes of useful information i.e. it should be complete, accurate, timely, relevant. To have an effective management information system (MIS).

(0.5+1+1+0.5+1+1+1+0.5+0.5) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Prioritize Key Factors – Focus on: a. Business Objective (pricing vs. cost control). b. Industry-Specific Needs (process/job costing). c. Statutory Compliance (CAS, audit trails).
2. Use Flow Logic – Start with macro (objectives/industry) → micro (process/data needs).
3. Add Examples – E.g., "Perishable goods need marginal costing to track breakeven points."

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to:

1. Listing Without Explanation – Many dump factors (e.g., "nature of business") without elaborating how it

impacts the costing system (e.g., process costing for refineries vs. job costing for advertising).

2. Ignoring Practical Implementation – Overlooking interdepartmental coordination (e.g., synchronizing cost data

with financial/statutory requirements).

3. Generic Statements – Writing vague points like "cost system should be accurate" instead of linking to specific

attributes (timeliness, compliance with CAS).

4. Missing Technical Nuances – Failing to highlight process-specific costing (e.g., by-product accounting in oil

refining) or marginal costing for perishable goods.

5. Overemphasis on Theory – Not providing industry examples (e.g., "pharma needs batch costing due to expiry

dates") to demonstrate application.

6. Neglecting Hierarchy Needs – Not tailoring factors to management levels (strategic vs. operational data

requirements).

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 45

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

etc.) used to calculate and allocate costs for products/services."

2. Industry-Specific Units – Memorize standard units: a. Automobile: Number (e.g., per car) . Steel/Cement: Ton. b. Chemicals: Litre/kg/ton. c. Power: kWh. d. Transport: Passenger-km/ton-km).

Examiner Observations Students often make these errors while answering this question:

1. Confusing Absorption vs. Marginal Costing Treatment – Many incorrectly state that fixed production

overheads are always part of product costs (ignoring marginal costing, where they are period costs).

2. Vague Examples – Listing "marketing costs" as period costs is correct, but top-scorers specify advertising, sales

commissions, or rent for admin offices to show clarity.

3. Inventory Valuation Misunderstanding – Weak answers fail to highlight that product costs capitalize into

inventory (appearing in Balance Sheet) while period costs hit P&L immediately.

4. Overlap in Definitions – Some mix direct vs. indirect costs with product/period costs (e.g., calling "factory

supervisor salary" a period cost—it’s a product cost under absorption costing).

5. Missing Marginal Costing Angle – A frequent oversight is not contrasting how fixed manufacturing costs shift

from product cost (absorption) to period cost (marginal).

## Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ’s)

Question 1. Which of the following is true about Cost control: (a) It is a corrective function (b) It challenges the set standards (c) It ends when targets achieved (d) It is concerned with future

(Study material)

Ans: (c) It ends when targets achieved Reason: Cost control refers to the process of monitoring and regulating the expenses of a business to keep them within the predefined limits or set targets. It involves comparing actual costs with standard or budgeted costs and taking corrective actions to minimize deviations. Once the pre-set cost targets are achieved, the process of cost control is considered complete for that activity or period — it does not continue beyond the achievement of targets.

Question 2. Which of the following is Not true about the cost control and cost reduction: (a) Cost control seeks to attain lowest possible cost under best conditions. (b) Cost control emphasises on past and present. (c) Cost reduction is a corrective function. It operates even when an efficient cost control system exists. (d) Cost control ends when targets are achieved.

(Study material)

Ans: (a) Cost control seeks to attain lowest possible cost under best conditions. Reason: This statement is not true about cost control — it actually describes cost reduction. Cost Control focuses on maintaining costs within set standards or budgets. It aims to adhere to predetermined cost limits and does not attempt to reduce costs beyond those set standards. In contrast, Cost Reduction is a more aggressive and continuous process that seeks to bring down costs to the lowest possible level, even if the current costs are already within the standards — and does so without compromising quality or performance.

Question 3. ……………….. is anything for which a separate measurement is required? (a) Cost unit (b) Cost object (c) Cost driver (d) Cost centre

(Study material)

Ans: (b) Cost object Reason: A Cost Object is anything for which separate cost measurement is desired. This could be a product, service, project, customer, activity, or department. It is the focus or target for accumulating and assigning costs.

Question 4. Cost units used in power sector is: (a) Kilometer (K.M) (b) Kilowatt-hour (kWh) (c) Number of electric points (d) Number of hours

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 50

(Study material)

Ans: (b) Kilowatt-hour (kWh) Reason: In the power sector, the standard cost unit used for measuring output and cost is the kilowatt-hour (kWh). It represents the amount of electrical energy consumed or produced over time and is used to compute cost per unit of electricity. This unit helps in:  Determining the cost of generating or distributing electricity,  Billing consumers based on energy consumption,  Comparing efficiency and cost performance.

Question 5. Process Costing method is suitable for (a) Transport sector (b) Chemical industries (c) Dam construction (d) Furniture making

(Study material)

Ans: (b) Chemical industries Reason: Process Costing is a costing method used where production is continuous, and units are homogeneous — meaning all units are similar and go through the same processes. Chemical industries are the best example of this, as they:  Produce identical units (e.g., paint, petrol, acid),  Use continuous and standardized processes,  Accumulate costs by process or department, not by individual unit.

Question 6. A taxi provider charges minimum Rs.80 thereafter Rs.12 per kilometer of distance travelled, the behaviour of conveyance cost is: (a) Fixed Cost (b) Semi-variable Cost (c) Variable Cost (d) Administrative cost.

(Study material)

Ans: (b) Semi-variable Cost Reason: The taxi fare has two components:

1. Fixed Component: Rs.80 minimum charge — this remains constant regardless of how many kilometres are

travelled (up to a point).

2. Variable Component: Rs.12 per kilometre — this increases with distance travelled.

Since the total cost includes both fixed and variable elements, it is classified as a semi-variable cost (also called mixed cost). These costs remain fixed up to a certain level and vary thereafter with the level of activity.

Question 1. Define Inventory Control and give its objectives. List down the basis to be adopted for Inventory Control.

[5 Marks | 7 Minutes\](PYP Nov’19)[Easy | ICAI Fav]

Answer1. Inventory Control: The Chartered Institute of Management Accountants (CIMA) defines Inventory Control as “The function of ensuring that sufficient goods are retained in stock to meet all requirements without carrying unnecessarily large stocks.” The objective of inventory control is to make a balance between sufficient stock and over - stock. The stock maintained should be sufficient to meet the production requirements so that uninterrupted production flow can be maintained. Insufficient stock not only pause the production but also cause a loss of revenue and goodwill. On the other hand, Inventory requires some funds for purchase, storage, maintenance of materials with a risk of obsolescence, pilferage etc. A trade-off between Stock-out and Over-stocking is required. The management may employ various methods of Inventory control to have a balance. Management may adopt the following basis for Inventory control:

Important Note:- This was a numerical question relating to the topic ‘Material cost’ to calculate EOQ and Total Inventory cost. Performance of the examinees was good.

(3+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Blitz Theory: Memorize CIMA’s definition verbatim (high marks for precision).
2. Tabular Format: Present "Basis" (ABC, VED, FSN) in bullet points for quick scoring.
3. Link to Practicality: Add 1 line on how basis aids decision-making (e.g., "ABC prioritizes high-value items").

Examiner Observations

1. Vague Definitions: Students often write incomplete definitions, missing CIMA’s formal definition.
2. Overlooking Trade-offs: Many fail to explain the critical balance between stock-out costs and overstocking

costs.

3. Generic Objectives: Listing objectives like "minimize costs" without linking to production continuity or

obsolescence risks.

4. Basis Misinterpretation: Confusing "basis" (e.g., ABC, VED) with "methods" (e.g., JIT, EOQ).
5. Numerical Neglect: In hybrid questions (theory + EOQ), students solve calculations correctly but skip

theoretical justification.

(4+4) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

Examiner Observations Students often make the following mistakes while solving ABC analysis questions:

1. Incorrect Cumulative % Calculation – Many students fail to sequentially add the percentages to reach the

70%, 20%, and 10% thresholds, leading to wrong classification.

2. Misranking Items – Some students rank items based on unit quantity rather than total cost, which is a

fundamental error.

3. Ignoring Partial Cumulation – A common mistake is not checking if the cumulative % crosses the © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 58

threshold (e.g., 70%) before assigning a category.

4. Rounding Errors – Approximating percentages too early can lead to incorrect categorization (e.g., stopping at

68% instead of reaching 70%).

5. Overlooking Small but High-Cost Items – Items like D (Rs. 220/unit) or G (Rs. 300/unit) may have low

quantities but contribute significantly, which students sometimes miss.

3. Ignoring Discount Impact on Purchase Cost – A few students compare EOQ vs. bulk order without adjusting

Question 9. EXPLAIN the advantages that would accrue in using the LIFO method of pricing for the valuation of raw material stock.

[5 Marks | 7 Minutes\](MTP April’21)[Easy | ICAI Fav]

Answer 9. The advantages that would accrue in using the LIFO method of pricing for the valuation of raw material stock are as follows:

- The cost of materials issued will be either nearer to and or will reflect the current market price. Thus, the cost of

goods produced will be related to the trend of the market price of materials. Such a trend in price of materials enables the matching of cost of production with current sales revenues.

- The use of the method during the period of rising prices does not reflect undue high profit in the income

statement as it was under the first-in-first-out or average method. In fact, the profit shown here is relatively lower because the cost of production takes into account the rising trend of material prices.

- In the case of falling prices profit tends to rise due to lower material cost, yet the finished products appear to be

more competitive and are at market price.

- Over a period, the use of LIFO helps to iron out the fluctuations in profits.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 61

- In the period of inflation LIFO will tend to show the correct profit and thus avoid paying undue taxes to some

extent.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Think Chronologically: Start with current cost matching → profit effects → tax impact.
2. Use Keywords: a. Inflation: "Lower reported profits → tax savings." b. Deflation: "Lower COGS → competitive pricing."
3. Prioritize Practical Benefits: Tax savings and profit stability are higher marks than generic matching.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with conceptual questions on LIFO due to these common errors:

1. Confusing LIFO with FIFO Effects – Many students incorrectly state that LIFO shows higher profits during

inflation (a FIFO characteristic) or fails to link it to tax benefits.

2. Overlooking Inflation Context – A key advantage of LIFO is tax savings during rising prices, but students often

miss this practical implication and focus only on "matching costs."

3. Vague Generalizations – Some write generic points like "better profit matching" without explaining how (e.g.,

by using current prices for COGS or stabilizing profits over time).

4. Ignoring Falling Price Scenarios – LIFO’s competitive advantage in deflation (lower COGS → competitive

pricing) is rarely mentioned.

5. Repetition of Points – Students often rephrase the same idea (e.g., "matches current prices" and "reflects

market trends") as separate advantages.

Relevant Cost of this order quantity Rs. Ordering cost =48,000 / 2,2,63 21.21, say 22 orders at Rs. 800 17,600.00 © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 62

Carrying cost = 1/2 × 2,263 × 15 16,972.50 Relevant cost 34,572.50 Differential cost = 44,992.50 – 34,572.50 = Rs. 10,420

Purchase Cost (48,000 × 80) 38,40,000.00 Purchase cost (48,000 × 72) 34,56,000.00 Ordering cost 22,950.00 Ordering cost 0.00 Carrying cost 22,042.50 Carrying cost½ × 48, 000 ×15 3,60,000.00 Total cost 38,84,992.50 38,16,000.00 This special offer at Rs. 72 per unit should be accepted as it saves Rs. 68,992.50 as compared to original offer.

(2+1+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. EOQ Formula: √(2 × 48,000 × 1,350 / 15) → 2,939 units.
2. Total Cost: a. Ordering = (48,000/2,939) ≈ 17 orders × Rs. 1,350. b. Carrying = ½ × 2,939 × 15.
3. Revised EOQ (Rs. 800 ordering cost): √ (2 × 48,000 × 800 / 15) → 2,263 units.
4. Bulk Offer: a. Compare original (EOQ) vs. bulk (Rs. 72) total costs. b. Key: Bulk saves Rs. 68,992.50 despite high carrying cost.

Examiner Observations Students often make these mistakes in EOQ and bulk discount problems:

1. Incorrect EOQ Formula Application: Misplacing values in √ (2AO/C), especially confusing annual demand

(A) with unit cost (C) or carrying cost (H).

2. Rounding Errors: Using fractional orders (e.g., 16.33) without rounding up to whole orders (17), leading

to understated ordering costs.

3. Carrying Cost Miscalculation: For bulk orders, students often forget to compute carrying cost for the full

48,000 units (½ × 48,000 × 15 = Rs. 3, 60,000).

4. Ignoring Differential Cost Logic: In part (ii), some students recompute EOQ but fail to compare total costs to

find the savings (Rs. 10,420).

5. Bulk Discount Misjudgment: Overlooking that ordering cost becomes zero in the bulk offer, or missing

the massive carrying cost impact.

(iv) Average stock level of A = (Refer to Working Note) = = 43,200 kg. Working note Maximum stock of A = ROL + ROQ – (Minimum consumption × Minimum re-order period) = 60,000 kg. + 12,000 kg. – [(550units × 12 kg.) × 2 weeks] = 58,800 kg.

(v) Re-order level of D Maximum re-order period × Maximum Usage = 3 weeks × (1,250 unit’s × 5 kg.) = 18,750 kg

(vi) Minimum stock of D Re-order level – (Average consumption × Average time required to obtain delivery) = 18,750 kg. – (900units × 5 kg. × 2 weeks) = 9,750 kg. (3+2+2+1)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Tabulate Data First: Create columns for usage rate, min/max production, and delivery periods to visualize

relationships.

2. Standardize Units: Convert all figures to kg immediately (units × kg/unit).
3. Formula Priority: a. ROL = Max usage × Max period

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 64

b. Min Level = ROL - (Avg usage × Avg period) c. Max Level = ROL + ROQ - (Min usage × Min period)

4. Part (iv) Requires 2 Steps: Calculate max stock before averaging.
5. Verification: Cross-check that minimum levels don't exceed maximum levels logically.

Examiner Observations Students frequently struggle with inventory level calculations due to these common errors:

1. Confusing Minimum/Maximum Formulas: Many students mix up the formulas for minimum stock level (Re-

order level - Avg. consumption) and maximum stock level (ROL + ROQ - Min. consumption). This leads to reversed answers.

2. Usage Rate Miscalculations: Failing to multiply weekly production by kg/unit (e.g., using 900 units instead of

900×12 kg for Material A) is a recurring mistake.

3. Time Period Errors: Using wrong delivery periods - average instead of maximum for ROL or vice versa for

minimum stock level.

4. Incomplete Working Notes: For average stock level (part iv), students often forget to first calculate maximum

stock, leading to incorrect averages.

5. Unit Consistency Issues: Some candidates maintain answers in units rather than converting to kgs as required.
6. Overcomplicating Solutions: For part (iii), both methods give the same answer, but students waste time doing

both when one suffices.

(3+2+3) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Skip Lead Time: Ignore lead time (irrelevant for EOQ/total cost).
2. Pre-Derive Formulas: Memorize EOQ = √(2AO/C) and Total Cost = Purchasing + (A/EOQ × O) + (EOQ/2 × C).
3. Unit Consistency: Ensure all costs (ordering, carrying) are per annum.
4. Shortcut for Carrying Cost: 8% of Rs. 50 = Rs. 4 (directly use in EOQ).

Examiner Observations Students frequently falter in three key areas:

1. Conceptual Errors: a. EOQ Misapplication: Using lead time or safety stock in EOQ formula, which is

unnecessary for basic EOQ. b. Cost Exclusion: Forgetting to include purchasing cost (Rs. 16 lakhs) in total inventory cost, focusing only on ordering/carrying costs.

2. Calculation Mistakes: a. Annual Demand: Errors in converting quarterly data (e.g., forgetting ×4 or ×2 kg/litre). b. Carrying Cost: Calculating storage/interest separately or misapplying rates (e.g., 8% of Rs. 40 instead of Rs. 50).
3. Presentation Issues: a. Unstructured Working: Jumbling steps (e.g., calculating ordering cost before EOQ). b. Unit Confusion: Mixing litres/kg or miswriting Rs./kg.

Question 13. A Company manufactures a special product which requires a component ‘Alpha’. The following particulars are collected for the year 2022-23: (i) Annual demand of Alpha 8,000 units (ii) Cost of placing an order Rs. 200 per order (iii) Cost per unit of Alpha Rs. 400 (iv) Carrying cost p.a. 20% The company has been offered a quantity discount of 4 % on the purchase of ‘Alpha’ provided the order size is 4,000 components at a time. Required: (i) COMPUTE the economic order quantity (ii) STATE whether the quantity discount offer can be accepted.

[8 Marks | 10 Minutes\](Study material) [Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 13. (i) Calculation of Economic Order Quantity

EOQ =√ =√ =200 units

(ii) Evaluation of Profitability of Different Options of Order Quantity (a) When EOQ is ordered

(Rs.) Purchase Cost (8,000 units× Rs. 400) 32,00,000 Ordering Cost [(8,000 units/200 units) ×Rs. 200] 8,000 Carrying Cost (200 units× Rs.400× ½ ×20/100) 8,000 Total Cost 32,16,000 (b) When Quantity Discount is accepted

(Rs.) Purchase Cost (8,000 units × Rs. 384\*) 30,72,000 Ordering Cost [(8,000 units/4000 units) × Rs. 200] × 400 Carrying Cost (4000 units × Rs. 384× ½× 20/100) 1,53,600 Total Cost 32,26,000 \*Unit Cost Rs. 400 Less Quantity Discount @ 4% = 16 Purchase Cost = 400- 16 =Rs.384 Advise – The total cost of inventory is lower if EOQ is adopted. Hence, the company is advised not to accept the quantity discount. (2+3+3)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. OQ First: Compute EOQ using undiscounted price (√ (2×8,000×200)/ (400×0.2) = 200 units.
2. Total Cost (EOQ): a. Purchase: 8,000 × 400 = Rs. 32,00,000 b. Ordering: (8,000/200) × 200 = Rs. 8,000 c. Carrying: (200/2) × 400 × 20% = Rs. 8,000 d. Total: Rs. 32, 16,000.
3. Total Cost (Discount): a. Purchase: 8,000 × 384 = Rs. 30,72,000 b. Ordering: (8,000/4,000) × 200 = Rs. 400 c. Carrying: (4,000/2) × 384 × 20% = Rs. 1, 53,600 d. Total: Rs. 32, 26,000.
4. Decision: Reject discount (Rs. 32, 16,000 < Rs. 32, 26,000).

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to:

1. Misapplication of EOQ Formula: a. Forgetting to adjust carrying cost (20% of Rs. 400 = Rs. 80/unit/year) in the denominator. b. Using the discounted price (Rs. 384) in EOQ calculation, which is incorrect—EOQ must be computed at the undiscounted price (Rs. 400).
2. Quantity Discount Evaluation Errors: a. Incorrect Purchase Cost: Calculating discount on total demand (8,000 × 4%) instead of per-unit (Rs. 400 – 4% = Rs. 384). b. Carrying Cost Miscalculation: Using EOQ (200 units) instead of the discount order size (4,000 units) for carrying cost under the discount scenario. c. Ordering Cost Oversight: Dividing annual demand by 4,000 (not EOQ) for ordering cost under discount.
3. Comparative Analysis Oversights:

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 67

a. Ignoring Total Cost Comparison: Only comparing EOQ vs. discount order size costs superficially without detailed calculations. b. Time Value of Discount: Missing that the discount’s benefit (Rs. 1, 28,000 savings) is offset by higher carrying costs (Rs. 1, 53,600).

4. Presentation Issues: a. Unstructured working notes, leading to arithmetic errors. b. Omitting units (Rs. /units) in cost breakdowns, losing clarity.

Question 14. WHAT will be your answer to the above question if there are no discounts offered and the price per ton is Rs. 1,500?

[5 Marks | 5 Minutes\](Study material)[Easy | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 14. If there will are no discount offer then the purchase quantity should be equal to EOQ. The EOQ is as follows:

EOQ =√

Where A = annual inventory requirement, O = ordering cost per order and C = carrying cost per unit per annum.

=√ = 200 units

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Identify Given Data: a. A = 5,000 units, O = Rs. 1,200, Price = Rs. 1,500, C = 20%.
2. Compute Carrying Cost (C): a. 20% of Rs. 1,500 = Rs. 300/unit/year.
3. Plug into EOQ Formula: a. √ (2 × 5,000 × 1,200) / 300 = √ (1, 20, 00,000 / 300) = √40,000 = 200 units.
4. Conclusion: Since no discount, order 200 units.

Examiner Observations Students often make these mistakes in this question:

1. Ignoring Carrying Cost Basis: a. Many incorrectly use Rs. 1,500 (price per ton) directly in the EOQ formula

without applying the 20% carrying cost (i.e., Rs. 1,500 × 20% = Rs. 300/unit/year).

b. Some wrongly assume carrying cost is given as a fixed value (e.g., Rs. 300) rather than a percentage.

2. Misplacing Values in EOQ Formula: a. Swapping ordering cost (O = Rs. 1,200) and carrying cost (C = 20% of Rs. 1,500) in the formula. b. Using annual demand (A = 5,000) correctly but failing to square root the final value properly.
3. Overcomplicating the Scenario: a. Since no discount is offered, EOQ is the only decision point, but students sometimes unnecessarily compare it with arbitrary order quantities. b. A few incorrectly assume that EOQ changes if the price per ton fluctuates (EOQ is independent of price unless carrying cost is price-sensitive).
4. Calculation & Unit Errors: a. Forgetting to convert carrying cost percentage into a per-unit value. b. Miswriting units (e.g., tons vs. units) leading to incorrect EOQ.

Question 15. Calculate EOQ and Total Variable Cost with the Current Unit Price

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 68

1. Annual Demand= 10,000 units 2. Unit Price= Rs. 30.00
3. Order Cost= Rs. 25.00 4. Storage Rate= 3% per annum
5. Interest Rate= 10% per annum 6. Obsolescence Rate= 7% per annum [6 Marks | 8 Minutes\](MTP April’21) [Medium| ICAI Fav]

Answer 15. Calculate EOQ and Total Variable Cost with the Current Unit Price Step 1: Calculate Carrying Cost per Unit per Annum Carrying Cost (C) = Storage Rate + Interest Rate + Obsolescence Rate C = 3% + 10% + 7% = 20% , C = 20% of Rs.30 = 0.20 × 30 = Rs.6

Step 2: Calculate EOQ

EOQ = √ = √ = √ = √ = 289 Units

Step 3: Calculate Total Variable Cost (a) Purchase Price for 10,000 units: Total Purchase Price = 10,000 × 30 = Rs.300, 000 (b) Ordering Cost: Number of Orders = 10,000/289 = 35 orders , Total Ordering Cost = 35 × 25 = Rs. 875 (c) Carrying Cost: Average Inventory = = = 144.5 units, Total Carrying Cost = 144.5 × 6 = Rs. 867 (d) Total Variable Cost: Total Variable Cost = Total Purchase Price + Total Ordering Cost + Total Carrying Cost Total Variable Cost = 300,000 + 875 + 867 = Rs. 301,742 (2+1+1+1+1)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Carrying Cost: a. Sum all % rates (3% + 10% + 7% = 20%). b. Multiply by unit price: 20% of Rs. 30 = Rs. 6.
2. EOQ Calculation: a. Use √ (2 × 10,000 × 25 / 6) = 289 units. No rounding until final TVC.
3. Total Variable Cost: a. Purchase Cost: Straightforward (10,000 × Rs. 30). b. Ordering Cost: 10,000/289 = 34.6 → 35 orders (always round up). c. Carrying Cost: 289/2 = 144.5 × Rs. 6.

Examiner Observations Students often stumble on EOQ and Total Variable Cost calculations due to:

1. Carrying Cost Misinterpretation: a. Many students incorrectly add percentages (e.g., 3% + 10% + 7% = 20%)

but fail to apply it to the unit price (Rs. 30). Some directly use 20% as Rs. 20 instead of Rs. 6 (20% of Rs. 30).

2. EOQ Formula Errors: a. Substituting wrong values in √ (2AO/C), like using unit price (Rs. 30) instead of ordering

cost (Rs. 25) or annual demand as monthly.

b. Rounding EOQ prematurely (e.g., taking 288.67 as 288 or 290) leading to cascading errors in ordering/carrying costs.

3. Total Variable Cost Calculation: a. Double-counting purchase price: Some exclude it (assuming only ordering +

carrying costs) or add it twice.

b. Miscounting orders: Using 10,000/288 = 34.72 orders → 35 orders is correct, but students often take 34 or 36, skewing costs. c. Carrying cost on full EOQ: Using 289 × Rs. 6 instead of average inventory (EOQ/2).

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 69

4. Unit Consistency: a. Mixing monthly/annual rates (e.g., using monthly demand or storage rates without

annualizing).

(i) EOQ = √ = √ = 2,000kgs

(ii) ROQ (Quarterly Purchase policy) - 5,000 Kgs Material Requirement - 22,630 Average Consumption - 62 Kgs Max usage – Min Usage = 100Kgs Max usage + Min Usage = 124Kgs (Formulating average usage with max & min) Hence Minimum Usage = 12 Kgs and Maximum Usage = 112 Kgs

Lead time – 4 to 8 days

ROQ Particulars EOQ ROQ Annual Requirement (A) 20,000 20,000 Quantity Ordered(B) 2,000 5,000 No. of Orders (C) = (A)/(B) 10 4 Order cost @ Rs.500 5,000 2,000 Average Inventory 1,000 2,500 Carrying Cost @ Rs.5 5,000 12,500 Associated Costs 10,000 14,500 Savings in EOQ 4,500

(2+1+2+1+1+2+3) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Yield Adjustment: a. Compute Material B needed = 10,000 units × 2.5 kgs = 25,000 kgs. b. Deduct opening stock: 25,000 – 2,630 = 20,000 kgs
2. EOQ & ROQ: a. EOQ = √ (2×20,000×500)/5 = 2,000 kgs b. ROQ = Quarterly order = 20,000/4 = 5,000 kgs
3. Re-Order Level & Stock: a. Re-Order Level = Max usage (112 kgs) × Max lead time (8 days) = 896 kgs.

b. Max Stock = 896 + 5,000 – (12×4) = 5,848 kgs.

4. Cost Comparison: a. Tabulate ordering + carrying costs for EOQ (Rs. 10,000) vs. ROQ (Rs. 14,500).
5. Discount Scenario: a. Recompute ROQ costs with 5% discount (Rs. 19/kg) and Rs. 4.75 carrying cost.

Examiner Observations Students frequently struggle with this multi-part inventory management question due to:

1. Yield Calculation Errors: a. Misinterpreting 80% yield (e.g., assuming 2 kgs directly instead of adjusting to 2.5

kgs/unit). b. Incorrectly calculating annual material requirement (e.g., ignoring opening stock adjustments).

2. EOQ vs. ROQ Confusion: a. Failing to distinguish between Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) and Re-Order

Quantity (ROQ) under quarterly policy. a. Using ROQ (5,000 kgs) in EOQ formula or vice versa.

3. Re-Order Level & Stock Formula: a. Miscalculating average usage (62 kgs/day) from max/min usage (12/112

kgs). b. Using EOQ instead of ROQ in max/min stock formulae, leading to incorrect values (e.g., 2,848 kgs vs. 5,848 kgs).

4. Discount Scenario Oversights: a. Not adjusting carrying cost for discounted price (Rs. 19 × 25% = Rs. 4.75). b. Missing net benefit calculation (Rs. 16,125 savings in ROQ due to discount).
5. Presentation Issues: a. Unstructured tables for cost comparison (EOQ vs. ROQ). b. Omitting units (kgs/days) in intermediate steps.

(2+1+1+1+3+1+1) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Prioritize Transactions – Start with opening stock, then process GRNs/MRNs in date order before material

issues.

2. Weighted Average Cost – Update after every receipt/return (e.g., after GRN-008, deduct MRN-003, then

recalculate rate).

3. Quick Calculations – Use a tabular format for the store ledger to avoid missing entries.
4. Stock Levels – Note that lead time and usage are based on extreme values (max/min), not averages.
5. Time-Saving Tip – For inventory turnover, use closing stock only if opening is zero; otherwise, average.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to the volume of transactions and weighted average cost calculations. Common mistakes include:

1. Incorrect Weighted Average Calculation – Many students fail to update the weighted average rate after each

receipt/return, leading to wrong stock valuations.

2. Ignoring MRN (Material Returned Notes) – Some students overlook the 500 and 400 units returned (MRN-

003 & MRN-004), leading to incorrect inventory balances.

3. Misinterpretation of Dates – The question mixes December and January transactions, causing confusion in

sequencing (e.g., Purchase Orders in December but GRNs in January).

4. Lead Time & Stock Level Formulas – Errors in identifying maximum/minimum usage and lead time result in

wrong re-order, max, and min stock levels.

5. Inventory Turnover Ratio – Students often use closing stock instead of average stock [(Opening + Closing)/2],

leading to incorrect ratios.

Question 18. An automobile company purchases 27,000 spare parts for its annual requirements. The cost per order is Rs. 240 and the annual carrying cost of average inventory is 12.5%. Each spare part costs Rs. 50. At present, the order size is 3,000 spare parts. (Assume that number of days in a year = 360 days) Find out: (i) How much the company's cost would be saved by opting EOQ model? (ii) The Re-order point under EOQ model if lead time is 12 days.

(iii) How frequently should orders for procurement be placed under EOQ model?

[8 Marks | 10 Minutes\](PYP Nov 20)[Medium | ICAI Fav]

Answer 18. Working Notes: Annual requirement (A) = 27,000 units Cost per order (O) = Rs.240 Inventory carrying cost (i) = 12.5% Cost per unit of spare (c) = Rs.50 Carrying cost per unit (i × c) = Rs.50 × 12.5% = Rs.6.25

Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) = √ = √ = 1440 Units

(i) Calculation of saving by opting EOQ:

Existing Order policy EOQ Model No. of orders

9 ( ) 18.75 or 19 ( ) A. Ordering Cost (Rs.) 2,160 (Rs. 240 × 9)

4,500, ( )- B. Carrying cost (Rs.)

9,375( ) 4,500( ) Total cost (A+B) (Rs.) 11,535 9,000 Savings of Cost by opting EOQ Model = Rs. 11,535 – Rs. 9,000 = Rs. 2,535

(ii) Re-order point under EOQ: Re-order point/ Re-order level = Maximum consumption × Maximum lead time Consumption per day = = 75 units Re-order point/ Re-order level = 75 units × 12 days = 900 units

(iii) Frequency of Orders (in days):

= = = 18.95 days or 19 days

(2+3+2+1) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. EOQ Formula – Use √(2AO/C) with C = Rs. 6.25 (not Rs. 50). Verify EOQ = 1,440 units.
2. Cost Comparison – a. Existing Policy: Ordering cost (9 × Rs. 240) + Carrying cost (½ × 3,000 × Rs. 6.25). b. EOQ Policy: Ordering cost (18.75 × Rs. 240) + Carrying cost (½ × 1,440 × Rs. 6.25).
3. Re-order Point = Daily usage (75 units) × Lead time (12 days) = 900 units.
4. Order Frequency = 360/18.75 = 19.2 days (round to 19 days).

Examiner Observations Students often face challenges in this EOQ-based question due to misapplication of formulas and logical gaps in interpreting costs. Common mistakes include:

1. EOQ Formula Errors – Incorrectly substituting values, especially carrying cost (C × i). Many students use Rs.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 75

50 instead of Rs. 6.25 (12.5% of Rs. 50), leading to wrong EOQ.

2. Ordering Cost Calculation – Using approximate no. of orders (e.g., 18.75 rounded to 19) without adjusting

total cost accurately. ICAI expects precise calculations.

3. Re-order Point Misinterpretation – Confusing lead time demand with safety stock or max consumption. The

question specifies lead time = 12 days, so no safety stock is involved.

4. Frequency of Orders – Calculating 360/18.75 = 19.2 days but rounding to 19 days without clarifying if partial

orders are allowed.

5. Total Cost Comparison – Neglecting to compare total costs (ordering + carrying) under both policies, leading

to incorrect savings.

Question 19. A Company uses three raw materials A, B and C for a particular product for which the following data apply: Raw Usage per unit Re-order Price per Delivery period Re-order Minimu Material of Product quantity Kg. (in weeks) level m level

(Kgs.) (Kgs.) (Kgs) (Kgs.)

Minimum Average Maximum A 10 10,000 10 1 2 3 8,000 ? B 4 5,000 30 3 4 5 4,750 ? C 6 10,000 15 2 3 4 ? 2,000 Weekly production varies from 175 to 225 units, averaging 200 units of the said product. COMPUTE the following quantities: (i) Minimum stock of A, (ii) Maximum stock of B, (iii) Re-order level of C, (iv) Average stock level of A.

[8 Marks | 10 Minutes\](Study material)[Medium | ICAI Twister | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 19. (i) Minimum stock of A Re-order level – (Average rate of consumption × Average time required to obtain fresh delivery) = 8,000 – (200 × 10 × 2) = 4,000 kgs.

(ii) Maximum stock of B Re-order level + Re-order quantity – (Minimum consumption × Minimum delivery period) = 4,750 + 5,000 – (175 × 4 × 3) = 9,750 – 2,100 = 7,650 kgs.

(iii) Re-order level of C Maximum delivery period × Maximum usage = 4 × 225 × 6 = 5,400 kgs. OR Re-order level of C = Minimum level of C + [Average rate of consumption × Average time required to obtain fresh delivery] = 2,000 + [(200 × 6) × 3] kgs = 5,600 kgs.

(iv) Average stock level of A = Minimum stock level of A + ½ Re-order quantity of A = 4,000 + ½ × 10,000 = 4,000 + 5,000 = 9,000 kgs © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 76

OR Average Stock level of A = = =10,125 Kgs Working note: Maximum stock of A = ROL+ ROQ – (Minimum consumption × Minimum re-order period) = 8,000 + 10,000 – [(175 × 10) × 1] = 16,250 kgs (2+2+2+2)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Decode Variables First: Note usage/unit (A: 10kg, B: 4kg, C: 6kg) and weekly production (175-225 units).
2. Consumption Rates: a. Min: 175 × usage/kg (e.g., A = 1,750 kgs/week). b. Avg: 200 × usage/kg (e.g., A = 2,000 kgs/week). c. Max: 225 × usage/kg (e.g., A = 2,250 kgs/week).
3. Key Formulas: a. ROL = Max usage × Max lead time (for C). b. Min Stock = ROL – (Avg usage × Avg lead time) (for A). c. Max Stock = ROL + ROQ – (Min usage × Min lead time) (for B).
4. Average Stock: Use ½ ROQ + Min Level for speed, or (Min + Max)/2 if time permits.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to multiple variables and formula misinterpretations. Common mistakes include:

1. Confusing Usage Rates – Mixing per-unit raw material usage (A: 10kg, B: 4kg, C: 6kg) with weekly production

units (175-225). Many students fail to multiply usage by production to get total kgs consumed.

2. Re-order Level (ROL) Missteps – For material C, ROL is missing. Students either: a. Use maximum usage × maximum lead time (correct: 225×6×4 = 5,400 kgs), or b. Incorrectly add minimum level to average consumption (5,600 kgs, which is not matching ICAI’s expected answer).
3. Minimum vs. Maximum Levels – a. For A, minimum stock = ROL – (Avg. consumption × Avg. lead time). Some students use minimum consumption instead of average. b. For B, maximum stock = ROL + ROQ – (Min. consumption × Min. lead time). Errors occur if lead time is taken in weeks but consumption is not scaled weekly.
4. Average Stock Level Formula Choice – ICAI accepts two methods: a. ½ Re-order Quantity + Minimum Level (9,000 kgs for A), or b. (Min. + Max. Stock)/2 (10,125 kgs for A). Students often miss calculating max stock (16,250 kgs) for the second method.

Question 20. From the details given below, CALCULATE: (i) Re-ordering level (ii) Maximum level (iii) Minimum level (iv) Danger level.

Re-ordering quantity is to be calculated on the basis of following information: Cost of placing a purchase order is Rs. 4,000

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 77

Number of units to be purchased during the year is 5, 00,000 Purchase price per unit, inclusive of transportation cost is Rs. 50 Annual cost of storage per unit is Rs.10. Details of lead time: Average - 10 days, Maximum - 15 days Minimum- 5 days, for emergency purchases- 4 days. Rate of consumption: Average: 1,500 units per day, Maximum: 2,000 units per day.

[6 Marks | 8 Minutes\](Study material)[Medium | ICAI Fav]

Answer 20. Basic Data: A (Number of units to be purchased annually) = 5, 00,000 units, O (Ordering cost per order) = Rs. 4,000 C (Annual cost of storage per unit) = Rs. 10, Purchase price per unit inclusive of transportation cost = Rs. 50

Computations: (i) Re-ordering level (ROL) = Maximum usage per period × Maximum lead time = 2,000 units per day × 15 days = 30,000 units

(ii) Maximum level = ROL + ROQ – [Min. rate of consumption × Min. lead time] (Refer to working notes 1 and 2) = 30,000 units + 20,000 units – [1,000 units per day×5 days] = 45,000 units

(iii) Minimum level = ROL–Average rate of consumption× Average re-order-period = 30,000 units – (1,500 units per day × 10 days) = 15,000 units

(iv) Danger level = Average consumption × Lead time for emergency purchases = 1,500 units per day × 4 days = 6,000 units

Working Notes: 1. Minimum rate of consumption per day Avg. rate of consumption =

1,500 units per day = or X = 1,000 units per day.

2. Re-order Quantity (ROQ) =√ =20,000 units (1+1+1+1+1+1)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Prioritize Formulas: Write down ROL, Max/Min Level formulas first to avoid confusion.
2. Derive Minimum Consumption Early: Solve for it immediately after noting average/maximum rates.
3. Use Emergency Lead Time Only for Danger Level: Isolate this to prevent mix-ups.
4. Quick ROQ Calculation: Plug values directly into √ (2AO/C) without overthinking.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to misinterpretation of lead times and consumption rates. Common mistakes include:

1. Confusing Maximum/Minimum Lead Time with Average: Using the wrong lead time (e.g., average instead of

maximum for ROL) drastically alters results.

2. Incorrect Minimum Consumption Calculation: Many fail to derive the minimum rate of consumption using the

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 78

average formula (1,500 = (Min + 2,000)/2), leading to errors in Maximum Level.

3. ROQ Formula Misapplication: Forgetting to square root or misplacing values in √(2AO/C).
4. Danger Level Oversight: Students often miss that it uses emergency purchase lead time (4 days), not regular

lead times.

5. Unit Consistency: Ignoring that lead times are in days while ROQ is annual, causing mismatched units.

Question 21. Rounak Ltd. is the manufacturer of monitors for PCs. A monitor requires 4 units of Part -M. The following are the details of its operation during 20X8: Average monthly market demand 2,000 Monitors Ordering cost Rs. 1,000 per order Inventory carrying cost 20% per annum Cost of Pat Rs. 350 per part Normal usage 425 parts per week Minimum usage 140 parts per week Maximum usage 710 parts per week Lead time to supply 3-5 weeks COMPUTE from the above: (i) Economic Order Quantity (EOQ). If the supplier is willing to supply quarterly 30,000 units of Part- M at a discount of 5%, is it worth accepting? (ii) Reorder level (iii) Maximum level of stock (iv) Minimum level of stock.

[8 Marks | 12 Minutes\](RTP Nov’18)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 21. A = Annual usage of parts = Monthly demand for monitors × 4 parts × 12 months = 2,000monitors × 4 parts × 12 months = 96,000 units O = Ordering cost per order = Rs. 1,000/- per order C1 = Cost per part =Rs. 350/- iC1 = Inventory carrying cost per unit per annum

= 20% × Rs. 350 = Rs. 70/- per unit, per annum Economic order quantity (EOQ): E.O.Q = √

= √ = 1,656 parts (approx.)

The supplier is willing to supply 30,000 units at a discount of 5%, therefore cost of each part shall be Rs. 350 – 5% of 350 = Rs. 332.5

Total cost (when order size is 30,000 units): = Cost of 96,000 units + ordering cost + carrying cost. = (96,000 units × Rs. 332.50) + (96,000 units / 30,000 units × ′1,000) + 1/2 (30,000 units × 20% × Rs. 332.50) = Rs. 3, 19, 20,000 + Rs. 3,200\* + Rs. 9, 97,500= Rs. 3, 29, 20,700

Total cost (when order size is 1,656 units): = (96,000 units × Rs. 350) + + (96,000 units / 1,656 units × ′1,000) + 1/2 (1,656 units × 20% × Rs. 350)

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 79

= Rs. 3, 36, 00,000 + Rs. 57,970\* + Rs. 57,960 = Rs. 3, 37, 15,930 Since, the total cost under the supply of 30,000 units with 5% discount is lower than that when order size is 1,656 units, therefore the offer should be accepted. Note: While accepting this offer consideration of capital blocked on order size of 30,000 units has been ignored. \*Order size can also be taken in absolute figure.

(1) Reorder level = Maximum consumption × Maximum re-order period = 710 units × 5 weeks = 3,550 units

(2) Maximum level of stock = Re-order level + Reorder quantity – (Min. usage × Min. reorder period) = 3,550 units + 1,656 units – (140 units × 3 weeks) = 4,786 units.

(3) Minimum level of stock = Re-order level – Normal usage × Average reorder period = 3,550 units – (425 units × 4 weeks) = 1,850 units.

(2+1+2+1+1+1) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Start with Annual Demand: Convert monthly monitor demand to annual part demand immediately.
2. EOQ First, Then Discount Comparison: Calculate EOQ, then compare total costs (purchase + ordering +

carrying) for both options.

3. Lead Time Caution: a. ROL: Max usage × Max lead time (5 weeks). b. Max Level: ROL + EOQ – (Min usage × Min lead time). c. Min Level: ROL – (Normal usage × Avg lead time).
4. Use Shortcuts: For carrying cost, compute 20% of unit cost once and reuse.

Examiner Observations Students frequently make the following mistakes in this question:

1. Incorrect Annual Demand Calculation: Many students fail to convert monthly monitor demand into annual

part demand (2,000 monitors × 4 parts × 12 months = 96,000 units). Some wrongly use weekly consumption directly.

2. EOQ vs. Discounted Bulk Order Comparison: a. Missing Total Cost Calculation: Students often calculate EOQ

but forget to compare it with the supplier’s bulk offer.

b. Ignoring Carrying & Ordering Costs: Some only compare purchase prices, neglecting carrying cost (20% of Rs. 332.5) and ordering cost (Rs. 1,000 per order).

3. Reorder Level Misinterpretation: Using average/normal usage (425 units/week) instead of maximum usage

(710 units/week) for ROL.

4. Maximum/Minimum Stock Levels: a. Wrong Lead Time: Using average (4 weeks) instead of minimum (3

weeks) for Maximum Level and average (4 weeks) for Minimum Level.

b. Formula Confusion: Mixing up "Normal usage" and "Minimum usage" in formulas.

Question 22. A company produces a product 'AB' by using two raw materials - 'Material Ae' and 'Material Be' in the ratio of 5:3. A sales volume of 50,000 kgs is estimated for the month of December by the managers expecting the trend will continue for entire year. The ratio of input and output is 8:5. © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 80

Other Information about Raw Material Ae is as follows: Purchase Price Rs. 150 per kg Re-order period 2 to 3 days Carrying Cost 12% Note: Material Ae is perishable in nature and if not used within 3.5 days of purchase it becomes obsolete. To place an order for material 'Ae’, the company has to incur an administrative cost of Rs. 375 per order. At present, material ‘Ae’ is purchased in a lot of 7,500 kgs. to avail the discount on purchase. Company works for 25 days in a month and production is carried out evenly. You are required to CALCULATE: (i) Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) for Material Ae; (ii) Maximum stock level for Material Ae.

[6 Marks | 8 Minutes\](MTP Sep’22)[Medium | ICAI Twister| High Chance for Exams]

Answer 22. (i) Monthly production of AB = 50,000 kgs Raw material required = 50,000/5 x 8 = 80,000 kgs Material Ae and Material Be ratio = 5:3 Therefore, material Ae = 80,000/8 x 5 =50,000 kgs

Calculation of EOQ= √ EOQ= √ = 5,000 kgs

(ii) Calculation of maximum stock level of Material Ae which is perishable in nature and is required to be used within 3.5 days. (a) Stock equals to 3.5 days consumption = 50,000 kgs/ 25 days x 3.5 days = 7,000 kgs (b) Maximum stock level for Material Ae Maximum stock = Reorder quantity + reorder level – (minimum consumption x minimum lead time) Where, reorder quantity = 7,500 kgs Reorder level = maximum consumption\* x maximum lead time = 50,000/ 25 x 3 days = 6,000 kgs Now, Maximum stock level = 7,500 kgs + 6,000 kgs – (50,000 /25 days x 2 days) = 9,500 kgs Stock required for 3.5 days consumption is lower than the maximum stock level calculated above. Therefore, maximum stock level will be 7,000 kgs. (\*since production is processed evenly throughout the month hence material consumption will also be even.)

(2+1+1+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Start with Annual Demand: Convert monthly to annual (50,000 × 12) for EOQ.
2. Prioritize Perishability: Calculate 3.5 days’ consumption first (7,000 kgs) as it caps the stock.
3. Quick EOQ Formula: Plug values directly into √(2AO/C) where: a. A = 6, 00,000 kg/year, O = Rs. 375, C = Rs. 18.
4. Compare Results: Traditional max stock (9,500 kgs) is invalid due to perishability.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to:

1. EOQ Calculation Errors: a. Using monthly (50,000 kg) instead of annual demand (50,000 × 12) in the EOQ

formula.

b. Incorrectly calculating carrying cost (12% of Rs. 150 = Rs. 18/unit/year).

2. Maximum Stock Level Misinterpretation: a. Ignoring the perishability constraint (3.5 days) and calculating

only the traditional formula.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 81

b. Not comparing 7,000 kgs (3.5 days’ consumption) with the formula-derived 9,500 kgs to arrive at the correct answer.

3. Reorder Level Confusion: a. Using average lead time (2.5 days) instead of maximum lead time (3 days) for

reorder level.

4. Unit Consistency: a. Mixing monthly and annual data without conversion (e.g., using monthly demand in

EOQ).

Examiner Observations Students generally perform well on this ABC analysis question, but common mistakes include:

1. Incorrect Ranking Basis: a. Some students rank items by unit quantity or unit cost instead of total inventory cost (Units × Unit Cost). b. Example: Item 102 (300 units) may seem "important" due to high quantity, but its Rs. 300 total cost makes it a 'C' item.
2. Misclassification in ABC Categories: a. Applying fixed percentage slabs (e.g., 80-15-5 rule) instead of the company’s given criteria (15%+ for A, ≤6% for C, rest B). b. Overlooking that two items (103 & 101) together form 70% of cost, requiring both to be 'A'.
3. Calculation Errors: a. Incorrectly computing % of Total Inventory Cost (e.g., dividing by total units instead of total cost). b. Missing cumulative % check for category assignment.
4. Presentation Issues: a. Not grouping items under A/B/C clearly in the final table.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to misclassification of costs and incorrect GST treatment. Common mistakes include:

1. GST Calculation Errors: a. Applying GST on the listed price (Rs. 2,50,000) instead of the net price after trade discount (Rs. 2,25,000). b. Forgetting that GST is non-creditable (since Sky & Co. is unregistered), so it must be added to the cost.
2. Cash Discount Misinterpretation: a. Including cash discount (10%) in cost calculation, even though it’s a finance charge (only applicable if paid within 30 days).
3. Abnormal vs. Normal Costs: a. Adding demurrage (Rs. 5,000) as a cost, though it’s a penalty (abnormal) and excluded. b. Deducting normal shortage (20%) from cost instead of adjusting units (5,000 → 4,000 good units).
4. Returnable Containers: a. Missing the net cost (Rs. 30,000 – Rs. 20,000 = Rs. 10,000) and treating the full deposit as expense.
5. Other Expenses (2%): a. Incorrectly calculating 2% on Rs. 2, 94,000 (should be Rs. 2,94,000 × 2/98 = Rs. 6,000).

Question 25. EXPLAIN the concept of "ABC Analysis" as a technique of inventory control.

[6 Marks | 8 Minutes\](Study material)[Medium | ICAI Fav]

Answer 25. ABC Analysis: This system exercises discriminating control over different items of inventory on the basis of the investment involved. Usually the items are classified into three categories according to their relative importance, namely, their value and frequency of replenishment during a period.

(i) ‘A’ Category: This category of items consists of only a small percentage i.e., about 10% of the total items handled by the stores but require heavy investment about 70% of inventory value, because of their high prices or heavy requirement or both. Items under this category can be controlled effectively by using a regular system which ensures neither over-stocking nor shortage of materials for production. Such a system plans its total material requirements by making budgets. The stocks of materials are controlled by fixing certain levels like maximum level, minimum level and re-order level.

(ii) ‘B’ Category: This category of items is relatively less important; they may be 20% of the total items of material handled by stores. The percentage of investment required is about 20% of the total investment in inventories. In the case of these items, as the sum involved is moderate, the same degree of control as applied in ‘A’ category of items is not warranted. The orders for the items, belonging to this category may be placed after reviewing their situation periodically.

(iii) ‘C’ Category: This category of items does not require much investment; it may be about 10% of total inventory value but they are nearly 70% of the total items handled by store. For these categories of items, there is © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 85

no need of exercising constant control. Orders for items in this group may be placed either after six months or once in a year, after ascertaining consumption requirements. In this case the objective is to economies on ordering and handling costs.

Advantages of ABC analysis: The advantages of ABC analysis are the following: (i) Continuity in production: It ensures that, without there being any danger of interruption of production for want of materials or stores, minimum investment will be made in inventories of stocks of materials or stocks to be carried. (ii) Lower cost: The cost of placing orders, receiving goods and maintaining stocks is minimized especially if the system is coupled with the determination of proper economic order quantities. (iii) Less attention required: Management time is saved since attention need to be paid only to some of the items rather than all the items, as would be the case if the ABC system was not in operation. (iv) Systematic working: With the introduction of the ABC system, much of the work connected with purchases can be systematized on a routine basis, to be handled by subordinate staff.

(2) Fast Moving, Slow Moving and Non-Moving (FSN) Inventory: It is also known as FNS (Fast, Normal and Slow moving) classification of inventory analysis. Under this system, inventories are controlled by classifying them on the basis of frequency of usage. The classification of items into these three categories depends on the nature and managerial discretion. A threshold range on the basis of inventory turnover is decided and classified accordingly. (i) Fast Moving- This category of items is placed nearer to store issue point and the stock is reviewed frequently for making of fresh orders. (ii) Slow Moving- This category of items is stored little far and stock is reviewed periodically for any obsolescence, and may be shifted to Non-moving category. (iii) Non-Moving- This category of items is kept for disposal. This category of items is reported to the management and an appropriate provision for loss may be created. Some of the reasons for slow moving and non-moving inventories are stated below: (i) Failure of production management to communicate the updated requirement to the stores management (ii) Technological upgradation in terms of new machine requiring new kind of material or existing material becoming obsolete. (iii) Lack of periodic review of inventories. By careful observation, timely identification and adoption of inventory management techniques such as maintenance of minimum level or just in time approach, one can manage slow moving and non-moving inventories. We may calculate inventory turnover ratio and present the reports of comparison of actual and standards with variations, if any to the management.

(3) Vital, Essential and Desirable (VED): Under this system of inventory analysis, inventories are classified on the basis of its criticality for the production function and final product. Generally, this classification is done for spare parts which are used for production. (i) Vital- Items are classified as vital when its unavailability can interrupt the production process and cause a production loss. Items under this category are strictly controlled by setting re-order level.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 86

(ii) Essential- Items under this category are essential but not vital. The unavailability may cause sub standardization and loss of efficiency in production process. Items under this category are reviewed periodically and get the second priority. (iii) Desirable- Items under this category are optional in nature, unavailability does not cause any production or efficiency loss. For instance, in hospital administration, stock of medicines and essential chemicals are categorized as VED or FSN inventory. In case of life saving, rare and critical drugs, they are being categorized as vital inventory. They are the ones whose unavailability can interrupt smooth service. Those inventories which are optional or substitutes, not leading to loss in efficiency would be categorized as desirable inventories. FNS categorization helps the store keepers in hospitals to keep a check on medicines whose expiry date is close and needs to be disposed off at the earliest. The quantity of slow-moving drugs are maintained accordingly.

(4) High Cost, Medium Cost, and Low Cost (HML) Inventory: Under this system, inventory is classified on the basis of the cost of an individual item, unlike ABC analysis where inventories are classified on the basis of overall value of inventory. A range of cost is used to classify the inventory items into the three categories. High-Cost inventories are given more priority for control, whereas Medium-cost and Low-cost items are comparatively given lesser priority.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Structured Format: Use bullet points for each technique (ABC/FSN/VED/HML) to avoid overlap.
2. Prioritize ABC: Spend 60% time on ABC (core concept), then briefly explain others.
3. Examples Matter: Add 1-line examples (e.g., "Hospital drugs under VED") to secure application marks.
4. Avoid Repetition: Clearly differentiate ABC (value) from FSN (usage) and VED (criticality).

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this theoretical question due to:

1. Overgeneralization of ABC Analysis: a. Many students describe the traditional 80-15-5 rule (70-20-10 for A-B-

C) but fail to adapt to scenario-specific % criteria (e.g., 15%+ for 'A' as in Q27).

b. Ignoring that ABC % thresholds vary across companies.

2. Confusing ABC with Other Techniques: a. Mixing up ABC (value-based) with FSN (usage frequency) or VED

(criticality) classifications.

b. For example, stating that ‘A’ items are "fast-moving" (FSN) instead of "high-value."

3. Incomplete Coverage: a. Missing advantages of ABC analysis (e.g., cost savings, systematic control) or other

techniques (FSN/VED/HML).

b. Overlooking practical examples (e.g., hospital inventory for VED).

4. Theoretical vs. Practical Disconnect: a. Failing to link ABC analysis to real-world applications (e.g., tighter

reorder levels for ‘A’ items).

Question 26. Write a short note on VED analysis of Inventory Control.

[4 Marks | 5 Minutes\](PYP July ‘21)[Easy | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 87

Answer 26. Vital, Essential and Desirable (VED): Under this system of inventory analysis, inventories are classified on the basis of its criticality for the production function and final product. Generally, this classification is done for spare parts which are used for production. (i) Vital- Items are classified as vital when its unavailability can interrupt the production process and cause a production loss. Items under this category are strictly controlled by setting re-order level.

(ii) Essential- Items under this category are essential but not vital. The unavailability may cause sub standardization and loss of efficiency in production process. Items under this category are reviewed periodically and get the second priority.

(iii) Desirable- Items under this category are optional in nature; unavailability does not cause any production or efficiency loss.

Important Note:- It was a theoretical question requiring examinees to write a short note on the concept of VED analysis of Inventory Control. Performance of the examinees was below average.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Structured Format: Use bullet points for each category (V/E/D).
2. Add Examples: Mention spare parts in factories or drugs in hospitals to secure application marks.
3. Link to Production Impact: Emphasize how Vital items halt production, while Desirable items don’t.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with VED analysis due to:

1. Lack of Conceptual Clarity: a. Many confuse VED (criticality-based) with ABC (value-based) or FSN (usage-based) classification. b. Example: Stating that "Vital" items are "high-value" (ABC) rather than "production-critical."
2. Incomplete Explanation: a. Missing real-world applications (e.g., spare parts in manufacturing, life-saving drugs in hospitals). b. Failing to explain control measures (e.g., strict reorder levels for vital items).
3. Overgeneralization: a. Not specifying that VED is primarily for spare parts/emergency items, not all inventory.
4. Weak Presentation: a. Writing in paragraphs instead of point-wise for clarity.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Step 1: Start with the opening stock (1,500 kg @ ₹48).
2. Step 2: Record receipts and issues date-wise, updating the weighted average rate after every receipt (not

issue).

3. Step 3: For weighted average, use: New Avg. Rate = [(Previous Qty × Prev. Rate) + (New Qty × New Rate)] /

Total Qty

4. Step 4: Deduct shortages only at period-end (31st May & 30th June).

Examiner Observations Students often make the following mistakes while solving this Stores Ledger Account problem:

1. Incorrect Opening Balance Handling – Many forget to account for the opening stock (1,500 kg @ ₹48)

properly, leading to errors in subsequent calculations.

2. Weighted Average Calculation Errors – Students frequently miscalculate the weighted average rate after

each receipt, especially when multiple receipts occur before an issue.

3. Shortage Adjustments Ignored – A common oversight is not deducting the stock shortages (80 kg on 31st

May and 60 kg on 30th June) from the closing balance.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 90

4. Date Sequencing Issues – Some students fail to follow the chronological order of transactions, leading to

incorrect stock valuations.

5. Rounding Off Mistakes – The weighted average rate should be rounded off systematically (preferably to two

decimal places), but students either ignore this or round inconsistently.

6. Final Valuation Errors – The closing stock value is often calculated incorrectly due to cumulative mistakes in

earlier steps.

Question 28. Explain: FIFO and LIFO method of stores issue.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes] (PYP May ‘18)[Easy | ICAI Fav]

Answer 28. First-in First-out (FIFO) method: It is a method of pricing the issues of materials, in the order in which they are purchased. In other words, the materials are issued in the order in which they arrive in the store or the items longest in stock are issued first. Thus each issue of material only recovers the purchase price which does not reflect the current market price. This method is considered suitable in times of falling price because the material cost charged to production will be high while the replacement cost of materials will be low.

Last-in-First-out (LIFO) method: It is a method of pricing the issues of materials. This method is based on the assumption that the items of the last batch (lot) purchased are the first to be issued. Therefore, under this method the prices of the last batch (lot) are used for pricing the issues, until it is exhausted, and so on. If however, the quantity of issue is more than the quantity of the latest lot than earlier (lot) and its price will also be taken into consideration. During inflationary period or period of rising prices, the use of LIFO would help to ensure that the cost of production determined on the above basis is approximately the current one.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Step 1: Start with crisp definitions (FIFO = First bought, first sold; LIFO = Last bought, first sold).
2. Step 2: Use a tabular example (2-3 transactions) to show how rates apply.
3. Step 3: Highlight real-world impact – FIFO inflates profit in rising prices, LIFO reduces taxable income.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with FIFO & LIFO methods due to:

1. Conceptual Confusion – Many mix up FIFO (oldest stock issued first) and LIFO (latest stock issued first),

especially during inflationary/deflationary scenarios.

2. Incorrect Batch Tracking – Students fail to track batches chronologically, leading to wrong pricing of issues

(e.g., using latest rates in FIFO or oldest rates in LIFO).

3. Partial Issue Mismanagement – When an issue quantity spans multiple batches, students either ignore

earlier/later lots or misallocate costs.

4. Real-World Relevance Ignored – Some write definitions but fail to explain why FIFO suits falling prices and

LIFO suits rising prices (impact on COGS and profit).

5. Closing Stock Valuation Errors – Under LIFO, closing stock may include oldest purchases, which students often

overlook.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Simple Average (SA): a. After each issue, identify remaining batches and average only their rates (e.g., Sep 5:

Only ₹10.20 remains post-issue).

b. Ignore exhausted rates (₹10.00 after Sep 5).

2. Weighted Average (WA): a. Update total cost & quantity after every receipt. b. For issues, use latest total cost/total quantity (e.g., Sep 5: ₹3,040/300 = ₹10.13).

Examiner Observations Students frequently make these errors while solving Simple Average (SA) vs. Weighted Average (WA) pricing problems:

1. Confusing SA with WA – Many students incorrectly average all available rates in WA (like SA) instead of

calculating total cost/total quantity after each receipt.

2. Incorrect Rate Selection in SA – For SA, students often:

a. Include rates of exhausted batches (e.g., after Sep 5 issue, using ₹10.00 despite only ₹10.20 stock remaining). b. Miscount active rates (e.g., for Sep 13 issue, some average 2 rates instead of 3).

3. Rounding Errors in WA – WA requires precise decimal calculations (e.g., ₹10.133 → ₹10.13). Students either

over-round or ignore decimals, distorting future balances.

4. Balance Verification Neglect – Few cross-check closing stock = Opening + Receipts – Issues leading to

undetected cumulative errors.

5. Chronological Order Mishaps – Transactions are sometimes recorded out of sequence (e.g., Sep 20 purchase

entered before Sep 18 issue).

(4+4) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with FIFO and LIFO inventory accounting due to these common errors:

1. Batch Tracking Errors a. In FIFO, students fail to exhaust the oldest batch first, especially when partial issues span multiple batches (e.g., March 18 issue of 220 units). b. In LIFO, they incorrectly use older rates instead of the latest available stock (e.g., March 25 issue should take 150 @ ₹230 first, but some use 50 @ ₹200).
2. Balance Mismanagement a.Skipping intermediate balances after each transaction, leading to incorrect stock valuations. b. Incorrect averaging (mixing rates) when balances have multiple batches (e.g., March 6 balance: 50 @ ₹200 + 200 @ ₹220).
3. Chronological Missteps a.Recording transactions out of sequence (e.g., March 24 purchase entered before March 18 issue).
4. Rounding/Calculation Slips a.Carrying forward errors from one transaction to the next due to minor miscalculations.
5. Closing Stock Confusion a.Under LIFO, the closing stock may include older, cheaper units (e.g., 50 @ ₹200 + 10 @ ₹220), which students often misprice.

4. Closing Stock Valuation a. Under FIFO, the closing stock (500 @ ₹11) must reflect the most recent purchase, but some include older batches. b. Under LIFO, the closing stock (100 @ ₹10 + 100 @ ₹14 + 300 @ ₹11) is often miscalculated due to incorrect layer tracking.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Simple Average: a. For each issue, average only the rates of remaining batches (e.g., March 5: ₹10.00 is

exhausted; use ₹10.20).

2. Weighted Average: a. Recalculate rate after every receipt: New Rate = (Total Cost + New Receipt Cost) /

(Total Qty + New Qty).

b. Issues use the latest WA rate (e.g., March 13: ₹10.63).

Examiner Observations

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 103

Students frequently make these mistakes when solving Simple Average (SA) vs. Weighted Average (WA) inventory pricing problems:

1. Simple Average Method Errors a. Incorrect Rate Pooling: Students often include exhausted rates (e.g., for March 5 issue, using ₹10.00 even though only ₹10.20 remains post-issue). b. Miscounting Active Rates: For March 13 issue, some average 2 rates instead of 3 (₹10.20, ₹10.50, ₹10.80).
2. Weighted Average Method Pitfalls a. Recalculation Neglect: Students fail to update the WA rate after every receipt, leading to cascading errors (e.g., March 10 WA rate should be ₹10.63, not ₹10.50). b. Rounding Errors: WA rates (e.g., ₹10.133 → ₹10.13) are often rounded incorrectly, distorting future balances.
3. Common Oversights a. Chronological Errors: Transactions recorded out of sequence (e.g., March 20 purchase entered before March 18 issue). b. Balance Verification: Few cross-check Closing Stock = Opening + Receipts – Issues, leading to undetected errors.
4. Closing Stock Valuation a. Under SA, students miscalculate the final rate (₹10.90) by averaging incorrect pools. b. Under WA, the closing stock (100 @ ₹10.78) is often wrong due to cumulative rounding mistakes.

Question 35. Case Scenarios The purchase committee of A Ltd. has been entrusted to review the material procurement policy of the company. The chief marketing manager has appraised the committee that the company at present produces a single product X by using two raw materials A and B in the ratio of 3:2. Material A is perishable in nature and has to be used within 10 days from Goods received note (GRN) date otherwise material becomes obsolete. Material B is durable in nature and can be used even after one year. Material A is purchased from the local market within 1 to 2 days of placing order. Material B, on the other hand, is purchased from neighboring state and it takes 2 to 4 days to receive the material in the store. The purchase price of per kilogram of raw material A and B is Rs.30 and Rs.44 respectively exclusive of taxes. To place an order, the company has to incur an administrative cost of Rs.1, 200. Carrying cost for Material A and B is 15% and 5% respectively. At present material A is purchased in a lot of 15,000 kg. to avail 10% discount on market price. GST applicable for both the materials is 18% and the input tax credit is availed. The sales department has provided an estimate that the company could sell 30,000 kg. In January 2024 and also projected the same trend for the entire year. The ratio of input and output is 5:3. Company works for 25 days in a month and production is carried out evenly.

Ans. - (b) Calculation of Maximum Stock level: Since, the Material A is perishable in nature and it required to be used within 10 days, hence, the Maximum Stock Level shall be lower of two:

(a) Stock equal to 10 days consumption = x 10 days =12,000 kg. (b) Maximum Stock Level for Material A: Re-order Quantity + Re-order level – (Min consumption\* × Min. lead time) Where, Re-order Quantity = 15,000 kg. Re-order level = Max. Consumption\* × Max. Lead time = 30,000/25 × 2 days = 2,400 kg. Maximum stock Level = 15,000 kg. + 2,400 kg. - (30,000/25 × 1 day) = 17,400 – 1,200 = 16,200 kg. Stock required for 10 days consumption is lower than the maximum stock level calculated through the formula. Therefore, Maximum Stock Level will be 12,000 kg. (\*Since, production is processed evenly throughout the month hence material consumption will also be even.)
