Examiner Observations

1. Perishability vs. EOQ Logic: a. Material A is perishable (must be used within 10 days), but EOQ assumes no perishability. The question silently forces you to compare EOQ with a policy that accounts for obsolescence losses. b. If you blindly calculate EOQ without considering the 10-day limit, you’ll miss the hidden loss due to spoilage when ordering EOQ (13,856 kg vs. 12,000 kg max usable in 10 days).
2. Discount vs. Obsolescence Trade-off: a. The current policy (15,000 kg) gets a 10% discount but results in obsolescence loss (since only 12,000 kg can be used in 10 days; the rest is wasted).

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 106

b. EOQ (13,856 kg) loses the discount but reduces obsolescence (only 1,856 kg wasted vs. 3,000 kg in current policy). c. The real conflict is between discount savings vs. obsolescence + carrying cost savings.

3. Misleading Carrying Cost Calculation: a. Carrying cost is applied to average stock (EOQ/2), but obsolescence loss is on the excess quantity beyond 10-day consumption (12,000 kg). b. The question doesn’t explicitly state that the carrying cost is irrelevant for the wasted portion, but the solution implies it by separately adding obsolescence loss.
4. GST and Input Credit Red Herring: a. GST (18%) and input tax credit are mentioned, but they don’t affect the decision because they’re neutral (credit offsets tax). Students might waste time on this irrelevant detail.
5. Production Ratio Distraction: a. The input-output ratio (5:3) is given but not needed for solving this part. It’s a decoy to test if you focus only on relevant data.

Question 36.STATE how normal and abnormal loss of material arising during storage are treated in Cost Accounts?

[8 Marks | 10 Minutes\](Study material)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 36. TREATMENT OF NORMAL AND ABNORMAL LOSS OF MATERIALS Loss of materials during handling, storage, process may occur any of the following forms: (i) Waste: The portion of raw material which is lost during storage or production and discarded. The waste may or may not have any value.

Treatment of Waste Normal- Cost of normal waste is absorbed by good production units. Abnormal- The cost of abnormal loss is transferred to Costing Profit and loss account. (ii) Scrap: The materials that result from production which are discarded and disposed-off without further treatment. Generally, scrap has either no value or insignificant value. Sometimes, it may be reintroduced into the process as raw material.

Treatment of Scrap Normal- The cost of scrap is borne by good units and income arises on account of realizable value is deducted from the cost. Abnormal- The scrap account should be charged with full cost. The credit is given to the job or process concerned. The profit or loss in the scrap account, on realization, will be transferred to the Costing Profit and Loss Account. (iii) Spoilage: It is the term used for materials which are badly damaged in manufacturing operations, that do not meet the specification required by the customers and they cannot be rectified economically and hence taken out of the process to be disposed off in some manner without further processing.

Treatment of Spoilage

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 107

Normal- Normal spoilage (i.e., which is inherent in the operation) costs are included in costs, either by charging the loss due to spoilage to the production order or by charging it to the production overhead so that it is spread over all the products. Any value realized from spoilage is credited to production order or production overhead account, as the case may be. Abnormal- The cost of abnormal spoilage (i.e., arising out of causes not inherent in manufacturing process) is charged to the Costing Profit and Loss Account. When spoiled work is the result of rigid specification, the cost of spoiled work is absorbed by good production while the cost of disposal is charged to production overhead. (iv) Defectives: It signifies those units or portions of production which do not meet the quality standards. Defectives arise due to sub-standard materials, bad-supervision, bad-planning, poor workmanship, inadequate- equipment and careless inspection. The defectives which can be re-made as per the quality standard by using additional materials are known as reworks. Reworks include repairs, reconditioning and refurbishing. Defectives which cannot be brought up to the quality standards are known as rejects. The rejects may either be disposed-off or re-cycled for production process.

Treatment of Defectives: Normal- An amount equal to the cost less realizable value on sale of defectives are charged to material cost of good production. Abnormal- Material cost of abnormal defectives are not included in material cost but treated as loss after giving credit to the realizable value of such defectives. The material cost of abnormal loss is transferred to costing profit and loss account. Reclamation of loss from defective units In the case of articles that have been spoiled, it is necessary to take steps to reclaim as much of the loss as possible. For this purpose: (i) All defective units should be sent to a place fixed for the purpose; (ii) These should be dismantled; (iii) Goods and serviceable parts should be separated and taken back into the stock; (iv) Parts which can be made serviceable by further work should be separated and sent to the workshop for the purpose and taken into stock after the defects have been removed; and (v) Parts which cannot be made serviceable should be collected in one place for being melted or sold off. Printed forms should be used to record quantities for all purposes aforementioned.

Difference between Waste and Scrap Waste Scrap It is connected with raw material or inputs to the It is the loss connected with the output production process. Waste of materials may be visible or invisible. Scraps are generally identifiable and has physical

substance. Generally, waste has no recoverable value. Scraps are termed as by-products and has small

recoverable value.

Difference between Scrap and Defectives © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 108

Scrap Defectives It is the loss connected with the output This type of loss is connected with the output as well as

the input. Scraps are not intended but cannot be eliminated due Defectives also are not intended but can be eliminated to the nature of material or process itself. through a proper control system. Generally, scraps are not used or rectified. Defectives can be used after rectification. Scraps have insignificant recoverable value. Defectives are sold at a lower value from that of the

good one. Distinction between Spoilage and Defectives: The difference between spoilage and defectives is that while spoilage cannot be repaired or reconditioned, defectives can be rectified and transferred, either back to the standard production or to the seconds. The problem of accounting for defective work is in relation to the costs of rectification or rework. (v) Obsolescence: Obsolescence is defined as “the loss in the intrinsic value of an asset due to its supersession”. In simple words, obsolescence refers to the loss in the value of an asset due to technological advancements. Treatment: Materials may become obsolete under any of the following circumstances: (i) where it is a spare part or a component of a machinery that is used in manufacturing and is now obsolete; (ii) where it is used in the manufacturing of a product which has now become obsolete; (iii) where the material itself is replaced by another material due to either improved quality or fall in price. In all the three cases, the value of the obsolete material held in stock is a total loss and immediate steps should be taken to dispose it off at the best available price. The loss arising out of obsolete materials is an abnormal loss and it does not form part of the cost of manufacture.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Bullet Points: Use headings (Normal/Abnormal) for each loss type.
2. Tabular Format: Compare treatments (e.g., scrap normal vs. abnormal).
3. Skip Irrelevant Data: Ignore GST, input-output ratios.
4. Prioritize Key Terms: Focus on spoilage (irreparable) and defectives (repairable).

Examiner Observations

1. Confusing Terminology: Students mix up waste, scrap, spoilage, and defectives, leading to incorrect

treatment (e.g., charging abnormal scrap to production overhead instead of P&L).

2. Normal vs. Abnormal Misclassification: Many fail to distinguish between inherent losses (normal)

and avoidable losses (abnormal), especially in spoilage/defectives.

3. Overlooking Realizable Value: Forgetting to deduct scrap/defective sale value from costs (e.g., normal scrap

reduces good units’ cost, but students treat it as pure loss).

4. Redundant Details: Wasting time on GST/input credit (irrelevant here) or production ratios (not needed for

this question).

5. Incomplete Treatment: Missing reclamation steps for defectives or obsolescence (often ignored as it’s less

common).

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 109

(iii) Cost of Returnable containers (iv) Central Goods and Service Tax (CGST) (v) Shortage due to abnormal reasons.

[5 Marks | 7 Minutes\](PYP Jan 21)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 37. Treatment of items in arriving at the value of cost of material Purchased S. No. Items Treatment (i) Detention charges/ Detention charges/ fines imposed for non- compliance of rule or law by any

Fine statutory authority. It is an abnormal cost and not included with cost of

purchase. (ii) Demurrage Demurrage is a penalty imposed by the transporter for delay in uploading or

offloading of materials. It is an abnormal cost and not included with cost of purchase. (iii) Cost of returnable Treatment of cost of returnable containers are as follows: Returnable

containers Containers: If the containers are returned and their costs are refunded, then

cost of containers should not be considered in the cost of purchase. If the amount of refund on returning the container is less than the amount paid, then, only the short fall is added with the cost of purchase. (iv) Central Goods and Central Goods and Service Tax (CGST) is paid on manufacture and supply of

Service Tax (CGST) goods and collected from the buyer. It is excluded from the cost of purchase if

the input credit is available for the same. Unless mentioned specifically CGST is not added with the cost of purchase. (v) Shortage due to Shortage arises due to abnormal reasons such as material mishandling,

abnormal reasons pilferage, or due to any avoidable reasons are not absorbed by the good units.

Losses due to abnormal reasons are debited to costing profit and loss account.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Rule-Based: Memorize: a. Abnormal = P&L (detention, demurrage, abnormal shortage). b. Containers = Net cost (refund-adjusted). c. CGST = Exclude if credit taken.
2. Tabular Format: Use a 2-column table (Item + Treatment) for clarity.

Examiner Observations

1. Misclassification of Abnormal Costs: Students often incorrectly include detention charges, demurrage, or

abnormal shortages in material cost, despite these being abnormal and chargeable to P&L.

2. CGST Confusion: Many assume CGST is always part of cost, forgetting the input tax credit rule (excluded if

credit is available).

3. Returnable Containers: Overlooking the refund adjustment—only the net non-refundable amount (if any) is

added to cost.

4. Vague Terminology: Using terms like "penalty" or "loss" without specifying normal vs. abnormal (e.g.,

demurrage is always abnormal).

5. Incomplete Answers: Missing exceptions (e.g., CGST inclusion if input credit is not available).

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 110

Question 38. Write down the treatment of following items associated with purchase of materials. (i) Cash discount (ii) IGST (iii) Demurrage (iv) Shortage (v) Basic Custom Duty

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](PYP May’22)[Medium | ICAI Fav]

Answer 38.

Treatment of items associated with purchase of materials is tabulated as below S.No. Items Treatment (i) Cash Discount Cash discount is not deducted from the purchase price. It is treated as interest

and finance charges. It is ignored. (ii) Integrated Goods Integrated Goods and Service Tax (IGST) is paid on inter- state supply of goods

and Service Tax and provision of services and collected from the buyers. It is excluded from the (IGST) cost of purchase if credit for the same is available. Unless mentioned specifically

it should not form part of cost of purchase. (iii) Demurrage Demurrage is a penalty imposed by the transporter for delay in uploading or

offloading of materials. It is an abnormal cost and not included with cost of purchase (iv) Shortage Shortage in materials are treated as follows:

Shortage due to normal reasons: Good units absorb the cost of shortage due to normal reasons. Losses due to breaking of bulk, evaporation, or due to any unavoidable conditions etc. are the reasons of normal loss. Shortage due to abnormal reasons: Shortage arises due to abnormal reasons such as material mishandling, pilferage, or due to any avoidable reasons are not absorbed by the good units. Losses due to abnormal reasons are debited to costing profit and loss account. (v) Basic Custom Duty Basic Custom duty is paid on import of goods from outside India. It is added with

the purchase cost.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Memorize Tax Rules: IGST/GST treatment depends on credit availability—always check the scenario.
2. Shortage Logic: Apply the "normal vs. abnormal" test—normal losses adjust unit cost; abnormal goes to P&L.

Examiner Observations Students often make the following mistakes while answering this question:

1. Cash Discount Treatment: Many incorrectly deduct it from purchase cost instead of treating it as a finance

charge.

2. IGST Exclusion: Some wrongly include IGST in purchase cost even when input credit is available.
3. Demurrage Classification: A frequent error is categorizing demurrage as a normal cost rather than an

abnormal expense.

4. Shortage Accounting: Students often fail to distinguish between normal and abnormal shortages, leading to

incorrect allocation (e.g., charging all shortages to Costing P&L).

5. Custom Duty Inclusion: A few miss adding basic customs duty to purchase cost, treating it as a separate

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 111

expense.

Question 39. Explain obsolescence and circumstances under which materials become obsolete. State the steps to be taken for its treatment.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](PYP Nov ‘18)[Medium | ICAI Fav]

Answer 39. Obsolescence: Obsolescence is defined as “the loss in the intrinsic value of an asset due to its supersession”. Materials may become obsolete under any of the following circumstances: (i) Where it is a spare part, or a component of a machinery used in manufacture and that machinery becomes obsolete; (ii) Where it is used in the manufacture of a product which has become obsolete; (iii) Where the material itself is replaced by another material due to either improved quality or fall in price.

Treatment: In all three cases, the value of the obsolete material held in stock is a total loss and immediate steps should be taken to dispose it off at the best available price. The loss arising out of obsolete materials on abnormal loss does not form part of the cost of manufacture.

Important Note:- This was a theoretical question on obsolescence of material. Below average performance was observed.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Memorize ICAI’s Definition: Use the exact phrase "loss in intrinsic value due to supersession" to secure full

marks.

2. Three-Point Circumstances: Think machinery → product → material to cover all scenarios.
3. Abnormal Loss Emphasis: Explicitly state that the loss does not affect product cost—this is often the

differentiating factor.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to:

1. Vague Definition: Many define obsolescence generically (e.g., "material no longer usable") without linking it

to loss in intrinsic value due to supersession, as per ICAI’s wording.

2. Incomplete Circumstances: Some list only 1–2 reasons (e.g., machinery obsolescence) but miss replacement

due to better quality/price—a key point.

3. Treatment Errors: A frequent mistake is suggesting gradual write-off instead of immediate disposal at best

price. Some also wrongly include the loss in manufacturing cost rather than treating it as an abnormal loss.

4. Lack of Clarity on Abnormal Loss: Students fail to explicitly state that the loss does not form part of

production cost, impacting costing accuracy.

Question 40. Anil & Company buys its annual requirement of 36,000 units in 6 instalments. Each unit costs RS.1 and the ordering cost is RS.25. The inventory carrying cost is estimated at 20% of unit value. FIND the total

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 112

annual cost of the existing inventory policy. CALCULATE, how much money can be saved by Economic Order Quantity?

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](Study material)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 40. (a) Total Annual Cost in Existing Inventory Policy Particulars (Rs.) Ordering cost (6 orders @ Rs. 25) 150 Carrying cost of average inventory (36,000 ÷ 6) = 6,000 units per order Average inventory = 3,000 units Carrying cost = 20% of Rs. 1 × 3,000 = 3,000 × 0.20 600 Total cost A 750

(b) Total Annual Cost in E.O.Q = EOQ =√ =3000 units

Particulars (Rs.) No. of orders = 36,000 ÷3,000 units = 12 orders Ordering cost (12 × Rs. 25) = 300 Carrying cost of average inventory (3,000 ×0.20) ÷ 2 = 300 Total Cost B 600 Savings due to E.O.Q Rs.(750 – 600) (A – B) 150 Note: As the units purchase cost of Rs. 1 does not change in both the computation, the same has not been considered to arrive at total cost of inventory for the purpose of savings. (2.5+2.5)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Use Shortcut Formulas: Memorize EOQ = √ (2AB/C), where C = carrying cost per unit (₹0.20 here).
2. Average Inventory = EOQ/2: Critical to avoid carrying cost error.
3. Exclude Purchase Cost: As per ICAI note, omit ₹36,000 to focus on ordering + carrying costs.
4. Double-Check Units: Ensure all values (e.g., 20% = ₹0.20) align before calculations.

Examiner Observations Students frequently make the following errors in this EOQ-based question:

1. Incorrect EOQ Formula Application: Some use wrong units (e.g., dividing by 0.2 instead of 20% of ₹1) or

miscalculate √ (2×36,000×25)/0.20, leading to wrong EOQ (e.g., 6,000 instead of 3,000).

2. Carrying Cost Misinterpretation: Many take full EOQ (3,000) as average inventory instead of EOQ/2 (1,500

units), doubling the carrying cost (₹600 vs. ₹300).

3. Ordering Cost Calculation: A few wrongly compute ordering cost for existing policy (e.g., 36,000/6,000 = 6

orders but forget ₹25 per order).

4. Ignoring Purchase Cost Clarification: Despite the note, some include ₹36,000 (36,000 × ₹1) in total cost,

complicating savings calculation unnecessarily.

Question 41. Which system of inventory management is known as 'Demand pull' or 'Pull through' system of production? Explain. Also, specify the two principles on which this system is based.

[4 Marks | 5 Minutes\](PYP Nov 22)[Easy | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 113

Answer 41. Just in Time (JIT) Inventory Management is also known as ‘Demand pull’ or ‘Pull through’ system of production. In this system, production process actually starts after the order for the products is received. Based on the demand, production process starts and the requirement for raw materials is sent to the purchase department for purchase. It is a system of inventory management with an approach to have a zero inventories in stores. According to this approach material should only be purchased when it is actually required for production. JIT is based on two principles (i) Produce goods only when it is required and (ii) The products should be delivered to customers at the time only when they want.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Keyword Focus: Use ICAI’s exact phrasing—"Demand Pull" = JIT. Avoid mixing with Kanban (a JIT tool, not the

system itself).

2. Two-Part Principles: Think "Production Trigger + Delivery Timing" to cover both principles succinctly.
3. Avoid Over-Explanation: JIT’s goal is inventory minimization, not absolute zero—clarify only if asked.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this conceptual question due to:

1. Confusing JIT with Other Systems: Many incorrectly label MRP (Material Requirements

Planning) or Kanban as the "Demand Pull" system, missing JIT’s core principle of zero inventory.

2. Vague Explanation of Pull System: Some describe JIT as "producing as per demand" but fail to explicitly link it

to post-order production initiation, a key distinction from push systems.

3. Incomplete Principles: A frequent error is listing only one principle (e.g., "produce when required") and

omitting the delivery timing aspect ("deliver when customers want").

4. Overcomplicating Zero Inventory: A few wrongly equate JIT with complete elimination of all inventory,

ignoring that it targets minimization (not absolute zero) through precise coordination.

Question 42. ABC Electronics Ltd. is facing challenges in managing its inventory. The company has been experiencing production delays due to stockouts, excessive inventory storage costs, and the presence of outdated components in its warehouse. The management is exploring methods to streamline their inventory management system to address these issues. To tackle these problems, they are considering the following strategies: (i) Danger Level (ii) Just in Time Inventory Management (iii) Maximum stock level and Minimum Stock level (iv) Obsolescence Write brief notes on the above strategies.

[8 Marks |10 Minutes\](Practice Question) [Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 42. (i) Danger level: It is the level at which normal issues of the raw material inventory are stopped and emergency issues are only made. It can be calculated as below: Danger Level = Average Consumption\* × Lead time for emergency purchase \*Some time minimum consumption is also used.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 114

(ii) Just in Time Inventory Management-JIT is a system of inventory management with an approach to have zero inventories in stores. According to this approach material should only be purchased when it is actually required for production. JIT is based on two principles (i) Produce goods only when it is required and (ii) The products should be delivered to customers at the time only when they want. It is also known as ‘Demand pull’ or ‘Pull through’ system of production. In this system, production process actually starts after the order for the products is received. Based on the demand, production process starts and the requirement for raw materials is sent to the purchase department for purchase.

(iii) Maximum Stock Level: It is the highest level of quantity for any material which can be held in stock at any time. Any quantity beyond this level cause extra amount of expenditure due to engagement of fund, cost of storage, obsolescence etc. It can be calculated as below: Maximum Stock Level = Re-order Level + Re-order Quantity - (Minimum Consumption Rate × Minimum Re-order Period) Here, Re-order Quantity may be EOQ And

Minimum Stock Level: It is lowest level of material stock, which must be maintained in hand at all times, so that there is no stoppage of production due to non-availability of inventory. It is calculated as below: Minimum Stock Level = Re-order Stock Level - (Average Consumption Rate × Average Re-order Period) (iv) Obsolescence- Obsolescence is defined as “the loss in the intrinsic value of an asset due to its supersession”. In simple words, obsolescence refers to the loss in the value of an asset due to technological advancements. Treatment: Materials may become obsolete under any of the following circumstances: (i) where it is a spare part or a component of a machinery that is used in manufacturing and is now obsolete; (ii) where it is used in the manufacturing of a product which has now become obsolete; (iii) where the material itself is replaced by another material due to either improved quality or fall in price. In all the three cases, the value of the obsolete material held in stock is a total loss and immediate steps should be taken to dispose it off at the best available price. The loss arising out of obsolete materials is an abnormal loss and it does not form part of the cost of manufacture.

(2+2+2+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Prioritize Key Terms: a. Underline "emergency purchase" for danger level. b. Use bullet points for JIT principles and obsolescence circumstances.
2. Formulas First: Write stock-level formulas immediately to secure marks even if explanations are brief.
3. Avoid Redundancy: For obsolescence, skip lengthy definitions—focus on 3 circumstances + abnormal loss.

Examiner Observations Students often make these errors in this inventory management question:

1. Danger Level Misconceptions: a. Many confuse it with reorder level or minimum stock level, failing to highlight it as an emergency

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 115

threshold. b. Some omit the formula or use average lead time instead of emergency purchase lead time.

2. JIT Over-Simplification: a. Students mention "zero inventory" but miss linking it to post-order production or the two principles (production timing + delivery timing). b. A few wrongly equate JIT with Kanban (a tool, not the system itself).
3. Stock Level Calculation Errors: a. For maximum stock level, students often exclude (Min Consumption × Min Reorder Period) or miscalculate reorder quantity (EOQ). b. For minimum stock level, some use normal lead time instead of average reorder period.
4. Obsolescence Treatment Gaps: a. Many list only 1–2 circumstances (e.g., machinery obsolescence) but miss replacement due to price/quality improvements. b. Some incorrectly include obsolescence loss in production cost instead of treating it as abnormal loss.

Question 43. Provide brief explanations on any three of the following topics: (i) Danger Level in Inventory Management (ii) Just in Time (JIT) Approach to Inventory Control (iii) Concept of Maximum and Minimum Stock Levels (iv) Obsolescence and its Effect on Inventory Value

[6 Marks | 8 Minutes] (Study material)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 43. (i) Danger Level: The Danger Level refers to the critical stock level of raw materials, below which normal inventory issues are stopped, and only emergency issues are made. It acts as a safeguard to ensure that production does not halt due to stockouts during emergency situations. The Danger Level can be calculated as: Danger Level = Average Consumption × Lead Time for Emergency Purchase In some cases, minimum consumption may be used instead of average consumption.

(ii) Just in Time (JIT) Inventory Management: Just in Time (JIT) is an inventory management strategy that aims to maintain minimal stock levels and avoid holding excess inventory. The key principle is that materials should be procured and delivered only when they are needed for production, thus reducing storage costs. JIT is based on two main principles:  Production when required: Goods are produced only when there is a demand.  Delivery when needed: Products are delivered to customers precisely at the time of need. This system is also known as the ‘Demand Pull’ or ‘Pull-through’ system, where the production process begins after customer orders are received. The requirement for raw materials is then communicated to the purchasing department based on actual demand.

(iii) Maximum Stock Level and Minimum Stock Level: Maximum Stock Level: The maximum stock level represents the highest quantity of a material that can be stored at any time. Exceeding this level incurs unnecessary costs related to storage, tied-up funds, and the risk of obsolescence. The calculation for Maximum Stock Level is:

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 116

Maximum Stock Level = Re-order Level + Re-order Quantity − (Minimum Consumption Rate × Minimum Re-order Period) In this calculation, the Re-order Quantity could be based on the Economic Order Quantity (EOQ). Minimum Stock Level: This is the lowest quantity of a material that must be maintained at all times to ensure continuous production without disruption. It prevents stockouts and keeps operations running smoothly. The formula for Minimum Stock Level is: Minimum Stock Level = Re-order Level − (Average Consumption Rate × Average Re-order Period)

(iv) Obsolescence: Obsolescence refers to the loss in value of an asset, typically due to changes in technology, market preferences, or improved alternatives. In the context of inventory, it refers to materials that are no longer usable or valuable due to these factors. Materials may become obsolete under the following conditions:  Spare parts or components that are no longer used in manufacturing due to technological advancements or machinery updates.  Finished products that are no longer in demand or have been replaced by superior alternatives.  Raw materials that have been replaced by better or cheaper substitutes. When materials become obsolete, they should be written off as a total loss, and steps should be taken to dispose of them at the best available price. The loss from obsolescence is an abnormal loss and should not be included in the cost of manufacture. (1+1+2+2)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Prioritize Key Elements: a. For Danger Level, highlight "emergency purchase" in the formula. b. For JIT, bullet-point the two principles first.
2. Use Short Formulas: Write stock-level formulas clearly (e.g., Max = ROL + EOQ - Min Usage).
3. Avoid Over-Explaining: For obsolescence, list the 3 causes concisely; no need for examples.

Examiner Observations Students often make these errors when answering this question:

1. Danger Level Confusion: a. Many mistake it for reorder level or safety stock, failing to emphasize it as the absolute emergency threshold where only critical issues are permitted. b. Some incorrectly use normal lead time instead of emergency purchase lead time in the formula.
2. JIT Oversimplification: a. While mentioning "zero inventory," students often miss: i. The pull-system nature (production starts only after order receipt). ii. The two critical principles (timely production + timely delivery). b. Some incorrectly describe JIT as Kanban (which is just an implementation tool).
3. Stock Level Calculation Errors: a. For maximum stock level, students: i. Forget to subtract (Min Consumption × Min Reorder Period). ii. Use EOQ incorrectly (e.g., not adjusting for lead time variability). b. For minimum stock level, some use normal reorder period instead of average.
4. Obsolescence Missteps: a. Students often: i. List only 1-2 causes (e.g., machinery obsolescence) but miss price/quality-driven replacement.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 117

ii. Wrongly include obsolescence loss in production cost rather than treating it as abnormal loss.

Descriptive Question Question 1. Z Ltd is working by employing 50 skilled workers. It is considering the introduction of an incentive scheme - either Halsey Scheme (with 50% Bonus) or Rowan Scheme - of wage payment for increasing the labour productivity to adjust with the increasing demand for its products by 40%. The company feels that if the proposed incentive scheme could bring about an average 20% increase over the present earnings of the workers, it could act as sufficient incentive for them to produce more and the company has accordingly given assurance to the workers. Because of this assurance, an increase in productivity has been observed as revealed by the figures for the month of April, 2020: Hourly rate of wages (guaranteed) Rs. 50 Average time for producing one unit by one worker at the previous performance (this 1.975 hours may be taken as time allowed) Number of working days in a month 24 Number of working hours per day of each worker 8 Actual production during the month 6,120 units Required: (i) Calculate the effective increase in earnings of workers in percentage terms under Halsey and Rowan scheme. (ii) Calculate the savings to Z Ltd in terms of direct labour cost per unit under both the schemes. (iii) Advise Z Ltd about the selection of the scheme that would fulfil its assurance of incentivizing workers and also to adjust with the increase in demand.

[8 Marks | 10 Minutes\](PYP Jan 21) (Old & New SM)[Difficult | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 1. Working Notes:

1. Total time wages of 50 workers per month: = No. of working days in the month × No. of working hours per day

of each worker × Hourly rate of wages × No. of workers = 24 days × 8 hrs. × Rs. 50 × 50 workers = Rs. 4, 80,000

2. Time saved per month: Time allowed per unit to a worker 1.975 hours

No. of units produced during the month by 50 workers 6,120 units Total time allowed to produce 6,120 units (6,120 × 1.975 hrs.) 12,087 hours Actual time taken to produce 6,120 units (24 days × 8 hrs. × 50 workers) 9,600 hours Time saved (12,087 hours – 9,600 hours) 2,487 hours

3. Bonus under Halsey scheme to be paid to 50 workers: Bonus = (50% of time saved) × hourly rate of wages

= 50/100 × 2,487 hours × Rs. 50 = Rs. 62,175 Total wages to be paid to 50 workers are (Rs. 4, 80,000 + Rs. 62,175) Rs. 5, 42,175, if Z Ltd. considers the introduction of Halsey Incentive Scheme to increase the worker productivity.

4. Bonus under Rowan Scheme to be paid to 50 workers:

Bonus = × 𝑇𝑖𝑚𝑒 𝑆𝑎𝑣𝑒𝑑 × ℎ𝑜𝑢𝑟𝑙𝑦 𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑒 = × 2,487 ℎ𝑜𝑢𝑟 × . 50 = . 98,764

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 119

Total wages to be paid to 50 workers are (Rs. 4, 80,000 + Rs. 98,764) Rs. 5, 78,764, if Z Ltd. Considers the introduction of Rowan Incentive Scheme to increase the worker productivity.

(i) (a) Effective hourly rate of earnings under Halsey scheme: (Refer to Working Notes 1, 2 and 3) = = = Rs. 56.48

Effective increase in earnings of worker (in %) = × 100 = 2.96%

(b) Effective hourly rate of earnings under Rowan scheme: (Refer to Working Notes 1, 2 and 4) = = = Rs. 60.29

Effective increase in earnings of worker (in %) = × 100 = 20.58%

(ii) (a) Saving in terms of direct labour cost per unit under Halsey scheme: (Refer to Working Note 3) Labour cost per unit (under time wage scheme) = 1.975 hours × Rs. 50 = Rs. 98.75 Labour cost per unit (under Halsey scheme) = = = Rs.88.60 Saving per unit = Rs. 98.75 – Rs. 88.60 = Rs. 10.15

(b) Saving in terms of direct worker cost per unit under Rowan Scheme: (Refer to Working Note 4) Labour cost per unit under Rowan scheme = Rs. 5, 78,764/6,120 units= Rs. 94.57 Saving per unit = Rs. 98.75 – Rs. 94.57 = Rs. 4.18

(iii) Calculation of Productivity: Normal Production Hours worked/Unit per Hour 4,861 (9,600/1.975) Actual Production Units 6,120 Increase in labour productivity 1,259 % Productivity i.e. increase in production/Normal production 25.9% Advice: Rowan plan fulfils the company’s assurance of 20% increase over the present earnings of workers. This would increase productivity by 25.9% only. It will not adjust with the increase in demand by 40%.

(2+2+2+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Quick Setup: Note guaranteed wages (24 days × 8 hrs × 50 workers × Rs. 50).
2. Time Saved: Compare actual hours (9,600) vs. allowed hours (6,120 × 1.975).
3. Bonus Formulas: a. Halsey: 50% × Time Saved × Rate. b. Rowan: (Time Taken/Time Allowed) × Time Saved × Rate.
4. Earnings Check: Verify if Rowan’s 20.58% hike meets the 20% assurance.
5. Demand Gap: Compare productivity rise (25.9%) vs. demand (40%). Conclude Rowan meets wage promise but

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 120

not demand.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to:

1. Misinterpretation of Time Saved – Many incorrectly calculate time allowed vs. time taken, leading to wrong

bonus computations under Halsey/Rowan schemes.

2. Incorrect Productivity Linkage – Overlooking the 40% demand increase vs. 20% earnings assurance, leading to

flawed advice on scheme selection.

3. Unit Cost Savings Miscalculation – Direct labour cost per unit savings are often derived from total wages

instead of comparing pre- and post-incentive costs.

4. Rowan Scheme Complexity – Errors in applying the Rowan bonus formula (Time Taken/Time Allowed × Time

Saved × Rate) due to improper fraction handling.

5. Hourly Rate vs. Percentage Increase – Confusing effective hourly rate increase with overall earnings boost,

missing the 20% target check.

Question 2. Discuss the accounting treatment of Idle time and overtime wages.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](MTP May’20, April ‘19, RTP May’19, Old & New SM)[Medium | ICAI Fav ]

Answer 2. Accounting treatment of idle time wages & overtime wages in cost accounts: Normal idle time is treated as a part of the cost of production. Thus, in the case of direct workers, an allowance for normal idle time is built into the labour cost rates. In the case of indirect workers, normal idle time is spread over all the products or jobs through the process of absorption of factory overheads.

Under Cost Accounting, the overtime premium is treated as follows: If overtime is resorted to at the desire of the customer, then the overtime premium may be charged to the job directly. If overtime is required to cope with general production program or for meeting urgent orders, the overtime premium should be treated as overhead cost of particular department or cost center which works overtime. Overtime worked on account of abnormal conditions should be charged to costing Profit & Loss Account. If overtime is worked in a department due to the fault of another department the overtime premium should be charged to the latter department.

OR Normal idle time: It is the time which cannot be avoided or reduced in the normal course of business. It is treated as a part of cost of production. Thus, in the case of direct workers an allowance for normal idle time is considered setting of standard hours or standard rate. In case of indirect workers, normal idle time is considered for the computation of overhead rate.

Abnormal idle time: Apart from normal idle time, there may be factors which give rise to abnormal idle time. Abnormal idle time cost is not included as a part of production cost and is shown as a separate item in the Costing Profit and Loss Account. The cost of abnormal idle time should be further categorized into controllable and uncontrollable. For each category, the break-up of cost due to various factors should be separately shown. This would help the management in fixing responsibility for controlling idle time. Management should aim at © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 121

eliminating controllable idle time and on a long- term basis reducing even the normal idle time. This would require a detailed analysis of the causes leading to such idle time.

Causes of Overtime and Treatment of Overtime premium in cost accounting

Causes Treatment (1) The customer may agree to bear the entire charge (1) If overtime is resorted to at the desire of the of overtime because urgency of work. customer, then overtime premium may be charged to

the job directly. (2) Overtime may be called for to make up any shortfall (2) If overtime is required to cope with general in production due to some unexpected development. production programmes or for meeting urgent orders,

the overtime premium should be treated as overhead cost of the particular department or cost centre which works overtime. (3) Overtime work may be necessary to make up a (3) If overtime is worked in a department due to the shortfall in production due to some fault of fault of another department, the overtime premium management. should be charged to the latter department. (4) Overtime work may be resorted to, to secure an (4) Overtime worked on account of abnormal out-turn in excess of the normal output to take conditions such as flood, earthquake etc., should not advantage of an expanding market or of rising demand be charged to cost, but to Costing Profit and Loss

Account.

(1+2+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Idle Time: a. Normal: Built into production costs (direct labor rates/overheads). b. Abnormal: Charge to P&L, with controllable/uncontrollable breakdown.
2. Overtime: a. Customer-Requested: Direct job cost. b. Production Urgency: Departmental overheads. c. Departmental Fault: Charge to faulty department. d. Abnormal Events (floods): P&L.
3. Key Insight: a. Cause Dictates Treatment – Map each scenario to its accounting outcome.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to:

1. Misclassification of Idle Time – Confusing normal vs. abnormal idle time and incorrectly charging abnormal

idle time to production costs instead of P&L.

2. Overtime Premium Allocation Errors – Failing to link overtime causes (customer urgency, production shortfall,

departmental fault) with the correct treatment (direct job charge, overheads, or P&L).

3. Overgeneralization – Treating all overtime uniformly instead of categorizing based on specific triggers (e.g.,

customer request vs. management failure).

4. Ignoring Controllability – Not segregating abnormal idle time into controllable vs. uncontrollable for

management reporting.

5. Formula Overemphasis – Focusing on calculations (absent in this theory question) instead of conceptual

clarity on accounting principles.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 122

Question 3. Discuss the steps involved in setting labour time standards.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](PYP Dec ‘21)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 3. Procedure of Setting Labour Time Standards The following are the steps involved in setting labour standards: (a) Standardization: Products to be produced are decided based on production plan and customer's order. (b) Labour specification: Types of labour and labour time is specified. Labour time specification is based on past records and it takes into account normal wastage of time. (c) Standardization of methods: Selection of proper machines to use proper sequence and method of operations. (d) Manufacturing layout: A plan of operation for each product listing the operations to be performed is prepared. (e) Time and motion study: It is conducted for selecting the best way of completing the job or motions to be performed by workers and the standard time which an average worker will take for each job. This also takes into account the learning efficiency and learning effect. (f) Training and trial: Workers are trained to do the work and time spent at the time of trial run is noted down. Important Note:- This theory question to discuss steps involved in setting Labour Time Standards. Majority of the examinees were unable to answer it correct. Performance of the examinees was poor.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Start with Macro-Level: a. Standardization (product/labor specs) → Methods (machines/sequences).
2. Critical Step: Time and Motion Study – Emphasize it sets benchmark time considering learning curves.
3. Practical Validation: a. Training ensures workers adapt. b. Trial runs validate standards.
4. Key Insight: Standards evolve with worker proficiency; not static.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to:

1. Incomplete Coverage: Missing key steps like time and motion study or training and trial runs, focusing only on

basic standardization.

2. Vague Explanations: Writing generic points like "study past records" without linking to labor

efficiency or learning effects.

3. Sequential Errors: Jumbling the order of steps (e.g., discussing manufacturing layout before method

standardization).

4. Overlooking Practical Aspects: Ignoring worker training or trial runs, which are critical for realistic standards.
5. Repetition: Rehashing the same point under different headings (e.g., merging labor specification with time

studies).

Question 4. Anirban Ltd. wants to ascertain the profit lost during the year 20X8-X9 due to increased labour turnover. For this purpose, they have given you the following information (1) Training period of the new recruits is 50,000 hours. During this period their productivity is 60% of the experienced workers. Time required by an experienced worker is 10 hours per unit. (2) 20% of the output during training period was defective. Cost of rectification of a defective unit was Rs.25. © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 123

(3) Potential productive hours lost due to delay in recruitment were 1, 00,000 hours. (4) Selling price per unit is Rs.180 and P/V ratio is 20%. (5) Settlement cost of the workers leaving the organization was Rs.1, 83,480. (6) Recruitment cost was Rs.1, 56,340 (7) Training cost was Rs.1, 13,180. You are required to CALCULATE the profit lost by the company due to increased labour turnover during the year 2018-19.

[8 Marks | 12 Minutes\](MTP April ’19 & Sep ‘23, RTP May ’18)[Difficult | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 4. Output by experienced workers in 50,000 hours = 50,000/10= 5,000 units Output by new recruits = 60% of 5,000 = 3,000 units Less of output = 5,000 – 3,000 = 2,000 units Total loss of output = 10,000 + 2,000 = 12,000 units Contribution per unit = 20% of 180 = Rs.36 Total contribution cost = 36 × 12,000 = Rs.4, 32,000 Cost of repairing defective units = 3,000 × 0.2 × 25 = Rs.15, 000 Profit forgone due to labour turnover

(Rs.) Loss of Contribution 4,32,000 Cost of repairing defective units 15,000 Recruitment cost 1,56,340 Training cost 1,13,180 Settlement cost of workers leaving 1,83,480 Profit forgone in 2018-19 9,00,000

(4+4) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Lost Output: a. Training Period: 50,000 hrs ÷ 10 = 5,000 units (experienced). New recruits produce 60% →

3,000 units → Loss = 2,000 units. b. Potential Loss: 1, 00,000 hrs ÷ 10 = 10,000 units.

2. Defects: 20% of 3,000 units = 600 units × Rs. 25 = Rs. 15,000.
3. Contribution: 20% of Rs. 180 = Rs. 36/unit → Total loss = 12,000 units × Rs. 36 = Rs. 4, 32,000.
4. Add Costs: Settlement (Rs. 1, 83,480) + Recruitment (Rs. 1, 56,340) + Training (Rs. 1, 13,180).
5. Total Profit Lost: Rs. 4, 32,000 + Rs. 15,000 + Rs. 4, 53,000 = Rs. 9, 00,000.

Examiner Observations Students frequently make these mistakes:

1. Productivity Miscalculation: Failing to adjust for the 60% efficiency of new recruits, leading to incorrect output

loss (e.g., using 50,000 hours directly without the 60% adjustment).

2. Defective Units Oversight: Missing the 20% defect rate or incorrectly applying it to total output instead of only

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 124

new recruits' output (3,000 units).

3. Contribution Margin Error: Using selling price (Rs. 180) instead of contribution (Rs. 36 = 20% of 180) for lost

profit calculation.

4. Double-Counting Hours: Adding potential lost hours (1,00,000) separately without converting them to lost

units (10,000 units = 1,00,000/10).

5. Cost Exclusion: Omitting settlement, recruitment, or training costs as part of profit forgone.

Question 5. RST Company Ltd. has computed labour turnover rates for the quarter ended 31st March, 2017 as 20%, 10% and 5% under flux method, replacement method and separation method respectively. If the number of workers replaced during that quarter is 50. Calculate: (i) Workers recruited and joined (ii) Workers left and discharged and (iii) Average number of workers on roll.

[6 Marks | 6 Minutes\](MTP Oct‘18)( MTP Mar’21, MTP Oct’22)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 5. Labour Turnover Rate (Replacement Method) = × 100 Or, = Thus, Average No. of workers = 500 Labour Turnover Rate (Separation Method) = × 100 Or, = Thus, No. of workers separated =25 Labour Turnover Rate (Flux Method) = × 100

Or, = Or, 100(25+No.of Accessions) = 10,000 Or, 25+No. of Accessions = 100 Thus, No. of Accessions = 100-25=75 Accordingly, (i) Workers recruited and Joined = 75 (ii) Workers left and discharged = 25 (iii) Average number of workers on roll = 500 (2+2+2)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Start with Replacement Method: a. Given: 10% rate, 50 replaced → Average workers = 50/(10/100) = 500.
2. Separation Method: a. 5% rate → Separations = 5% of 500 = 25.
3. Flux Method: a. 20% rate → Separations (25) + Accessions = 20% of 500 = 100 → Accessions = 75.
4. Key Insight: a. Replacements (50) are subset of accessions (75 new + 50 replaced = 125 total accessions), but

flux method only uses new accessions (75) + separations (25).

Examiner Observations Students commonly make these errors:

1. Formula Mix-Up: Confusing the numerators for different methods: a. Using replacements instead of separations in the separation method. b. Incorrectly adding replacements (50) to accessions in the flux method (should be separations + accessions).
2. Calculation Order: Solving for average workers last instead of first, leading to cascading errors.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 125

3. Accessions Misinterpretation: Assuming "accessions" = only new recruits (ignoring replacements are part of

accessions).

4. Percentage Application: Misplacing decimal points (e.g., using 0.20 instead of 20/100).
5. Incomplete Answers: Providing only final numbers without showing working notes (losing method marks).

1. Guaranteed Hourly Rate: a. Multiply actual hours × hourly rate (e.g., Worker III: 540 × Rs. 60 = Rs. 32,400).
2. Piecework Earnings: a. Calculate per-unit rates: (Standard minutes × Rs. 1) → Rs. 15/20/30 for A/B/C. b. 3. Rowan Bonus: a. Time Allowed: Total standard minutes ÷ 60 (e.g., Worker I: 24,150 ÷ 60 = 402.5 hours). b. Bonus: (Time Taken/Time Allowed) × Time Saved × Hourly Rate.

Examiner Observations Students frequently struggle with this question due to:

1. Wage Scheme Confusion: Mixing up the three schemes (guaranteed hourly, piecework, and Rowan bonus)

leading to incorrect earnings calculations.

2. Piece Rate Errors: a. Calculating piece rates per minute but failing to convert to per unit (e.g., Product A: 15

minutes × Rs. 1 = Rs. 15/unit). b. Missing the 50% guarantee clause and wrongly applying the 75% rule even when earnings exceed 50% of basic pay. © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 127

3. Rowan Bonus Missteps: a. Incorrectly computing time saved (Time Allowed – Time Taken) or using the wrong

formula for bonus. b. Forgetting to multiply by the hourly rate in the bonus calculation.

4. Time Allowed Miscalculation: a. Not converting total standard minutes to hours (÷60) for time allowed. b. Omitting products with zero production (e.g., Worker II’s Product A and B).
5. Data Organization: Failing to tabulate computations, leading to disorganized and error-prone answers.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Step 1: Opening Balances: a. Deduct given roles (810 + 120 + 6 + 12 + 90) from 1,158 → 120 remaining

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 129

employees.

b. Apply 3:3:2 ratio to Legal Secretary (45), Staff Attorney (45), Associate Attorney (30).

2. Step 2: Closing Balances: a. Adjust openings with joinings/separations (e.g., Legal Secretary: 45 + 90 = 135).
3. Step 3: Categorize Movements: a. Separations: Left (315) + Transferred out (90 + 15). b. New Recruitments: Joined (1,686) + Transferred in (12 + 39). c. Replacements: Subset of joinings (e.g., HR Manager: 30 replaced).
4. Step 4: Calculate Rates: a. Average Workforce: (1,158 + 2,694)/2 = 1,926. b. Replacement Method: 165/1,926 × 100 = 8.57%. c. Flux Method: (1,851 + 315)/1,926 × 100 = 112.46%.

Examiner Observations Students frequently struggle with this question due to:

1. Data Organization Errors: Failing to systematically categorize employees (transfers vs. separations vs. new

recruitments), leading to incorrect totals.

2. Ratio Misapplication: Incorrectly calculating opening strengths of Legal Secretary, Staff Attorney, and

Associate Attorney (3:3:2 ratio) from the remaining 120 employees.

3. Flux Method Misunderstanding:

a. Omitting new recruitments (1,686) in the flux rate, resulting in an incorrect verification (24.92% vs. actual 112.46%). b. Treating transfers to subsidiaries as separations but missing transfers from subsidiaries as new recruitments.

4. Replacement vs. New Recruitment:

a. Confusing replacements (165) with total joinings (1,851), leading to wrong replacement method calculations.

5. Average Workforce Miscalculation: Using incorrect opening/closing figures (e.g., excluding transferred

employees).

Question 8. Following information is given of a newly setup organization for the year ended on 31st March, 2021\. st (ii) Equivalent Employee Turnover Rates for (i) above, given that the organization was setup on 31 January, 2021\.

[6 Marks | 7 Minutes\](PYP July ‘21)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 8. (i) Employee Turnover rate: Using Separation method: = × 100 = × 100= 5%

Using Flux method: = × 100 = × 100= 15%

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 130

(ii) Equivalent Employee Turnover Rate: = × 365 Using Separation method = 5/60 X 365 = 30.42% Or, = 5/60 X 360 = 30% Or, 5/2 X 12 = 30% Using Flux method = 15/60 × 365 =91.25% Or, = 15/60 X 360 = 30% Or, 15/2 X 12 = 30%

Important Note:- It was a practical problem requiring computation of Employee turnover rates and Equivalent employee turnover rates by using separation method and flux method. Most of the examinees were not well acquainted with the concept of equivalent employee turnover rates. Performance of the examinees was below average.

(3+3) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Step 1: Identify separations (25) and replacements (50) from data.
2. Step 2: Apply formulas directly: a. Separation Rate = (25/500) × 100 = 5% b. Flux Rate = (25+50)/500 × 100 = 15%
3. Step 3: For equivalent rates, note the 60-day period (Jan 31–Mar 31). Annualize by: a. Separation Equivalent = (5%/60) × 365 = 30.42% b. Flux Equivalent = (15%/60) × 365 = 91.25%

Examiner Observations Many students struggled with this question due to:

1. Misunderstanding Flux Method – Some incorrectly considered only replacements or separations instead of

both.

2. Equivalent Turnover Rate Calculation – A significant number failed to adjust for the short period (2 months vs.

annualized 365 days). Common errors included: a. Using full-year denominators (12 months/365 days) instead of actual 60 days. b. Incorrectly applying 360 days (corporate year) without clarity.

3. Formula Confusion – Mixing up Separation and Flux formulas or omitting the "×100" for percentage

conversion.

4. Ignoring Setup Date – Overlooking that the organization was operational only from 31st January 2021, leading

to incorrect annualization.

Question 9. Rowan Premium Bonus system does not motivate a highly efficient worker as a less efficient worker and a highly efficient worker can obtain same bonus under this system. Discuss with an example.

[6 Marks | 7 Minutes\](PYP July 21)[Medium | ICAI Twister | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 9. Rowan Premium Plan: According to this system a standard time allowance is fixed for the performance of a job and bonus is paid if time is saved. Under Rowan System, the bonus is that proportion of the time wages as time saved bears to the standard time. Bonus = × 𝑇𝑖𝑚𝑒 𝑆𝑎𝑣𝑒𝑑 × ℎ𝑜𝑢𝑟𝑙𝑦 𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑒 Example explaining highly efficient worker and less efficient worker obtaining same bonus: © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 131

Time rate (per Hour) Rs. 60 Time allowed 8 hours. Time taken by ‘X’ 6 hours. Time taken by ‘Y’ 2 hours. Bonus = × 𝑇𝑖𝑚𝑒 𝑆𝑎𝑣𝑒𝑑 × ℎ𝑜𝑢𝑟𝑙𝑦 𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑒

For ‘X' = × 6 ℎ𝑜𝑢𝑟 × . 60 = Rs. 90, For ‘Y’ = × 2 ℎ𝑜𝑢𝑟 × . 60 = Rs. 90 From the above example, it can be concluded that a highly efficient worker may obtain same bonus as less efficient worker under this system.

Important Note:- It was a theoretical question on Rowan Premium Bonus Plan testing the knowledge of the examinees that in what situation efficient and less efficient workers will get the same bonus. Majority of examinees did not answer properly. Performance of the examinees was below average.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Step 1: Memorize the Rowan formula: Bonus = (Taken/Allowed) × Saved × Rate.
2. Step 2: Pick extreme time-saving scenarios (e.g., 2 hrs vs. 6 hrs taken for 8 hrs allowed).
3. Step 3: Plug values: a. Worker X (6 hrs): (6/8) × 2 × 60 = Rs. 90. b. Worker Y (2 hrs): (2/8) × 6 × 60 = Rs. 90.
4. Key Insight: The (Taken/Allowed) ratio offsets higher time savings, capping rewards for top performers.

Examiner Observations Many students struggled with this question due to:

1. Misapplication of the Rowan Formula – Some incorrectly calculated bonus using Time Saved × Hourly

Rate directly, ignoring the (Time Taken / Time Allowed) adjustment.

2. Failure to Identify Equal Bonus Scenario – A significant number could not demonstrate how a highly efficient

worker (saving 6 hours) and a less efficient worker (saving 2 hours) could receive the same bonus (Rs. 90).

3. Lack of Conceptual Clarity – Students often missed the diminishing returns aspect of Rowan Plan, where

higher efficiency does not proportionally increase the bonus.

4. No Real-World Context – Answers lacked practical reasoning (e.g., why this demotivates top performers

compared to Halsey or Straight Piece Rate systems).

Question 10. PQR Limited has replaced 72 workers during the quarter ended 31st March 2022. The labour rates for the quarter are as follows: Flux method 16% Replacement method 8% Separation method 5% You are required to ascertain: (i) Average number of workers on roll (for the quarter), (ii) Number of workers left and discharged during the quarter, (iii) Number of workers recruited and joined during the quarter, (iv) Equivalent employee turnover rates for the year.

[8 Marks | 10 Minutes\](PYP May’22, Old & New SM)[Medium | ICAI Fav] © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 132

Answer 10. Working Note: (i) Average number of workers on roll (for the quarter): Employee Turnover rate using Replacement method = × 100 Or, = × 100 Average number of workers on roll = 900 (ii) Number of workers left and discharged: Employee turnover rate (Separation method)= × 100 = = Or, S = 45 Hence, number of workers left and discharged comes to 45 (iii) Number of workers recruited and joined: Employee turnover rate (Flux method) = Or, - Or, \* + =99

Using Flux method = × 4= 64%

Using Replacement method= × 4= 32%

Using Separation method= × 4= 20% (3+2+3)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Start with Replacement Method: a. 8% = 72 replacements → Average workforce = 72 ÷ 0.08 = 900.
2. Calculate Separations: a. 5% of 900 = 45 workers (left/discharged).
3. Solve for Accessions via Flux Method: a. 16% of 900 = 144 total flux (S + A). b. A = 144 – 45 = 99 new hires.
4. Annualize Rates: Multiply quarterly rates by 4: a. Flux: 16% × 4 = 64%, Replacement: 8% × 4 = 32%,

Separation: 5% × 4 = 20%.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to:

1. Formula Confusion: Many mix up the Flux, Replacement, and Separation methods, using wrong

numerators/denominators (e.g., using replacements instead of separations in the Separation method).

2. Inconsistent Base Calculation: Errors in deriving the average workforce (900) from the Replacement method

(8% = 72 workers) lead to incorrect answers for separations and accessions.

3. Flux Method Misapplication: A frequent mistake is failing to recognize that Flux = Separations (S) + Accessions

(A), leading to wrong calculations for new hires (A = 99). Some students subtract replacements (72) instead of separations (45).

4. Annualization Errors: For part (iv), students either: a. Forget to multiply quarterly rates by 4 for annual

equivalents. b. Incorrectly use 365 days instead of quarters.

5. Calculation Slips: Simple arithmetic errors (e.g., 16% of 900 = 144) are common, especially under exam

pressure.

Question 11. DISCUSS the two types of cost associated with labour turnover.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](Study material)[Easy | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 133

Answer 11. Cost of Employees (Labour) Turnover: Two types of costs which are associated with employee turnover are: (a) Preventive Costs: The cost incurred to prevent employee turnover or keep it as lowest as possible. Cost incurred for prevention of employee turnover includes the following: (i) Cost of medical benefit provided to the employees; (ii) Cost incurred on employees’ welfare like pension etc. (iii) Cost on other benefits with an objective to retain employees.

(b) Replacement Costs: These are the costs which arise due to employee turnover. If employees leave soon after they acquire the necessary training and experience of good work, additional costs will have to be incurred on new workers, i.e., cost of recruitment, training and induction, abnormal breakage and scrap and extra wages and overheads due to the inefficiency of new workers. It is obvious that a company will incur very high replacement costs if the rate of employee turnover is high. Similarly, only adequate preventive costs can keep Employee turnover at a low level. Each company must, therefore, work out the optimum level of Employee turnover keeping in view its personnel policies and the behaviour of replacement cost and preventive costs at various levels of Employee turnover rates.

(2.5+2.5) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Preventive Costs: Think "retention tools"—welfare, benefits, bonuses.
2. Replacement Costs: Think "consequences of leaving"—recruitment ads, trainer hours, production delays.
3. Structure: Use bullet points for examples (saves time vs. paragraphs).
4. Key Insight: Add 1 line on cost trade-off (e.g., "Investing in wellness programs reduces future hiring costs").

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this conceptual question due to:

1. Overgeneralization: Many fail to categorize costs clearly into preventive vs. replacement, mixing examples like

"training costs" (replacement) with "welfare benefits" (preventive).

2. Incomplete Examples: Lists are often too brief (e.g., only mentioning "recruitment costs" for replacement)

without critical details like abnormal scrap due to new hires' inefficiency.

3. Missing Link to Turnover Impact: Few connect how high turnover escalates replacement costs or

how preventive costs stabilize workforce retention.

4. Theoretical Gaps: Some ignore the trade-off between preventive and replacement costs, missing the "optimum

turnover level" concept.
