Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Standard Output First: Always start with 96 units/week (8 hrs × 2 units × 6 days).
2. Efficiency %: Compare actual output to 96 units.
3. Scheme Shortcuts: a. Emerson: 20% + (Efficiency% – 100) as bonus %. b. Merrick: 120% piece rate for 100-120% efficiency. c. Taylor: 125% if output ≥ standard (else 83%).
4. Avoid Time-Piece Mixups: a. Emerson uses time rates (hourly wages). b. Merrick/Taylor use piece rates (per-unit wages).
5. Cross-Check Units: Ensure final earnings match the scheme’s base (hours vs. units).

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 135

Examiner Observations Students frequently struggle with this question due to:

1. Incentive Scheme Confusion: a. Emerson’s System: Many misapply the bonus slab (e.g., 20% for >100%

efficiency + 1% for each 1% beyond), leading to incorrect rates (e.g., 57.5% instead of 37.5%). b. Merrick vs. Taylor: Students often interchange piece rates, forgetting Merrick uses graduated rates (120% for 100-120% efficiency) while Taylor uses binary rates (125% only for standard+).

2. Efficiency Calculation Errors: a. Some use daily output instead of weekly output for efficiency %, causing

cascading mistakes. b. Incorrectly treat 96 units as the daily standard (it’s weekly).

3. Wage Rate Missteps: a. Forgetting to convert daily wages to hourly rates (Rs.360 ÷ 8 = Rs.45/hour) before applying bonuses. b. Using time rates for piece-rate systems (Merrick/Taylor).
4. Unit Consistency: a. Calculating piece rates per hour instead of per unit (e.g., Rs.27/unit, not Rs.216/hour).

Question 13. R Ltd. is facing increasing employee turnover in the factory and before analysing the causes and taking remedial steps; the management wants to have an idea of the profit foregone as a result of employee turnover in the last year. Last year sales amounted to Rs. 99, 63,960 and P/V ratio was 20%. The total number of actual hours worked by the direct employee force was 5.34 lakhs. The actual direct employee hours included 36,000 hours attributable to training new recruits, out of which half of the hours were unproductive. As a result of the delays by the Personnel Department in filling vacancies due to employee turnover 1, 20,000 potentially productive hours (excluding unproductive training hours) were lost. The costs incurred consequent on employee turnover revealed, on analysis, the following: Settlement cost due to leaving Rs. 52,584 Recruitment costs Rs. 32,088 Selection costs Rs. 15,300 Training costs Rs. 36,588 Assuming that the potential production lost as a consequence of employee turnover could have been sold at prevailing prices, FIND the profit foregone last year on account of employee turnover.

[8 Marks | 12 Minutes\](MTP April ’22) (Old & New SM)[Difficult | ICAI Twister | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 13. Workings: (i) Computation of productive hours Actual hours worked 5,34,000 Less: Unproductive training hours 18,000 Actual productive hours 5,16,000

(ii) Productive hours lost: Loss of potential productive hours + Unproductive training hours = 1, 20,000 + 18,000 = 1, 38,000 hours (iii) Loss of contribution due to unproductive hours: Sales value / Actual productive hours ×Total unproductive hours = Rs. 99, 63,960 / 5, 16,000 hrs. × 1, 38,000 hours = Rs. 26, 64,780 Contribution lost for 1, 38,000 hours = Rs. 26, 64,780/100 × 20= Rs. 5, 32,956 © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 136

Computation of profit forgone on account of employee turnover

(Rs.) Contribution foregone (as calculated above) 5,32,956 Settlement cost due to leaving 52,584 Recruitment cost 32,088 Selection cost 15,300 Training costs 36,588 Profit foregone 6,69,516

(2+1+2+3) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Isolate Productive Hours: Deduct only unproductive training (18,000 hrs) from total.
2. Compute Lost Hours: Sum potential loss (1.20L) + unproductive training (18,000).
3. Sales Rate: Divide sales by productive hours (5.16L), not total hours.
4. Contribution: Multiply lost sales (1.38L × Rs. 193.10) by P/V ratio (20%).
5. Sum All Costs: Add direct turnover costs (Rs. 1.37L) to lost contribution.
6. Cross-Check: Ensure no double-counting (e.g., training costs are standalone).

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to:

1. Misclassification of Hours: a. Many fail to distinguish between productive vs. unproductive hours, especially ignoring that 50% of training hours (18,000) were unproductive. b. Some incorrectly include all 36,000 training hours as lost productive hours.
2. Contribution Calculation Errors: a. Using total sales (Rs. 99.64L) directly instead of sales per productive hour (Rs. 99.64L ÷ 5.16L hrs = Rs. 193.10/hr). b. Forgetting to apply P/V ratio (20%) to compute lost contribution (Rs. 26.65L × 20% = Rs. 5.33L).
3. Overlooking Turnover Costs: a. Omitting non-production costs (settlement, recruitment, selection, training) while summing up profit foregone. b. Double-counting training costs by including them in both lost hours and direct costs.
4. Formula Misapplication: a. Incorrectly using total actual hours (5.34L) instead of productive hours (5.16L) for sales/hour calculations.

Question 14. A total of 108 labour hours have been put in a particular job card for repair work engaging a semiskilled and skilled labour (Mr. Deep and Mr. Sam respectively). The hours devoted by both the workers individually on daily basis for this particular job are given below:

Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday 10.5 8.0 10.5 9.5 10.5 The skilled labour also worked on Saturday for 10 hours.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 137

Sunday is a weekly holiday and each worker has to work for 8 hours on all week days and 5 hours on Saturdays; the workers are however paid full wages for Saturday (8 hours for 5 hours worked). Semi-skilled and skilled worker is paid ordinary wage @ Rs. 400 and Rs. 600 respectively per day of 8 hours labour. Further, the workers are also paid dearness allowance @ 20%. Extra hours worked over and above 8 hours are also paid at ordinary wage rate however, overtime premium of 100% of ordinary wage rate is paid if a worker works for more than 9 hours in a day AND 48 hours in a week. You are required to COMPUTE the wages payable to Mr. Deep (Semi-skilled) and Mr. Sam (Skilled).

[8 Marks | 15 Minutes\](RTP May ’22)[Difficult | ICAI Twister | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 14. Calculation of total normal hours to be paid for Mr. Deep (Semi-skilled):

Day Normal hours Extra hours Overtime Equivalent normal hours Total normal

hours for overtime worked hours A B C D = C×2 E = A+B+D Monday 8 1 1½ 3 12 Tuesday 8 -- -- -- 8 Wednesday 8 1 1½ 3 12 Thursday 8 1 ½ 1 10 Friday 8 1 1½ 3 12 Saturday -- -- -- -- Total 40 4 5 10 54

Calculation of total normal hours to be paid for Mr. Sam (Skilled):

Day Normal hours Extra hours Overtime Equivalent normal hours Total normal

hours for overtime worked hours A B C D = C×2 E = A+B+D Monday 8 1 1½ 3 12 Tuesday 8 -- -- -- 8 Wednesday 8 1 1½ 3 12 Thursday 8 1 ½ 1 10 Friday 8 1 1½ 3 12 Saturday 5 3\*+1 1\*\* 2 11 Total 45 8 6 12 65 Mr. Sam will be paid for equivalent 8 normal working hours at ordinary wage rate, though 5 hours of working is required on Saturday. Further, extra 9th hour worked will also be paid at ordinary wage rate. \*\* Overtime of 1 hour worked over and above 9 hours will be paid at overtime rate. Wages payable:

Mr. Deep Mr. Sam Basic Wages per hour (Rs. 400/8, Rs. 600/8) (Rs.) 50 75 Dearness allowance per hour (@ 20%) (Rs.) 10 15 Hourly rate (Rs.) 60 90 Total equivalent normal hours 54 65

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 138

Total Wages payable (Rs.) 3,240 5,850

(3+3+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Tabulate Daily Hours: a. Weekdays: Mark normal (8), extra (up to 9), overtime (>9). b. Saturday: 5 hours = 8 paid; additional hours = extra/overtime.
2. Weekly Total: a. Check if >48 hours for overtime premium.
3. Equivalent Hours: a. Overtime hours × 2 (100% premium).
4. Hourly Rates: a. Basic (Daily wage ÷ 8) + DA (20%).
5. Final Sum: a. Total equivalent hours × (Basic + DA).

Examiner Observations Students frequently make these mistakes in wage calculation problems:

1. Misclassification of Hours: a. Many fail to distinguish between normal hours (8/day), extra hours (up to 9/day), and overtime hours (>9/day or >48/week). b.Some treat Saturday's 5-hour requirement as overtime, ignoring it's paid as 8 normal hours.
2. Overtime Premium Errors: a. Incorrectly apply 100% premium to all extra hours instead of only hours beyond 9/day or 48/week. b.Miss that Saturday's 10th hour (Mr. Sam) qualifies for overtime premium (1 hour @ double rate).
3. Weekly Hour Calculation: a. Forget to check total weekly hours (48 threshold) for overtime eligibility. b.Overlook that Saturday's base 5 hours count as 8 paid hours in weekly totals.
4. Wage Rate Application: a. Use daily rates instead of hourly rates (Rs. 400/8 = Rs. 50/hr for semi-skilled). b. Omit dearness allowance (20%) or add it to basic wages incorrectly.
5. Skilled vs. Semi-Skilled Differences: a. Apply the same rules to both workers, ignoring Saturday's 10-hour work for skilled labor (Mr. Sam).

Question 15. A skilled worker is paid a guaranteed wage rate of Rs. 120 per hour. The standard time allowed for a job is 6 hour. He took 5 hours to complete the job. He is paid wages under Rowan Incentive Plan. (i) Calculate his effective hourly rate of earnings under Rowan Incentive Plan. (ii) If the worker is placed under Halsey Incentive Scheme (50%) and he wants to maintain the same effective hourly rate of earnings, calculate the time in which he should complete the job.

[6 Marks | 8 Minutes\](RTP Nov ’23)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 15. (i) Effective hourly rate of earnings under Rowan Incentive Plan Earnings under Rowan Incentive plan = (Actual time taken X wage rate) + × Time taken × Wage rate

= (5 hours X Rs. 120) + ( × 5 ℎ𝑜𝑢𝑟 × . 120) = Rs. 600 +Rs. 100 = Rs. 700 (ii) Let time taken = X ∴ Effective hourly rate = © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 139

Or, Effective hourly rate under Halsey Incentive plan

= Or, Rs.140 =

Or, 140X = 120X + 360 – 60X, Or, 80X = 360 Or, X = = 4.5 hours Therefore, to earn effective hourly rate of Rs.140 under Halsey Incentive Scheme worker has to complete the work in 4.5 hours.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Part (i) – Rowan Plan: a.Time Saved = 6 – 5 = 1 hour. b. Earnings = (5 × 120) + (1/6 × 5 × 120) = Rs. 700. c. Effective Rate = 700 ÷ 5 = Rs. 140.
2. Part (ii) – Halsey Plan: a. Let X = time taken. b. Equation: 140 = [120X + 60 × (6 – X)] ÷ X. c. Simplify: 140X = 120X + 360 – 60X → X = 4.5 hours.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to:

1. Rowan vs. Halsey Confusion: a. Many interchange formulas, applying Halsey’s 50% bonus to Rowan or vice versa. b. Some forget Rowan’s unique (Time Saved/Time Allowed) × Time Taken × Rate structure.
2. Effective Rate Misunderstanding: a. In part (i), students stop at total earnings (Rs. 700) but forget to divide by actual hours (5) to get Rs. 140/hour. b. In part (ii), they fail to set up the equation to maintain Rs. 140/hour under Halsey.
3. Algebraic Errors: a. While solving for X (time taken) in part (ii), students make arithmetic mistakes (e.g., mishandling 50% of Rs. 120 × (6 – X)).
4. Time Saved Miscalculation: a. Incorrectly compute time saved as 2 hours (instead of 1 hour) under Rowan, leading to wrong earnings.
5. Guaranteed Rate Oversight: a. Ignore that Rs. 120/hour is guaranteed, even if the incentive calculation yields lower earnings.

Question 16. How would you account for idle capacity cost in Cost Accounting?

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](RTP Nov ’23)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 16. Idle capacity costs are treated in the following ways in Cost Accounts: (i) If the idle capacity cost is due to unavoidable reasons: A supplementary overhead rate may be used to recover the idle capacity cost. In this case, the costs are charged to the production capacity utilised. (ii) If the idle capacity cost is due to avoidable reasons: Such as faulty planning, etc. the cost should be charged to Costing Profit and Loss Account. (iii) If the idle capacity cost is due to trade depression, etc.: Being abnormal in nature the cost should also be charged to the Costing Profit and Loss Account.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 140

(iv) If the idle capacity cost is due to seasonal factors, then the cost should be charged to cost of production by inflating overhead rate.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Categorize First: a. Is idle capacity avoidable /unavoidable /abnormal /seasonal?
2. Apply Rules: a. Unavoidable: Supplementary rate. b. Avoidable/Abnormal: P&L. c. Seasonal: Higher overhead absorption.
3. Add Examples: a. Unavoidable: "Machine repairs." b. Avoidable: "Overstaffing."
4. Use Headings: a. Clearly label each type for readability.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this theoretical question due to:

1. Misclassification of Idle Capacity Causes: a. Many fail to distinguish between avoidable (e.g., faulty planning) vs. unavoidable (e.g., seasonal) idle capacity, leading to incorrect accounting treatment. b. Some treat seasonal idle capacity as "abnormal" and wrongly charge it to Costing P&L.
2. Overhead Recovery Errors: a. For unavoidable idle capacity, students either: i. Forget to use a supplementary overhead rate or ii. Incorrectly inflate the primary overhead rate instead of creating a separate rate.
3. Abnormal vs. Normal Confusion: a. Trade depression (abnormal) is often confused with seasonal factors (normal), resulting in wrong allocation to production costs.
4. Practical Application Gaps: a. Answers lack real-world examples (e.g., "machine breakdown" for unavoidable, "poor demand forecasting" for avoidable).
5. Presentation Issues: a. Bullet points or fragmented explanations without logical flow lose marks despite correct content.

Question17. Explain the treatment of over and under absorption of overheads in cost accounts.

[6 Marks | 7 Minutes\](RTP Nov ’23)[Medium | ICAI Fav]

Answer17. Treatment of over and under absorption of overheads are: (i) Writing off to costing P&L A/c: Small difference between the actual and absorbed amount should simply be transferred to costing P&L A/c, if difference is large then investigate the causes and after that abnormal loss/ gain shall be transferred to costing P&L A/c. (ii) Use of supplementary Rate: Under this method the balance of under and over absorbed overheads may be charged to cost of W.I.P., finished stock and cost of sales proportionately with the help of supplementary rate of overhead. (iii) Carry Forward to Subsequent Year: Difference should be carried forward in the expectation that next year the position will be automatically corrected. © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 141

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Check Variance Size: a. <5% of total overheads? → P&L. b. >5%? Investigate → Use supplementary rate if normal, else P&L.
2. Supplementary Rate Steps: a. Compute rate = (Under/Over-absorption) ÷ (Total output). b. Apply to WIP, finished goods, COGS.
3. Carry Forward Only If: a. Next year’s operations will offset the variance (e.g., cyclical demand). b. Time-Saver: Use a flowchart: Small → P&L → Large → Normal? (Supplementary) : Abnormal? (P&L).

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to:

1. Misapplication of Methods: a. Many wrongly apply supplementary rates for minor variances (which should go to P&L) or carry forward insignificant differences. b. Some treat all under/over-absorption as abnormal without investigation.
2. Threshold Confusion: a. Fail to distinguish between small vs. large variances (e.g., "small" differences go to P\&L; "large" ones need analysis).
3. Proportional Allocation Errors: a. When using supplementary rates, students often skip WIP/finished goods and allocate the entire variance to COGS.
4. Carry-Forward Misuse: a. Suggest carrying forward variances indiscriminately, even for seasonal businesses where correction is unlikely.
5. Lack of Justification: a. Answers lack decision logic (e.g., why choose P&L vs. supplementary rate).

Question 18. Distinguish between cost allocation and cost absorption.

[2 Marks | 2 Minutes\](RTP Nov ’23)[Easy | ICAI Fav]

Answer 18. Distinguish between Cost allocation and Cost absorption: Cost allocation is the allotment of whole item of cost to a cost centre or a cost unit. In other words, it is the process of identifying, assigning or allowing cost to a cost centre or a cost unit. Cost absorption is the process of absorbing all indirect costs or overhead costs allocated or apportioned over particular cost center or production department by the units produced.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this conceptual distinction due to:

1. Definition Confusion: a. Many interchange the terms, stating cost absorption is about assigning costs to cost centers (which is allocation). b. Some describe absorption as "assigning direct costs," confusing it with cost assignment.
2. Scope Misunderstanding: a. Fail to highlight that allocation is for whole costs (e.g., rent to departments), while absorption is for

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 142

overheads per unit. b. Overlook that allocation precedes absorption in the cost flow.

3. Practical Examples Missing: a. Answers lack real-world illustrations (e.g., allocating electricity to departments vs. absorbing factory overheads into product costs).
4. Process vs. Outcome: a. Few clarify that allocation is a process of assigning, while absorption is the final recovery of overheads by output units.
5. Over-Simplification: a. Some reduce the answer to "allocation is for centers, absorption is for units," missing the hierarchical relationship between the two.

Question 19. M/s Zeba Private Limited allotted a standard time of 40 hours for a job and the rate per hour is Rs. 75\. The actual time taken by a worker is 30 hours. You are required to calculate the total earnings under the following plans: (i) Halsey Premium Plan (Rate 50%) (ii) Rowan Plan (iii) Time Wage System (iv) Piece Rate System (v) Emerson Plan

[8 Marks | 10 Minutes\](PYP May ‘19)[Medium | ICAI Fav]

Answer 19. (i) Halsey Premium plan: = (Time taken × Rate per hour) + ( )

= (30 hours × Rs. 75) + ( )

(ii) Rowan Premium plan: = (Time taken × Rate per hour) + ( ) = (30 hours × Rs. 75) + (40 × 30 × Rs. 75) = Rs. 2,250 + Rs. 375 = Rs. 2,625 = Rs. 2,250 + Rs. 562.5 = Rs. 2,812.5 or Rs. 2,813

(iii) Time wage system: = Time taken × Rate per hour = 30 × Rs. 75 = Rs. 2,250

(iv) Piece Rate System: = Std. Time × Rate per hour = 40 × Rs. 75 = Rs. 3,000

(v) Emerson plan: Efficiency level = 40/30 = 133.33% Time taken × (120% + 33.33%) of Rate = 30 hours × 153.33% of Rs. 75 = Rs. 3,450

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 143

Important Note: In this numerical problem of ‘Employee Cost’ students were asked to calculate earnings under various plans. Candidate failed to calculate earnings in job/piece rate system and Emerson’s plan. Performance of the examinees was average. (1+2+1+2+2)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Prioritize Plans: Solve Halsey, Rowan, Time Wage first (simpler formulas).
2. Emerson Efficiency: a. Efficiency = (40/30) × 100 = 133.33%. b. Bonus = 20% (base) + 33.33% = 53.33%. c. Rate = 153.33% of Rs. 75.
3. Piece Rate: Use standard time (40 hrs), not actual.
4. Cross-Check: a. Rowan earnings > Halsey (for high efficiency). b. Emerson > Piece Rate (for efficiency > 100%).

Examiner Observations Students frequently make these errors in incentive plan calculations:

1. Formula Confusion: a. Halsey vs. Rowan: Many interchange formulas, applying Halsey's 50% fixed bonus to Rowan's proportional bonus (Time Saved/Time Allowed). b. Emerson Missteps: Students often miscalculate efficiency (e.g., 133.33% = 40/30) and skip the 20% base bonus + 1% per 1% above standard.
2. Piece Rate System: a. Incorrectly use actual time (30 hrs) instead of standard time (40 hrs) to calculate earnings.
3. Time Wage System: a. Some wrongly add bonuses (Halsey/Rowan) to basic time wages.
4. Calculation Errors: a. Rowan Plan: Errors in computing (Time Saved/Time Allowed) × Time Taken × Rate (e.g., 10/40 × 30 × 75 = Rs. 562.5). b. Emerson Plan: Forget to add the 20% base bonus to incremental 33.33% (total 153.33% of Rs. 75).
5. Unit Mix-ups: a. Use hours for piece rate (should be output-based) or rates inconsistently.

Question 20. Discuss any four objectives of 'Time keeping' in relation to attendance and payroll procedures.

[3 Marks | 3 Minutes\](PYP Nov 20)[Easy | ICAI Fav]

Answer 20. The objectives of time-keeping in relation to attendance and payroll procedures are as follows: (i) For the preparation of payrolls. (ii) For calculating overtime. (iii) For ascertaining and controlling employee cost. (iv) For ascertaining idle time. (v) For disciplinary purposes. (vi) For overhead distribution

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Keyword Focus: Use terms like "compliance," "cost allocation," and "audit trails" to align with ICAI’s

preference for technical precision.

2. Flowchart Mindset: Visualize the payroll-to-cost-control chain to avoid missing linkages.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 144

Examiner Observations

1. Vague Linkage to Payroll: Students list objectives generically (e.g., "for payroll preparation") but fail to

explain how timekeeping ensures accuracy in wage calculation, tax withholdings, or compliance with labor laws.

2. Misinterpretation of Idle Time: Many define idle time as "unproductive hours" but omit its impact on cost

control (e.g., machine downtime vs. employee idleness).

3. Overlooking Disciplinary Context: Few connect timekeeping to policy enforcement (e.g., tardiness patterns

triggering corrective action)

4. Ignoring Overhead Distribution: Rarely do students tie timekeeping to allocating indirect costs (e.g., utilities

per department based on logged hours)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Ignore Irrelevant Data: Skip the 25% demand/20% earnings assurance—focus on time saved and formulas.
2. Tabulate Key Figures: a. Time Allowed = 2 hrs/unit × 1,250 units = 2,500 hrs. b. Actual Time = 25 days × 8 hrs × 10 workers = 2,000 hrs.
3. Use Shortcuts: a. Rowan Bonus = (Actual Time/Time Allowed) × Time Saved × Rate. b. Halsey Bonus = 0.5 × Time Saved × Rate.
4. Verify Units: Ensure final answers are in Rs./hour (for earnings) and Rs./piece (for savings).

Examiner Observations

1. Incorrect Bonus Calculation: a. Halsey: Some students calculate 50% bonus on total wages instead of time saved. b. Rowan: Many use Time Saved/Time Allowed (incorrect) instead of Time Taken/Time Allowed (correct), leading to inflated bonuses.

2. Savings Misinterpretation: a. Comparing savings per piece against original time wages (Rs.80) is often missed. Students assume savings are against current earnings, not the baseline.
3. Hourly Rate Errors: a. Forgetting to divide total wages by total hours (2,000) for effective earnings/hour, resulting in Rs.90,000/1,250 = Rs.72 (wrong unit).
4. Overcomplicating Productivity Links: a. Unnecessary focus on the 25% demand increase or 20% earnings hike, which are contextual but irrelevant to calculations.

(3+3) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Quick Time Calculation: a. Standard Time = 1,250 units × 2 hours = 2,500 hours. b. Actual Time = 25 days × 8 hours × 10 workers = 2,000 hours.
2. Bonus Shortcuts: a. Halsey: 50% × (Time Saved × Rate). b. Rowan: (Time Saved / Standard Time) × Actual Wages.
3. Key Check: a. Rowan’s bonus is higher (Rs. 800 vs. Halsey’s Rs. 500), but Halsey gives more savings per unit

(Rs. 0.40 vs. Rs. 0.16).

Examiner Observations Students often make the following mistakes while solving this question:

1. Misunderstanding Time Saved Calculation: Some students incorrectly calculate "time saved" as (Actual Time –

Standard Time) instead of (Standard Time – Actual Time), leading to negative values or wrong bonuses.

2. Ignoring Guaranteed Wages: The question specifies a guaranteed hourly wage (Rs. 2/hour), but students

sometimes skip verifying if incentive earnings exceed guaranteed wages (though not required here since time saved exists).

3. Rowan Bonus Formula Errors: The Rowan bonus is (Time Saved / Standard Time) × Actual Time × Rate.

Students often misplace the denominator (Standard Time vs. Actual Time) or incorrectly multiply by Time Saved directly.

4. Effective Rate Confusion: Some students divide total wages by standard hours (2,500) instead of actual hours

(2,000), leading to incorrect hourly earnings.

5. Savings Calculation Oversight: Direct labour cost savings must compare original cost (Rs. 4/unit) with incentive

cost. Students sometimes compare Halsey vs. Rowan instead of both against the original.

6. Assurance Misinterpretation: Shivi’s assurance is a 20% increase in earnings, but students fail to check if either

scheme meets this. Here, both do (Halsey: 12.5%, Rowan: 20%), but Rowan aligns better with the assurance.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 152

Question 26. PR Ltd. totally understands the importance of employee motivation and retention, thus, it has implemented a structured wage policy. The basic wage rate is set at Rs. 100 per hour along with Dearness Allowance (DA) of 50%, which is competitive within the industry. To encourage productivity and compensate for the demands of overtime, the company offers enhanced rates for hours worked beyond the standard schedule. The normal working days are from Monday to Saturday, and the worker would be paid overtime premium of- 75% of basic wage rate (inclusive of DA) for working before and after normal working hours, and 125% of basic wage rate (inclusive of DA) for working on Sundays. Throughout the previous year, the following hours were worked- Normal time 4,00,000 hours Overtime before and after normal working hours 80,000 hours Overtime on Sundays 20,000 hours Total 5,00,000 hours However, the hours recorded for job ‘PR123’ are as follows: Normal time 4,000 hours Overtime before and after normal working hours 400 hours Overtime on Sundays 100 hours Total 4,500 hours You are required to CALCULATE the employee cost chargeable to job ‘PR123’ and the treatment of overtime premium: (i) Where overtime is worked regularly throughout the year as a policy due to the workers’ shortage. (ii) Where overtime is worked irregularly to meet the requirements of production.

[8 Marks | 12 Minutes\](MTP May 2025)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 26. Workings Basic wage rate = Rs. (100 + Rs. 50 for DA) per hour = Rs. 150 per hour Overtime wage rate before and after working hours = Rs. 150 + 75% of Rs. 150 = Rs. 262.50 per hour Overtime wage rate for Sundays = Rs. 150 + 125% of Rs. 150 = Rs. 337.50 per hour

Computation of average inflated wage rate (including overtime premium) Particulars (Rs.) Annual wages for the previous year for normal time (4, 00,000 hrs. × Rs. 150) 6,00,00,000 Wages for overtime before and after working hours (80,000 hrs. × Rs. 262.50) 2,10,00,000 Wages for overtime on Sundays (20,000 hrs. × Rs. 337.50) 67,50,000 Total wages for 5, 00,000 hrs. 8,77,50,000 Average inflated wage rate = = Rs. 175.50

(i) Where overtime is worked regularly as a policy due to workers’ shortage: The overtime premium is treated as a part of employee cost and job is charged at an inflated wage rate. Hence, employee cost chargeable to job ‘PR123’ = Total hours × Inflated wage rate = 4,500 hrs. × Rs. 175.50 = Rs. 7, 89,750

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 153

(ii) Where overtime is worked irregularly to meet the requirements of production: Basic wage rate is charged to the job and overtime premium is charged to factory overheads as under: Employee cost chargeable to Job ‘PR123’ = 4,500 hours @ Rs. 150 per hour = Rs. 6, 75,000 Factory overhead = {400 hrs. × Rs. (75% of Rs. 150)} + {100 hrs. × Rs. (125% of Rs. 150)} = {Rs.45, 000 + Rs.18, 750} = Rs.63, 750

(3+2+3) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Quick Rate Calculation: a. Basic + DA = Rs. 150/hour. b. Overtime (Weekdays) = 150 + (75% × 150) = Rs. 262.50/hour. c. Overtime (Sundays) = 150 + (125% × 150) = Rs. 337.50/hour.
2. Part (i) Shortcut: a. Total Annual Wages / Total Hours = Rs. 175.50/hour. b. Job Cost = 4,500 × 175.50 = Rs. 7, 89,750.
3. Part (ii) Logic: a. Job Cost = 4,500 × 150 = Rs. 6, 75,000. b. Overhead = (400 × 112.50) + (100 × 187.50) = Rs. 63,750.

Examiner Observations Students frequently make the following mistakes in this question:

1. Incorrect Overtime Rate Calculation: a. Some students fail to add Dearness Allowance (DA) to the basic wage rate before calculating overtime premiums (e.g., using Rs. 100 instead of Rs. 150). b. Misapplying percentages: 75% and 125% premiums are applied to the total wage (Rs. 150), not just the basic Rs. 100.
2. Inflated Wage Rate Misuse: a. In part (i), students often skip calculating the average inflated rate and directly charge overtime premiums to the job without justification. b. In part (ii), they incorrectly include overtime premium in job cost instead of treating it as overhead.
3. Treatment of Overtime Premium: a. Regular vs. Irregular Overtime Confusion: i. For regular overtime, the inflated rate must be used. ii. For irregular overtime, only the basic wage rate is charged to the job, and the premium is overhead. b. Students often reverse these treatments or apply both premiums to overhead.
4. Factory Overhead Calculation Errors: a. In part (ii), some students forget to segregate premiums (75% for weekdays, 125% for Sundays) or miscalculate the amounts.
5. Time Allocation Mismanagement: a. Spending too much time on recalculating rates instead of using the given data efficiently.

2. Allocation Logic: a. Pi’s Ordinary Wages (Rs. 19,410): i. A (30%) = Rs. 5,823 ii. S (30%) = Rs. 5,823 iii. D (40%) = Rs. 7,764 b. Overtime (Rs. 1,371): 100% to Job S. c. Qu’s Wages (Rs. 24,263): i. A (30%) = Rs. 7,279 ii. S (50%) = Rs. 12,131 iii. D (20%) = Rs. 4,853

Examiner Observations This question tests wage computation, overtime treatment, and cost allocation across jobs. Common mistakes include:

1. Overtime Calculation Errors: a. Students often miss the "twice the sum of basic + DA" rule, using only basic wages or incorrect multipliers. b. Misallocating overtime: Overtime is only for Job S, but some students distribute it across all jobs.
2. Dearness Allowance (DA) Oversight: a. DA is 50% of basic wages, but students sometimes exclude it from overtime or gross wages.
3. Provident Fund (PF) & ESI Miscalculations: a. PF and ESI contributions are based on basic wages only, but students wrongly apply them to gross wages (including DA/overtime). b. Employer’s contributions are often forgotten, though they are part of employee cost.
4. Incorrect Allocation Ratios: a. Pi’s ordinary wages are split 30:30:40 (A:S:D), but Qu’s are 30:50:20. Students sometimes mix these ratios. b. Overtime is 100% allocated to Job S, but some students prorate it.
5. Net vs. Gross Wages Confusion: a. Net wages (after deductions) are irrelevant for cost allocation; gross wages + employer contributions matter.

(2+2+2+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Quick Time Calculations: a. Cee: 21 units × 8 = 168 hours allowed; 168 – 78 = 90 hours saved. b. Dee: 30 units × 8 = 240 hours allowed; 240 – 114 = 126 hours saved.
2. Halsey Shortcut: a. Bonus = 50% × Time Saved × Rs. 5. b. Cee: 50% × 90 × 5 = Rs. 225.
3. Rowan Formula: a. Bonus = (Time Saved / Time Allowed) × Time Taken × Rs. 5. b. Cee: (90/168) × 78 × 5 = Rs. 208.93.
4. Loss Focus: a. Only Rs. 5 excess is considered for loss (not full Rs. 65).

Examiner Observations This question tests wage calculation under Halsey and Rowan schemes, loss computation due to rate errors, and comparative savings analysis. Common mistakes include:

1. Incorrect Bonus Calculation: a. Halsey Scheme: Students often forget the 50% multiplier or apply it to the wrong base (e.g., total wages instead of time saved). b. Rowan Scheme: Misplacing the formula (Time Saved / Time Allowed) × Time Taken × Rate. Some students reverse the numerator/denominator or skip "Time Taken."
2. Excess Rate Misapplication: a. The Rs. 5 excess (Rs. 65 – Rs. 60) applies only to the incorrect rate, but students sometimes apply it to the entire wage.
3. Time Saved Errors: a. Time Saved = Time Allowed – Time Taken, but students may use Time Taken – Time Allowed, leading to negative values.
4. Loss Computation Oversights: a. For Rowan loss (Part ii), students often skip recalculating bonus under the new scheme and reuse Halsey values.
5. Savings Misinterpretation (Part iii): a. The question asks for savings if Rowan were followed, but students compare Halsey vs. Rowan under incorrect rates instead of correct vs. incorrect rates.

Question 29. The board of the J Ltd. has been appraised by the General Manager (HR) that the employee attrition rate in the company has increased. The following facts has been presented by the GM (HR): (1) Training period of the new recruits is 50,000 hours. During this period their productivity is 60% of the experienced workers. Time required by an experienced worker is 10 hours per unit. (2) 20% of the output during training period was defective. Cost of rectification of a defective unit was Rs.25. (3) Potential productive hours lost due to delay in recruitment were 1, 00,000 hours. (4) Selling price per unit is Rs. 180 and P/V ratio is 20%. (5) Settlement cost of the workers leaving the organization was Rs. 1, 83,480. (6) Recruitment cost was Rs.1, 56,340 (7) Training cost was Rs. 1, 13,180 You being an associate finance to GM (HR), has been asked the following questions:

[5×2=10 Marks | 8 Minutes\](Study material) [Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

(i) How much quantity of output is lost due to labour turnover? (a) 10,000 units (b) 8,000 units (c) 12,000 units (d) 12,600 units

Answer.- (c) Output by experienced workers in 50,000 hours = =5,000 units  Output by new recruits = 60% of 5,000 = 3,000 units Loss of output = 5,000 – 3,000 = 2,000 units Total loss of output = Due to delay recruitment + Due to inexperience = 10,000 + 2,000 = 12,000 units

(ii) How much loss in the form of contribution, the company incurred due to labour turnover? (a) Rs. 4, 32,000 (b) Rs. 4, 20,000 (c) Rs. 4, 36,000 (d) Rs. 4, 28,000

Answer. - (a) Contribution per unit = 20% of Rs.180 = Rs.36 Total contribution lost = Rs.36 × 12,000 units = Rs.4, 32,000

(iii) What is the cost repairing of defective units? (a) Rs. 75,000 (b) Rs. 15,000 (c) Rs. 50,000 (d) Rs. 25,000

Answer. - (b) Cost of repairing defective units = 3,000 units × 0.2 × Rs. 25 = Rs. 15,000

(iv) Calculate the profit lost by the company due to increased labour turnover. © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 159

(a) Rs.7, 50,000 (b) Rs. 15, 00,000 (c) Rs. 5, 00,000 (d) Rs. 9, 00,000

Answer. - (d) Calculation of loss of profit due to labour turnover

(Rs.) Loss of Contribution 4,32,000 Cost of repairing defective units 15,000 Recruitment cost 1,56,340 Training cost 1,13,180 Settlement cost of workers leaving 1,83,480 Profit forgone in 2022-23 9,00,000

(v) How much quantity of output is lost due to inexperience of the new worker? (a) 1,000 units (b) 2,600 units (c) 2,000 units (d) 12,600 units

Answer. - (c) Output by experienced workers in 50,000 hours = =5,000 units  Output by new recruits = 60% of 5,000 = 3,000 units

Loss of output = 5,000 – 3,000 = 2,000 units

Examiner Observations This question tests attrition cost analysis with a focus on lost output due to inexperienced workers. Common mistakes include:

1. Misinterpreting Productivity Loss: a. Students often ignore the 60% productivity of new recruits and assume they produce at 100% efficiency, leading to incorrect lost output (e.g., 5,000 vs. 3,000 units).
2. Defective Units Distraction: a. The 20% defective output is a red herring for this sub-question. It’s irrelevant to calculating lost output due to inexperience but is often wrongly factored in.
3. Hours vs. Units Confusion: a. Some students divide training hours (50,000) by 10 hours/unit but forget to apply the 60% productivity, resulting in 5,000 units instead of 3,000.
4. Overcomplicating the Problem: a. The question asks only for lost output due to inexperience, but students sometimes include potential lost hours (1, 00,000) or rectification costs, which are not required here.
5. Formula Misapplication: a. Incorrectly using P/V ratio or selling price (given for later parts) in this calculation, despite no relevance to lost units.

(2+2+1+1+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Prioritize Amended Systems: a. Start with piece-rate (simplest), then Rowan/Halsey (time-saving focus).
2. Rowan Shortcut: a. Time Allowed = (2.5/15 × 270) × 1.5 = 67.5 hrs. b. Bonus = (27.5/67.5) × 40 × Rs. 160 = Rs. 2,607.41.
3. Halsey Shortcut: a. Bonus = 0.5 × 27.5 × Rs. 160 = Rs. 2,200.

Examiner Observations This question tests multiple wage payment systems (time-rate, piece-work, Rowan, Halsey) and their impact on earnings, productivity, and unit labor cost. Common mistakes include:

1. Misapplication of Premium Rates: a. Rowan System: Students often reverse the Time Saved/Time Allowed ratio or use Time Taken instead of Time Allowed in the denominator. b. Halsey System: Forgetting the 50% multiplier on time saved or miscalculating time saved.
2. Piece-Rate Calculation Errors: a. Basic Time Allowed: Miscomputing hours for 270 articles (should be 2.5 hrs/15 × 270 = 45 hrs). b. 20% Bonus: Applying it to total wages instead of basic piece-rate earnings (Rs. 7,200 × 20%).
3. Time-Rate Oversights:

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 162

a. Including late-shift premiums (Rs. 225/hr) in amended systems (they only apply to the existing time-rate system).

4. Unit Cost Miscalculations: a. Dividing weekly earnings by wrong output (e.g., using 240 articles instead of 270 for amended systems).
5. Rowan vs. Halsey Confusion: a. Rowan's bonus is variable (depends on efficiency), while Halsey's is fixed at 50%. Students often mix formulas.

Question 31. Discuss the remedial steps to be taken to minimize the labour turnover.

[6 Marks | 7 Minutes\](MTP Oct‘19)[Medium | ICAI Fav]

Answer 31. The following steps are useful for minimizing labour turnover: (a) Exit interview: An interview to be arranged with each outgoing employee to ascertain the reasons of his leaving the organization. (b) Job analysis and evaluation: to ascertain the requirement of each job. (c) Organization should make use of a scientific system of recruitment, placement and promotion for employees. (d) Organization should create healthy atmosphere, providing education, medical and housing facilities for workers. (e) Committee for settling workers grievances.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Cause → Solution Mapping: For each step, ask: Which turnover cause does this fix? (e.g., job evaluation →

wage inequity).

2. Bullet Format: Use headings + 1-line explanations (ICAI prefers clarity over essays).
3. Skip Definitions: No need to define "labour turnover" — jump straight to remedies.

Examiner Observations Students often make these mistakes:

1. Generic Answers: Merely listing points without explaining how each step reduces turnover (e.g., "exit interview

helps" but not how it identifies systemic issues).

2. Missing Linkage: Failing to connect remedial steps to specific causes of turnover (e.g., job evaluation addresses

wage dissatisfaction).

3. Overlooking Non-Monetary Factors: Ignoring psychological/social aspects (e.g., "healthy atmosphere" but not

detailing work-life balance initiatives).

4. Repetition: Writing overlapping points (e.g., "scientific recruitment" and "placement" as separate ideas).

Question 32. Explain the treatment of Overtime Premium in following situations: (i) SV & Co. wants to grab some special orders, and overtime is required to meet the same. (ii) Dept. X has to work overtime to make up a shortfall in production due to some fault of management in dept. Y. (iii) S Ltd. has to work overtime regularly throughout the year as a policy due to the workers' shortage. (iv) Due to flood in Odisha, RS Ltd. has to work overtime to complete the job. (v) A customer requested the company MN Ltd. to expedite the job because of his urgency of work. © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 163

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](PYP May’22)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 32. Treatment of Overtime premium in different situations

Situation Treatment (i) SV & Co. wants to grab some special orders, and If overtime is required to cope with general production overtime is required to meet the same. programmes or for meeting urgent orders, the

overtime premium should be treated as overhead cost of the particular department or cost centre which works overtime. (ii) Dept. X has to work overtime to make up a shortfall If overtime is worked in a department due to the fault in production due to some fault of management in of another department, the overtime premium should dept. Y. be charged to the latter department (Y). (iii) S Ltd. has to work overtime regularly throughout The overtime premium is treated as a part of employee the year as a policy due to the workers’ shortage. cost and job is charged at an effective average wage

rate. (iv) Due to flood in Odisha, RS Ltd. has to work Overtime worked on account of abnormal conditions overtime to complete the job. such as flood, earthquake etc., should not be charged

to cost, but to Costing Profit and Loss Account. (v) A customer requested the company MN Ltd. to Where overtime is worked at the request of the expedite the job because of his urgency of work. customer, overtime premium is also charged to the

job/ customer directly.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Cause-Based Classification: a. Internal Fault? → Charge to responsible dept. (ii). b. Abnormal? → P&L (iv). c. Customer-Driven? → Direct charge (v).
2. Tabular Format: Use two columns ("Situation" + "Treatment") for clarity and speed.

Examiner Observations Students often make these mistakes:

1. Overgeneralization: Treating all overtime premiums uniformly without analyzing the specific reason behind

overtime (e.g., charging all premiums to overheads).

2. Misallocation of Fault: Failing to identify which department bears the cost when overtime is due to another

department’s fault (e.g., charging Dept. X instead of Y in situation ii).

3. Ignoring Abnormal Conditions: Not segregating abnormal overtime (floods, strikes) from routine, leading to

incorrect charging to production costs.

4. Policy vs. Exception Confusion: Missing the distinction between regular policy-driven overtime (worker

shortage) and one-off cases (customer urgency).

5. Customer-Driven Overtime: Forgetting to directly charge premiums to the customer when overtime

is requested by them.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 164

Question 33. A skilled worker, in PK Ltd., is paid a guaranteed wage rate of Rs.15.00 per hour in a 48- hour week. The standard time to produce a unit is 18 minutes. During a week, a skilled worker -Mr. ‘A’ has produced 200 units of the product. The Company has taken a drive for cost reduction and wants to reduce its labour cost. You are required to: (i) Calculate wages of Mr. ‘A’ under each of the following methods: (A) Time rate, (B) Piece -rete with a guaranteed weekly wage, (C) Halsey Premium Plan (D) Rowan Premium Plan (ii) Suggest which bonus plan i.e. Halsey Premium Plan or Rowan Premium Plan, the company should follow.

[8 Marks | 10 Minutes] (PYP Nov 22)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 33. (i) Calculation of wages of Mr. ‘A’ under different wage schemes: A. Time rate: Wages = Time Worked × Rate for the time = 48 hours x Rs.15 = Rs.720

B. Piece rate with a guaranteed weekly wage: Wages = Number of units produced × Rate per unit = 200 units x Rs.4.50\* = Rs.900, (Rs.15 / 60 minutes) x 18 minutes = Rs.4.50

C. Halsey Premium Plan: Wages = Time taken × Time rate + 50% of time saved × Time rate Wages = Time taken × Time rate + 50% (Standard time – Actual time) × Time rate = (48 hours x Rs.15) + 50% of (60 hours# – 48 hours) x Rs.15 = Rs.720 + Rs.90 = Rs.810 (200 units x 18 minutes) / 60 minutes = 60 hours

D. Rowan Premium Plan: Wages = Time taken X Rate per hour + X Time taken X Rate per hour

= (48 hours X Rs.15) + ( ) = Rs.720 + Rs.144 = Rs.864

(ii) The company may follow Halsey Premium Plan over Rowan Premium Bonus Plan as the total wages paid is lower than that of Rowan Premium Bonus Plan. (2+2+2+2)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Standard Time First: a. Immediately calculate total standard time (200 × 18/60 = 60 hrs). b. Helps in Halsey & Rowan calculations.
2. Guaranteed Wage Check: a. Always compare piece-rate earnings vs. guaranteed wage (higher is paid).
3. Formula Memorization: a. Halsey: (Actual Time × Rate) + (50% × Time Saved × Rate). b. Rowan: (Actual Time × Rate) + (Time Saved/Time Allowed × Actual Time × Rate).
4. Time-Saving Tip: a. Use a table format for clear presentation (Method | Calculation | Wages).

Examiner Observations Common Mistakes Students Make:

1. Incorrect Standard Time Calculation: a. Students often miscalculate the total standard time (e.g., failing to convert 18 minutes per unit into hours for 200 units). b. Wrong: Using 18 minutes directly without converting to hours (60 hours = 200 × 18/60).
2. Misapplication of Piece Rate Guarantee:

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 165

a. Forgetting to compare piece-rate earnings (Rs. 900) with guaranteed wages (Rs. 720). b. Incorrectly assuming piece rate always overrides guaranteed wages.

3. Halsey vs. Rowan Formula Errors: a. Halsey: Using actual time saved (12 hours) but applying 50% incorrectly (e.g., 50% of 60 hours instead of 12). b. Rowan: Miscalculating the Time Saved/Time Allowed ratio (12/60 × 48 × 15 = Rs. 144).
4. Bonus Plan Suggestion Without Analysis: a. Simply stating "Halsey is better because wages are lower" without considering worker motivation, cost control, or efficiency impact.

Question 34. DISCUSS the effect of overtime payment on productivity.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](MTP May 2025)[Easy | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 34. Effect of overtime payment on productivity: Overtime work should be resorted to only when it is extremely essential because it involves extra cost. The overtime payment increases the cost of production in the following ways:

1. The overtime premium paid is an extra payment in addition to the normal rate.
2. The efficiency of operators during overtime work may fall and thus output may be less than normal output.
3. In order to earn more the workers may not concentrate on work during normal time and thus the output

during normal hours may also fall.

4. Reduced output and increased premium of overtime will bring about an increase in cost of production. Approach & Time-Saving Tips
1. Cause-Effect Chain: a. Use arrows to link: Overtime → Fatigue → Errors → Rework → Cost ↑.
2. Two-Sided View: a. Pros: Meets deadlines. Cons: Long-term inefficiency.
3. Pre-Memorized Keywords: a. "Fatigue," "premium cost," "slowdown," "burnout," "attrition."
4. Bullet Format: a. Avoid paragraphs; list 4-5 crisp points with bold headings.

Examiner Observations Common Mistakes Students Make:

1. One-Sided Analysis: a. Only discussing negative effects (fatigue, cost increase) while ignoring short-term benefits (meeting deadlines, urgent orders).
2. Generic Statements: a. Writing vague points like "productivity decreases" without explaining how (e.g., fatigue → errors → rework).
3. Missing Cost-Productivity Link: a. Failing to connect overtime premium to per-unit cost escalation due to lower output.
4. Overlooking Behavioral Aspects: a. Not mentioning worker demotivation or intentional slowdowns during normal hours to justify overtime.
5. No Structured Flow: a. Jumbling cost and productivity effects instead of categorizing them logically.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 166

1. Incorrect Time Calculations: a. Miscalculating standard man-hours (6,400 hrs) vs. available hours (4,800 hrs), leading to wrong overtime (1,600 hrs). b. Using 8 units/hour for overtime scenario (should be 6 units/hour before incentive).

The rate of change of labour force in a company during the year ending 31st March, 2023 was calculated as 13%,8% and 5% respectively under 'Flux Method', 'Replacement method' and 'Separation method'. The number of workers separated during the year is 40. You are required to calculate: (i) Average number of workers on roll. (ii) Number of workers replaced during the year. (iii) Number of new accessions i.e. new recruitment. Number of workers at the beginning of the year.

[6 Marks | 10 Minutes\](MTP Oct ’23)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 39. (i) Labour Turnover Rate (Separation Method) = Or, = Or, Average no. of workers on roll = 800

(ii) Labour Turnover Rate (Replacement method) = Or, = Or, No. of workers replaced = 64

(iii) Labour Turnover Rate (Flux Method) = Or, = Or, 100 (40 + No. of Accessions) = 10,400 Or, No. of new accessions = 64

(iv) No. of workers at the beginning of the year Let workers at the beginning of the year were ‘X’ Average no. of workers on roll =

Approach & Time-Saving Tips © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 172

1. Start with Separation Method: a. It gives Avg. Workers (800) directly.
2. Replacement Method Next: a. Simple % calculation (8% of 800 = 64).
3. Flux Method Last: a. Subtract separations (40) from total flux (104) to get new accessions (64).
4. Beginning Workers Formula: a. Memorize: Avg. Workers = [X + (X + Accessions - Separations)] / 2.
5. Time-Saver: a. Underline key numbers (40 separations, 13% flux) to avoid confusion.

Examiner Observations Common Mistakes Students Make:

1. Formula Confusion: a. Mixing up Flux Method (Accessions + Separations) with Replacement Method (only Replacements). b. Using wrong denominators (e.g., using "workers at beginning" instead of "average workers on roll").
2. Average Workers Miscalculation: a. Incorrectly assuming "average workers = workers at beginning" instead of (Beginning + End)/2. b. Failing to adjust for new accessions (64) and separations (40) in the closing balance.
3. Accessions vs. Replacements: a. Treating "new accessions" and "replacements" as the same (replacements are a subset of accessions).
4. Algebraic Errors: a. Errors in solving for X (beginning workers), especially in balancing the equation: 800 = [X + (X + 64 - 40)] / 2.

Question 41. SMC Company Limited is producing a particular design of toys under the following existing incentive system: Normal working hours in the week 48 hours Late shift hours in the week 12 hours Rate of payment Normal working: Rs.150 per hour

Late shift: Rs.300 per hour Average output per operator for 60 hours per week (including late shift hours): 80 toys. The company's management has now decided to implement a system of labour cost payment with either the Rowan Premium Plan or the Halsey Premium Plan in order to increase output, eliminate late shift overtime, and reduce the labour cost. The following information is obtained: The standard time allotted for ten toys is seven and half hours.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 174

Time rate: Rs.150 per hour (as usual). Assuming that the operator works for 48-hours in a week and produces 100 toys, you are required to calculate the weekly earnings for one operator under- (i) The existing Time Rate, (ii) Rowan Premium Plan and, (iii) Halsey Premium Plan (50%).

[8 Marks | 12 Minutes\](May ‘23)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 41. Working Notes: (1) Effective rate per hour: Incentive for 60 hours = (Rs.150 × 48 hours + Rs.300 × 12 hours) = 7,200 + 3,600 = Rs.10, 800 = Rs.10, 800 ÷ 60 hours = Rs.180 per hour (2) Time taken/ allowed to produce 100 toys: = (60 hours ÷ 80 toys) × 100 toys = 75 hours (3) Time saved = Time Allowed – Time Taken = 75 hours – 48 hours = 27 hours (i) Calculation of weekly earnings for one operator under the existing time rate: = (48 hours x Rs.150) + (12 hours x Rs.300) = Rs.10, 800

Alternative solution = Effective rate per hour (WN-1) × Time required for 100 toys (WN-2) = Rs.180 × 75 hours = Rs.13, 500 (ii) Calculation of weekly earnings for one operator under Rowan Premium plan: (Time taken × Rate per hour) + (Time Saved/ Time Allowed × Time taken × Rate per hour) = (48 hours × Rs.150) + [(27 ÷ 75) × 48 × Rs.150] = 7,200 + 2,592 = Rs.9, 792 (iii) Calculation of weekly earnings for one operator under Halsey Premium plan: (Time taken × Rate per hour) + (50% of Time Saved × Rate per hour) = (48 hours × Rs.150) + (50% of 27 hours × Rs.150) = Rs.7, 200 + Rs.2, 025 = Rs.9, 225

(2+1+1+1+2+1) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Standard Time First: a. Immediately calculate 75 hrs for 100 toys (7.5×10)
2. Three-Column Format: a. Create columns for Existing, Rowan, Halsey systems
3. Highlight Time Saved: a. Clearly show 27 hrs saved as it's used in both premium plans
4. Formula Shortcuts: a. Rowan: Remember (Time Taken/Time Allowed)×Time Saved × Rate b. Halsey: Simple 50% of Time Saved × Rate
5. Time-Saver: a. Pre-calculate components: 48×150=7,200; 27×150=4,050

Examiner Observations Common Mistakes Students Make:

1. Incorrect Time Allowed Calculation a. Students often miscalculate standard time for 100 toys by using the original 80-toy productivity rate (60 hours) instead of the given standard (7.5 hours per 10 toys). b. Correct Approach: i. Standard time for 100 toys = (7.5 hrs/10 toys) × 100 = 75 hours.
2. Ignoring Late Shift Elimination in New Plan a. The question specifies eliminating late shifts under new plans, but students sometimes include overtime rates in Rowan/Halsey calculations.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 175

3. Rowan vs. Halsey Formula Errors a. Rowan: Forgetting the ratio (Time Taken/Time Allowed) and using Time Saved directly. b. Halsey: Using 100% instead of 50% of time saved.
4. Effective Rate Misapplication a. Calculating effective rate (Rs. 180/hour) but incorrectly applying it to Rowan/Halsey plans (should only use base rate of Rs. 150/hour).
5. Comparison Oversight a. Not analyzing which plan reduces labor costs more (Halsey: Rs. 9,225 vs. Rowan: Rs. 9,792 vs. Existing: Rs. 10,800).

Question 42. How does the high employee turnover increase the cost of production? Explain.

[6 Marks | 6 Minutes\](May ‘23) [Medium | ICAI Fav]

Answer 42. High Employee Turnover increases the cost of production Replacement costs are the costs which arise due to employee turnover. If employees leave soon after they acquire the necessary training and experience of good work, additional costs will have to be incurred on new workers, i.e., cost of recruitment, training and induction, abnormal breakage and scrap and extra wages and overheads due to the inefficiency of new workers. It is obvious that a company will incur very high replacement costs if the rate of employee turnover is high. Similarly, only adequate preventive costs can keep Employee turnover at a low level. Each company must, therefore, work out the optimum level of Employee turnover keeping in view its personnel policies and the behaviour of replacement cost and preventive costs at various levels of Employee turnover rates.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Quick Framework: Use the "Direct + Indirect Costs" approach: a. Direct: Recruitment, training. b. Indirect: Lower output quality, downtime.
2. Time-Saver: Pre-memorize 3-4 cost examples (e.g., "abnormal breakage" is a keyword ICAI rewards).
3. ICAI Expectation: Link every cost to higher per-unit production cost explicitly.

Examiner Observations Students often make the following mistakes while answering this question:

1. Vague Explanation of Replacement Costs – Many fail to break down specific costs (recruitment, training,

inefficiency losses) and instead give a generic definition.

2. Ignoring Preventive Costs – While replacement costs are highlighted, students miss discussing how preventive

measures (better wages, work culture) can reduce turnover.

3. Lack of Linkage to Production Costs – Some explain turnover in HR terms but don’t connect it clearly to per-

unit production cost increases (e.g., inefficiency = higher labor cost/unit).

4. Overlooking Indirect Costs – Scrap, rework, and supervision costs due to new hires are often omitted.
5. No Mention of Optimum Turnover – ICAI expects a brief note on balancing turnover (some attrition is healthy;

excessive is costly).

Question 43. EXPLAIN the meaning of Idle time and SHOW the treatment for the following causes of Idle time. Causes Treatment © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 176

1. The time lost between factory gate and the place of work,
2. The interval between one job and another,
3. Idle time may also arise due to abnormal factors like lack of coordination

4. Power failure, Breakdown of machines [5 Marks | 6 Minutes] (MTP May 2025)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 43. Idle Time - The time during which no production is carried-out because the worker remains idle but are paid. In other words, it I s the difference between the time paid and the time booked. Idle time can be normal or abnormal. The time for which employees are paid includes holidays, paid leaves, allowable rest or off time etc. Causes Treatment

1. The time lost between factory gate and the place of It is treated as a part of cost of production. Thus, in the

work, case of direct workers an allowance for normal idle

2. The interval between one job and another, time is considered setting of standard hours or standard rate. In case of indirect workers, normal idle time is considered for the computation of overhead rate
3. Idle time may also arise due to abnormal factors like Abnormal idle time cost is not included as a part of

lack of coordination production cost and is shown as a separate item in the

4. Power failure, Break-down of machines Costing Profit and Loss Account.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Quick Framework: Use the "Normal vs. Abnormal" dichotomy: a. Normal: Routine, unavoidable → Production cost. b. Abnormal: Avoidable, inefficiency → P&L.
2. Time-Saver: Pre-memorize 2-3 ICAI-standard treatments (e.g., "machine breakdown → always abnormal").
3. ICAI Expectation: Explicitly state where costs are recorded (e.g., "overhead rates" for indirect workers).

Examiner Observations Students frequently commit the following errors in this question:

1. Confusing Normal vs. Abnormal Idle Time – Many fail to clearly distinguish between normal (expected,

unavoidable) and abnormal (avoidable, inefficiency-related) idle time.

2. Incomplete Treatment Explanations – Some list causes but don’t specify how each is treated (e.g., "power

failure" should explicitly state "charged to Costing P&L").

3. Overlooking Direct vs. Indirect Workers – Normal idle time treatment differs for direct (absorbed in production

cost via standard time) and indirect (included in overhead rates), but students generalize.

4. Missing Practical Examples – Examiners expect specifics (e.g., "time between jobs" is normal for batch

production, but "machine breakdown" is abnormal).

5. No Link to Cost Accounting Standards – ICAI prefers terms like "AS 2 (Valuation of Inventories)" for normal

idle time absorption.

1. Leave Days vs. Working Days Confusion – Many incorrectly deduct 30 leave days from 310 working days

(double-counting), failing to recognize these are either separate or inclusive.

2. Misinterpreting Idle Time – Normal idle time (70 hours) is often added to working hours instead of deducted,

inflating the cost per hour.

3. Welfare Cost Allocation – Some miss dividing total welfare cost (Rs. 6,61,500) by 175 employees, leading to

because of inconsistent working-hour assumptions.

5. Bonus/PF Calculation Errors – Overlooking that these are % of salary (not basic pay) or misapplying

percentages (e.g., 25% of total cost).

Question 45. A worker takes 15 hours to complete a piece of work for which time allowed is 20 hours. His wage rate is Rs. 5 per hour. Following additional information are also available: Material cost of work Rs. 50 Factory overheads 100% of wages Calculate the factory cost of work under the following methods of wage payments: (i) Rowan Plan (ii) Halsey Plan

[6 Marks | 8 Minutes] (PYP May ‘18)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 45.

Rs. (i) Rowan Plan: Normal time wage = 15 hours @ Rs. 5 = 75 Bonus = Time saved /Time allowed × (Time taken × Time rate) = 5/20 x (15 x 5) 18.75

93.75 (ii) Halsey Plan: Normal time wage = 15 hours @ Rs. 5 = 75 Bonus = 50% of (Time saved x Time rate) = 50% of (5x5) = 12.5

87.5

Rowan Plan Rs. Halsey Plan Rs. Materials 50 50 Direct Wages 93.75 87.5 Prime Cost 143.75 137.5 Factory Overhead (100% of Direct wages) 93.75 87.5 Factory Cost 237.5 225

(3+3) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Focus on Bonus Formulas: a. Rowan: Bonus = (Time saved/Time allowed) × Time taken × Rate. b. Halsey: Bonus = 50% × Time saved × Rate.
2. Shortcut: For Halsey, Time saved × Rate × 0.5 = 5 × 5 × 0.5 = Rs. 12.5.
3. Overhead Clarity: Factory overheads are always applied to direct wages, not total cost.

Examiner Observations Students commonly make these errors in wage payment method questions:

1. Confusing Bonus Formulas – Many mix up Rowan (Time saved/Standard time × Time taken × Rate)

and Halsey (50% of Time saved × Rate), leading to incorrect bonus calculations.

2. Incorrect Time Saved Calculation – Some subtract Time taken (15) from Time allowed (20) wrongly (e.g., 20 –

15 = 10 hours instead of 5).

3. Overhead Application Errors – Factory overheads (100% of wages) are sometimes applied to total factory

cost instead of only direct wages.

4. Material Cost Omission – A few forget to include material cost (Rs. 50) in prime cost, affecting the final factory

cost.

5. Partial Solutions – Stopping at wage calculation and not proceeding to factory cost (material + wages +

overheads).

Examiner Observations Students often make these critical errors in such wage calculation problems:

1. Overtime Miscalculations: a. Missing that overtime starts after 8 hours (not 9), leading to incorrect hours counted (e.g., 10-hour day = 2 OT hours, not 1). b. Using basic rate only for OT instead of (Basic + DA) × 2.
2. Holiday/Sunday Pay Errors: a. Forgetting to add double basic pay for 15th August (holiday) and Sunday. b. Excluding allowances (HRA, transport) for holiday work when they are still applicable.
3. Effective Hourly Rate Missteps: a. Dividing total wages by 26 days × 8 hours (208) instead of actual hours worked (186.5). b. Overlooking employer PF/Pension contributions in total wages.
4. Transport Allowance: a. Calculating for 26 days instead of 23 worked days.
5. Job Costing Blunders: a. Charging full monthly wages to Job HT200 instead of 100 hours × effective rate.

3. Time Saved Miscalculations: a. Incorrectly computing allowed hours (e.g., 15 pieces × 8 hours = 120 for M). b. Using actual hours instead of saved hours for bonus calculations.
4. Comparative Analysis Oversights: a. Failing to compare Halsey vs. Rowan losses in part (iii), leading to incorrect "savings" conclusions. b. Not recognizing that Rowan’s loss is higher (Rs. 192) than Halsey’s (Rs. 3,168).

Question 2. Labour turnover is measured by- (a) Number of persons replaced/ average number of workers (b) Numbers of persons separated / number of workers at the beginning of the year (c) (Number of persons replaced + number of persons separated)/ (number of persons at the beginning + the number of persons at the end of the year) (d) None of the above

(Study material)

Answer: (a) Number of persons replaced/ average number of workers

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 188

Reason: Labour turnover refers to the rate at which employees leave and are replaced in an organization. There are three main methods to measure it, and the one mentioned in the question is the Replacement Method, which is: Labour Turnover (Replacement Method) = (Number of persons replaced / Average number of workers) × 100 This method focuses on how many workers were replaced, not just how many left.

Question 3. Important factors for control of employee cost can be- (a) Time and Motion Study (b) Control over idle time and overtime (c) Control over employee turnover (d) All of the above

(Study material)

Answer: (d) All of the above Reason: All options help control employee cost: (a) Time and Motion Study → improves efficiency (b) Control over idle time and overtime → avoids unnecessary wage cost (c) Control over employee turnover → reduces hiring and training expenses

Question 4. Mr. A works in a manufacturing company where he is paid bonus according to the Halsey 50% plan, besides the normal wages. The relevant data is as below: Time Rate (per hour) Rs. 100 Time allowed 10 hours Time taken 5 hours Time saved 5 hours Mr. A believes that his bonus under Halsey system is getting reduced by 50%, thus intending to shift towards Rowan Premium Plan. You are required to CALCULATE the total earnings of Mr. A as per Halsey plan and Rowan Premium plan & ENUMERATE the reason for difference in both the earnings. (a) Total earnings as per Halsey plan- Rs. 500 and as per Rowan Premium plan- Rs.750. Earnings under Halsey Plan is lower than that of Rowan Premium plan as the bonus is getting reduced by 50%. (b) Total earnings as per Halsey plan- Rs.750 and as per Rowan Premium plan- Rs.500. Earnings under Rowan Premium plan is lower than that of Halsey plan as the actual time taken is 50% of the time allowed. (c) Total earnings as per Halsey plan- Rs.750 and as per Rowan Premium plan- Rs.750. When the actual time taken is 50% of the time allowed, the earnings under Halsey and Rowan Plans are equal. (d) Total earnings as per Halsey plan- Rs.250 and as per Rowan Premium plan- Rs.250. Total earnings under both the Plans are equal as the time taken under both the plans are same.

(RTP may 2025)

Answer: (c) Total earnings as per Halsey plan- Rs.750 and as per Rowan Premium plan- Rs.750. When the actual time taken is 50% of the time allowed, the earnings under Halsey and Rowan Plans are equal. Calculation of total earnings: As per Halsey 50% plan = Time taken × Time rate + (50% of Time saved × Time rate) © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 189

= 5 hrs. × Rs.100 + [1/2 × (5 hrs. × Rs.100)] = Rs.500 + Rs.250 = Rs.750 As per Rowan Premium plan =Time taken × Rate per hour + ( ) × Time taken × Rate per hour)

=5 hours × Rs.100 + ( ) × Time taken × Rate per hour) = Rs.500 + Rs.250 = Rs.750 When the actual time taken is 50% of the time allowed, the earnings under Halsey and Rowan Plans are equal.

Sometimes, the workers needs to work late at night which was 3 nights of 3 hours each for the current week. The average output produced per worker for the week is 120 units. Information regarding incentive rate is as follows: Rate of Payment Day shift: Rs. 320 per hour Night shift: Rs. 450 per hour However, this time-basis payment made workers lazy, making their expected output lower. As workers started doing more of the night shifts for higher earnings with minimal impact on the outputs, the company decided to shift on to a system of payments on output basis. Information regarding amended incentive rate is as follows: Time-rate (as usual):Rs. 320 per hour Basic time allowed for 15 units: 5 hours Piece-work rate: Add 15% to basic piece-rate In the amended incentive system, the normal weekly working hours remained the same while production increased to 135 units. CALCULATE the labour cost per unit as per the existing incentive system, along with the amended incentive system. (a) Rs. 140.42 and Rs. 122.67 respectively (b) Rs. 124.81 and Rs. 138.00 respectively (c) Rs. 124.81 and Rs. 122.67 respectively (d) Rs. 140.42 and Rs. 138.00 respectively

(RTP Jan 2025)

Answer: (a) Rs. 140.42 and Rs. 122.67 respectively Calculation of existing labour cost per unit (time basis) Normal weekly hours = 5 days x 8 hours = 40 hours Night shift hours = 3 nights x 3 hours = 9 hours Average production per week = 120 units Weekly wages: Normal shift (40 hours × Rs. 320) Rs. 12,800 Night shift (9 hours × Rs. 450) Rs. 4,050 Total wages Rs. 16,850 Labour cost per unit Rs. 140.42

( ) Calculation of amended labour cost per unit (piece basis) © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 190

15 units are produced in 5 hours Therefore, to produce 135 units, hours required is 135 units =45 hours. Labour cost of producing 135 units: At basic time rate (45 hours × Rs. 320) = Rs. 14,400 Add: Bonus @ 15% on basic Piece rate

15%] 135 units =Rs. 2,160 Earning for the week = Rs. 16,560 Labour cost per unit = ( ) = Rs. 122.67

Question 6. Idle time is the time under which- (a) Full wages are paid to workers (b) No productivity is given by the workers (c) Both (a) and (b) (d) None of the above

(Study material)

Answer: (c) Both (a) and (b) Reason: Idle time refers to the time during which: (a) Workers are paid full wages, but (b) They do not produce any output due to reasons like machine breakdown, lack of materials, etc.

Question 7. Cost of idle time due to non- availability of raw material is- (a) Charged to overhead costs (b) Charged to respective jobs (c) Charged to costing profit and loss account (d) None of the above

(Study material)

Answer: (c) Charged to costing profit and loss account Reason: Idle time due to abnormal causes like non-availability of raw material is considered abnormal idle time. Its cost is not related to normal production activity, so it is not included in job or overhead costs. Instead, it is directly charged to the costing Profit and Loss Account to reflect it as an abnormal loss.

Question 8. Standard time of a job is 60 hours and guaranteed time rate is Rs.0.30 per hour. What is the amount of wages under Rowan plan if job is completed in 48 hours? (a) Rs.16.20 (b) Rs.17.28 (c) Rs.18.00 (d) Rs.14.40

(Study material)

Answer: (b) Rs.17.28 Reason: Under the Rowan Plan, a worker is paid: Wages = Time taken × Rate + Bonus Bonus = (Time saved / Standard time) × Time taken × Rate This method rewards efficiency but controls the bonus, so workers don’t earn excessively by rushing. In this case: Standard Time = 60 hours

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 191

Time Taken = 48 hours Time Rate = Rs.0.30/hour Time Saved = 12 hours So, wages = (48 × 0.30) + [(12 / 60) × 48 × 0.30] = Rs.14.40 + Rs.2.88 = Rs.17.28

Question 9. Suppose the units of a product are produced at the rate of 4 units per useful direct labour hour. Direct labour idle time is 10% of hours paid for. Sales of 1,000 units are budgeted and finished goods stock is expected to rise by 100 units. The budgeted direct labour hours for the production would be: (a) 306 (b) 250 (c) 275 (d) 400

(RTP Sep. 2025)

Answer: (a) 306 Total production required = Budgeted sales + Increase in finished goods stock = 1,000 + 100 =1,100 units Production rate = 4 units per useful direct labour hour Useful hours = = 275 hours Useful hours = 90% of paid hours: Paid hours = 275/90% = 305.55 = 306 hours

Question 10. Out of the following methods attendance is marked by recognizing an employee based on physical and behavioral traits- (a) Punch Card Attendance method (b) Bio- Metric Attendance system (c) Attendance Register method (d) Token Method

(Study material)

Answer: (b) Bio- Metric Attendance system Reason: The Bio-Metric Attendance System identifies employees using physical and behavioral traits such as fingerprints, facial recognition, or iris scan. This ensures accurate and tamper-proof attendance records.

Question 11. Time and motion study is conducted by- (a) Time keeping department (b) Personnel department (c) Payroll department (d) Engineering department

(Study material)

Answer: (d) Engineering department Reason: Time and Motion Study involves analyzing:  Time taken to complete tasks (Time study), and  Movements involved in performing them (Motion study) to improve work efficiency and productivity. This technical and analytical work is typically carried out by the Engineering Department, as it requires understanding of processes, machinery, and workflow design.

Question 12. Identify, which one of the following, does not account for increasing labour productivity- (a) Job satisfaction (b) Motivating workers © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 192

(c) High labour turnover (d) Proper supervision and control

(Study material)

Answer: (c) High labour turnover Reason: High labour turnover means frequent exit and replacement of employees, which disrupts workflow, increases training costs, and reduces overall efficiency — thus lowering labour productivity.

Question 13. Time booking refers to a method wherein ……………… of an employee is recorded. (a) Attendance (b) Food expenses (c) Health status (d) Time spent on a particular job

(Study material)

Answer: (d) Time spent on a particular job Reason: Time booking refers to the method of recording the actual time an employee spends on a specific job, task, or activity. It helps in:  Calculating labour cost per job  Analyzing efficiency and productivity  Preparing accurate job costing

Question 14. Employee Cost includes- (a) Wages and salaries (b) Allowances and incentives (c) Payment for overtime (d) All of the above

(Study material)

Answer: (d) All of the above Reason: Employee Cost includes all payments and benefits given to employees for services rendered. This covers: (a) Wages and salaries → Basic compensation (b) Allowances and incentives → Dearness allowance, bonuses, performance incentives (c) Payment for overtime → Extra wages for hours worked beyond normal time

Question 15. If the time saved is less than 50% of the standard time, then the wages under Rowan and Halsey premium plan on comparison gives- (a) More wages to workers under Rowan plan than Halsey plan (b) More wages to workers under Halsey plan than Rowan plan (c) Equal wages under two plans (d) None of the above

(Study material)

Answer: (a) More wages to workers under Rowan plan than Halsey plan Reason: When time saved is less than 50% of standard time: The Rowan Plan gives a higher bonus because the bonus is proportional to both time saved and actual time taken, leading to a more gradual increase in bonus. The Halsey Plan gives 50% of the time saved as a bonus, which grows linearly.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 193

So, for smaller savings (less than 50%), the Rowan Plan yields higher total wages than the Halsey Plan.

Question 16. If overtime is required for meeting urgent orders, the overtime premium should be charged as- (a) Respective job (b) Overhead cost (c) Costing P& L A/c (d) None of above

(Study material)

Answer: (a) Respective job Reason: When overtime is worked specifically to meet urgent customer orders, the overtime premium (extra wages paid over normal rate) is directly attributable to that job. Therefore, it should be charged to the respective job, as it forms part of the cost incurred to complete that particular job on time.

1. First Priority: Allocate service departments correctly before computing production rates
2. Key Distinction: a. Predetermined rates use budgeted figures b. Performance report uses actual hours × predetermined rates

4. ICAI Expectation: Show complete working notes for allocations and rate calculations.

Examiner Observations Students frequently struggle with this comprehensive overhead absorption problem due to:

1. Service Department Allocation Errors: Many fail to properly allocate S1 (equal basis) and S2 (2:1 ratio) costs

before calculating predetermined rates, leading to incorrect overhead rates for P1 and P2.

2. Actual vs Budgeted Hour Confusion: A common mistake is using budgeted hours (1.5/1 hr for P1) instead of

actual hours (6,100/4,150) when computing absorbed overheads in the performance report.

3. Rate Application Mistakes: Some students reverse the application - applying machine hour rate to P2 (labor

hours) or vice versa, despite clear question instructions.

4. Performance Report Formatting Issues: Candidates often miss comparing budgeted vs actual figures side-by-

side or forget to include all cost elements (materials, labor, overheads).

5. Working Note Neglect: Overlooking the need to show machine/labor hour calculations (Working Note 1) and

actual rate computations (Working Note 3) leads to partial marks.

Examiner Observations Students frequently make these errors in solving comprehensive overhead distribution problems:

1. Incorrect Basis Selection for Apportionment – Many students use wrong allocation bases (e.g., using floor

space for power instead of HP hours). This leads to incorrect primary distribution.

2. Service Dept. Re-distribution Errors – A common mistake is misapplying the simultaneous equation

method (e.g., wrong % allocation for Stores and General Plant). Some students also forget to include reciprocal charges.

3. Calculation Mistakes in Ratios – Errors in ratio calculations (e.g., 7:1:0:2 for Power) distort overhead

apportionment.

4. Overlooking Allocated vs. Apportioned Costs – Some students miss pre-allocated costs (e.g., indirect labor,

supervisor’s salary) and only focus on apportioned overheads.

5. Final Absorption Confusion – After solving simultaneous equations, students sometimes incorrectly transfer

service costs to production departments (e.g., wrong % split for General Plant).

1. Priority Order: a. Primary Distribution: Verify all bases (e.g., power = HP × machine hrs). b. Service Reallocation: i. Simultaneous Equations: Fastest for exams; solve algebraically. ii.
