(3+2+2+3) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Cost Allocation (Part i): a. Compute rates: i. Labour: Rs. 10/hour (Rs. 3 lakhs ÷ 30,000 hours).

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 280

ii. Runs: Rs. 300/run (Rs. 1.8 lakhs ÷ 600 runs). iii. Inspections: Rs. 30/inspection (Rs. 2.4 lakhs ÷ 8,000). b. Multiply rates by actual usage per product.

2. Unused Capacity (Part ii): a. Subtract actual usage from capacity (e.g., 600 runs – 540 = 60 unused runs). b. Multiply unused units by rates (e.g., 60 × Rs. 300 = Rs. 18,000).
3. Product 'S' Cost Sheet (Part iii): a. Direct Costs: Material (Rs. 18,000) + Labour (1,500 hours × Rs. 10) + Design (Rs. 3,750). b. Indirect Costs: Runs (15 × Rs. 300) + Inspections (250 × Rs. 30). c. Add 20% markup to total cost (direct + indirect).

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to:

1. Incorrect Cost Driver Rate Calculation: a. Misallocating total capacity (e.g., using actual usage instead of capacity for rate calculation). b. Wrongly computing rates (e.g., Rs. 300/run = Rs. 1, 80,000 ÷ 540 runs instead of 600).
2. Unused Capacity Errors: a. Calculating unused capacity as total cost minus allocated cost but missing the per-unit rate (e.g., 6,000 unused labour hours × Rs. 10 = Rs. 60,000). b. Overlooking total capacity vs. actual usage (e.g., unused inspections = 8,000 – 7,000 = 1,000).
3. Product 'S' Cost Sheet Mistakes: a. Incorrect segregation of direct/indirect costs (e.g., treating design cost as indirect). b. Misallocating initial design cost (not dividing Rs. 30,000 by 8 quarters). c. Markup application errors: Adding 20% to only direct costs or excluding ABC overheads.
4. Time Mismanagement: a. Spending excessive time on Parts (i) and (ii) and rushing through Part (iii), leading to calculation errors.

Question 19. STATE what are the practical applications of ABC?

[8 Marks | 10 Minutes\](Study material)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 19. PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS OF ACTIVITY BASED COSTING As a Decision-Making Tool ABC can act as a decision making tool in the following ways: (i) ABC along with some other cost management technique can be utilized to improve performance and profitability of an organization.

(ii) Wholesale distributors can gain significant advantage in the decision-making process through implementation of ABC concepts by correlating costs to various activities. Introduction of new product or vendor can be better decided through ABC.

(iii) ABC can assist in decisions related to facility and resource expansion. Often the basis for relocation or opening of a new distribution center is based on cost associations. Reduction in freight or other logistic costs can offset

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 281

the expense of the new facility, staff or equipment. The ABC model can identify the specific cost elements being targeted, providing a much clearer picture which aids in management actions.

(iv) ABC augments decision support for human resources. Since the activity (and therefore costs) can be associated to an individual, new levels of financial performance can be determined. This might be evident in the case of branch management or sales.

(v) Companies who wish to determine price based on cost plus markup basis find ABC method of costing very relevant and are able to determine competitive prices for their products.

As Activity Based Management Meaning of Activity Based Management: The term Activity Based Management (ABM) is used to describe the cost management application of ABC. The use of ABC as a costing tool to manage costs at activity level is known as Activity Based Management (ABM). ABM is a discipline that focuses on the efficient and effective management of activities as the route to continuously improving the value received by customers. ABM utilizes cost information gathered through ABC.

Various analysis in Activity Based Management The various types of analysis involved in ABM are as follows: (1) Cost Driver Analysis: The factors that cause activities to be performed need to be identified in order to manage activity costs. Cost driver analysis identifies the causal factors. (2) Activity Analysis. (a) Value-Added Activities (VA): The value-added activities are those activities which are indispensable in order to complete the process. The customers are usually willing to pay (in some way) for these services. For example, polishing furniture by a manufacturer dealing in furniture is a value added activity. (b) Non-Value-Added Activities (NVA): The NVA activity represents work that is not valued by the external or internal customer. NVA activities do not improve the quality or function of a product or service, but they can adversely affect costs and prices. Moving materials and machine set up for a production run are examples of NVA activities. (3) Performance Analysis: Performance analysis involves the identification of appropriate measures to report the performance of activity centres or other organisational units, consistent with each unit’s goals and objectives.

Activity Based Management in Business Activity Based Management can be used in the following ways (i) Cost Reduction: ABM helps the organisation to identify costs against activities and to find opportunities to streamline or reduce the costs or eliminate the entire activity, especially if there is no value added. (ii) Business Process Re-engineering: Business process re-engineering involves examining business processes and making substantial changes to how organisation currently operates. ABM is a powerful tool for measuring business performance, determining the cost of business output and is used as a means of identifying opportunities to improve process efficiency and effectiveness.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 282

(iii) Benchmarking: Benchmarking is a process of comparing of ABC-derived activity costs of one segment of company with those of other segments. It requires uniformity in the definition of activities and measurement of their costs. (iv) Performance Measurement: Many organisations are now focusing on activity performance as a means of facing competitors and managing costs by monitoring the efficiency and effectiveness of activities. Area Measure Quality of purchased component Zero defects Quality of output % yield Customer awareness Orders; number of complaints

Facilitate Activity Based Budgeting Meaning of Activity Based Budgeting (ABB): Activity based budgeting analyse the resource input or cost for each activity. It provides a framework for estimating the amount of resources required in accordance with the budgeted level of activity. Actual results can be compared with budgeted results to highlight both, in financial and non-financial terms, those activities with major discrepancies from budget for potential reduction in supply of resources. It is a planning and control system which seeks to support the objectives of continuous improvement. It means planning and controlling the expected activities of the organization to derive a cost-effective budget that meet forecast workload and agreed strategic goals. ABB is the reversing of the ABC process to produce financial plans and budgets.

Key Elements of ABB: The three key elements of activity based budgeting are as follows:-  Type of work to be done  Quantity of work to be done  Cost of work to be done

Benefits of ABB: Few benefits of activity based budgeting are as follows:- (i) Activity Based Budgeting (ABB) can enhance accuracy of financial forecasts and increasing management understanding. (ii) When automated, ABB can rapidly and accurately produce financial plans and models based on varying levels of volume assumptions. (iii) ABB eliminates much of the needless rework created by traditional budgeting techniques.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. ABC Applications: Focus on pricing, resource allocation, and profitability analysis with examples (e.g.,

wholesale distributors).

2. ABM Framework: a. Cost Driver Analysis: Identify root causes of costs. b. VA vs. NVA: Use examples (e.g., polishing furniture = VA; material movement = NVA). c. Performance Measures: Link to quality, customer satisfaction.
3. ABB: Define as "reverse ABC" for budgeting, highlighting work type, quantity, and cost.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this theoretical question due to:

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 283

1. Overgeneralization of Applications: a. Listing vague benefits like "cost reduction" without linking to specific ABC applications (e.g., pricing decisions, process re-engineering).
2. Confusing ABM with ABC: a. Failing to distinguish Activity-Based Costing (ABC) (cost allocation tool) from Activity-Based Management (ABM) (strategic cost management).
3. Missing Key Terminology: a. Omitting critical terms like value-added (VA) vs. non-value-added (NVA) activities, cost driver analysis, or benchmarking.
4. Incomplete Coverage of ABB: a. Neglecting to explain Activity-Based Budgeting (ABB) or its three key elements (type, quantity, and cost of work).
5. Lack of Structured Presentation: a. Jumbling points without clear headings (e.g., mixing ABM benefits with ABC applications).

Examiner Observations Students often make these errors in this question:

1. Incorrect Overhead Allocation in Traditional Costing: a. Misapplying the machine hour rate (Rs. 6/hour) to labour hours instead of machine hours. b. Forgetting to multiply machine hours per unit by production volume (e.g., 10 hours × 3,000 units for P).
2. ABC Cost Pool Calculation Errors: a. Misallocating % of overheads: Using 20% of total machine hours (Rs. 24 lakhs) instead of total overheads (Rs. 24 lakhs × 20% = Rs. 4.8 lakhs for setups). b. Wrong cost driver totals: Miscalculating batches (e.g., 20,000 ÷ 1,000 = 20 for R) or inspections (5 × 20 = 100 for P).
3. Cost Driver Rate Mistakes: a. Dividing setup costs by total units (3,000 + 5,000 + 20,000) instead of total batches (50). b. Using Rs. 1.80/hour for machine ops but not linking it to 30% of Rs. 24 lakhs = Rs. 7.2 lakhs ÷ 4 lakh hours.
4. Unit Cost Aggregation: a. Adding total costs but forgetting to divide by units (e.g., Rs. 12.81 lakhs ÷ 3,000 for P). b. Overlooking purchase-related costs (10% of overheads).

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to:

1. Incorrect Overhead Allocation in Traditional Costing: a. Misapplying the machine hour rate (Rs. 30/hour) to labour hours instead of machine hours. b. Forgetting to multiply machine hours per unit by production volume (e.g., 10 hours × 9,000 units for Hand towels).
2. ABC Cost Pool Calculation Errors: a. Misallocating % of overheads: Using 20% of total machine hours (Rs. 3.6 crores) instead of total overheads (Rs. 3.6 crores × 20% = Rs. 72 lakhs for setups). b. Wrong cost driver totals: Miscalculating batches (e.g., 60,000 ÷ 3,000 = 20 for Gym towels) or inspections (5 × 20 = 100 for Hand towels).
3. Cost Driver Rate Mistakes: a. Dividing setup costs by total units (9,000 + 15,000 + 60,000) instead of total batches (50). b. Using Rs. 7.5/hour for machine ops but not linking it to 25% of Rs. 3.6 crores = Rs. 90 lakhs ÷ 12 lakh hours.
4. Unit Cost Aggregation: a. Adding total costs but forgetting to divide by units (e.g., Rs. 1.88 crores ÷ 9,000 for Hand towels). b. Overlooking store delivery costs (10% of overheads).

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

Step 3: Allocate overheads (e.g., Gold utilities: 5 ops × Rs. 1.70).

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to:

1. Material Weight Calculation Errors: a. Misinterpreting 0.8 kg/litre for oils and 1 kg/litre for water, leading to incorrect total weight per unit. b. Forgetting to include chemicals in total weight (e.g., Gold: 60ml oils × 0.8 + 30ml water × 1 + 20g butter + 10g chemicals).
2. ABC Cost Driver Missteps: a. Forklifting costs: Using total units instead of total weight (9,84,000g) for rate calculation (Rs. 0.06/g). b. Utilities: Miscalculating total machine operations (e.g., Gold: 4,000 × 5 = 20,000).
3. Overhead Allocation in Traditional Costing: a. Applying Rs. 33/hour to direct labour cost instead of hours (e.g., Gold: 30 mins = 0.5 hours × Rs. 33 = Rs. 16.50).
4. Unit Cost Aggregation: a. Adding direct costs but missing per-unit overheads (e.g., Diamond: Rs. 248.50 + Rs. 10 + Rs. 7.02 + Rs. 10.20).
5. Time Wastage: a. Over-calculating direct material costs (already provided in working note) instead of focusing on ABC steps.

Examiner Observations Students frequently make these errors in this question:

1. Machine Department Cost Apportionment: a. Incorrectly splitting Rs. 2,52,000 in 4:3:2 ratio (Set-up: Rs. 1,12,000, Stores: Rs. 84,000, Inspection: Rs. 56,000). b. Forgetting to add original activity costs (e.g., Set-up = Rs. 80,000 + Rs. 1,12,000 = Rs. 1,92,000).
2. Batch Calculations: a. Confusing production runs (48 units/batch) with dispatch batches (24 units/batch). b. Miscalculating batches (e.g., Product D: 1,008 ÷ 48 = 21 runs, not 42).
3. Cost Driver Rate Errors: a. Using total requisitions (200) instead of 50 per product for store receiving. b. Wrong material handling rate (Rs. 54/batch) applied to production runs instead of dispatch batches (192).
4. Overhead Allocation: a. Allocating store receiving costs equally (Rs. 36,000 each) due to 50 requisitions per product. b. Missing per-unit cost calculation after total overhead allocation.
5. Time Mismanagement: a. Over-calculating machine hours for traditional costing, leaving less time for ABC.

Question 25. Discuss with example the level of activity method of segregating semi-variable costs into fixed and variable costs. © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 297

[6 Marks | 8 Minutes\](MTP Oct. ‘18)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 25. Level of activity method: Under this method, the variable overhead may be determined by comparing two levels of output with the amount of expenses at those levels. Since the fixed element does not change, the variable element may be ascertained with the help of the following formula. \= Suppose the following information is available:

Production Units Semi-variable expenses (Rs.) January 100 260 February 140 300 Difference 40 40 The variable cost: = =1 Thus, in January, the variable cost will be 100 × Re. 1 = Rs. 100 and the fixed cost element will be (Rs. 260 – Rs.

100. or Rs. 160. In February, the variable cost will be 140 × Re. 1 = Rs. 140 whereas the fixed cost element will

remain the same, i.e., Rs. 160.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Step 1: Identify Data Points a. Select two activity levels (e.g., Jan: 100 units, Feb: 140 units) and their costs (Rs. 260, Rs. 300).
2. Step 2: Apply Formula a. Variable Cost/Unit = (Rs. 300 − Rs. 260) / (140 − 100) = Rs. 1/unit.
3. Step 3: Compute Fixed Costs a. For Jan: Fixed Cost = Rs. 260 − (100 × Rs. 1) = Rs. 160. b. Validate with Feb: Rs. 300 − (140 × Rs. 1) = Rs. 160 (consistent).

Examiner Observations Students often make these errors when applying the Level of Activity Method:

1. Incorrect Data Selection: a. Choosing non-representative periods (e.g., months with outliers like strikes or

shutdowns) to compare costs and output. b. Using total costs instead of semi-variable costs, leading to wrong variable/fixed splits.

2. Calculation Errors: a. Misapplying the formula: i. Correct: Variable Cost/Unit = (Change in Cost) / (Change in Units). ii. Incorrect: Using absolute values or averaging costs. b. Forgetting to subtract variable costs to derive fixed costs (e.g., Fixed Cost = Total Cost − (Units × Variable Rate)).
3. Assumption Oversights: a. Ignoring that the method assumes linearity (fixed costs remain constant, variable

costs change uniformly). b. Failing to validate if the selected data points align with normal operations.

4. Unit Confusion: a. Using differing units (e.g., comparing Rs. with \$ or kg with liters) without conversion.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 298

Question 26. WRITE DOWN the corresponding cost drivers related to the following activity cost pools: Inspecting and testing costs, Setting-up machines cost, Machining costs, Supervising Costs, Ordering and Receiving Materials cost.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes] (MTP Sep’22)[Easy | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 26. Activity Cost Pools Related Cost Drivers Inspecting and testing costs Number of tests Setting up machines cost Machining costs Number of set-ups Machine hours Supervising Costs Direct labour hours Ordering and Receiving Materials cost Number of purchase orders

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Focus on Causality: Choose drivers that directly cause the activity cost.

a. Example: More tests → Higher inspecting costs → Driver: Number of tests.

2. Standardize Metrics: Use quantifiable and trackable units (hours, orders, tests).
3. Avoid Redundancy: Ensure no overlap (e.g., "machine hours" ≠ "set-up hours").

Examiner Observations Students often make these errors when identifying cost drivers:

1. Mismatched Pairings: a. Linking supervising costs to "number of employees" instead of direct labour hours. b. Assigning machining costs to "number of machines" rather than machine hours.
2. Overcomplication: a. Proposing complex drivers (e.g., "skill level of workers" for supervising) instead

of quantifiable metrics (labour hours).

3. Ambiguity in Terms: a. Confusing "number of set-ups" (for setting up machines) with "number of batches". b. Using "number of inspections" instead of "number of tests" for inspecting costs.
4. Omission of Key Drivers: a. Missing purchase orders for material receiving costs, substituting with "material

weight" or "supplier count."

(ii) Factors to be considered for dropping a customer: Dropping customers should be the last resort to be taken by an entity. Factors to be considered should include:

- What is the expected future profitability of each customer?

2. Step 2: Calculate COGS & Gross Margin: a. COGS = Units × Rs. 5,400. b. Gross margin = Actual revenue − COGS.
3. Step 3: Allocate Operating Costs: a. Delivery costs: km/delivery × deliveries × Rs. 7.5. b. Expedited delivery: Rs. 13,500 if applicable.
4. Step 4: Derive Operating Income: a. Subtract total operating costs from gross margin.

Examiner Observations Students often make these errors in customer profitability analysis:

1. Discount Calculation Errors: a. Miscalculating discounts by using listed price × units sold instead of (listed price − actual price) × units. b. For Customer A (no discount), some students incorrectly deduct Rs. 6,480 − Rs. 6,480 = Rs. 0 as a "discount."
2. Activity Cost Allocation Mistakes: a. Delivery costs: Using total deliveries instead of km traveled (e.g., Customer E: 20 deliveries × 30 km × Rs. 7.5 = Rs. 4,500). b. Expedited deliveries: Overlooking the one-time cost for Customer E (Rs. 13,500).
3. Gross Margin vs. Operating Income Confusion: a. Subtracting operating costs before COGS, leading to incorrect gross margin. b. Missing product handling costs (Rs. 22.50/unit), which are part of operating activities.
4. Future Profitability Factors: a. Listing generic reasons like "customer behavior" instead of quantitative metrics (e.g., avoidable costs, restructuring potential).

Question 31. STATE what is Activity based costing. How are product costs determined in ABC?

[6 Marks | 7 Minutes\](Study material)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 307

Answer 31. MEANING AND DEFINITION: Activity Based Costing is an accounting methodology that assigns costs to activities rather than products or services. This enables resources & overhead costs to be more accurately assigned to products & services that consume them. ABC is a technique which involves identification of cost with each cost driving activity and making it as the basis for apportionment of costs over different cost objects/ jobs/ products/customers or services.

ABC assigns cost to activities based on their use of resources. It then assigns cost to cost objects, such as products or customers, based on their use of activities. ABC can track the flow of activities in organization by creating a link between the activity (resource consumption) and the cost object. CIMA defines ‘Activity Based Costing’ as “An approach to the costing and monitoring of activities which involves tracing resource consumption and costing final outputs. Resources are assigned to activities, and activities to cost objects based on consumption estimates. The latter utilize cost drivers to attach activity costs to outputs.”

TRADITIONAL ABSORPTION COSTING VS ABC: Cost Allocation under Traditional and Activity Based Costing System In traditional absorption costing overheads are first related to cost centres (Production & Service Centres) and then to cost objects, i.e., products. In ABC overheads are related to activities or grouped into cost pools. Then they are related to the cost objects, e.g., products. The two processes are, therefore, very similar, but the first stage is different, as ABC uses activities instead of functional departments (cost centres). The problem with functional departments is that they tend to include a series of different activities, which incur a number of different costs that behave in different ways. Activities also tend to run across functions; for instance, procurement of materials often includes raising a requisition note in a manufacturing department or stores. It is not raised in the purchasing department where most procurement costs are incurred. Activity costs tend to behave in a similar way to each other i.e., they have the same cost driver. Therefore, ABC gives a more realistic picture of the way in which costs behave.

Difference between Activity Based Costing and Traditional Absorption Costing

Activity Based Costing Traditional Absorption Costing

activities can be eliminated. Thus, the corresponding Hence, not suitable for cost control. costs are also reduced/ minimized. Hence ABC aids cost control.

STAGES IN ACTIVITY BASED COSTING (ABC) The different stages in ABC calculations are listed below: (1) Identify the different activities within the organisation: Usually the number of cost centres that a traditional overhead system uses is quite small, say up to fifteen. In ABC, the number of activities will be much more, say 200; the exact number will depend on how the management subdivides the organisation’s activities. It is possible to break the organisation down into many very small activities. But if ABC is to be acceptable as practical system it is necessary to use larger groupings, say, 40 activities may be used in practice. The additional number of activities over cost centres means that ABC should be more accurate than the traditional method regardless of anything else. Some activities may be listed as follows:-

- Production schedule changes
- Customer liaison
- Purchasing
- Production process set up
- Quality control
- Material handling
- Maintenance

(2) Relate the overheads to the activities, both support and primary, that caused them. This creates ‘cost pools’ or ‘cost buckets’. This will be done using resource cost drivers that reflect causality.

(3) Support activities are then spread across the primary activities on some suitable base, which reflects the use of the support activity. The base is the cost driver that is the measure of how the support activities are used.

(4) Determine the activity cost drivers that will be used to relate the overheads collected in the cost pools to the cost objects/products. This is based on the factor that drives the consumption of the activity. The question to ask is – what causes the activity to incur costs? In production scheduling, for example, the driver will probably be the number of batches ordered.

(5) Calculate activity cost driver rates for each activity, just as an overhead absorption rate would be calculated in the traditional system. Activity cost driver rate =

The activity driver rate can be used not only to identify cost of products, as in traditional absorption costing, but it can also be used for costing other cost objects such as customers/customer segments and distribution channels. The possibility of costing objects other than products is part of the benefit of ABC. The activity cost driver rates will be multiplied by the different amounts of each activity that each product/other cost object consumes.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 309

Examples of Cost Drivers Some of the examples of cost drivers for different activity pools in a production department are stated below:

Activity Cost Pools Related Cost Drivers Ordering and Receiving Materials cost Number of purchase orders Setting up machines costs Number of set-ups Machining costs Machine hours Assembling costs Number of parts Inspecting and testing costs Number of tests Painting costs Number of parts Supervising Costs Direct labour hours

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. First 2 mins: Define ABC + Traditional Costing difference (bullet points).
2. Next 3 mins: Explain 5 stages (focus on support activity allocation & cost driver logic).
3. Last 2 mins: Give 2-3 cost driver examples (e.g., "No. of setups → Setup costs").

Examiner Observations

1. Mixing Traditional & ABC Concepts: a. Writing that ABC uses department-wise allocation (wrong—it’s activity-wise). b. Assuming machine/labour hours are the only cost drivers (ABC uses multiple drivers like setups, orders, inspections).
2. Incomplete Stages Explanation: a. Missing support activity allocation (Stage 3) or cost driver selection logic (Stage 4). b. Not giving real-world examples (e.g., "purchase orders" as driver for procurement costs).
3. Overlooking Practical Benefits: a. ABC helps in cost control by eliminating non-value activities, but students only focus on costing accuracy.

Question 32. STATE what is Activity based Management. How does ABC help ABM?

[6 Marks | 7 Minutes\](Study material)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 32. As Activity Based Management Meaning of Activity Based Management: The term Activity Based Management (ABM) is used to describe the cost management application of ABC. The use of ABC as a costing tool to manage costs at activity level is known as Activity Based Management (ABM). ABM is a discipline that focuses on the efficient and effective management of activities as the route to continuously improving the value received by customers. ABM utilizes cost information gathered through ABC.

Various analysis in Activity Based Management The various types of analysis involved in ABM are as follows: (1) Cost Driver Analysis: The factors that cause activities to be performed need to be identified in order to manage activity costs. Cost driver analysis identifies the causal factors. © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 310

(2) Activity Analysis. (a) Value-Added Activities (VA): The value-added activities are those activities which are indispensable in order to complete the process. The customers are usually willing to pay (in some way) for these services. For example, polishing furniture by a manufacturer dealing in furniture is a value added activity. (b) Non-Value-Added Activities (NVA): The NVA activity represents work that is not valued by the external or internal customer. NVA activities do not improve the quality or function of a product or service, but they can adversely affect costs and prices. Moving materials and machine set up for a production run are examples of NVA activities. (3) Performance Analysis: Performance analysis involves the identification of appropriate measures to report the performance of activity centres or other organisational units, consistent with each unit’s goals and objectives.

Activity Based Management in Business Activity Based Management can be used in the following ways (i) Cost Reduction: ABM helps the organisation to identify costs against activities and to find opportunities to streamline or reduce the costs or eliminate the entire activity, especially if there is no value added.

(ii) Business Process Re-engineering: Business process re-engineering involves examining business processes and making substantial changes to how organisation currently operates. ABM is a powerful tool for measuring business performance, determining the cost of business output and is used as a means of identifying opportunities to improve process efficiency and effectiveness.

(iii) Benchmarking: Benchmarking is a process of comparing of ABC-derived activity costs of one segment of company with those of other segments. It requires uniformity in the definition of activities and measurement of their costs.

(iv) Performance Measurement: Many organisations are now focusing on activity performance as a means of facing competitors and managing costs by monitoring the efficiency and effectiveness of activities.

Area Measure Quality of purchased component Zero defects Quality of output % yield Customer awareness Orders; number of complaints

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. First 2 mins: Define ABM + key difference from ABC (ABM = management tool, ABC = costing tool).
2. Next 3 mins: Explain 3 analyses (Cost Driver, VA/NVA, Performance) + 1 example each.
3. Last 2 mins: Cover business applications (focus on cost reduction & benchmarking).

Examiner Observations

1. Treating ABM as Just an Extension of ABC: a. Writing "ABM is ABC" (wrong—ABM uses ABC data for decision-making, cost control, process

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 311

improvement). b. Not explaining practical business applications (e.g., re-engineering, performance measurement).

2. Superficial Analysis of Value vs Non-Value Activities: a. Defining VA/NVA but not connecting to cost reduction (e.g., "setups are NVA → ABM eliminates them"). b. Missing real-world examples (e.g., "moving materials = NVA → ABM reduces logistics costs").
3. Ignoring Performance Metrics: a. Listing benchmarking & performance measures but not explaining how ABM tracks them (e.g., "% yield" for quality).
4. Weak Link Between ABC & ABM: a. Not stating clearly: "ABC provides activity cost data → ABM uses it to optimize processes."

(2+2+2+2+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Start with Traditional Costing – Allocate Rs. 90,000 store support costs based on COGS ratio (Lemon: 20%,

Grapes: 50%, Papaya: 30%).

2. For ABC, Compute Rates First – Calculate per-order, per-delivery, per-hour, and per-item rates before

allocating.

3. Use Tables for ABC Allocation – Organize data in columns (Lemon, Grapes, Papaya) to avoid errors.
4. Verify Total Costs Match – Ensure Rs. 90,000 is fully allocated in both methods.
5. Quick % Calculation – Divide operating income by respective product revenue, not total.

Examiner Observations Students often make the following mistakes while solving this question:

1. Incorrect Allocation Base in Traditional Costing – Many students allocate store support costs incorrectly under

the traditional method, failing to realize it is based on COGS proportion and not revenue.

2. Missing Directly Traced Costs (Bottle Returns) – A common oversight is ignoring directly traceable costs (like

bottle returns for Lemon) while calculating ABC costs.

3. Wrong Activity Driver Rates – Students sometimes miscalculate ABC allocation rates (e.g., dividing total cost

by incorrect driver quantity). For example, using total deliveries as 300 instead of 315 leads to wrong per-delivery costs.

4. Operating Income % Calculation Errors – Some students divide operating income by total revenue instead of

product-wise revenue, distorting percentages.

5. Misclassification of Costs – A few students wrongly include COGS in store support costs, leading to double-

counting.

6. Time Mismanagement – Due to the detailed calculations, students spend too much time on ABC allocation,

leaving less time for comparison and interpretation.

Question 36. EXPLAIN in brief the problems of traditional costing where overhead costs are allocated based on volume.

[8 Marks | 9 Minutes\](Study material)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 36. Overhead, in Traditional Costing System, overhead costs are grouped together under cost center and then absorbed into product costs on either of the basics such as direct labour hours, machine hours, volume etc.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 320

In certain cases, this traditional costing system gives inaccurate cost information. Though, it should not be assumed that all traditional absorption costing systems are not accurate enough to give adequate information for pricing purposes or other long-run management decision purposes. Some traditional systems treat overheads in a detailed way and relate them to service cost centres as well as production cost centres. The service centre overheads are then spread over the production cost centres before absorption rates are calculated. The main cause of inaccuracy is in the calculation of the overhead rate itself, which is usually based on direct labour hours or machine hours. These rates assume that products that take longer to make, generate more overheads and so on.

Organisations, who do not wish to know how much it costs to make a product with precise accuracy, may be happy with traditional costing system. Others, however, fix their price on cost basis and need to determine it with reasonable accuracy. The latter organisations have been greatly benefitted from the development of activity- based costing (ABC), which is considered as a modern absorption costing method, and was evolved to give more accurate product costs.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Define Traditional Costing – Briefly explain volume-based allocation (e.g., labor/machine hours).
2. List Problems – a. Overcosts simple, high-volume products. b. Undercosts complex, low-volume products. c. Ignores non-volume drivers (e.g., setups, inspections).
3. Mention Validity in Simple Cases – E.g., single-product firms.
4. Contrast with ABC – ABC uses activity drivers, improving accuracy for diverse products.
5. Conclude – Traditional costing is faster but less precise; ABC is detailed but costly.

Examiner Observations Students often make the following mistakes while answering this question:

1. Overgeneralizing Traditional Costing’s Flaws – Some students vaguely criticize traditional costing without

explaining specific problems like distorted product costs due to volume-based allocation.

2. Ignoring Context Where Traditional Costing Works – Many wrongly claim that traditional costing is always

inaccurate, failing to acknowledge that it can be sufficient for simple, high-volume production environments.

3. Lack of Comparison with ABC – The question expects a contrast with ABC, but students often miss explaining

how ABC improves accuracy by using multiple cost drivers.

4. Misunderstanding Overhead Absorption – Some students incorrectly assume that traditional costing uses

only direct labor hours, ignoring other bases like machine hours or units produced.

5. Superficial Explanation – Instead of delving into real-world implications (e.g., underpricing low-volume,

complex products), answers remain theoretical and unapplied.

6. Repetitive Points – Many repeat the same idea (e.g., "traditional costing is less accurate") without structured

arguments or examples.

(iv) Challenges faced in assigning total operating cost of Rs. 8, 27,970:

- Choosing an appropriate cost driver for activity area.
- Developing a reliable data base for the chosen cost driver.
- Deciding, how to handle costs that may be common across several activities.
- Choice of the time period to compute cost rates per cost driver.
- Behavioural factors. (3+2+2+1+2+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tipsc
1. Prioritize Part (i) & (ii) – These are formulaic and quick (gross margin = revenue – COGS; ABC rates = total cost / total units).
2. Use Tables for Part (iii) – Organize calculations in columns (General, Drugstore, Chemist) to avoid repetition.
3. Leverage Given Data – For shelf-stocking, directly use avg. hours × deliveries × rate (no need for total hours).
4. Comment Strategically – Compare operating cost/revenue ratios (Chemist Shops’ 3.17% vs. 0.58% for Supermarkets).

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 324

5. List Challenges Concisely – Focus on ICAI’s keywords: cost driver selection, data reliability, cross-activity costs, behavioral factors.

Examiner Observations Students frequently make the following errors when attempting this ABC costing question:

1. Incorrect Gross Margin Calculation – Some students calculate gross margin as a percentage of total revenue

instead of channel-wise revenue, leading to distorted profitability analysis.

2. Misallocation of Activity Costs – A common mistake is using wrong multipliers (e.g., multiplying carton costs

by total deliveries instead of cartons per delivery × deliveries).

3. Overlooking Per-Unit Rates – Many fail to compute activity rates per cost driver (e.g., Rs. 3 per line item)

before allocating costs, causing cascading errors.

4. Ignoring New Insights from ABC – The question demands comparative analysis (e.g., Chemist Shops consume

more resources), but students often skip this critical commentary.

5. Superficial Treatment of Challenges – For part (iv), generic answers like "cost allocation is hard" are given

instead of specific issues (e.g., behavioral resistance, data reliability).

6. Time Mismanagement – Due to multi-step calculations, students spend excessive time on part (iii) and rush

through part (iv), losing easy marks.

Revenues (At list price) (Refer to working 6,06,528 9,20,160 40,17,600 24,62,400 6,35,040 note) Less: Discount (Refer to working note) - 10,224 3,72,000 1,73,280 63,504 Revenue (At actual price) 6,06,528 9,09,936 36,45,600 22,89,120 5,71,536 Less: Cost of goods sold (Refer to working 5,05,440 7,66,800 33,48,000 20,52,000 5,29,200 note) Gross margin 1,01,088 1,43,136 2,97,600 2,37,120 42,336 Less: Customer level operating activities 34,944 51,696 1,73,280 1,12,320 51,840 costs (Refer to working note) Customer level operating income 66,144 91,440 1,24,320 1,24,800 (9,504)

II. Comments Customer Dee in comparison with Customer Cee: Operating income of Customer Dee is more than that of Customer Cee, despite having only 61.29% (38,000 units) of the units’ volume sold in comparison to Customer Cee (62,000 units). Customer Cee receives a higher percent of discount i.e. 9.26% (Rs. 6) while Customer Dee receive a discount of 7.04% (Rs. 4.56). Though the gross margin of customer Cee (Rs. 2,97,600) is more than that of Customer Dee (Rs. 2,37,120) but total cost of customer level operating activities of Cee (Rs. 1,73,280) is more in comparison to Customer Dee (Rs. 1,12,320). As a result, operating income is more in case of Customer Dee.

Customer Eey in comparison with Customer Aey: Customer Eey is not profitable while Customer Aey is profitable. Customer Eey receives a discount of 10% (Rs. 6.48) while Customer Aey doesn’t receive any discount. Sales Volume of Customer Aey and Eey is almost same. However, total cost of customer level operating activities of Eey is far more (Rs. 51,840) in comparison to Customer Aey (Rs. 34,944). This has resulted in occurrence of loss in case of Customer Eey.

Important Note:- This was a numerical problem from the topic ‘Concepts of Activity Based Costing (ABC)’ which required preparing customer level operating income using cost driver rates and examining the result and commenting on the customer by comparison of result/ other parameters. Performance of the examinees was above average.

(3+4+3+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Skip List Price Revenue – Directly calculate actual revenue = cases × actual price.
2. Use Tables for Costs – Organize activity costs in columns (Aey to Eey) to avoid repetition.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 327

3. Prioritize Key Comparisons: a. Dee vs. Cee: Highlight discount % (7.04% vs. 9.26%) + delivery efficiency. b. Eey vs. Aey: Emphasize discount (10%) + 60 km delivery cost.
4. Comment Concisely – Use ratios: a. Operating income/Revenue (%) b. Cost of activities/Revenue (%)
5. Verify Expedited Costs – Ensure Rs. 240 is added only for Eey.

Examiner Observations Students often make these errors in this ABC costing question:

1. Discount Calculation Errors – Many incorrectly compute discounts by using list price (Rs. 64.80) minus actual

price but fail to multiply by cases sold, leading to wrong revenue figures.

2. Misapplication of Cost Drivers – A frequent mistake is using total deliveries instead of delivery kilometers ×

Rs. 4.80 for delivery costs. Some also miss expedited deliveries (e.g., Eey’s 2 deliveries × Rs. 120).

3. Incomplete Comparisons – For part (ii), students state operating incomes but fail to analyze key

differences (e.g., Dee’s lower volume but higher profitability vs. Cee due to lower discounts and operating costs).

4. Overlooking Negative Profitability – Some ignore Eey’s loss (−Rs. 9,504) or attribute it only to discounts,

missing the impact of high delivery costs (Rs. 11,520 due to 60 km/delivery).

5. Formulaic Comments – Instead of insightful comparisons, answers like "Cee has higher sales" are given

without linking to cost drivers or discounts.

6. Time Wastage on List Price Revenue – Unnecessarily calculating revenue at list price first, instead of directly

computing actual revenue = cases sold × actual price.

(4+4+4) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Start with Absorption Costing: a. Compute machine (Rs. 4/hr) + assembly (Rs. 2.5/hr) rates. b. Allocate department-wise (no mixing!).
2. ABC: Calculate Rates First: a. Use given cost pools ÷ driver quantities (e.g., Rs. 50/set-up).
3. Product-Wise ABC Allocation: a. Use actual activity data (e.g., 4,500 set-ups for X).
4. Highlight Key Shifts: a. Product Y: a. Lower profit in ABC due to high order/set-up costs. b. Products X/Z: Losses persist but change marginally.
5. Verify Total Profit Matches: Cross-check Rs. 3.7L for both methods.

Examiner Observations Students frequently make these errors in this absorption vs. ABC costing question:

1. Incorrect Overhead Allocation in Absorption Costing – Many students: a. Use total overheads (Rs. 64.3L) instead of department-wise (Rs. 36.8L + Rs. 27.5L). b. Misapply machine/labor hour rates (e.g., using Rs. 4 for assembly or Rs. 2.5 for machine dept.).
2. ABC Cost Driver Rate Miscalculations – Common mistakes include: a. Dividing total pool costs by wrong quantities (e.g., using 9,200 set-ups instead of 9,000). b. Overlooking purchase orders (800) or customer orders (7,200), leading to wrong per-order rates.
3. Product-Wise Activity Allocation Errors – Students often: a. Multiply set-up costs by production units instead of actual set-ups (4,500/3,000/1,500). b. Miss purchasing costs for Product Z (150 orders × Rs. 250).
4. Profit Comparison Oversights – While both methods show total profit = Rs. 3.7L, students fail to analyze: a. Product Y’s inflated profit under absorption costing (Rs. 15.2L vs. Rs. 14.82L in ABC). b. Product X/Z’s losses due to unallocated set-up/order costs in absorption costing.
5. Time Mismanagement – Spending excessive time on absorption costing and rushing through ABC analysis.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 331

Question 40. KD Ltd. is following Activity based costing. Budgeted overheads, cost drivers and volume are as follows:

Cost pool Budgeted overheads (Rs.) Cost driver Budgeted volume Material procurement 18,42,000 No. of orders 1,200 Material handling 8,50,000 No. of movement 1,240 Maintenance 24,56,000 Maintenance hours 17,550

Set-up 9,12,000 No. of set-ups 1,450 Quality control 4,42,000 No. of inspection 1,820

The company has produced a batch of 7,600 units, its material cost was Rs.24, 62,000 and wages Rs.4, 68,500. Usage activities of the said batch are as follows: Material orders 56 Material movements 84 Maintenance hours 1,420 hours Set-ups 60 No. of inspections 18

Required: (i) CALCULATE cost driver rates. (ii) CALCULATE the total and unit cost for the batch.

[8 Marks | 12 Minutes\](MTP April ’23) (Same concept different figures RTP Nov’20)[Medium | ICAI Fav]

Answer 40.(i) Calculation of cost driver rate: Cost pool Budgeted overheads (Rs.) Cost driver Cost driver rate (Rs.) Material procurement 18,42,000 1,200 1,535.00 Material handling 8,50,000 1,240 685.48 Maintenance 24,56,000 17,550 139.94 Set-up 9,12,000 1,450 628.97 Quality control 4,42,000 1,820 242.86

(ii) Calculation of cost for the batch: Particulars Amount (Rs.) Amount (Rs.) Material cost 24,62,000.00 Wages 4,68,500.00 Overheads:

- Material procurement (Rs.1,535×56 orders) 85,960.00
- Material handling (Rs.685.48×84 movements) 57,580.32
- Maintenance (Rs.139.94×1,420 hours) 1,98,714.80
- Set-up (Rs.628.97×60 set-ups) 37,738.20

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 332

- Quality control (Rs.242.86×18 inspections) 4,371.48 3,84,364.80

Total Cost 33,14,864.80 No. of units 7,600 Cost per units 436.17

(3+5) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Compute Rates First: a. Use exact fractions (e.g., 8,50,000 ÷ 1,240 = Rs. 685.48).
2. Batch Cost Calculation: a. Material/Wages: Directly given (Rs. 24.62L + Rs. 4.68L). b. Overheads: Multiply actual usage (56/84/1,420/60/18) by rates.
3. Verify Totals: a. Cross-check Rs. 3,84,364.80 overheads before adding to direct costs.
4. Unit Cost: a. Divide Rs. 33,14,864.80 by 7,600 units = Rs. 436.17/unit.
5. Use Calculator Efficiently: a. Store rates in memory to avoid re-entry.

Examiner Observations Students often make these errors while solving this ABC costing problem:

1. Incorrect Cost Driver Rates – Many students: a. Round off rates prematurely (e.g., Rs. 685.48 → Rs. 685), causing significant cost deviations. b. Misdivide (e.g., Material handling = 8,50,000 ÷ 1,200 instead of 1,240).
2. Overhead Allocation Errors – Common mistakes include: a. Using budgeted volume (1,200 orders) instead of actual usage (56 orders) for calculations. b. Missing units conversion (e.g., calculating total cost but forgetting to divide by 7,600 units).
3. Calculation Slips – Students frequently: a. Miscompute maintenance costs (1,420 hrs × Rs. 139.94 = Rs. 1,98,714.80) due to complex multiplication. b. Overlook quality control costs (only 18 inspections) as it appears minor.
4. Presentation Issues – Some: a. Fail to label units (Rs./unit) in the final answer. b. Mix up cost pools (e.g., assigning set-up costs to material handling).
5. Time Wastage – Spending too much time on rate calculations and rushing through the total cost summary.

Students frequently make these errors in this ABC vs. Traditional Costing problem:

1. Incorrect Support Cost Allocation in Traditional Method – Many students: a. Calculate 30% of COGS correctly but forget to add bottle return costs (Rs. 60,000) for soft drinks. b. Misallocate the total support cost (Rs. 45L) by using revenue % instead of COGS %.
2. ABC Cost Driver Misapplications – Common mistakes: a. Use wrong ratios for activity allocation (e.g., 360:840:360 for ordering but 300:2190:660 for delivery). b. Miss direct tracing of bottle returns (only for soft drinks). c. Miscalculate per-unit rates (e.g., Rs. 100/hour for shelf-stocking instead of Rs. 100).
3. Operating Income % Errors – Students often: a. Divide total operating income (Rs. 10.2L) by individual revenues instead of product-wise income. b. Misinterpret Fresh Produce’s low profitability (0.6%) under ABC, assuming it’s an error.
4. Time Mismanagement – Spending too much time on traditional costing and rushing through ABC calculations.

Finally choose the best product in both methods on the basis of income as percentage of revenue. Most of the students answered will in the second part of the question. Performance of the examinees was good.

(4+2+4+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Traditional Costing First: a. Allocate 40% of COGS (Rs. 92.1L ÷ Rs. 230.25L) + add Drug License Fee (2:3:5).
2. ABC: Calculate Rates First: a. Ordering: Rs. 415/order (Rs. 8.3L ÷ 2,000). b. Delivery: Rs. 650/delivery (Rs. 18.2L ÷ 2,800).
3. Allocate Activity Costs: a. Use actual usage (e.g., 1,250 shelf-hours × Rs.720 = Rs. 9L for Drug B).
4. Highlight Key Shifts: a. Drug A: 22.12% → 8.81% due to high ordering/shelf-stocking costs. b. Drug C: 9.32% → 15.78% as ABC fairly allocates costs.
5. Verify Totals: Ensure Rs. 50.15L profit matches in both methods.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 338

Examiner Observations Students frequently make these errors in this ABC vs. Traditional Costing problem:

1. Incorrect Support Cost Allocation in Traditional Method – Many students: a. Calculate 40% of COGS correctly but forget to distribute Drug License Fee (2:3:5 ratio) separately. b. Misallocate the total support cost (Rs. 92.1L) by using revenue % instead of COGS %.
2. ABC Cost Driver Misapplications – Common mistakes: a. Use wrong ratios for activity allocation (e.g., 560:810:630 for ordering but 950:1000:850 for delivery). b. Miss the fixed Drug License Fee allocation (2:3:5 for A:B:C). c. Miscalculate per-unit rates (e.g., Rs. 720/hour for shelf-stocking instead of Rs. 720).
3. Operating Income % Errors – Students often: a. Divide total operating income (Rs. 50.15L) by individual revenues instead of product-wise income. b. Misinterpret Drug A’s profitability drop (22.12% → 8.81%) under ABC, assuming it’s an error.
4. Time Mismanagement – Spending too much time on traditional costing and rushing through ABC calculations.

Question 43. STATE what are the limitations of ABC?

[4 Marks | 5 Minutes\](Study material)[Easy | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 43. LIMITATIONS OF ACTIVITY BASED COSTING The main limitations using Activity Based Costing are: (i) It is more expensive, particularly in comparison with traditional costing system. (ii) It is not helpful to the small organizations. (iii) It may not be applied to organizations with limited products. (iv) Selection of the most suitable cost driver may not be easy/ may be difficult or complicated.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Structured Format: Use bullet points for clarity.
2. Prioritize Key Limitations: a. High Cost: Explain setup/maintenance expenses. b. Small Firms: ABC’s complexity outweighs benefits for low-volume businesses. c. Cost-Driver Issues: Hard to identify/measure drivers (e.g., R&D costs).
3. Add Unique Points: a. Behavioral: Staff may resist new systems. b. Dynamic Changes: ABC requires frequent updates.
4. Avoid Fluff: Skip definitions; focus on limitations.

Examiner Observations Students often make these errors when answering about ABC limitations:

1. Vague or Generic Points – Many write "ABC is complex" without explaining why (e.g., high implementation

costs, need for detailed data).

2. Missing Key Limitations – Overlook critical points like: a. Behavioral Resistance: Employees may resist ABC due to process changes. b. Dynamic Environments: ABC struggles with frequent product/process changes.
3. Overemphasis on Cost – Only state "ABC is expensive" but fail to compare cost vs. benefits (e.g., better

decisions justify costs). © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 339

4. Irrelevant Examples – Cite limitations like "ABC needs computers" (outdated) instead of practical

challenges (e.g., cost-driver selection).

5. Repetition – List "not useful for small firms" and "not for limited products" as separate points when they

are interlinked.

Comment on the results: Customer D is the most profitable customer. D’s profits are even higher than C (whose revenue is the highest) despite having only 52.30% of the unit volume of customer C. The main reason is that C receives a discount of Rs. 9 per case while customer D receives only a Rs.3.60 discount per case. Customer E is the least profitable. The profits of E is even less than A (whose revenue is least) Customer E received a discount of Rs. 10.80 per case, makes more frequent orders, requires more customer visits and requires more delivery kms. in comparison with customer A.

(ii) Insight gained by reporting both the list selling price and the actual selling price for each customer: Separate reporting of both-the listed and actual selling prices enables Alpha Ltd. to examine which customer has received what discount per case, whether the discount received has any relationship with the sales volume. The data given below provides us with the following information;

Sales volume Discount per case (Rs.) C (1,36,800 cases) 9.00 D (71,550 cases) 3.60 B (19,688 cases) 1.80 E (8,775 cases) 10.80 A (4,680 cases) 0

The above data clearly shows that the discount given to customers per case has a direct relationship with sales volume, except in the case of customer E. The reasons for Rs. 10.80 discount per case for customer E should be explored. (5+3+2)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Calculate Actual Revenue: a. List price × cases sold → Subtract discount (list - actual price) × cases.
2. Compute Activity Costs: a. Use cost driver rates (e.g., Rs. 5.75/km × kms × deliveries). b. Expedited delivery: Only for E (1 × Rs. 2,250).
3. Tabulate Results: a. Compare gross margin vs. operating costs to spot anomalies (e.g., Customer E).
4. Comment Strategically: a. Highlight D’s efficiency (lower discounts, moderate costs) vs. C’s high volume but

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 342

lower margins.

b. Flag E’s outlier discount for investigation.

Examiner Observations Students often make these errors in this customer profitability analysis question:

1. Discount Calculation Errors: a. Many students incorrectly compute discounts by subtracting actual price from list price but fail to multiply by cases sold, leading to wrong revenue figures. b. Example: For Customer C, discount should be (108 - 99) × 1,36,800 = Rs. 12,31,200, but some students only calculate Rs. 9 per case without scaling.
2. Delivery Cost Miscalculations: a. A frequent mistake is using total deliveries instead of delivery kms × Rs. 5.75. b. Example: For Customer E, it’s 20 deliveries × 30 km × Rs. 5.75 = Rs. 3,450, not 20 × Rs. 5.75.
3. Overlooking Expedited Deliveries: a. Only Customer E has 1 expedited delivery (Rs. 2,250), but many students miss this cost.
4. Misinterpretation of Profitability: a. Students often assume highest revenue (Customer C) = highest profit, but fail to see Customer D is more profitable due to lower discounts and operating costs. b. Customer E’s near-zero profit (Rs. 274) is often ignored in analysis.
5. Incomplete Insights on Pricing: a. For part (ii), students state "discounts vary" but miss the anomaly with Customer E (high discount despite low volume).

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Skip Manual Rate Calculation – Use the provided activity rates directly to save time.
2. Tabulate ABC Costs First – Allocate marketing, website, credit card fees, etc., in a table format to avoid

repetition.

3. Separate Direct Costs – Keep COGS (only for cafeteria) and digital media costs (for halls only) outside ABC.
4. Quick Verification – Cross-check if total ABC costs (₹15,37,500) match the sum of individual department

allocations.

5. Focus on Conclusion – For part (ii), a single line comparing cafeteria’s negative 12% margin suffices to validate

the supervisor’s view.

Examiner Observations Students often make the following mistakes while attempting this question:

1. Incorrect Allocation of Costs – Many students fail to correctly allocate activity-based costs (ABC) to each

department, especially missing the activity driver linkage (e.g., using wrong multipliers like square feet for marketing costs).

2. Ignoring Non-ABC Costs – Some exclude digital media costs or COGS for the cafeteria, leading to incorrect

operating income calculations.

3. Calculation Errors in Activity Rates – Miscomputing activity rates (e.g., dividing total cost by wrong capacity)

distorts the entire allocation.

4. Overlooking Negative Profitability – Even after calculating losses in the cafeteria, students may not justify the

supervisor’s contention clearly.

5. Time Mismanagement – Due to the volume of data, students spend excessive time on computations instead of

focusing on key requirements.

1. Incorrect Production Runs Calculation – Many forget that production runs = (Total units ÷ Batch size). Here,

2. Wrong Cost Driver Allocation – Some students allocate assembly costs to Product Q, which does not use

assembly hours.

3. Miscounting Cost Drivers – Errors in totalling machine hours (1,32,000 hrs) or requisitions (120) distort activity

rates.

4. Overlooking Zero Assembly Hours for Q – A common oversight is assigning assembly costs to Q, despite the

question stating it requires only machine hours.

5. Time Wastage on Manual Calculations – Instead of using given data smartly, students recalculate totals,

wasting time.

Question 49. DEFINE the following terms: (i) Cost driver (ii) Activity cost pool © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 354

[4 Marks | 5 Minutes] (Study material)[Easy | ICAI Fav]

Answer 49. (i) Activity: Activity, here, refers to an event that incurs cost. (ii) Cost Object: It is an item for which cost measurement is required e.g. a product or a customer. (iii) Cost Driver: It is a factor that causes a change in the cost of an activity. There are two categories of cost driver.

- Resource Cost Driver: It is a measure of the quantity of resources consumed by an activity. It is used to

assign the cost of a resource to an activity or cost pool.

- Activity Cost Driver: It is a measure of the frequency and intensity of demand, placed on activities by

cost objects. It is used to assign activity costs to cost objects. (iv) Cost Pool: It represents a group of various individual cost items. It consists of costs that have same cause and effect relationship. Example machine set-up.

Examples of Cost Drivers: Business Functions Cost Driver Research and Development • Number of research projects

- Personnel hours on a project

Design of products, services and procedures • Number of products in design

- Number of parts per product
- Number of engineering hours

Customer Service • Number of service calls

- Number of products serviced
- Hours spent on servicing products

Marketing • Number of advertisements

- Number of sales personnel
- Sales revenue

Distribution • Number of units distributed

- Number of customers

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Stick to ICAI’s Keywords – Use phrases like "cause-effect relationship," "homogeneous costs," and "measure of

frequency."

2. Pre-Memorize Examples – Standard examples (e.g., "number of batches" for setup cost pool) save time.
3. Avoid Overwriting – Definitions should be 30-40 words max. Example:

a. Cost Driver: "A factor influencing activity costs, e.g., machine hours for maintenance costs."

4. Use Bullet Points – Clearly separate types (resource vs. activity driver) for better readability. (2+2) Examiner Observations

Students often make these errors in definition-based questions:

1. Vague Definitions – Using generic phrases like "cost driver affects costs" without specifying cause-effect

relationship or types (resource/activity driver).

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 355

2. Missing Examples – ICAI expects real-world examples (e.g., "number of setups" for cost pool). Many write

definitions but skip illustrations.

3. Confusing Cost Pool with Cost Driver – Some incorrectly define cost pool as a "cost category" without linking it

to homogeneous activities (e.g., machine setup costs grouped under one pool).

4. Overcomplicating Answers – Unnecessary details like ABC steps dilute clarity. Definitions should be concise yet

complete.

5. Ignoring Sub-Categories – For cost drivers, failing to distinguish between resource cost driver (assigns resource

costs to activities) and activity cost driver (assigns activity costs to cost objects).

Question 50. A manufacturing company in India wants to replace its traditional costing system by ABC. It produces a number of products, each having complex production process of different degree. SUGGEST various requirements for installing activity based costing.

[5 Marks | 8 Minutes\](Study material)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 50. REQUIREMENTS IN ABC IMPLEMENTATION A number of distinct practical stages are required in the ABC implementation which are given as below:

(1) Staff Training: The co-operation of the workforce is critical to the successful implementation of ABC. Staff training should be done to create an awareness on the purpose of ABC.

(2) Process Specification: Informal, but structured interviews with key members of personnel will identify the different stages of the production process, the commitment of resources to each, processing times and bottlenecks.

(3) Activity Definition: The activities must be defined clearly in the early stage in order to manage the problems, if any, effectively. There might be overloading of information from the new data, but the same is needed in codification.

(4) Activity Driver Selection: Cost driver for each activity shall be selected.

(5) Assigning Cost: A single representative activity driver can be used to assign costs from the activity pools to the cost objects.

(1+1+1+1+1) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Use the "APIPA" Framework – Activities → Pools → Integration → Pilot → Adoption.
2. Prioritize Practicality – Focus on actionable steps (e.g., "Use barcodes for material movement tracking") over

theory.

3. Leverage Keywords – Include terms like "heterogeneous processes," "GST-compliant cost

tracking," and "activity-based budgeting."

4. Add a Closing Line – "Regularly review ABC data to align with dynamic production needs." (Shows depth).

Examiner Observations © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 356

Students often make these mistakes while answering ABC implementation requirements:

1. Generic Points – Listing vague steps like "identify activities" without explaining how (e.g., process mapping,

interviews with department heads).

2. Missing Indian Context – Overlooking challenges specific to Indian manufacturing (e.g., labor-intensive

processes, GST compliance in cost tracking).

3. Ignoring Cost-Benefit Analysis – Not mentioning the need to evaluate ROI of ABC vs. traditional costing before

implementation.

4. Overlooking Behavioral Aspects – Skipping resistance management (e.g., training for staff, top-management

buy-in).

5. Technical Gaps – Failing to specify software/tools (e.g., ERP integration, data analytics) for accurate activity

tracking.

6. Repetition – Rewriting the same point in different words (e.g., "identify cost drivers" and "analyze activities" as

separate points).

XYZ Constructions has a policy to price all jobs at budgeted total cost plus 50%. Overheads are currently absorbed on a labour-hour basis. The company believes that switching to activity-based costing (ABC) to absorb overheads would reduce the costs associated with RBC and make them more competitive.

You are provided with the following data:

(c) Possible pricing strategies for the two services offered by XYZ Constructions  The pricing policy is a matter for XYZ Constructions to decide. They could elect to maintain the current 50% mark-up on cost and if they did the price of the RBC would fall by around 7% in line with the costs. This should make them more competitive in the market.  They could also reduce the prices by a little less than 7% (say 5%) in order to increase internal margins a little.

Reasons other than high prices for the current poor sales of RBC:

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 358

 If the quality of work or the reputation and reliability of the builder are questionable, lowering prices is unlikely to boost sales. While it is possible that XYZ Constructions has a strong reputation for IPC but not for RBC, it is more likely that a poor reputation would impact all their products. Poor service or inflexibility in meeting customer needs may also hurt sales and can't be fixed by lowering prices. ي Poor marketing strategies also discourage customers from selecting XYZ Constructions.  XYZ Constructions faces competition and may need to adopt a more competitive pricing strategy, such as 'going rate pricing,' instead of simply adding a markup to costs.  XYZ Constructions could enter the market by pricing some projects competitively to establish a foothold. Completed projects could then be leveraged to attract new customers. (3+3+2+2)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Segregate Overheads – Split ₹600L into labour-hour (₹400L) and ABC-driven (₹200L) costs first.
2. Pre-Compute Rates – Calculate ₹800/labour hr, ₹0.2L/visit, ₹0.2667L/doc upfront.
3. Tabulate Costs – Use a table for RBC/IPC to avoid repetition.
4. Pricing Strategy – Link RBC’s 7% cost drop to market penetration pricing, IPC’s 2% hike to value-based

pricing.

5. Non-Price Reasons – Think RBC-specific: "No brand recall in residential segment" or "IPC-focused sales team."

Examiner Observations Students often make these errors in ABC costing questions:

1. Incorrect Overhead Rate Calculation – Misallocating overheads by using total labour hours (50,000) for all

activities instead of specific drivers (site visits, planning docs).

2. Ignoring Activity Drivers – Applying property-related costs (₹400L) to all activities instead of only labour-hour-

based costs.

3. Profit Markup Errors – Adding 50% to only direct costs instead of total cost (material + labour + overheads).
4. Unit Confusion – Mixing lakhs and rupees (e.g., quoting ₹20,000/site visit instead of ₹0.2L).
5. Pricing Strategy Oversights – Suggesting uniform price cuts without considering competitive positioning (e.g.,

RBC needs aggressive pricing, IPC can sustain hikes).

6. Non-Price Factors – Listing generic reasons like "competition" without specifics (e.g., poor RBC marketing, lack

of customer trust in residential projects).

Question 52. A manufacturing company based in India is planning to transition from its traditional costing system to Activity-Based Costing (ABC) in order to improve cost accuracy and gain better insights into product profitability. Given the company's diverse product portfolio and the complexity of its production processes, the implementation of ABC is expected to provide a more precise allocation of overheads. You are required to SUGGEST the key practical stages involved in successfully implementing an Activity-Based Costing system.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](RTP Sep. 2025)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 52. A number of distinct practical stages that are required in the ABC implementation are given below: (1) Staff Training: The co-operation of the workforce is critical to the successful implementation of ABC. Staff training should be done to create an awareness on the purpose of ABC.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 359

(2) Process Specification: Informal, but structured interviews with key members of personnel will identify the different stages of the production process, the commitment of resources to each, processing times and bottlenecks.

(3) Activity Definition: The activities must be defined clearly in the early stage in order to manage the problems, if any, effectively. There might be overloading of information from the new data, but the same is needed in codification.

(4) Activity Driver Selection: Cost driver for each activity shall be selected.

(5) Assigning Cost: A single representative activity driver can be used to assign costs from the activity pools to the cost objects. (1+1+1+1+1)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Think Chronologically – ABC follows a logical flow: People → Processes → Activities → Drivers → Cost

Assignment.

2. Focus on Practicality – Avoid theoretical jargon; emphasize real-world steps like interviews (Stage 2) and

simple driver selection (Stage 4).

3. Use Mnemonics – Remember "SPADA": a. Staff Training b. Process Specification c. Activity Definition d. Driver Selection e. Assigning Costs

Examiner Observations Students often make the following errors while answering this question:

1. Missing Critical Stages – Some students skip Process Specification (Stage 2), assuming ABC implementation is

purely about cost allocation without analyzing production workflows.

2. Overlooking Staff Training (Stage 1) – Many treat ABC as a technical exercise, ignoring the human factor.

Resistance to change can derail implementation, making training crucial.

3. Confusing Activity Definition (Stage 3) with Cost Allocation – Students sometimes merge Stages 3 & 5, failing

to distinguish between defining activities and assigning costs, leading to unstructured answers.

4. Incorrect Driver Selection (Stage 4) – Some suggest arbitrary cost drivers (e.g., machine hours for all activities)

instead of activity-specific drivers (e.g., setup time for batch-related costs).

5. Overcomplicating Stage 5 – Instead of using a single representative driver, students propose complex multi-

driver models, missing the practical simplicity needed in initial ABC adoption.

Question 53. Explain 'Activity Based Budgeting'.

[5 Marks | 7 Minutes] (PYP Nov ‘18)[Medium | ICAI Fav]

Answer 53. Activity Based Budgeting (ABB)

- Activity based budgeting analyse the resource input or cost for each activity.
- It provides a framework for estimating the amount of resources required in accordance with the budgeted level

of activity.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 360

- Actual results can be compared with budgeted results to highlight both in financial and non- financial terms

those activities with major discrepancies from budget for potential reduction in supply of resources.  It is a planning and control system which seeks to support the objectives of continuous improvement.

- It means planning and controlling the expected activities of the organization to derive a cost- effective budget

that meet forecast workload and agreed strategic goals.

- ABB is the reversing of the ABC process to produce financial plans and budgets. Approach & Time-Saving Tips
1. Start with ABC Connection – Clarify ABB as "ABC in reverse" (budgeting based on activity drivers).
2. Use the P-C-S Framework: a. Planning: Forecast workload → Estimate resources. b. Control: Compare actual vs. budgeted activity costs. c. Strategy: Align budgets with strategic goals.
3. Highlight Key Terms: a. "Activity-driven," "resource input analysis," "continuous improvement."

Examiner Observations Students often make the following mistakes while answering this question:

1. Confusing ABB with Traditional Budgeting – Many students define ABB as just another budgeting method

without highlighting its activity-driven approach, missing the key differentiator.

2. Overlooking the Link to ABC – A significant error is failing to explain that ABB reverses the ABC process (using

cost drivers to forecast budgets rather than allocate costs).

3. Ignoring Non-Financial Aspects – Some focus only on financial discrepancies, skipping ABB’s role in continuous

improvement and strategic goal alignment.

4. Vague Explanations – Instead of concrete steps (e.g., analyzing resource inputs per activity), students provide

generic definitions like "ABB helps in planning."

5. Missing the Control Angle – ABB is not just planning but also a control tool (comparing actual vs. budgeted

activity costs). Many omit this critical function.

(4+2+4) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Prioritize ABC (Part ii) – It’s more complex and carries 6 marks. Solve it first.
2. Use Tabular Format – For ABC driver rates: a. Activity Cost / Total Driver Volume = Rate (e.g., 22,

50,000/1,500 = Rs. 1,500/order).

3. Batch Overheads = Rate × Batch Activity (e.g., 1,500 × 48 orders = Rs. 72,000).
4. Absorption Costing (Part i) – Quick steps: a. OAR = Total Overheads / Prime Cost × 100 = 17.18%. b. Batch Overheads = 30, 13,900 × 17.18% = Rs. 5, 17,930.

Examiner Observations Students frequently commit these errors in this question:

1. Incorrect Absorption Rate Calculation – Many students miscalculate the overhead absorption rate (OAR) by

using total overheads instead of prime cost as the base, leading to wrong product costs in part (i).

2. Misallocating ABC Overheads – In part (ii), some students: a. Use total batch activities instead of activity driver rates (e.g., dividing total setup cost by 40 setups for the batch instead of 2,250 total setups). b. Overlook inspection costs (e.g., using 5 inspections instead of recalculating rates per 2,710 inspections).
3. Ignoring Prime Cost in ABC – A few exclude direct costs (materials + wages) in ABC calculations, focusing only

on overheads.

4. Unit Cost Rounding Errors – Final per-unit costs are often rounded incorrectly (e.g., Rs. 235.46 → Rs. 235 or

236), losing precision.

5. Time Mismanagement – Students spend excessive time on part (i) (absorption costing), leaving inadequate

time for part (ii) (ABC), which carries higher weightage.

Question 55. Star Limited manufacture three products using the same production methods. A conventional product costing system is being used currently. Details of the three products for a typical period are: Product Labour Hrs. per unit Machine Hrs. per unit Materials per Unit1 Volume in Units

AX 1.00 2.00 35 7,500

3. Unit Cost Calculation Oversights – Forgetting to: a. Add direct costs (materials + labor) in ABC. b. Divide total ABC costs by units for per-unit cost.
