Chapter 7

Cost Accounting System

Question 1. A manufacturing company disclosed a net loss of Rs.3, 47,000 as per their cost accounts for the year ended March 31,20X8. The financial accounts however disclosed a net loss of Rs. 5, 10,000 for the same period. The following information was revealed because of scrutiny of the figures of both the sets of accounts. (i) Factory Overheads under-absorbed 40,000 (ii) Administration Overheads over-absorbed 60,000 (iii) Depreciation charged in Financial Accounts 3,25,000 (iv) Depreciation charged in Cost Accounts 2,75,000 (v) Interest on investments not included in Cost Accounts 96,000 (vi) Income-tax provided 54,000 (vii) Interest on loan funds in Financial Accounts 2,45,000 (viii) Transfer fees (credit in financial books) 24,000 (ix) Stores adjustment (credit in financial books) 14,000 (x) Dividend received 32,000 PREPARE a memorandum Reconciliation Account.

[6 Marks | 8 Minutes\](MTP March ‘19, RTP Nov 20)(Old & New SM)[Medium | ICAI Fav]

Answer 1. Memorandum Reconciliation Accounts

(Rs.) (Rs.) To Net Loss as per Costing books 3,47,000 By Administration overheads over 60,000

Recovered in cost accounts To Factory overheads under 40,000 By Interest on investment not included in 96,000 absorbed in Cost Accounts Cost Accounts To Depreciation under charged in 50,000 By Transfer fees in Financial books 24,000 Cost Accounts To Income- Tax not provided in 54,000 By Stores adjustment(Credit in financial 14,000 Cost Accounts books) To Income- Tax not provided 54,000 By Dividend received in financial books 32,000 in Cost Account To Interest on Loan Funds in 2,45,000 Financial Accounts

By Net loss as per Financial books 5,10,000 7,36,000 7,36,000

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Start with Cost Loss (₹3, 47,000).
2. Add expenses only in financial books (loan interest, tax, factory under-absorption, extra depreciation).
3. Deduct incomes only in financial books (dividend, transfer fees, stores adjustment, admin over-absorption).

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 442

4. Ignore common items (already reflected in both accounts).

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with reconciliation problems due to incorrect classification of adjustments (additions vs. deductions) and overlooking items not recorded in cost accounts. Common mistakes include:

1. Misidentifying Over/Under Absorption: Factory overhead under-absorption is added to cost loss (since it’s an

extra cost), but administration overhead over-absorption is deducted (it’s income in cost accounts). Many students reverse these.

2. Depreciation Handling: Missing the difference (₹50,000) between financial (₹3,25,000) and cost (₹2,75,000)

depreciation. Students either ignore it or double-count.

3. Non-Cost Items: Items like interest on investments (₹96,000), dividend (₹32,000), and transfer fees (₹24,000)

are deducted from cost loss (as they’re income in financial books but absent in cost books). Students often add them.

4. Loan Interest & Tax: Interest on loans (₹2,45,000) and tax (₹54,000) are added to cost loss (expenses in

financial books only). Students deduct them or skip tax.

5. Stores Adjustment: Credit in financial books (₹14,000) is deducted (income not in cost books). Students treat it

as an expense.

Question 2. “Is reconciliation of cost accounts and financial accounts necessary in case of integrated accounting system?” EXPLAIN.

[3 Marks | 4 Minutes\](MTP, March ’19, April ‘23 & Sep ’23)(RTP May ’22)[Easy | ICAI Fav]

Answer 2. In integrated accounting system cost and financial accounts are kept in the same set of books. Such a system will have to afford full information required for Costing as well as for Financial Accounts. In other words, information and data should be recorded in such a way so as to enable the firm to ascertain the cost (together with the necessary analysis) of each product, job, process, operation or any other identifiable activity. It also ensures the ascertainment of marginal cost, variances, abnormal losses and gains. In fact all information that management requires from a system of Costing for doing its work properly is made available. The integrated accounts give full information in such a manner so that the profit and loss account and the balance sheet can be prepared according to the requirements of law and the management maintains full control over the liabilities and assets of its business.

Since, only one set of books are kept for both cost accounting and financial accounting purpose so there is no necessity of reconciliation of cost and financial accounts.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Start with a crisp definition: "In an integrated system, cost and financial accounts are maintained in a single set

of books."

2. Directly state the conclusion: "Hence, reconciliation is unnecessary as there are no separate records to

reconcile."

3. Add a one-line justification: "All transactions are recorded once, ensuring consistency between cost and

financial figures."

4. Avoid lengthy explanations—stick to the core logic.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 443

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to a lack of clarity on the key difference between integrated and non-integrated accounting systems. Common mistakes include:

1. Misunderstanding Integration: Some students incorrectly assume that reconciliation is always required, even

in an integrated system, due to confusion between separate vs. single-book accounting.

2. Over-Explaining Non-Integrated Systems: Instead of focusing on why reconciliation is unnecessary in

integrated systems, they waste time describing reconciliation in traditional systems.

3. Missing the Core Logic: The critical point—a single set of books eliminates discrepancies—is often

underemphasized. Students fail to highlight that integrated systems inherently avoid dual recording (which causes mismatches).

4. Unnecessary Details: Some add irrelevant points like "advantages of integrated accounting" without tying them

to the reconciliation question.

Question 3. BRIEF OUT advantages of Integrated Accounts.

[3 Marks | 4 Minutes\](MTP April ’22, Old & New SM)[Easy | ICAI Fav]

Answer 3. Advantages of Integrated Accounts are as follows: (i) No need for Reconciliation- The Question of reconciling costing profit and financial profit does not arise, as there is only one figure of profit. (ii) Less efforts- Due to use of one set of books, there is a significant saving in efforts made. (iii) Less time consuming- No delay is caused in obtaining information as it is provided from books of original entry. (iv) Economical process- It is economical also as it is based on the concept of “Centralisation of Accounting function”.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Memorize 5 Keywords: Reconciliation, Centralization, Time-saving, Cost Control, and Economical.
2. Follow the "1+1 Rule": 1 advantage + 1-line explanation per point. Example: a. "No reconciliation needed – Single profit figure eliminates mismatch disputes."
3. Prioritize ICAI’s Favourites: Always include centralization and cost monitoring (high-weightage).

Examiner Observations Students often underperform in this question due to generic or incomplete answers. Common mistakes include:

1. Listing Without Explanation: Many students just bullet-point advantages (e.g., "No reconciliation

needed") without elaborating why it’s beneficial. For full marks, a 1-line explanation for each point is expected.

2. Missing Key ICAI Keywords: ICAI prefers terms like "centralized accounting," "eliminates duplication," "real-

time data access." Students often use vague phrasing like "saves time" without technical depth.

3. Overlooking Cost-Control Aspect: A unique but expected point is that integrated accounts enable better cost

monitoring (since financial and cost data sync instantly). Most students miss this.

4. Repetition of "No Reconciliation": While important, overemphasizing this (without other points) makes the

answer look incomplete.

(1) Materials issued: Direct Rs. 6,50,000 Indirect (to factory) Rs. 2,30,000 (2) Allocation of wages (25% indirect) Rs. 9,00,000 (3) Under/Over absorbed overheads: Factory (Over) Rs. 60,000 Administration (Under) Rs. 50,000 (4) Payment to Creditors (Trade payables) Rs. 9,00,000 (5) Collection from Debtors (Trade receivables) Rs. 8,00,000

[6 Marks | 8 Minutes\](MTP May 20)[Medium | ICAI Fav]

Answer 4. Journal Entries under Integrated system of accounting

Particulars Rs. Rs. (i) Work-in-Progress Control A/c Dr. 6,50,000 Factory Overhead Control A/c Dr. 2,30,000 To Stores Ledger Control A/c 8,80,000 (Being issue of Direct and Indirect materials) (ii) Work-in Progress Ledger Control A/c Factory Dr. 6,75,000 Overhead control A/c Dr. 2,25,000 To Wages Control A/c 9,00,000 (Being allocation of Direct and Indirect wages) (iii) Factory Overhead Control A/c Dr. 60,000 To Costing Profit & Loss A/c 60,000 (Being transfer of over absorption of Factory overhead) (iv) Costing Profit & Loss A/c Dr. 50,000 To Administration Overhead Control A/c 50,000 (Being transfer of under absorption of Administration overhead) (v) Trade Payables A/c Dr. 9,00,000 To Cash/ Bank A/c 9,00,000 (Being payment made to creditors) (vi) Cash/ Bank A/c Dr. 8,00,000 To Trade receivables A/c 8,00,000 (Being payment received from debtors)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Follow the "Control A/c" Rule: a. All costs flow through Control Accounts (Stores, WIP, Overhead).
2. Over/Under Absorption Shortcut: a. Ask: "Is the system recovering too little (under) or too much (over)?" i. Over = Credit P&L (extra income). ii. Under = Debit P&L (extra expense).
3. Use Proportions for Wages: a. 25% indirect = ₹2, 25,000 to Factory Overhead, rest to WIP.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 445

4. Skip Intermediate Steps: a. Directly record payments/receipts against Trade Payables/Receivables.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with journal entries in integrated accounting due to:

1. Confusing Control Accounts: a. Using incorrect heads like "Material A/c" instead of "Stores Ledger Control A/c" or "Work-in-Progress Control A/c". b. Misallocating indirect costs (e.g., crediting "Factory Overhead" instead of debiting it for under-absorption).
2. Over/Under Absorption Errors: a. Reversing entries for over/under-absorbed overheads (e.g., debiting P&L for over-absorption instead of crediting). b. Missing the Costing P&L A/c entirely, treating adjustments as balance sheet items.
3. Wage Allocation Mistakes: a. Failing to split wages (25% indirect) correctly, leading to incorrect debits to WIP vs. Factory Overhead.
4. Ignoring Trade Receivables/Payables: a. Recording payments/receipts directly in Cash A/c without involving Trade Payables/Receivables.
5. Formatting Issues: a. Omitting "Being..." narratives, which are crucial for clarity in exams.

Question 5. Explain integrated accounting system and state its advantages.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes] (PYP May ‘19)[Easy | ICAI Fav]

Answer 5. Integrated Accounting System: Integrated Accounts is the name given to a system of accounting, whereby cost and financial accounts are kept in the same set of books. Obviously, then there will be no separate sets of books for Costing and Financial records. Integrated accounts provide or meet out fully the information requirement for Costing as well as for Financial Accounts. For Costing it provides information useful for ascertaining the cost of each product, job, and process, operation of any other identifiable activity and for carrying necessary analysis. Integrated accounts provide relevant information which is necessary for preparing profit and loss account and the balance sheets as per the requirement of law and also helps in exercising effective control over the liabilities and assets of its business. (2 marks)

Advantages of Integrated Accounting System The main advantages of Integrated Accounts are as follows: (i) No need for Reconciliation - The question of reconciling costing profit and financial profit does not arise, as there is only one figure of profit. (ii) Less efforts - Due to use of one set of books, there is a significant saving in efforts made. (iii) Less time consuming - No delay is caused in obtaining information as it is provided from books of original entry. (iv) Economical process - It is economical also as it is based on the concept of “Centralization of Accounting function”. (3 marks)

Important Note:- This theoretical question was related to advantages of ‘Integrated Accounting’. Average performance of the examinees was observed. © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 446

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Memorize the Definition: Use ICAI’s phrasing: "Cost and financial accounts maintained in the same set of

books."

2. List Advantages with Keywords: a. No reconciliation (single profit figure). b. Centralization (reduces manpower/software costs). c. Real-time data (no lag in cost/financial reporting). d. Statutory compliance (seamless P&L/Balance Sheet prep).
3. Avoid Examples: No need for case studies—stick to concepts.
4. Use Bullet Points: Saves time and improves readability.

Examiner Observations Students often underperform in this question due to:

1. Vague Definitions: Many fail to clearly define "same set of books"—the core concept of integrated accounting.

Instead, they write generic statements like "cost and financial accounts are combined."

2. Incomplete Advantages: While most list "no reconciliation needed", they miss critical ICAI-preferred

points like: a. Real-time data access (since all entries are unified). b. Better cost control (instant tracking of financial & cost impacts).

3. Repetitive Explanations: Students elaborate excessively on "economical" or "time-saving" but skip legal

compliance (how it simplifies statutory reporting).

4. No Structure: Answers often lack headings (Definition, Advantages) or bullet points, making them harder to

evaluate.

Question 6. Explain what are the pre-requisites of integrated accounting.

[4 Marks | 5 Minutes\](PYP Nov 20, RTP May’23) (SM May 22, MTP Mar’22)[Medium | ICAI Fav]

Answer 6.The essential pre-requisites for integrated accounts include the following steps:

- The management’s decision about the extent of integration of the two sets of books. Some concerns find it

useful to integrate up to the stage of prime cost or factory cost while other prefers full integration of the entire accounting records.

- A suitable coding system must be made available so as to serve the accounting purposes of financial and cost

accounts.

- An agreed routine, with regard to the treatment of provision for accruals, prepaid expenses, other adjustment

necessary for preparation of interim accounts.

- Perfect coordination should exist between the staff responsible for the financial and cost aspects of the

accounts and an efficient processing of accounting documents should be ensured.

- Under this system there is no need for a separate cost ledger. Of course there will be a number of subsidiary

ledgers; in addition to the useful Customers’ Ledger and the Bought Ledger, there will be: (a) Stores Ledger; (b) Stock Ledger and (c) Job Ledger.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Use the "5-Point Framework": Memorize:

a. Management decision → Coding → Adjustments → Coordination → Subsidiary ledgers.

2. Explain Briefly: 1 line per point (e.g., "A unified coding system ensures cost/financial data is captured

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 447

simultaneously").

3. Highlight Subsidiary Ledgers: Explicitly name stores, stock, and job ledgers (ICAI expects these).
4. Avoid Redundancy: Skip examples—focus on concepts.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to:

1. Missing Key Pre-requisites: Many only mention coding systems and coordination, but overlook critical points

like: a. Management decision on integration level (prime cost vs. full integration). b. Treatment of accruals/prepaid expenses (essential for interim accounts).

2. Vague Explanations: Stating "a suitable coding system is needed" without elaboration on how it enables dual

reporting (financial + cost).

3. Ignoring Subsidiary Ledgers: Failing to specify stores, stock, and job ledgers as mandatory components.
4. Disorganized Structure: Answers often lack logical flow (e.g., discussing subsidiary ledgers before coding

systems).

5. Overemphasis on Obvious Points: Excessive focus on "no separate cost ledger" while neglecting process

adjustments (accruals, prepayments).

Question 7. Briefly explain the essential features of a good Cost Accounting System.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](PYP May’22, RTP Nov’18, MTP Oct’22)[Easy | ICAI Fav]

Answer 7. The essential features, which a good cost accounting system should possess, are as follows: (a) Informative and simple: Cost accounting system should be tailor-made, practical, simple and capable of meeting the requirements of a business concern. The system of costing should not sacrifice the utility by introducing inaccurate and unnecessary details.

(b) Accurate and authentic: The data to be used by the cost accounting system should be accurate and authenticated; otherwise it may distort the output of the system and a wrong decision may be taken.

(c) Uniformity and consistency: There should be uniformity and consistency in classification, treatment and reporting of cost data and related information. This is required for benchmarking and comparability of the results of the system for both horizontal and vertical analysis.

(d) Integrated and inclusive: The cost accounting system should be integrated with other systems like financial accounting, taxation, statistics and operational research etc. to have a complete overview and clarity in results.

(e) Flexible and adaptive: The cost accounting system should be flexible enough to make necessary amendment and modifications in the system to incorporate changes in technological, reporting, regulatory and other requirements.

(f) Trust on the system: Management should have trust on the system and its output. For this, an active role of management is required for the development of such a system that reflects a strong conviction in using information for decision making.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 448

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Use the "6-Feature Framework": Memorize: a. Simple → Accurate → Uniform → Integrated → Flexible →

Trusted.

2. One-Line Justification per Point: a. "Integration with taxation/operations research avoids data silos."
3. Prioritize ICAI Keywords: a. Benchmarking (for uniformity), Regulatory agility (for flexibility). b. Avoid Examples: Stick to conceptual clarity.

Examiner Observations Students often underperform in this question due to:

1. Superficial Explanations: Many list features like "simple" or "accurate" without justifying why they matter

(e.g., "Simple systems avoid unnecessary complexity that delays decision-making").

2. Missing Key Features: Overlooking critical ICAI-preferred points like: a. Integration with other systems (taxation, operations research). b. Management trust (system output must be reliable for decision-making).
3. Redundancy: Repetitive emphasis on "accuracy" or "flexibility" without distinct elaboration for each point.
4. Disorganized Structure: Answers lack logical flow (e.g., discussing "flexibility" before "uniformity").
5. Ignoring Practical Implications: Failing to link features to real-world outcomes (e.g., "Uniformity enables

benchmarking across periods").

Question 8. EXPLAIN what the essential pre-requisites of Integrated Accounting are System.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](Study Material)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 8. Essential pre-requisites for Integrated Accounts The essential pre-requisites for integrated accounts include the following steps:

1. The management’s decision about the extent of integration of the two sets of books. Some concerns find it

useful to integrate up to the stage of prime cost or factory cost while other prefers full integration of the entire accounting records.

2. A suitable coding system must be made available so as to serve the accounting purposes of financial and cost

accounts.

3. An agreed routine, with regard to the treatment of provision for accruals, prepaid expenses, other adjustment

necessary for preparation of interim accounts.

4. Perfect coordination should exist between the staff responsible for the financial and cost aspects of the

accounts and an efficient processing of accounting documents should be ensured. Under this system there is no need for a separate cost ledger. Of course, there will be a number of subsidiary ledgers; in addition to the useful Customers’ Ledger and the Purchase Ledger, there will be: (a) Stores Ledger; (b) Stock Ledger and (c) Job Ledger.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Use the "5-Point Framework": Memorize: a. Management decision → Coding → Adjustments → Coordination → Subsidiary ledgers.
2. Explain Briefly: 1 line per point (e.g., "A unified coding system ensures cost/financial data is captured

simultaneously").

3. Highlight Subsidiary Ledgers: Explicitly name stores, stock, and job ledgers (ICAI expects these).
4. Avoid Redundancy: Skip examples—focus on concepts.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 449

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this question due to:

1. Incomplete Coverage: Many miss critical pre-requisites like: a. Level of integration (prime cost vs. full integration). b. Subsidiary ledgers (stores, stock, job ledgers).
2. Vague Explanations: Stating "a coding system is needed" without elaborating on how it enables dual reporting

(financial + cost).

3. Ignoring Adjustment Routines: Overlooking accruals/prepayments treatment, which is crucial for interim

accounts.

4. Disorganized Structure: Answers often lack logical flow (e.g., discussing subsidiary ledgers before coding

systems).

5. Overemphasis on Obvious Points: Excessive focus on "no separate cost ledger" while

neglecting coordination and document processing.

Question 9. STATE what are the advantages of Integrated Accounting?

[4 Marks | 5 Minutes\](Study Material)[Easy | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 9. The main advantages of Integrated Accounts are as follows: (a) No need for Reconciliation- The question of reconciling costing profit and financial profit does not arise, as there is only one figure of profit.

(b) Less efforts- Due to use of one set of books, there is a significant saving in efforts made.

(c) Less time consuming- No delay is caused in obtaining information as it is provided from books of original entry.

(d) Economical process- It is economical also as it is based on the concept of “Centralization of Accounting function”.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Memorize the "Core 4" Advantages: a. No reconciliation → Effort/time-saving → Economical →

Centralization.

2. Add 1-Line Explanations: a. "Centralization eliminates duplicate data entry, reducing costs."
3. Prioritize ICAI Keywords: a. "Single profit figure," "books of original entry," "centralization."

Examiner Observations Students often underperform in this question due to:

1. Listing Without Explanation: Many students merely bullet-point advantages (e.g., "No reconciliation

needed") without justifying why it’s beneficial (e.g., "Eliminates disputes between cost and financial teams").

2. Missing Key Advantages: Overlooking ICAI-preferred points like: a. Real-time decision-making (data is instantly available). b. Regulatory compliance (seamless adherence to Companies Act).
3. Superficial Treatment of "Economical": Stating it’s "cost-effective" without elaboration (e.g., "Reduces

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 450

software, manpower, and training costs").

4. Repetition: Overemphasizing "time-saving" or "effort-saving" without distinct reasoning.
5. No Structure: Answers often lack headings or logical flow, making them harder to evaluate.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Follow the Transaction Flow: a. Purchases → Issues → Wages → Overheads → Production → Sales.
2. Use Control Accounts Religiously: a. All costs flow through Control Accounts (Stores, WIP, Overheads).
3. Highlight Key Splits: a. 50% credit terms for purchases/sales. b. 50% direct wages to WIP, rest to overheads.
4. Verify Overheads: a. Ensure Rs. 1,00,000 charged to WIP includes Rs. 80,000 incurred + Rs. 20,000 over-

absorbed.

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with integrated accounting journal entries due to:

1. Control Account Confusion: a. Using generic names like "Material A/c" instead of "Stores Ledger Control A/c" or "Work-in-Process Control A/c". b. Misallocating entries (e.g., debiting "Factory Overhead" directly to P&L instead of control accounts).
2. Wage Allocation Errors: a. Failing to split direct (50%) vs. indirect wages correctly. b. Omitting the Wages Control A/c as an intermediary.
3. Overhead Treatment Mistakes: a. Incorrectly recording overhead absorption (e.g., not matching incurred vs. charged amounts). b. Missing the Selling & Distribution Overhead entry entirely.
4. Credit Sales/Purchases Oversights: a. Not segregating cash vs. credit transactions (50% credit terms given). b. Incorrectly recording debtors/creditors movements.
5. Cost of Sales Calculation: a. Forgetting to include Selling Overheads in cost of sales. b. Double-counting or omitting Finished Goods transfers.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 452

(i) Credit Purchase of Material Rs. 27,000 (ii) Manufacturing overhead charged to Production Rs. 6,000 (iii) Selling and Distribution overheads recovered from Sales Rs. 4,000 (vi) Indirect wages incurred Rs. 8,000 (v) Material returned from production to stores Rs. 9,000

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](PYP Nov’19, MTP Oct ’21)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 11. Journal entries are as follows:

Dr. Cr. (Rs.) (Rs.) (i) Stores Ledger Control A/c…………………… Dr. 27,000 To Cost Ledger Control A/c 27,000 (ii) Work-in-Process Control A/c........................... Dr. 6,000 To Manufacturing Overhead Control A/c 6,000 (iii) Cost of Sales A/c……………………………… Dr. 4,000 To Selling & Dist. Overhead Control A/c 4,000 (iv) (1) Wage Control A/c…………………… Dr. 8,000 To Cost Ledger Control A/c 8,000 (2) Manufacturing Overhead Control A/c……… Dr. 8,000 To Wages Control A/c 8,000

OR Manufacturing Overhead Control A/c……………. Dr. 8,000 To Cost Ledger Control A/c 8,000 (v) Stores Ledger Control A/c ……………………… Dr. 9,000 To Work-in-Process Control A/c 9,000

Important Note:- This was a theoretical question based on Non-Integrated system of accounting. Average performance was observed by the examinees.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Identify Non-Integrated System – Ensure entries are purely within cost books (no financial accounts like

Creditors/Cash).

2. Follow Cost Accounting Flow – Material → WIP → Overheads → Sales, maintaining control accounts.
3. Indirect Wages Focus – Remember indirect wages first hit Wage Control A/c before being transferred to

Overhead A/c (or direct entry).

4. Quick Checks – a. All entries must involve Cost Ledger Control A/c (credit side for expenses). b. Overheads must align with their respective control accounts.

Examiner Observations Students often commit the following errors while attempting this question:

1. Confusing Non-Integrated with Integrated System – Some students incorrectly treat Cost Ledger Control A/c as

part of financial books, leading to wrong entries like debiting Creditors A/c instead of Stores Ledger Control A/c.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 453

2. Incorrect Treatment of Overheads – Manufacturing overheads charged to production (entry ii) are sometimes

debited to Cost of Sales A/c instead of WIP Control A/c.

3. Double Entry for Indirect Wages – Many students miss the dual entry (Wage Control A/c → Manufacturing

Overhead A/c) and directly credit Cost Ledger Control A/c, ignoring the intermediate wage control account.

4. Material Returns Misclassification – Material returned to stores (entry v) is often credited to Stores Ledger

Control A/c instead of WIP Control A/c, disrupting inventory tracking.

5. Overhead Recovery Confusion – Selling overheads recovered from sales (entry iii) are occasionally debited to

Overhead Control A/c instead of Cost of Sales A/c.

1. Incorrect Absorption Rates – Misapplying factory overheads (20% of prime cost) or administrative overheads

(10% of factory cost), leading to wrong cost calculations.

2. Closing Stock Valuation Errors – Using financial accounting stock value (₹1,50,000) instead of cost accounting

value (₹2,05,846) in reconciliation.

3. Overhead Mismanagement – Failing to identify over/under-absorption of factory, administrative, and selling

expenses, causing reconciliation mismatches.

4. Dividend & Non-Cost Items – Omitting dividend income (₹80,000) or preliminary expenses (₹70,000) in

reconciliation, as they do not appear in cost accounts.

5. Profit Balancing Mistake – Incorrectly computing profit in cost accounts due to arithmetic errors in cost sheet

preparation.

6. Reconciliation Format Errors – Not structuring adjustments properly (additions vs. deductions) or missing key

reconciling items.

The financial accounts however disclosed a net profit of Rs. 6, 94,000 for the same period. The following information was revealed as a result of scrutiny of the figures of both the sets of accounts.

(Rs.) (i) Factory Overheads under-absorbed 80,000 (ii) Administration Overheads over-absorbed 1,20,000 (iii) Depreciation charged in Financial Accounts 6,50,000 (iv) Depreciation charged in Cost Accounts 5,50,000 (v) Interest on investments not included in Cost Accounts 1,92,000 (vi) Income-tax provided 1,08,000 (vii) Interest on loan funds in Financial Accounts 4,90,000 (viii) Transfer fees (credit in financial books) 48,000 (ix) Stores adjustment (credit in financial books) 28,000 (x) Dividend received 64,000 PREPARE a Reconciliation statement.

[6 Marks |8 Minutes\](MTP April 23, March ’21)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 13 Statement of Reconciliation

Particulars Amount (Rs.) Amount (Rs.) Net profit as per Cost accounts 10,20,000 Add: Administration Overheads over-absorbed 1,20,000 Interest on investments 1,92,000 Transfer fees 48,000 Stores adjustment 28,000 Dividend received 64,000 4,52,000 Less: Factory Overheads under-absorbed 80,000

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 456

Depreciation under charged 1,00,000 Income-tax provided 1,08,000 Interest on loan funds 4,90,000 (7,78,000) Net profit as per Financial accounts 6,94,000

Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Segregate Adjustments – a. Add: Over-absorbed admin overheads, non-cost incomes (interest, dividends,

fees). b. Deduct: Under-absorbed factory overheads, tax, loan interest, and depreciation shortfall.

2. Depreciation Focus – Deduct the difference (₹1,00,000) since cost accounts undercharged it.
3. Non-Operating Items – Add transfer fees (₹48,000) and stores adjustment (₹28,000) as they’re financial

credits.

4. Quick Verification – Ensure adjustments reconcile ₹10,20,000 (cost) to ₹6,94,000 (financial).

Examiner Observations Students often struggle with this reconciliation question due to:

1. Misclassification of Adjustments – Confusing additions (e.g., over-absorbed overheads, non-cost incomes)

with deductions (e.g., under-absorbed overheads, financial expenses).

2. Depreciation Discrepancy – Missing the ₹1,00,000 difference (₹6,50,000 – ₹5,50,000) as a deduction, treating

it as a standalone item instead of a reconciling adjustment.

3. Non-Cost Items Ignored – Overlooking interest on investments (₹1, 92,000), transfer fees (₹48,000), or

dividend (₹64,000) as additions since they’re excluded in cost accounts.

4. Tax and Interest Errors – Failing to deduct income tax (₹1,08,000) and loan interest (₹4,90,000) as these are

financial-only items.

5. Stores Adjustment Misinterpretation – Incorrectly treating the ₹28,000 credit (financial books) as a deduction

instead of an addition.

6. Arithmetic Mistakes – Miscalculating the net effect of adjustments, leading to mismatched profits.

overheads).

Performance of the examinees was above average. Overall performance in this compulsory question was average.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips To solve this quickly, always follow a two-column thought process:

1. Cost Items (Add/Deduct): Identify items in cost books that are not in financial accounts (like under/over-

recovered overheads, obsolescence, provisions). Place them on the debit or credit side accordingly.

2. Financial Items (Add/Deduct): Identify incomes or charges in financial books absent in cost books (dividends,

interest, depreciation differences, store adjustments).

3. Depreciation Shortcut: Instead of recalculating total, directly take the difference between cost recovered and

financial charged.

4. Final Check: Ensure total debits = total credits.

Examiner Observations This question tests a candidate’s ability to reconcile profits between cost and financial accounts, a standard ICAI topic. Common mistakes observed in exams include:

1. Misclassification of items: Students often confuse items to be added or deducted. For instance, “Works

Overhead under-recovered” should always be added to cost profit, while “Office Overhead over-recovered” should be deducted. Some candidates wrongly treat both as adjustments in the same direction.

2. Omission of income items: Dividend and interest income are often ignored, reducing marks unnecessarily.
3. Depreciation adjustments: Students frequently miscalculate the difference between depreciation charged in

financial accounts and recovered in cost books. Correct identification of “overcharged” vs. “recovered” is crucial.

4. Stores adjustments and obsolescence: Many overlook these adjustments or misplace them on the wrong side

of the memorandum account.

5. Mechanical errors: Addition and balancing errors are surprisingly common, given the numbers are relatively

simple.

Question 17. GK Ltd. showed net loss of Rs. 2, 43,300 as per their financial accounts for the year ended 31st March, 2018. However, cost accounts disclosed net loss of Rs. 2, 48,300 for the same period. On scrutinizing both the set of books of accounts, the following information were revealed:

Rs. (i) Works overheads over recovered 30,400 30,000 (ii) Selling overheads under recovered 20,300 (iii) Administrative overheads under recovered 27,700 (iv) Depreciation over charged in cost accounts 35,100 (v) Bad debts w/off in financial accounts 15,000 (vi) Preliminary Exp. w/off in financial accounts 5,000 (vii) Interest credited during the year in financial accounts 7,500

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 462

Prepare a reconciliation statement reconciling losses shown by financial and cost accounts by taking costing net loss as base.

[6 Marks |8 Minutes\](PYP May’18)[Medium | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 17

Reconciliation Statement Particulars Rs. Rs. Loss as per Cost Accounts (2,48,300) Add: Works overheads over recovered 30,400 Depreciation over charged in cost accounts 35,100 Interest credited during the year in financial accounts 7,500 73,000 Less: Selling overheads under recovered 20,300 Administrative overheads under recovered 27,700 Bad debts w/off in financial accounts 15,000 Preliminary Exp. w/off in financial accounts 5,000 (68,000) Loss as per Financial Accounts (2,43,300)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips A quick method is to classify adjustments into two types:

1. Cost items causing difference: Over/under recovery, depreciation difference. Check whether these increase

or decrease loss relative to cost accounts.

2. Financial items not in cost accounts: Interest income, bad debts, preliminary expenses. Decide addition or

deduction based on effect on financial loss.

Examiner Observations This question requires reconciling losses between cost and financial accounts, with cost loss as the base. Common mistakes observed in exams include:

1. Incorrect sign treatment: Students frequently misplace over-recoveries and under-recoveries. For example,

“Works overheads over-recovered” should be added to cost loss (since cost accounts understate profit/loss), but many treat it as a deduction. Similarly, under-recovered selling/administrative overheads should be deducted.

2. Confusion between additions and deductions: Items like interest credited or depreciation overcharged are

sometimes incorrectly added or deducted. Accurate interpretation of “overcharged” vs “undercharged” is crucial.

3. Omission of financial charges: Preliminary expenses and bad debts are often ignored in reconciliation, reducing

marks.

4. Mechanical mistakes in calculation: Simple addition and subtraction errors occur due to large numbers.
5. Misinterpretation of question base: Using financial loss as base instead of costing loss (as specifically asked) is

a common error.

In the preparation of the cost sheet, examinees faced problems in the identification of absorbed indirect expenses on the basis of normal production capacity. Performance of the examinees was below average.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips To solve quickly and avoid errors:

1. Classify overheads first: Identify variable vs. fixed components and absorb fixed overheads on normal capacity,

while variable overheads are fully applied.

2. Prepare a mini cost sheet: Start with prime cost → factory/admin overheads → works cost → cost of

production → cost of sales → profit.

3. Reconciliation shortcut: Compare profit per cost account with financial profit. Add non-cost incomes

(dividend), subtract costs or losses not included in cost accounts.

4. Time-saving tip: Use balancing figure method for profit instead of recalculating every component from scratch.

Examiner Observations This question integrates cost sheet preparation with reconciliation of profits, testing both cost accounting and financial accounting concepts. Common mistakes observed include:

1. Incorrect classification of overheads: Students often misclassify fixed and variable components. For example,

treating factory overheads as fully fixed or selling overheads as partially fixed leads to incorrect absorption.

2. Errors in proportioning fixed overheads: Apportioning fixed overheads based on actual production instead of

normal production capacity is a frequent error. Many candidates calculate fixed factory/admin overheads on the 15,000 units produced rather than scaling from 20,000 units normal capacity.

3. Ignoring notional rent: Some students omit the notional rent charged in cost accounts, reducing the accuracy

of the reconciliation.

4. Misalignment in reconciliation adjustments: Dividend received, loss on sale of investments, or

under/overcharged overheads are sometimes added/deducted incorrectly.

5. Mechanical errors: Balancing the cost sheet and the reconciliation statement with large numbers causes

addition/subtraction mistakes.

Important Note:- Question was on preparation of reconciliation statement to calculate the profit as per financial records. This sub part can be considered as an easy one and most of the examinees attempted in the correct line. Performance of the examinees was good.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips To solve quickly:

1. Classify adjustments into two categories:  Items in cost accounts but not in financial accounts (e.g., over/under recovery, stock valuation).  Items in financial accounts but not in cost accounts (e.g., rent, bad debts, tax, loss on assets).
2. Determine impact on profit: Ask: “Does this adjustment increase or decrease profit when moving from cost to

financial accounts?”

3. Use mini two-column approach: Add items that increase profit; deduct items that decrease profit.
4. Time-saving tip: Avoid recalculating net profit; use the balancing figure method.

Examiner Observations This question tests the candidate’s ability to reconcile profit between cost and financial accounts, a fundamental topic in Cost Accounting. Performance was generally good, but typical mistakes included:

1. Incorrect classification of items: Students sometimes misinterpret which items should be added or deducted.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 466

For instance, over-recovery of selling overheads in cost accounts increases profit, so it should be added, while under-recovery of administration overheads reduces profit, so it should be deducted. Misplacing these adjustments is a common error.

2. Ignoring financial account items: Some candidates omit adjustments like income tax, rent received, or loss on

sale of capital assets, leading to incorrect reconciliation.

3. Mechanical mistakes: Errors in addition/subtraction, especially with multiple items, are frequent despite the

problem being simple.

4. Overlapping adjustments: Overvaluation of closing stock in cost accounts vs financial accounts is sometimes

misunderstood. Candidates may double-count or omit it.

Question 20. Indicate, for following items, whether to be shown in the Cost Accounts or Financial Accounts: (i) Preliminary expenses written off during the year (ii) Interest received on bank deposits (iii) Dividend, interest received on investments (iv) Salary for the proprietor at notional figure though not incurred (v) Charges in lieu of rent where premises are owned (vi) Rent receivables (vii) Loss on sale of Fixed Assets (viii) Interest on capital at notional figure though not incurred (ix) Goodwill written off (x) Notional Depreciation on the assets fully depreciated for which book value is Nil.

[5 Marks | 5 Minutes\](PYP Nov 22)[Easy | ICAI Fav | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 20 S. No. Items Accounts (i) Preliminary expenses written off during the year Financial Accounts (ii) Interest received on bank deposits Financial Accounts (iii) Dividend, interest received on investments Financial Accounts (iv) Salary for the proprietor at notional figure though not incurred Cost Accounts (v) Charges in lieu of rent where premises are owned Cost Accounts (vi) Rent receivables Financial Accounts (vii) Loss on the sales of Fixed Assets Financial Accounts (viii) Interest on capital at notional figure though not incurred Cost Accounts (ix) Goodwill written off Financial Accounts (x) Notional Depreciation on the assets fully depreciated for which book value is Cost Accounts

nil

Approach & Time-Saving Tips To solve quickly:

1. Identify nature of item: Ask, “Is this related to production cost or actual financial transaction?”
2. Notional items belong to cost accounts: Any expense not involving cash but related to production or capital

usage (proprietor’s salary, notional rent, interest on capital, notional depreciation) goes to cost accounts.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 467

3. Actual cash/investment transactions belong to financial accounts: Dividend, rent received, bad debts,

preliminary expense write-off, goodwill write-off, and losses on asset sale are financial.

4. Use simple mental shortcuts: “Notional = Cost, Cash/Statutory = Financial.” This avoids confusion and speeds

up answering.

Examiner Observations This question tests the candidate’s conceptual clarity on the distinction between Cost Accounts and Financial Accounts, which is fundamental in Cost Accounting. Common mistakes observed in exams include:

1. Notional or theoretical items: Many students incorrectly classify notional charges such as proprietor’s salary,

notional rent, interest on capital, and notional depreciation. These are cost items even if not incurred in cash, but some candidates mistakenly treat them as financial items.

2. Capital vs revenue items: Items like preliminary expenses written off or goodwill written off are financial

account items, but students sometimes classify them under cost accounts due to their “expense” nature.

3. Income items confusion: Rent receivable, interest, and dividend income are often misclassified as cost account

adjustments rather than financial account items.

4. Losses on fixed assets: Some candidates incorrectly include this in cost accounts, though it only affects financial

accounts.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips  Classify costs first: Direct costs → WIP, Indirect costs → Factory/Admin OH Control.  Over/Under absorption treatment: Over-absorbed OH → Credit P&L, Under-absorbed OH → Debit P&L.  Stock deficiency: Normal loss is part of overheads → charge to Factory OH, not P&L directly.  Mental shortcut: For integrated accounts, think in sequence: Materials → WIP → Factory/Admin OH → Costing P&L → Financial P&L.  Time-saving: Prepare a small template with Dr/Cr placements and standard narration lines; plug in figures directly.

Examiner Observations This question tests a candidate’s understanding of integrated accounting, specifically the journal entries for direct/indirect costs and over/under absorption of overheads. Performance was moderate, but common mistakes observed include:

1. Misclassification of accounts: Some students confuse Factory Overhead Control A/c with Costing P&L A/c for

over/under absorption entries. Over absorption should be credited to Costing P&L, while under absorption is debited from Costing P&L.

2. Incorrect treatment of stock deficiencies: Normal loss in raw materials should be charged to Factory Overhead

Control, not directly to P&L or WIP. Many students incorrectly posted it to Stores Ledger Control only.

3. Mixing direct and indirect costs: Direct materials must be posted to WIP Ledger Control, while indirect wages

go to Factory Overhead Control. Some students reversed this treatment.

4. Omission of narration: Proper narration is essential in ICAI exams; missing or incorrect narration can lead to

loss of marks.

5. Mechanical errors: Addition/subtraction errors or reversed Dr/Cr postings are common due to large numbers.

Question 22. EXPLAIN why it is necessary to reconcile the Profits between the Cost Accounts and Financial Accounts.

[4 Marks | 5 Minutes\](Study Material)[Easy | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 22. When the cost and financial accounts are kept separately, it is imperative that these should be reconciled to make the cost accounts reliable. It is necessary for reconciliation of the two sets of accounts that sufficient details are available to locate the differences and the reasons for the same. It is, therefore, important that in the financial accounts, the expenses should be analysed in the same way as in the cost accounts.

The General Ledger Adjustment Account in the Cost Ledger may be studied to know the items which are included here and how differently these are presented in the financial accounts. The reconciliation of the balances of two sets of accounts is possible by preparing a Memorandum Reconciliation Account. In this account, the items charged in one set of accounts but not in the other or those charged in excess as compared to the other are identified and collected. These items of differences are either added or subtracted from the profit as shown by

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 469

one of the accounts. Finally the profits from two sets of accounts are reconciled. The procedure is similar to those which are followed for reconciling bank balance as per bank ledger with the balance as shown in bank statement. It is important, however, to know the causes which, generally, give rise to differences in the Cost and Financial Accounts.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips When attempting theory questions like this, first define reconciliation, then explain why it is required, followed by how it is done and finally state examples/causes. A quick 4-step framework is: (a) Reliability of cost accounts, (b) Analysis of differences, (c) Memorandum Reconciliation Account, (d) Similar to Bank Reconciliation.

Examiner Observations This theoretical question is straightforward but requires conceptual clarity and structured presentation. Many students did not score full marks because of the following common mistakes:

1. Incomplete coverage: Some students only wrote “to find out the difference between profits in Cost and

Financial Accounts” without explaining the reliability and control function of reconciliation.

2. Lack of examples: Good answers mention items like under/over absorption of overheads, notional charges,

purely financial incomes/expenses. Many students ignored examples, which cost them marks.

3. Confusing reconciliation with rectification: Some students wrongly assumed reconciliation means correction of

errors. Examiners noted that reconciliation is about identifying and explaining differences, not correcting them.

4. Poor structure: Instead of logical steps (objective → need → method → causes), students wrote in long

paragraphs, making it unclear.

5. Missing linkage with Cost Audit: ICAI expects students to connect reconciliation with making cost data reliable

for decision-making. Very few students highlighted this.

Question 23. STATE what are the reasons for disagreement of profits as per Cost Accounts and Financial Accounts? Discuss.

[6 Marks | 5 Minutes\](Study Material)[Easy | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 23. 1. Items included in Financial Accounts only- (a) Purely Financial Expenses: (i) Interest on loans or bank mortgages. (ii) Expenses and discounts on issue of shares, debentures etc. (iii) Other capital losses i.e., loss by fire not covered by insurance etc. (iv) Losses on the sales of fixed assets and investments (v) Income tax, donations, subscriptions (vi) Expenses of the company’s share transfer office, if any. (b) Purely Financial Income (i) Interest received on bank deposits, loans and investments (ii) Dividends received (iii) Profits on the sale of fixed assets and investments (iv) Transfer fee received. (v) Rent receivables (2 marks)

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 470

2. Item included in Cost Accounts only (notional expenses):

(i) Charges in lieu of rent where premises are owned (ii) Interest on capital at notional figure though not incurred (iii) Salary for the proprietor at notional figure though not incurred (iv) Notional Depreciation on the assets fully depreciated for which book value is nil. (1 mark)

3. Items whose treatment is different in the two sets of accounts: The objective of cost accounting is to provide

information to management for decision making and control purposes while financial accounting conforms to external reporting requirements. Hence there are chances that certain items are treated differently in the two sets of accounts. For example, LIFO method for inventory valuation is not recommended by Accounting Standards for Financial Reporting purpose but this method may be adopted for cost accounting purpose if management feels it suitable for making any decision. Similarly cost accounting may use a different method of depreciation than what is allowed under financial accounting. (2 marks)

4. Varying basis of valuation: It is another factor which sometimes is responsible for the difference. It is well

known that in financial accounts stock are valued either at cost or market price, whichever is lower. But in Cost Accounts, stocks are only valued at cost. (1 mark)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips For this type of theory, use a classification approach: (i) Financial items only, (ii) Notional items only, (iii) Different treatment, (iv) Valuation differences.

Examiner Observations This question is purely conceptual and requires systematic coverage of the four main heads of differences. While it is a direct question, many students failed to score full marks due to the following mistakes:

1. Incomplete listing: Students often stop after writing “purely financial incomes/expenses” and forget to include

notional charges and differences in valuation methods. Examiners noted this as the most common reason for losing marks.

2. Lack of examples: ICAI expects at least one or two examples under each head. Many students only mentioned

“interest, dividend, rent” without citing items like share transfer expenses, LIFO vs. AS-2 conflict, notional depreciation, etc.

3. Poor structure: Students often write in a paragraph form rather than a classified format (Items in financial

accounts only, items in cost accounts only, different treatments, valuation differences). This reduces clarity.

4. Confusion with reconciliation: Some students wrongly wrote the reconciliation procedure instead of reasons

for disagreement.

5. Overwriting obvious points: Many wrote that “cost accounts are for internal use and financial for external use”

but did not connect this with impact on profit differences.

Question 24. STATE when the Reconciliation statement of Cost and Financial accounts is not required.

[3 Marks | 4 Minutes\](Study Material)[Easy | ICAI Fav]

Answer 24. Procedure for Reconciliation There are 3 steps involved in the procedure for reconciliation.

1. Ascertainment of profit as per Financial Accounts

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 471

2. Ascertainment of profit as per Cost Accounts
3. Reconciliation of both the profits

Circumstances where reconciliation statement can be avoided: When the Cost and Financial Accounts are integrated - there is no need to have a separate reconciliation statement between the two sets of accounts. Integration means that the same set of accounts fulfil the requirement of both i.e., Cost and Financial Accounts.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips For a quick and precise answer:  First, directly state the condition: “Reconciliation not required when cost and financial accounts are integrated.”  Then, briefly explain integration in one line: “Integration means the same accounting entries serve both purposes; hence no differences arise.”  Avoid repeating reconciliation procedure, examples, or reasons for differences, as this wastes time.

Examiner Observations This is a conceptual question that tests candidates’ understanding of integrated accounts. While the answer is short, many students make the following mistakes:

1. Describing reconciliation procedure unnecessarily: Many students wrote the 3-step procedure of

reconciliation even though the question specifically asks when it is not required. This wastes time and shows lack of focus.

2. Vague or incomplete answers: Some students wrote “when accounts are correct” or “when profits match”

without explaining the concept of integration, which is the key point. Examiners noted that mere mention of “no need” without justification loses marks.

3. Mixing with reconciliation of branch/ledger accounts: Occasionally, students confuse this with bank

reconciliation or branch profit reconciliation, which is irrelevant here.

4. Not mentioning the definition of integrated accounts: ICAI expects the answer to briefly define integrated

accounts to justify why reconciliation is unnecessary.

(6+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips  Stepwise posting: Start from Stores and Wages, then post to WIP, Finished Goods, and Costing P&L. Track Building Construction separately.  Direct vs Indirect costs: Always classify carefully—direct materials/wages → WIP, indirect → OH Control.  Loss treatment: Loss on materials → Factory OH, not P&L directly.  Absorption of overheads: Over/under absorption should be posted to Costing P&L A/c.  Gross Profit margin: Use GP% to compute Finished Goods valuation for COGS.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 475

 Quick Tip: Prepare a cost flow diagram before entering accounts—it reduces posting errors and saves time.

Examiner Observations This is a comprehensive practical question testing candidates’ understanding of job costing, historic costing, and control accounts in a non-integrated system. Performance was moderate to low. Common mistakes included:

1. Misallocation of materials and wages: Students often failed to split direct and indirect wages correctly among

WIP, Factory OH, and Building Construction. Similarly, issuing materials to building construction or maintenance was sometimes omitted or misposted.

2. Incorrect treatment of under/over absorption: Many students did not post under-absorbed overheads to

Costing P&L A/c, or posted over-absorbed amounts incorrectly.

3. Handling of losses in raw materials: Some students charged the loss directly to P&L instead of treating it as

part of Factory OH, which distorted WIP and Finished Goods balances.

4. Balancing control accounts: Errors in calculating closing balances of Stores, WIP, Finished Goods led to trial

balance mismatch.

5. Flow of costs to COGS and profit calculation: Candidates often ignored gross profit margin, leading to errors in

Finished Goods valuation and Costing P&L.

Fixed costs must be absorbed on normal capacity, not actual production.  Prepare Cost Sheet: Start with direct costs, add absorbed overheads proportionally, then calculate profit as balancing figure.  Reconciliation: Add incomes like interest/dividend and adjust undercharged overheads to arrive at profit per

Examiner Observations This is a practical question combining financial and cost accounting, testing candidates’ understanding of absorption costing, fixed/variable costs, and reconciliation of profits. Performance was moderate. Common mistakes included:

1. Incorrect splitting of fixed and variable portions: Many students did not separate factory, administrative, and

selling overheads correctly, leading to errors in the cost sheet.

2. Improper absorption based on normal production: Students often used actual production only for fixed costs,

instead of adjusting proportionally to normal production (50,000/60,000 units).

3. Treatment of selling/administrative expenses: Confusion arose in splitting fixed and variable portions, or

adding total actual expenses directly to cost accounts without absorption adjustment.

4. Reconciliation errors: Some students forgot to add interest/dividend income in reconciliation or miscalculated

the undercharged amounts.

5. Balancing figure mistakes: Errors in calculating profit as per cost accounts arose due to rounding or

misallocation of absorbed overheads.

Examiner Observations This question tests candidates’ understanding of profit/loss reconciliation between cost and financial accounts. Overall performance was average, with students generally able to identify items but often making errors in classification and calculation. Common mistakes included:

1. Incorrect treatment of depreciation: Many students failed to correctly calculate the difference between

depreciation charged in financial accounts and recovered in cost accounts (overcharged or undercharged), leading to wrong adjustment.

2. Mixing items to debit/credit sides: Items like administration over-recovered or factory under-recovered

overheads were sometimes wrongly placed, causing balancing errors.

3. Omission of financial incomes: Items like interest on investments, transfer fees, or stores adjustments

credited in financial books were frequently ignored, reducing marks.

4. Misinterpretation of tax impact: Students often treated income-tax as a cost item instead of a financial

account adjustment.

5. Balancing figure errors: Errors in totaling the debit and credit sides of the memorandum reconciliation account

were common.

Examiner Observations

1. Common Mistakes:  Students often confuse overhead absorption rates and apply them incorrectly. For example, applying factory overhead on cost of production instead of prime cost, or miscalculating administrative and selling overheads per unit.  Many ignore closing stock adjustments (both WIP and finished goods) or use financial records values instead of cost figures, leading to wrong cost of goods sold.  Misclassification of capital nature items like advertisement expenses; students sometimes include them in the P&L account.  Errors in reconciliation statement: Adding/subtracting overhead differences incorrectly, or omitting income like dividend/interest, which distorts the reconciliation.  Calculation mistakes in per-unit overhead rates (e.g., Rs. 4.8/unit or Rs. 6.4/unit) because of rounding or wrong COGS/units base.
2. Positive Observations:  Clear stepwise preparation of costing P&L and financial P&L helps in scoring full marks in ICAI exams, as examiners look for proper reconciliation logic.  Students who highlight unique adjustments like under/over-absorbed overheads separately gain extra marks.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips  Start with Stores Ledger Control A/c – Post opening balance, purchases, issues to WIP, maintenance, building, and loss.  Post Wages Control A/c – Split into direct (WIP), indirect (Factory OH), and building construction wages.  Prepare Factory Overhead Control A/c – Include indirect wages, materials loss, actual overhead, under/over absorption, and building allocation.  Record Royalty – Directly to WIP.  Update Work-in-Process Control A/c – Include materials, wages, overhead, royalty, opening balance; post © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 487

transfer to Finished Goods; balance is closing WIP.  Prepare Finished Goods Control A/c – Include opening FG, WIP transferred, calculate COGS using GP margin, and balance remaining FG.  Prepare Cost of Goods Sold A/c – Take COGS from Finished Goods, post to Costing P&L.  Post Selling, Distribution & Admin OH – Directly to Costing P&L through the control account.  Complete Cost Ledger Control A/c – Bring all totals together to reconcile with Costing P&L.  Building Construction A/c – Post opening, materials, wages, and overhead; balance clears to Cost Ledger since construction is completed.  Use Given Closing Balances – Saves time; don’t recalculate unless needed.  Maintain Sequential Posting – Stores → Wages → Factory OH → WIP → FG → COGS → Costing P&L → Building.

Examiner Observations This question requires careful attention to detail, and students often make several common mistakes.

1. Incorrect Allocation of Overheads: A frequent error is misclassifying factory overheads, especially the

allocation of indirect wages, materials issued to maintenance, and factory overheads in the Building Construction Account. Students sometimes fail to correctly allocate costs absorbed in the building construction account, which could lead to errors in the Factory Overhead Control Account.

2. Handling of Loss in Materials: The loss in the raw materials account should be treated as factory overheads.

Students often fail to incorporate this loss properly in the Stores Ledger and Factory Overhead accounts, leading to discrepancies in the accounts.

3. Mismanagement of Under-Absorbed Overheads: Under-absorbed factory overheads are a tricky point. Many

students fail to treat these correctly, either by not recognizing them in the Costing P&L A/c or placing them incorrectly in the wrong ledger.

4. Closing Balances: A key mistake is miscalculating or not reflecting the closing balances of raw materials and

work-in-process in the control accounts. These balances must be carried forward correctly and reconciled in the final trial balance.

5. Wrong Application of Gross Profit Margin: Incorrect calculation of the cost of goods sold (COGS) based on the

gross profit margin is another common mistake. Since the gross profit margin is 20% on sales, the COGS should be 80% of the sales, i.e., Rs. 2, 16,000. Misapplying this can lead to incorrect entries in the Finished Goods Control Account and Cost of Goods Sold Account.

(5+2+1) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Note Opening Balances: Start with given opening balances for all control accounts (Stores, WIP, Finished

Goods, etc.).

2. Materials Transactions:  Record purchases and materials issued to production in Stores Ledger and WIP Control.  Adjust for returns to suppliers.
3. Wages and Overheads:  Debit WIP and Manufacturing Overhead for direct and indirect wages.  Record overhead costs and amounts charged to production.
4. Sales and Sales Return:  Transfer finished goods to Cost of Sales for sales.  Adjust for sales returns.
5. Cost Ledger Control:  Transfer totals from relevant accounts (Materials, Wages, Overheads) to Cost Ledger Control A/c.
6. Closing Balances:  Calculate and record closing balances for each control account.
7. Prepare Trial Balance:  Ensure debits and credits are balanced to finalize the trial balance.

Examiner Observations This question is centered around preparing various control accounts, including Cost Ledger Control, Stores Ledger, Work-in-Process (WIP), Finished Stock, Manufacturing Overhead, and others. While attempting such questions, students often make common mistakes that can be easily avoided by following a systematic approach.

1. Incorrectly Handling of Sales Returns: Sales returns at cost are a key adjustment in Finished Goods Control A/c

and Cost of Sales A/c. Many students forget to adjust the sales return cost in the Finished Goods account, leading to incorrect final balances. In this case, Rs. 90,000 sales return should be considered.

2. Mismanagement of Manufacturing Overheads: A significant mistake is the incorrect allocation of under-

recovered overheads. The under-absorption of manufacturing overheads (Rs. 50,000) is a tricky point. Students often fail to correctly transfer this under-recovery to the Profit & Loss account, affecting the final balance in the Manufacturing Overhead Control A/c.

3. Closing Balances: Misplacing the closing balance in the Cost Ledger Control A/c or incorrectly treating the

ending balance in other control accounts (like WIP or Finished Stock) can lead to imbalances in the trial balance.

4. Wages and Overheads Allocation: Another common issue arises when students misclassify direct wages and

indirect wages in the control accounts. In this case, indirect wages should go to the Manufacturing Overhead Control A/c, and direct wages should be classified under the Wages Control A/c.

5. Time Management: This question requires the preparation of multiple control accounts, so students should

plan their time carefully and not linger too long on one step. Efficiently handling this question involves setting a

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 491

clear structure and moving through the accounts systematically.

Apply the given absorption rates for factory and administrative overheads.  Reconcile the Profit: Reconcile the profit by adjusting the differences in overheads, stock valuation, and non- manufacturing items (like interest, dividends, etc.) between financial and costing records.

Examiner Observations When solving this question, students often make the following mistakes:

1. Misapplication of Absorption Rates: Some students fail to properly apply the absorption rates for factory

overheads and administration overheads. The factory overheads should be based on direct wages (70% of direct wages), and the administration overheads should be calculated as 15% of factory cost, which can be confusing if not done step by step.

2. Overvaluing Stocks: Students often incorrectly value opening and closing stocks, especially the finished goods.

The opening stock should be calculated based on the correct unit cost, and closing stock is also valued correctly, based on the cost of production per unit.

3. Incorrect Treatment of Sales and Distribution Costs: While calculating the cost of sales, some students forget

to account for the proper selling and distribution overheads per unit, leading to discrepancies. © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 494

4. Cost of Goods Manufactured: Careful calculation of units produced and the proper allocation of raw materials,

direct labour, and factory overheads are essential to ensure accurate costing. Missing out on any of these steps will cause errors.

Important Note:- This numerical question was related to Non Integrated Accounts. Four different ledgers are required to be prepared. Performance of the examinees was average. The examinees have made mistakes in the posting of particular transaction in concerned account.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips  Systematic Posting: Always start with the opening balances for each account and post transactions in order (raw material purchases, wages, factory overheads, etc.). Follow the logical sequence from one control account to the next.  Focus on Adjustments: Pay close attention to adjustments for sales returns, raw material losses, and work-in- progress rejections. These are often tricky points and are easy to overlook, but they significantly affect the final balances.  Track Flow of Costs: Ensure you understand the flow of costs—raw materials to work-in-progress, work-in- progress to finished goods, and finished goods to cost of goods sold. This will help maintain consistency in your postings.  Cross-Verify: After preparing each ledger, cross-check with the previous step. This will help identify missing entries or mispostings early on.

Examiner Observations In this question, students often make the following mistakes:

1. Incorrect Posting of Transactions: The most common error is posting transactions into the wrong control

accounts. For example, students might mix up entries for raw materials, factory overheads, or wages between different accounts. Correctly identifying which account to debit or credit is crucial to avoid these mistakes.

2. Failure to Account for Losses in Raw Material: The treatment of raw material losses (inventory audit) is often

overlooked, leading to incorrect calculations in the Raw Material Control Account. Students should ensure they account for such losses in the correct manner, either through the P&L account or adjustments.

3. Mismanagement of Work-in-Progress: The Work-in-Progress Control Account should reflect not only raw

materials but also direct wages, factory overheads, and rejections. Some students fail to correctly calculate the cost of rejected work-in-progress and might omit such entries.

4. Factory Overheads Handling: The factory overheads are allocated to the Work-in-Progress account but need

careful posting. Students sometimes mistakenly credit or debit factory overheads to the wrong accounts or fail to match them with the corresponding amounts in work-in-progress.

5. General Ledger Adjustment Account: Students sometimes fail to adjust for the proper entries in the General

Ledger Adjustment Account, especially when reconciling balances like sales returns, raw material credit, and inventory losses. They might overlook or misinterpret certain balancing figures, which could lead to discrepancies.

The chief accountant of the company has provided following information from the Financial Accounts and Cost Accounts: Sr. No Particulars (Rs.) (i) Legal Chargers Provided in Financial accounts 15,250

(ii) Interim Dividend received credited in financial accounts 4,50,000 (iii) Preliminary Expenses written off in financial accounts 25,750 (iv) Over recovery of selling overheads in cost accounts 11,380 (v) Profit on sale of capital asset credited in financial accounts 30,000 (vi) Under valuation of closing stock in cost accounts 25,000 (vii) Over recovery of production overheads in cost accounts 10,200 (viii) Interest paid on Debentures shown in financial accounts 50,000 Required: Find out the Profit (Loss) as per Cost Accounts by preparing a Reconciliation Statement.

[5 Marks | 5 Minutes\](PYP Nov 22)[Difficult | ICAI Twister | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 34

Reconciliation Statement (Reconciliation the profit as per financial records with the profit as per costing records)

Particulars (Rs.) Total (Rs.) Profit as per Financial Accounts 5,50,000 Add: Legal Charges 15,250

Preliminary expenses written off 25,750 Interest paid 50,000 91,000

6,41,000 Less: Under-valuation of closing stock in cost book 25,000

Approach & Time-Saving Tips  Start with the Profit from Financial Accounts: The reconciliation begins with the net profit from financial accounts, which is Rs. 5, 50,000.  Add Items to Adjust for Differences: Items such as legal charges, preliminary expenses, and interest paid should be added to the financial profit because they appear in the financial records but not in the cost records.  Subtract Items Impacting Cost Accounts: Deduct the profit on the sale of capital assets, interim dividend, and over-recovery of overheads as these do not affect the cost records.  Ensure Accuracy: Carefully verify each addition and subtraction. The key is ensuring the right treatment for each item—adding back items that belong to financial accounts but not costing records, and subtracting those that are in cost accounts but not in financial records.

Examiner Observations In this reconciliation question, the key mistakes students often make include:

1. Incorrect Treatment of Items: Students sometimes miss the correct addition or subtraction of certain items.

For example, legal charges, preliminary expenses, and interest paid are expenses recorded in financial accounts

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 498

but are not included in the cost accounts, so they should be added back when reconciling the profits.

2. Mismanagement of Over-Recovery Adjustments: The over-recovery of selling overheads and production

overheads in the cost accounts should be subtracted, but students may mistakenly add them, leading to a wrong profit reconciliation.

3. Profit on Sale of Capital Asset: The profit on sale of capital assets is a non-operating income recorded in the

financial accounts. It should be subtracted from the profit as it does not affect the cost accounts.

4. Handling of Interim Dividend: The interim dividend received is credited in the financial accounts and should be

deducted in the reconciliation, but students sometimes forget to subtract it.

5. Under-Valuation of Closing Stock: The under-valuation of closing stock in the cost accounts must be added to

the financial profit, but students may forget this adjustment or fail to perform it correctly.

6. Formula and Calculation Errors: Some students may get confused about how to balance the adjustments,

resulting in errors in final profit calculation.

 Careful Work-in-Process Calculation: Ensure that direct materials, direct labor, and overheads are correctly included when calculating work-in-process (Step D).  Balance Accounts Accurately: Pay attention to the Stores Ledger Control Account and Work-in-Process Control Account, ensuring all debits and credits are properly accounted for.  Recheck Overheads Absorption: Finally, calculate any under- or over-absorbed overheads (Step G), as this can often be overlooked.

Examiner Observations This question tests the candidate’s understanding of accounting for materials, labour, overheads, and work-in- progress under a Non-Integrated Accounting System. Some common mistakes that students often make while attempting this question include:

1. Incorrect Calculation of Overheads: Students sometimes fail to correctly apply the overhead recovery rate. The

overhead recovery rate is based on direct labor hours, and incorrect allocation could lead to errors in overhead applied (Step C).

2. Misunderstanding of Work-in-Process: The balance of work-in-process should include not just material and

labor, but also overheads applied. Often, students neglect to add overheads while calculating the total cost of unfinished jobs (Step D).

3. Store Ledger Control Account Balancing: Many students forget to properly balance the Stores Ledger Control

Account, especially when handling transactions related to purchases and work-in-process (Step F).

4. Handling of Creditors: When calculating materials purchased, it’s easy to miss adjustments for the opening and

closing balances of creditors. This affects the accuracy of material purchased (Step A).

5. Calculation of Direct Materials Consumed: Some students may miscalculate material consumption, especially

when balancing material costs across different accounts. Always ensure the correct balancing figure in the Work- in-Process Control Account (Step E).
