(2+2+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips  Focus on Equivalent Production First: Begin by determining the equivalent production for each type of cost (material, labour, and overhead). Focus on calculating the completion percentage for opening WIP and closing WIP carefully. This is the most time-consuming part, so be thorough but efficient.  Handle Scrap Separately: In the second part of the question, ensure that you deduct the sale of scrap from the total material cost before proceeding to calculate the cost per unit. This is a critical adjustment that students sometimes miss, leading to errors.  Use FIFO Logic for WIP Handling: When calculating costs for opening WIP, remember that it should be completed first in FIFO, and then the new units are processed. Keep this in mind when working through equivalent production.  Be Methodical in Cost per Unit Calculation: Ensure your account for the correct total costs and divide them by the equivalent units to arrive at the correct cost per unit. This helps streamline the process and reduce errors.

Examiner Observations  Calculation of Equivalent Units: Students often make mistakes when calculating the equivalent units in FIFO method, especially when handling opening work-in-process and closing work-in-process. In FIFO, the opening WIP is considered separately and completed first before new units are processed, so it requires special treatment, which students sometimes overlook. This can lead to incorrect equivalent units for both material and labour/overhead.  Handling of Abnormal Gain: Abnormal gain can cause confusion, especially when calculating the equivalent production. The FIFO method requires careful tracking of normal loss and abnormal gain. Any abnormal gain must be deducted from the units to adjust the total equivalent units correctly, which some students might forget.  Sale of Scrap: The calculation of the value of scrap is critical. It needs to be deducted from the material costs, but students sometimes forget to do this or incorrectly apply it. In this case, the sale of scrap must be deducted from the input material cost before determining the total cost per unit.  Cost per Unit Calculation: The cost per unit is often mishandled. Students might forget to adjust the total input costs by deducting scrap proceeds or may fail to apply the correct number of equivalent units for labour and © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 664

overhead while calculating the unit costs.

This is the key step that determines how the joint costs are distributed and affects subsequent calculations.  Calculate Further Processing Costs: Next, calculate the further processing costs for each product. These costs © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 666

are separate from joint costs and must be handled distinctly.  Analyze Incremental Profit: For each product, calculate the incremental revenue from further processing (i.e., the difference between the price after further processing and the price at split-off). Compare this to the additional processing costs to determine if further processing is beneficial.  Make Processing Decisions: Once the analysis is done, determine whether the products should be processed further or sold at split-off, and adjust your profit calculations accordingly.

Examiner Observations  Incorrect Apportionment of Joint Costs: A common mistake students make is improperly apportioning joint costs based on sales value at split-off. The split-off value needs to be calculated correctly and proportionately allocated to each product based on the sales value at the point of split-off. Incorrect sales value can lead to errors in the joint cost allocation, affecting subsequent calculations.  Further Processing Cost Miscalculation: Students sometimes confuse joint costs with further processing costs. Further processing costs must be calculated separately for each product after the split-off stage. It’s essential to distinguish these costs clearly and ensure they are not mixed up.  Failing to Consider Opportunity Cost: The incremental revenue from further processing must be compared to the further processing costs. Some students may fail to analyze whether the further processing will result in higher profits. This analysis is critical for recommending whether a product should be processed further or sold at the split-off stage.  Not Identifying the Right Decision for Each Product: Students often miss the distinction between which product should be sold at split-off and which should undergo further processing. The decision should be based on whether the incremental revenue from further processing exceeds the further processing costs for each product.

Deduct management and selling expenses to determine the overall profit or loss.

Question 44. An article passes through three successive operations from raw materials stage to the finished product stage. The following data are available from the production records for the month of March, 2021: Operation No. of pieces (Input) No. of pieces (Rejected) No. of pieces (Output)

1 1,80,000 60,000 1,20,000 2 1,98,000 18,000 1,80,000 3 1,44,000 24,000 1,20,000

(i) DETERMINE the input required to be introduced in the first operation in no. of pieces in order to obtain finished output of 500 pieces after the last operation. (ii) CALCULATE the cost of raw material required to produce one piece of finished product, if the weight of the finished piece is 0.5 kg. and the price of raw material is Rs. 80 per kg.

[5 Marks | 6 Minutes\](MTP April ’21) [Medium]

Answer 44

Statement of production Operation Input Rejections Output

Total % of output 1 1,80,000 60,000 50 1,20,000 2 1,98,000 18,000 10 1,80,000 3 1,44,000 24,000 20 1,20,000

(i) Determination of input required to obtain 500 pieces of finished output:

Particulars No. of pieces Output required after operation 3 500 Add: Rejection in operation 3 (20%) 100 Output required after operation 2 600 Add: Rejection in operation 2 (10%) 60 Output required after operation 1 660 Add: Rejection in operation 1 (50%) 330 Input required in operation 1 990

ii) Calculation of cost of raw material: To produce 500 pieces of final output, 990 pieces of inputs are required at operation 1. Thus, to get a finished piece of 0.5 kg. of output, the weight of input required is: =0.5/500 × 990 = 0.99 kg. The cost of raw material would be Rs. 80 × 0.99 kg. = Rs.79.20 (1+3+1)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips  Reverse Calculation: Start from the required finished output and move backward through each operation. For each operation, calculate the number of units that need to be input by considering the rejection percentages at

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 671

that operation. This helps in calculating the total input required for each operation to achieve the desired output.  Quick Calculation for Weight: Once you have the required input quantity for the first operation, use that to calculate the weight of raw material. Use the given weight per finished piece and the total input quantity to find the weight. Multiply by the raw material price to get the total cost.

Examiner Observations  Misunderstanding Rejections: A frequent mistake is that students forget to account for the rejections at each operation correctly. This includes ensuring that the rejection percentages are applied to the input or output at each stage. Failure to properly add the rejections before moving to the next operation often leads to inaccurate results.  Confusing Output and Input Relationships: Students sometimes struggle with determining the correct input required for the first operation. The question asks for the required input to achieve a specific finished output, which is a reverse calculation. Students often forget to adjust for the rejections at each stage before calculating the necessary input.  Incorrect Weight Calculation: The weight of raw material required for producing a finished product is derived based on the input quantity. A common mistake is applying the weight to the output directly instead of adjusting it based on the total input required at the first operation. This mistake leads to errors in cost calculations.  Skipping Percentages in Operations: Another common error is skipping the percentage of rejections in each operation. For example, not adding 50% rejection in operation 1, 10% in operation 2, and 20% in operation 3 when determining the input/output flow. This results in discrepancies when trying to calculate the input needed to produce a specified number of finished units.

Examiner Observations This question requires a clear understanding of process costing, FIFO method, and calculation of equivalent units. Students often make the following mistakes:

1. Incorrect Calculation of Raw Material Input: Students may struggle with understanding the balancing figure

concept for raw material input and fail to account for normal loss while calculating the quantity of raw material

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 674

introduced during the month.

2. Wrong Allocation of Losses: Identifying and differentiating between normal and abnormal losses can be

confusing. The normal loss is calculated based on fresh input, and any remaining loss is abnormal. Students often mix these losses up.

3. Failure to Value Closing WIP Correctly: The valuation of closing work-in-process can be tricky, especially when

dealing with different completion percentages for labor and overheads. Students may forget to apply the correct percentage for each cost element.

4. Overlooking Scrap Value: While calculating the total value of raw material, students may neglect to add the

scrap value of the normal loss.

5. Process Flow Understanding: Students tend to overlook the relationship between input, output, and losses. The

proper inflow and outflow management, including raw materials, losses, and WIP, should be carefully tracked.

Question 46. eSalt is the biggest producer of sodium hydroxide in India. This main product of the company has a strong reactivity with other organic compounds. It is highly versatile and is alkaline in nature. However, the basic material required for the production of this product is salt along with the electricity. However, the common use is in disinfection like for purifying drinking water or swimming pool water. It is also an important ingredient of toothpaste. Examiner Observations This question is a detailed case on joint product costing and decision-making, focusing on the apportionment of joint costs using various methods like physical units, sales value, and net realizable value. The main errors students make are:

1. Misinterpretation of Apportionment Methods: Students often confuse how joint costs should be apportioned

between the products, especially when using the physical unit method versus the sales value method or net realizable value.

2. Incorrect Calculation of Joint Costs: Some students overlook how to calculate the joint cost properly,

particularly in the case of increased production and conversion cost. The base material cost and conversion cost need careful handling, especially when these are increased by multiples.

3. Not Considering Further Processing Profitability: In the decision to further process Halogen, students

sometimes fail to compare the incremental revenue with the incremental cost properly, leading to incorrect decisions. The key is to focus on the difference in revenue versus cost for a clear decision.

4. Neglecting Correct Units and Values: While calculating the net realizable value (NRV) or incremental revenue,

students sometimes miscalculate the figures, especially when the further processed product (Vinyl) is introduced.

5. Forgetting to Include Conversion Costs in Further Processing: The incremental processing cost is crucial when

deciding whether to further process Halogen. Some students forget to incorporate this in their calculations.

Examiner Observations

1. Inter-process Profit Calculation:  A common mistake students make is overlooking the inter-process profit when calculating transfer prices. Students often miss out on adding the 25% profit margin for Processes I and II or 33.33% for Process III to Finished Stock.
2. Cost and Transfer Price Confusion:  Students often confuse cost with transfer price. The question specifically asks for the transfer price, which

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 681

includes both cost plus profit. Failing to calculate this correctly results in incorrect answers.

3. Closing Stock Adjustment:  Incorrect calculation or failure to adjust for closing stock leads to miscalculation of transfer prices. Many students neglect the closing stock impact when determining the base cost for the next stage.
4. Prime Cost Focus:  Some students focus only on the prime cost (direct material, wages, and overheads) but forget to adjust for the inter-process profit and closing stock. This can result in missing out on profit calculations and thus impacting the overall transfer pricing.
5. Not Using the Correct Profit Percentage:  A common mistake is misapplying the profit margin for each transfer. The question requires 25% profit for transfers between Processes I and II, and 33.33% for Process III to Finished Stock. Incorrectly using one profit margin for all processes can lead to wrong answers.
6. Handling of Opening and Closing Stocks:  Students often struggle with the correct treatment of opening and closing stock, which directly affects the transfer price. The inter-process profit embedded in opening stock should be carefully handled to avoid errors in calculations.
7. Time Management:  This question involves several steps of calculation and checking. Many students may rush through the steps or skip intermediate calculations, resulting in incorrect answers. Adequate time for reviewing steps is crucial.
8. Conceptual Understanding:  The question tests both conceptual understanding and practical application of cost accounting principles. Students need to grasp multi-stage process costing and how profits are handled at each stage.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 682

## Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ’s)

Question 1. The type of process loss that should not be allowed to affect the cost of good units is: (a) Abnormal loss (b) Normal loss (c) Seasonal loss (d) Standard loss

(Study Material)

Answer: (a) Abnormal loss Reason: Abnormal loss refers to losses that occur beyond the expected or normal level in the production process, and these losses are not part of the regular production costs. Since abnormal losses are unexpected, they should not be allowed to affect the cost of good units. The costs associated with abnormal losses are typically treated separately and are not included in the cost per unit of the good units produced.  Normal loss is the expected or inherent loss during the production process, and its cost is absorbed into the cost of the good units.  Seasonal loss and standard loss are not common terms in cost accounting, but they might refer to specific losses depending on the context or industry.

Question 2. 100 units are processed at a total cost of Rs. 160, normal loss is 10%, & scrap units are sold @ Rs.0.25 each. If the output is 80 units, then the value of abnormal loss is: (a) Rs.2.50 (b) Rs.16 (c) Rs.17.50 (d) Rs.17.75

(Study Material)

Answer: (c) Rs.17.50 Reason: Normal loss = 10 units, expected output = 90 units. Actual output = 80 units, so abnormal loss = 10 units. Cost per unit = Rs.1.60 (Rs.160 / 100 units). Cost of abnormal loss = 10 units \* Rs.1.60 = Rs.16. Scrap value = 10 units \* Rs.0.25 = Rs.2.50. Value of abnormal loss = Rs.16 (cost) - Rs.2.50 (scrap value) = Rs.17.50.

Question 3. When average method is used in process costing, the opening inventory costs are: (a) Subtracted from the new costs (b) Added to the new costs (c) Kept separate from the costs of the new period (d) Averaged with other costs to arrive at total cost

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) Added to the new costs Reason: Under the average method in process costing, the costs from the opening inventory (previous period) are combined with the costs incurred during the current period to calculate the total cost. This method averages the costs over the total units produced during the period, including those from the opening inventory. The opening

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 683

inventory costs are added to the new costs to determine the total cost for the period, which is then allocated to both the completed and in-process units.

Question 4. Spoilage that occurs under inefficient operating conditions and is ordinarily controllable is called: (a) Normal spoilage (b) Abnormal spoilage (c) Normal defectives (d) None of the above

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) Abnormal spoilage Reason: Abnormal spoilage refers to spoilage that occurs under inefficient operating conditions and is typically controllable. It is not considered a normal part of the production process and goes beyond the expected or normal level of loss. Abnormal spoilage results from issues such as poor processes, defective machinery, or inadequate supervision, and is generally treated separately from the cost of good units.  Normal spoilage is the expected or inherent loss in production, which is accounted for as part of the normal cost.  Normal defectives are products that do not meet quality standards but are still considered part of the normal process.

Question 5. The cost of normal process loss is - (a) Absorbed by good units produced and amount realised by the sale of loss units should be debited to the process account. (b) Debited to costing profit and loss account. (c) Absorbed by good units produced. (d) Debited to costing profit and loss account and amount realised by the sale of loss units should be credited to the process account.

(Study Material)

Answer: (c) Absorbed by good units produced. Reason: Normal process loss is considered an inherent part of the production process, and its cost is absorbed by the good units produced. This means that the costs associated with normal spoilage or loss are distributed across the units that are successfully produced. Since normal losses are expected and unavoidable, the cost is spread out to maintain a realistic cost per unit for the good units.  Option (a) refers to the treatment of abnormal loss, not normal loss.  Option (b) and (d) would apply to abnormal losses, not normal losses.

Question 6. The value of abnormal loss is equal to: (a) Total cost of materials (b) Total process cost less realizable value of normal loss (c) Total process cost less cost of scrap (d) Total process cost less realizable value of normal loss less value of transferred out goods.

(Study Material)

Answer: (d) Total process cost less realizable value of normal loss less value of transferred out goods. © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 684

Reason: The value of abnormal loss is calculated by taking the total process cost and subtracting both the realizable value of normal loss (from the sale of scrap or waste) and the cost of the good units transferred out. This gives the cost of the units that are lost due to abnormal circumstances, which are not part of the normal process.  Total process cost includes the cost of materials, labor, and overheads incurred during the production process.  Realizable value of normal loss is the value recovered from scrap or waste from the normal loss.  Transferred out goods refer to the good units that have been completed and transferred to the next stage, and their cost is subtracted from the total cost. Thus, the abnormal loss is the cost associated with the production loss that exceeds the expected (normal) loss.

Question 7. 200 units were introduced in a process in which 20 units is the normal loss. If the actual output is 150 units, then there is: (a) No abnormal loss (b) No abnormal gain (c) Abnormal loss of 30 units (d) Abnormal gain of 30 units

(Study Material)

Answer: (c) Abnormal loss of 30 units Reason: Units introduced = 200 units Normal loss = 20 units Expected output = 200 units - 20 units (normal loss) = 180 units Actual output = 150 units The expected output is 180 units, but the actual output is only 150 units. This results in an abnormal loss of: Abnormal loss = Expected output - Actual output = 180 units - 150 units = 30 units Since the actual output is lower than the expected output due to this abnormal loss, the answer is abnormal loss of 30 units.

Question 8. Lean Labs develops 55mm film using a four-step process that moves progressively through four departments. The company specializes in overnight service and has the largest drug store chain as its primary customer. Currently, direct labor, direct materials, and overhead are accumulated by departments. The cost accumulation system that best describes the system Lean Labs is using is: (a) Operation costing. (b) Activity-based costing. (c) Job-order costing. (d) Process costing.

(Study Material)

Answer: (d) Process costing. Reason: Lean Labs is using a four-step process that moves progressively through four departments, which is characteristic of process costing. This method is typically used in industries where production is continuous and units are homogeneous, with costs accumulated by departments or processes. The company accumulates direct labor, direct materials, and overhead by departments, which aligns with the process costing system, where costs are tracked for each process or stage of production, and then allocated to all units produced during that stage.  Operation costing is a hybrid system combining aspects of job-order and process costing, typically used in industries where products have some variations but are produced in large quantities.  Activity-based costing (ABC) assigns costs based on activities performed, not by department or process.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 685

 Job-order costing is used when products are custom-made or unique, and costs are accumulated for each individual job or order.

Question 9. When compared with normal spoilage, abnormal spoilage: (a) Arises more frequently from factors that are inherent in the manufacturing process. (b) Is given the same accounting treatment as normal spoilage. (c) Is generally thought to be more controllable by purchase department than production department. (d) Is not typically influenced by the "tightness" of production standards.

(Study Material)

Answer: (d) Is not typically influenced by the "tightness" of production standards. Reason: Abnormal spoilage refers to spoilage that occurs due to factors beyond the normal production process, often caused by inefficiencies or unusual circumstances. It is not typically influenced by the "tightness" of production standards because such spoilage is unexpected and occurs under abnormal or inefficient conditions. In contrast, normal spoilage is an inherent part of the process and is generally anticipated based on production standards. (a) is incorrect because abnormal spoilage arises from factors outside normal manufacturing conditions, not from inherent process factors. (b) is incorrect because abnormal spoilage is accounted for separately and is not treated the same way as normal spoilage. (c) is incorrect because abnormal spoilage is more directly influenced by production issues rather than purchasing factors.

Question 10. Assume 550 units were worked on during a period in which a total of 500 good units were completed. Normal spoilage consisted of 30 units; abnormal spoilage, 20 units. Total production costs were Rs. 2,200. The company accounts for abnormal spoilage separately on the income statement as loss due to abnormal spoilage. Normal spoilage is not accounted for separately. What is the cost of the good units produced? (a) Rs.2, 080 (b) Rs.2, 115 (c) Rs.2, 200 (d) Rs.2, 332

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) Rs.2, 115 Reason: The total production cost of Rs.2, 200 is for 550 units worked on. Cost per unit = Rs.2, 200 ÷ 550 = Rs.4. The cost for 500 good units = 500 × Rs.4 = Rs.2, 000. The cost for normal spoilage (30 units) = 30 × Rs.4 = Rs.120. Abnormal spoilage is accounted separately, so it's excluded from the good units' cost. Total cost of good units = Rs.2,000 (good units) + Rs.120 (normal spoilage) = Rs.2,115.

Question 11. IC Limited uses process costing systems and inspects its goods post manufacturing. An engineer noticed on May 31st the following:

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 686

Good units completed 15,000 Normal spoilage (units) 300 Abnormal spoilage (units) 100 Unit costs were: Material Rs.2.50 and conversion costs (Labour & overheads) Rs.6.00. The number of units that company would transfer to its finished goods stock and the related cost of these units are: (a) 15,000 units transferred at a cost of Rs.127, 500 (b) 15,000 units transferred at a cost of Rs.130, 050 (c) 15,000 units transferred at a cost of Rs.135, 000 (d) 15,300 units transferred at a cost of Rs.130, 050

(Study Material)

Answer-(b) 15,000 units transferred at a cost of Rs.130, 050 Reason: 15,000 good units are transferred to finished goods. Total cost per unit = Rs. 2.50 (Material) + Rs. 6.00 (Conversion) = Rs. 8.50. Total production cost is based on 15,300 units (15,000 good units + 300 normal spoilage). Total cost of production = 15,300 units × Rs. 8.50 = Rs. 130,050. 15,000 good units are transferred at this total cost.

Question 12. A process account is debited by abnormal gain, the value is determined as: (a) Equal to the value of normal loss (b) Cost of good units less realizable value of normal loss (c) Cost of good units less realizable value of actual loss (d) Equal to the value of good units less closing stock

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) Cost of good units less realizable value of normal loss Reason: When there is an abnormal gain, it means that more good units were produced than expected (i.e., more than the normal units), and the process account is debited with the value of the abnormal gain. The value of the abnormal gain is determined by:  Cost of good units: This is the cost of the units that were actually completed and transferred.  Realizable value of normal loss: The amount that can be recovered from the scrap or waste due to normal spoilage. Therefore, the value of the abnormal gain is calculated as the cost of good units less the realizable value of normal loss. This reflects the cost savings or profit derived from producing more than the expected good units.

Question 13. Under Weighted Average (Average) Method: (a) The cost to complete the opening WIP is ignored. (b) The cost to complete the opening WIP and other completed units are calculated separately. (c) The cost of opening work-in-process and cost of the current period are aggregated and the aggregate cost is divided by output in terms of completed units. (d) Closing stock of work in process is valued at current cost.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 687

(Study Material)

Answer: (c) The cost of opening work-in-process and cost of the current period are aggregated and the aggregate cost is divided by output in terms of completed units. Reason: Under the Weighted Average Method in process costing, the costs of the opening work-in-process (WIP) and the current period are combined (aggregated). This aggregate cost is then averaged over the total units produced, including both completed units and ending WIP, to determine the cost per unit. This method does not differentiate between the costs of the opening WIP and the costs incurred in the current period. Instead, it averages the costs, providing a simplified approach compared to the FIFO method, where opening WIP costs are handled separately.

Question 14. Inter-process profit is calculated, because: (a) A process is a cost centres (b) Each process has to report profit (c) The efficiency of the process is measured (d) The wages of employees are linked to the process profitability.

(Study Material)

Answer: (c) The efficiency of the process is measured Reason: Inter-process profit is calculated to measure the efficiency of a process. It reflects the profit that arises when one process transfers goods to the next process at a price higher than its cost. This helps in evaluating how efficiently each process is operating and managing its costs. The inter-process profit also provides insights into the value added at each stage of production. (a) A process being a cost center does not directly explain the need to calculate inter-process profit; it is primarily for performance evaluation. (b) Each process does not necessarily need to report a profit, but the calculation of inter-process profit is for efficiency analysis. (d) While wages can be linked to productivity, they are not the primary reason for calculating inter-process profit.

Question 15. A firm introduced 3,000 units of material in the manufacturing process. During the period 2,500 units were completed and transferred to next process. However, the degree of completion on remaining 500 units was 100%, 60%, and 30% for materials, labour and overheads respectively. Which one of the following is the equivalent complete units with regard to labour? (a) 2,500 (b) 2,800 (c) 2,650 (d) 2,500

(Study Material)

Answer: (b) 2,800 units Equivalent Units = Units Completed + (Units in Process x Degree of Completion) Equivalent Units for Labour = 2,500 + (500 x 0.60) = 2,800 units

Approach & Time-Saving Tips To solve this question quickly, the student should focus on:

1. Focus on Selling Prices: Understand how the selling prices relate to the allocation of joint costs.
2. By-Product Credit: Keep track of the by-product (B) and remember that it helps reduce the joint costs of the

main products.

3. Systematic Calculation: Follow a step-by-step approach—first calculate the allocation ratios, then the net joint

costs, and finally the profit margins.

4. Avoiding Over-Calculation: Don't get bogged down by excessive calculations; focus on getting the key allocation

ratios correct.

Examiner Observations Mistakes Students May Make:

1. Incorrect Allocation of Joint Costs: One common mistake students make is failing to properly allocate the joint

costs based on the sales price ratio or the allocation ratio. In this question, the allocation is based on the respective sales prices of X, Y, and Z, which requires careful attention.

2. Overlooking the By-Product: Some students might neglect the by-product’s contribution to reducing the joint

costs. It’s crucial to remember that the by-product (B) should be credited to the joint cost to lower the amount of net joint costs allocated to the main products.

3. Incorrect Margin Calculations: Many students might mistakenly compute the margins on cost and sales. The

problem specifies a 25% margin based on cost or 20% margin on sales, but students may get confused and use a wrong figure when calculating margins.

4. Failure to Use the Correct Selling Prices for Margin: Students might incorrectly subtract the margin from the

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 691

selling price, not understanding that the margin is calculated on cost. This impacts the overall allocation and profit margin percentage calculation.

5. Skipping Post-Split Costs: The post-split-off costs need to be deducted from the selling price when calculating

the joint cost per unit and net margin. Missing out on this can lead to incorrect answers.

percentage for products X differs from the others. Make sure you properly account for these adjustments.

4. Double-Check Apportionments: Review the apportionments and ensure that the final calculations align with

the sales and closing inventory values.

5. Don’t Rush COGS Calculations: Finally, compute the Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) by adding the relevant

additional costs and adjusting for inventory correctly.

Examiner Observations Mistakes Students May Make:

1. Misunderstanding the Net Realizable Value (NRV) Method: One of the most common mistakes is failing to

properly apply the NRV method to allocate joint costs. Students should understand that joint costs are allocated based on the net realizable value of the products, i.e., the sale value minus additional costs. Some may skip calculating the NRV and directly apply the joint costs, leading to incorrect allocation.

2. Incorrect Inventory Treatment: Another frequent error is in the treatment of closing inventories. Students

might forget to adjust for the cost of closing inventory when calculating the Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) or fail to apply the correct percentage for each product, especially for the closing inventory of X, which is a unique case in this question.

3. Incorrect Apportionment of Costs: When apportioning the joint costs, students often make errors in

calculating the proportion of costs based on the net realizable value (NRV). This mistake can lead to incorrect joint cost allocation for each product.

4. Sales Revenue Calculation: Some students might mistakenly calculate the sales revenue using incorrect

quantities or fail to multiply by the correct sale prices, resulting in incorrect gross profit figures.

5. Omitting Additional Costs: Failing to add the direct labor and manufacturing overhead costs for further

processing in departments 2 and 3 to the cost of goods sold can cause significant errors in the final answer.

Question 3. DISTINGUISH between Joint products and By-products.

[6 Marks | 8 Minutes\](Study Material) [Medium| ICAI Fav]

Answer 3. MEANING OF JOINT PRODUCTS AND BY PRODUCTS: Agricultural product industries, chemical process industries, sugar industries, and extractive industries are some of the industries where two or more products of equal or unequal importance are produced either simultaneously or in the course of processing operation of a main product.

In all such industries, the management is faced with the problems such as, valuation of inventory, pricing of product and income determination, problem of taking decision in matters of further processing of by-products and/or joint products after a certain stage etc. In fact, the various problems relate to (i) apportionment of common costs incurred for various products and (ii) Aspects other than mere apportionment of costs incurred up to the point of separation. Before taking up the above problems, we first define the various necessary concepts.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 694

(i) Joint Products - Joint products represent “two or more products separated in the course of the same processing operation usually requiring further processing, each product being in such proportion that no single product can be designated as a major product”. In other words, two or more products of equal importance, produced, simultaneously from the same process, with each having a significant relative sale value are known as joint products. For example, in the oil industry, gasoline, fuel oil, lubricants, paraffin, coal tar, asphalt and kerosene are all produced from crude petroleum. These are known as joint products.

(ii) By-Products - These are defined as “products recovered from material discarded in a main process, or from the production of some major products, where the material value is to be considered at the time of severance from the main product.” So in a nutshell By product is a product which is recovered incidentally from the material used in the manufacture of main or desired products, such a by-product having either a net realizable value or a usable value which is relatively insignificant in comparison with the saleable value of the main or desired products. By-product may be further processed to increase their realizable value Thus by-products emerge as a result of processing operation of another product or they are produced from the scrap or waste of materials of a process. In short a by-product is a secondary or subsidiary product which emanates as a result of manufacture of the main product.

The point at which they are separated from the main product or products is known as split-off point. The expenses of processing are joint till the split –off point.

Split of Point – this is a point in a production process where joint products emerging from the process gets separately identifiable. Split of Point has its importance in the joint product costing as joint cost incurred up to this point only and needs to be borne jointly by the products emerging from the common process. Any cost incurred after Split of Point is a product specific cost and to be borne by the product concerned. Examples of by-products are molasses in the manufacture of sugar, tar, ammonia and benzole obtained on carbonisation of coal and glycerin obtained in the manufacture of soap.

Distinction between Joint-Product and By-Product - The main points of distinction as apparent from the definitions of Joint Products and By-Products are: (a) Joint products are of equal importance whereas by-products are of small economic value. (b) Joint products are produced simultaneously but the by-products are produced incidentally in addition to the main products.

(iii) Co-Products - Joint products and co-products are used synonymously in common parlance, but strictly speaking a distinction can be made between two. Co-products may be defined as two or more products which are contemporary but do not emerge necessarily from the same material in the same process. For instance, wheat and gram produced in two separate farms with separate processing of cultivation are the co-products. Similarly, timber boards made from different trees are co-products.

(3+3) Approach & Time-Saving Tips To solve this question quickly and accurately:

1. Be Concise in Definitions: Start by clearly defining joint products and by-products without over-complicating.

This sets a solid foundation. © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 695

2. Focus on Key Differences: The crux of this question lies in distinguishing joint products from by-products.

Focus on two aspects: the relative importance (equal vs. small value) and the method of production (simultaneously vs. incidentally).

3. Examples to Illustrate: Use specific examples like crude oil products for joint products (gasoline, kerosene) and

sugar production by-products (molasses, tar) to cement your understanding.

4. Avoid Over-elaboration: Stick to the points of distinction. Avoid getting into unnecessary details about co-

products unless asked.

Examiner Observations Mistakes Students May Make:

1. Confusing Joint Products with Co-Products: Some students confuse joint products with co-products, leading to

incorrect definitions. Joint products are produced from a common process, whereas co-products come from different materials or processes. Students must clearly understand this distinction, especially when they mention examples.

2. Overgeneralization: The terms "equal importance" and "insignificant value" must be explained carefully.

Often, students may incorrectly use these terms without understanding their specific implications in real-life scenarios, which could affect their answer's accuracy. Joint products have comparable values, while by-products are incidental and have relatively low value in comparison.

3. Misunderstanding of the Split-off Point: The split-off point is critical in distinguishing joint products from by-

products. Students might fail to explain this concept or provide its relevance in cost allocation. A clear understanding of where joint costs are split between products is crucial for accurate answers.

4. Incomplete Explanation of By-Products: Some students may not sufficiently explain how by-products can be

further processed to add value, which is a key aspect of by-product handling in cost accounting.

5. Not Using Examples Effectively: While examples are given, students should ensure they use them to solidify

their explanations. Failing to do so makes the answer less practical and unclear.

Question 4. DISCUSS the treatment of byproduct cost in Cost Accounting.

[4 Marks | 6 Minutes\](Study Material) [Medium| ICAI Fav]

Answer 4. TREATMENT OF BY-PRODUCT COST IN COST ACCOUNTING By-product cost can be dealt in cost accounting in the following ways: (a) When they are of small total value: When the by-products are of small total value, the amount realised from their sale may be dealt in any one the following two ways:

1. The sales value of the by-products may be credited to the Costing Profit and Loss Account and no credit

be given in the Cost Accounts. The credit to the Costing Profit and Loss Account here is treated either as miscellaneous income or as additional sales revenue.

2. The sale proceeds of the by-product may be treated as deductions from the total costs. The sale

proceeds in fact should be deducted either from the production cost or from the cost of sales.

(b) When the by-products are of considerable total value: Where by-products are of considerable total value, they may be regarded as joint products rather than as by-products. To determine exact cost of by-products the costs incurred up to the point of separation, should be apportioned over by-products and joint products by using

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 696

a logical basis. In this case, the joint costs may be divided over joint products and by-products by using relative market values; physical output method (at the point of split off) or ultimate selling prices (if sold).

(c) Where they require further processing: In this case, the net realisable value of the by-product at the split-off point may be arrived at by subtracting the further processing cost from the realisable value of by-products. If total sales value of by-products at split-off point is small, it may be treated as per the provisions discussed above under (a). In the contrary case, the amount realised from the sale of by-products will be considerable and thus it may be treated as discussed under (b). (2+1+1)

Approach & Time-Saving Tips This question requires clear understanding of different by-product cost treatments:

1. Focus on Small vs. Large By-products: Start by highlighting the distinction between low-value by-products and

those with significant value. This is the key point.

2. Concise Treatment: Explain the two main approaches for small-value by-products — either crediting the profit

and loss account or deducting from total costs. For large-value by-products, mention when they are treated as joint products.

3. Handling Further Processing: Don't miss explaining that when by-products require further processing, the net

realizable value is adjusted by subtracting processing costs.

4. Example Use: Incorporate an example (like molasses in sugar production) for clarity.

Examiner Observations Mistakes Students May Make:

1. Incorrect Treatment of By-product Sales Proceeds: Some students may confuse the two methods of dealing

with small-value by-products. They might mix up where the sale proceeds should be credited — to the Costing Profit and Loss Account versus as a deduction from costs. Failing to differentiate clearly between these methods leads to inaccurate answers.

2. Not Differentiating Based on Value: Students might overlook the distinction between the treatment for small-

value and high-value by-products. This distinction is crucial, especially when discussing when by-products should be treated as joint products.

3. Inadequate Discussion on Further Processing of By-products: The treatment of by-products requiring further

processing should be explained clearly. Some students may neglect the importance of considering net realizable value after processing, which can impact cost allocation and profitability.

4. Lack of Examples: Including relevant examples makes the explanation clearer. Many students fail to use real-

life scenarios (like molasses from sugar production) to illustrate points, which weakens their answer.

Question 5. How apportionment of joint costs up-to the point of separation amongst the joint products using market value at the point of separation and net realizable value method is done? DISCUSS.

[3 Marks | 4 Minutes\](MTP Nov ’21, RTP May ’21) [Medium | High Chance for Exams]

Answer 5. Apportionment of Joint Cost amongst Joint Products using: Market value at the point of separation: This method is used for apportionment of joint costs to joint products up to the split off point. It is difficult to apply if the market value of the product at the point of separation is not available. It is useful method where further processing costs are incurred disproportionately. © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 697

Net realizable value Method: From the sales value of joint products (at finished stage) the followings are deducted:  Estimated profit margins  Selling & distribution expenses, if any  Post- split off costs. The resultant figure so obtained is known as net realizable value of joint products. Joint costs are apportioned in the ratio of net realizable value.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips  Start with a Short Definition: In the first few sentences, define joint costs and why apportionment is necessary. Then, introduce the two methods.  Explain the Market Value Method First: This is simpler — just mention that the market value at the split-off point is used to apportion costs but only when available.  Elaborate on the Net Realizable Value Method: This is where the core marks are. Break down the method step-by-step, stressing the deductions (selling expenses, profit margins, post-split-off costs) before moving to the apportionment.  Finish with Limitations: Discuss why some industries may prefer one method over the other, depending on product characteristics or the availability of market prices.

Examiner Observations Mistakes Students May Make:

1. Confusion Between Methods: Students often mix up the Market Value at the Point of Separation method and the Net Realizable Value (NRV) method. It is crucial to differentiate them clearly. For example, some may confuse that NRV includes post-split-off costs, while Market Value at the split-off point does not.
2. Incorrect Deduction in NRV Method: When discussing the NRV method, students might fail to mention all the necessary deductions such as estimated profit margins and selling expenses, which are key to calculating the net realizable value.
3. Lack of Practical Application: Students might not elaborate on scenarios where these methods are useful, particularly when they can’t get market values at the split-off point or when further processing costs are disproportionately large.
4. Failure to Discuss Limitations: A common oversight is not addressing the limitations of both methods. For example, the Market Value method can be difficult if no market value exists or is unreliable.

Question 6. DESCRIBE briefly, how joint costs upto the point of separation may be apportioned amongst the joint products under the following methods: (i) Average unit cost method (ii) Contribution margin method (iii) Market value at the point of separation (iv) Market value after further processing (v) Net realizable value method.

[6 Marks | 8 Minutes\](Study Material) [Medium| ICAI Twister]

Answer 6. METHODS OF APPORTIONMENT OF JOINT COST TO JOINT PRODUCTS : Proper apportionment of joint cost over the joint products is of considerable importance, as this affects (a) Valuation of closing inventory; (b) Pricing of products; and (c) Profit or loss on the sale of different products. As the relations between materials, processes and joint products are complex and unobservable, there is no way to determine the cost of the

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 698

different production factors used in the processes for the production of each of the joint products. Therefore, the costs incurred in the manufacture of each of the joint products cannot be correctly identified. It can only be apportioned to the joint products by using some rational methods.

The commonly used methods for apportioning total process costs upto the point of separation over the joint products are as follows: (i) Physical Units Method (ii) Net Realisable Value at split-off point (iii) Using Technical Estimates

Some other methods, which managers may also use for making decisions are: (i) Market value at the point of separation (ii) Market value after further processing (iii) Average unit cost method (iv) Contribution margin method

(i) Physical Unit Method: This method is based on the assumption that the joint products are capable of being measured in the same units. Accordingly, joint costs here are apportioned on the basis of some physical base, such as weight, numbers etc. In other words, the basis used for apportioning joint cost over the joint products is the physical volume the joint products at the point of separation. Any loss arises during the joint production process is also apportioned over the products on the same basis.. In situation where physical units are different, the joint products must be converted to a common unit of measurement. In case, the same cannot be converted to a common unit of measurement, this method cannot be applied. The main defect of this method is that it gives equal importance and value to all the joint products.

This method of apportioning is mostly followed when sale price of all the products is uniform. (ii) Net Realisable Value at Split-off Point Method: To arrive at the sales value at the split-off point, following are deducted from the sales value of joint products at final stage i.e. after processing: (i) Directly attributable Selling and distribution expenses like freight, royalty, commission, etc. and (ii) Post split- off processing cost.

This method has advantage as relative sales value serves as a proxy for relative benefit received by each product from the joint cost. When selling prices for all products exist at split off, the sales value at split off method is the preferred technique. It is a relatively simple technique that depends on a common basis for cost allocation – revenues

The resultant figure so obtained is known as net realisable value of joint products. Joint costs are apportioned in the ratio of net realisable value. The net realisable value at split-off point method is widely used in the industries. This method is used when the realisable value of joint products at split –off is not known.

(iii) Using Technical Estimates: This method uses technical estimates to apportion the joint costs over the joint products. This method is used when the result obtained by the above methods does not match with the resources consumed by joint products or the realisable value of the joint products are not readily available. © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 699

Other Methods The followings are the methods which are used by management for taking managerial decisions: (i) Market value at the point of separation: This method is used for the apportionment of joint costs to joint products up to the split off point. It is difficult to apply this method if the market value of the products at the point of separation is not available. It is a useful method when the realisable value of joint products at split-off (point of separation) is known and where further processing costs are incurred disproportionately. To determine the apportionment of joint costs over joint products, a factor known as multiplying factor is determined. This multiplying factor on multiplication with the sales values of each joint product gives rise to the proportion of joint cost. Multiply in factor: x100 Total Sales Revenue is sum of production quantity multiplied by the market price for each of the joint products.

(ii) Market value after further processing: Here the basis of apportionment of joint cost is the total sales value of finished products and involves the same principle as discussed above. The use of this method is unfair where further processing costs after the point of separation are disproportionate or when all the joint products are not subjected to further processing. The net realisable value method which is discussed as above overcomes the shortcoming of this method.

(iii) Average Unit Cost Method: Under this method, total process cost (upto the point of separation) is divided by total units of joint products produced. On division average cost per unit of production is obtained. Average unit cost = Total process cost (upto the point of separation) ÷ Total units of joint product produced. This is a simple method. The effect of application of this method is that all joint products will have uniform cost per unit. If this method is used as the basis for price fixation, then all the products may have more or less the same price. Under this method customers of high quality items are benefitted as they have to pay less price on their purchase.

(iv) Contribution Margin Method: According to this method, joint costs are segregated into two parts - variable and fixed. The variable costs are apportioned over the joint products on the basis of units produced (average method) or physical quantities. In case the products are further processed after the point of separation, then all variable cost incurred be added to the variable costs determined earlier. In this way total variable cost is arrived which is deducted from their respective sales values to ascertain their contribution. The fixed costs are then apportioned over the joint products on the basis of the contribution ratios.

(1+1+1+1+1+1) Approach & Time-Saving Tips

1. Read the Question Carefully: Identify the key methods mentioned (Average Unit Cost, Contribution Margin,

Market Value at Separation, etc.) and their relevance to joint cost apportionment.

2. Brief Introduction: Start by providing a short explanation of joint cost apportionment and its importance in

areas like inventory valuation and pricing (1 mark).

3. Method-wise Explanation:  Average Unit Cost Method: Explain how total joint costs are divided by total units produced, giving a uniform cost per unit (1 mark).  Contribution Margin Method: Describe how joint costs are divided based on the contribution margin, particularly focusing on variable costs and contribution ratios (1 mark).

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 700

 Market Value at the Point of Separation: Highlight how joint costs are apportioned based on the market value of products at the split-off point (1 mark).  Market Value After Further Processing: Explain how joint costs are allocated based on the market value after additional processing, and the limitations of this method (1 mark).  Net Realisable Value Method: Discuss how joint costs are divided based on the net realisable value (after accounting for post-split-off costs and selling expenses) at the split-off point (1 mark).

4. Conclusion: Provide a quick summary of the different methods, focusing on their applicability and why certain

methods may be preferred over others in different scenarios (1 mark).

5. Clarity and Conciseness: Ensure each method is explained clearly and in a concise manner, avoiding overly

technical jargon.

Examiner Observations  Lack of Clear Differentiation: Students often fail to differentiate between similar methods, such as Market Value at the Point of Separation and Market Value After Further Processing. Clear distinctions are necessary.  Confusion in Applicability: Many students struggle to explain when a particular method should be used. For example, the Average Unit Cost Method is misapplied when joint products have significantly different market values or qualities.  Misunderstanding of Further Processing Costs: Students sometimes confuse further processing costs with joint costs when discussing methods like Market Value After Further Processing, leading to incorrect cost apportionment.  Inadequate Explanation of Net Realisable Value: Some students do not explain the Net Realisable Value Method sufficiently, particularly how post-split-off costs (processing and selling) affect the final net value.  Over-simplification of Methods: Students may oversimplify explanations of complex methods like the Contribution Margin Method, failing to mention how it handles variable and fixed costs separately.  Omission of Practical Scenarios: Students often miss explaining how each method is used in real-world scenarios, reducing the clarity and practical relevance of the answer.  Over-reliance on One Method: Some students over-focus on one method and don’t adequately explain the others, missing out on valuable marks. A balanced explanation of all methods is required.  Inadequate Conclusion: Some students forget to briefly summarize which method might be more suitable under specific circumstances, which weakens the overall answer.

Question 7. NN Manufacturing Company uses joint production process that produces three products at the split off point. Joint productions costs during September were Rs. 8, 40,000. Product information for September was as follows:

Particulars Product A Product B Product C Units produced 1,500 3,000 4,500 Units sold 2,000 6,000 7,500 Sales prices: At the split-off Rs. 100 After further processing Rs. 150 Rs. 175 Rs. 50 Costs to process after split-off Rs. 1,50,000 Rs. 1,50,000 Rs. 1,50,000 © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 701

Assume that product C is treated as a by-product and the company accounts for the by-product at net realizable value as a reduction of joint cost. Assume also that Product B&C must be processed further before they can be sold. FIND OUT the total cost of Product A in September if joint cost allocation is based on net realizable values?

[6 Marks | 8 Minutes\](Study Material) [Medium| ICAI Twister]

Answer 7. Product A can be sold at the split-off point, because the question says that "Products B and C must be processed further before they can be sold." Since product A is not included in that, we know that Product A can be sold at the split-off point. Furthermore, the cost to process Product A after the split-off point is Rs.150, 000, whereas the additional revenue to be earned by processing it further is only Rs.75, 000 (Rs.50 increase in selling price per unit multiplied by the 1,500 units produced during September). Therefore, Product A will not be processed further, and we use the sales value at split-off for A for allocating the joint costs. The sales value at the split-off for A is Rs. 100 × 1,500 units, or Rs.1, 50,000.

Since Product B must be processed further, we use its net realizable value for the joint cost allocation. The net realizable value of Product B is Rs.3, 75,000 [(Rs.175 selling price after further processing × 3,000 units produced) – Rs.1, 50,000 in further processing costs]. Product C, the by-product, must also be processed further to be sold. The net realizable value of Product C is Rs. 75,000 [(Rs. 50 sales price after further processing × 4,500 units produced) – Rs. 1, 50,000 in further processing costs].

Joint production costs total Rs. 8, 40,000. Since the by-product C is accounted for as a reduction to the joint costs, the joint costs to be allocated are Rs. 7, 65,000 (Rs. 8, 40,000 minus the Rs. 75,000 NRV of Product C), to be allocated between Product A (sales value Rs. 1, 50,000) and Product B (net realizable value Rs. 3, 75,000). So, the total on which the allocation of the joint costs is based is Rs. 1, 50,000 + 3, 75,000 = Rs. 5, 25,000. Product A represents 28.571% of the total (Rs. 1, 50,000 ÷ Rs. 5, 25,000).

Since Product A has no further processing costs, the total cost of Product A is equal to its allocated joint costs, which are 28.571% of the net joint costs of Rs. 7, 65,000, or Rs. 2, 18,568.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips  Identify the key concepts: Focus on understanding which products need further processing (Product B & C) and which can be sold at split-off (Product A).  Calculate the NRV: For Product B & C, subtract the further processing costs from their after-processing sales revenue to arrive at the NRV.  Deduct the NRV of the by-product: For Product C, subtract its NRV from the total joint costs before allocating the remaining joint costs between Product A and Product B.  Allocate the Joint Costs: Use the sales values (for A) and NRV (for B) to determine the allocation of the remaining joint costs.  Final Answer: Calculate Product A's share of the joint costs and conclude with the total cost of Product A.

Examiner Observations  Confusion About By-Products: Students often mistakenly treat by-products like Product C as regular joint © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 702

products, allocating full joint costs to them. In this case, Product C should only be accounted for at net realizable value (NRV), and its value is deducted from the total joint costs.  Misunderstanding of NRV Concept: Some students fail to calculate the net realizable value correctly, especially for Product B and Product C. They may incorrectly include processing costs or fail to subtract them when calculating the NRV.  Overcomplicating the Calculation: A common mistake is overcomplicating the joint cost allocation by including unnecessary steps or details. Students should focus on the split-off point sales values and net realizable value to allocate the joint costs efficiently, without redundant calculations.  Not Considering Product A’s Sale at Split-off: Students sometimes overlook that Product A is sold at the split- off point and doesn’t require further processing. This can lead to incorrect assumptions and over complication.  Incorrect Application of Further Processing Costs: Students sometimes incorrectly apply further processing costs to all products, even if the product is not further processed (like Product A). It's crucial to distinguish between products that are processed further and those that are not.  Skipping the Deduction of By-Product NRV: Sometimes students fail to subtract the NRV of Product C (the by- product) from the total joint cost before allocating the remaining costs between the other products.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips  Step 1: Calculate Total Joint Costs: Add up direct material, direct labor, variable overheads, and fixed overheads to determine total joint costs (1 mark).  Step 2: Apportion Joint Costs:

 Physical Quantity Method: Divide joint costs based on the physical volume of products produced. Ensure the correct ratio for each product (2 marks).  Contribution Margin Method: Calculate the contribution margin for each product (Sales Revenue - Variable Costs). Apportion fixed costs to the product with a positive contribution margin (2 marks).  Step 3: Profit or Loss Calculation: Deduct the apportioned costs from the sales value to determine profit or loss for both methods (2 marks).  Step 4: Final Answer: Clearly mention the profit or loss for both methods under the required headings.

© Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 704

Examiner Observations  Incorrect Apportionment of Fixed Costs: One common mistake students make is the incorrect apportionment of fixed overheads in the Contribution Margin Method. The fixed cost of Rs. 64,000 should be apportioned based on the contribution margin, but if the contribution margin for one product is negative (like for Cream), students often forget that the entire fixed cost will be allocated to the product with a positive contribution margin (Ghee). This must be carefully noted.  Misapplication of the Physical Quantity Method: When using the Physical Quantity Method, students sometimes apply the formula incorrectly or misinterpret the physical quantities. The apportionment should be based on the relative quantities of the two products, so errors in calculating the total volume of products or distributing the joint costs in proportion to the quantities produced can lead to mistakes.  Ignoring Contribution Margin for Profitability: In the Contribution Margin Method, students often overlook the concept of contribution margin and its role in profitability analysis. They may fail to calculate the contribution margin first (i.e., Sales Revenue - Variable Costs) before applying the fixed cost apportionment, which affects the final profit or loss for each product.  Overcomplicating the Calculation: Sometimes, students overcomplicate the process by including irrelevant details or skipping simple calculations that are key to accurate cost allocation.  Failure to Identify the Correct Profit/Loss Computation: Students may make the mistake of calculating only sales revenue and joint costs but neglect to compute the profit/loss after the cost allocation step. This is crucial for the final answer.

Question 9. A company produces two joint products A and B from the same basic materials. The processing is completed in three departments. Materials are mixed in Department I. At the end of this process, A and B get separated. After separation, A is completed in the Department II and B in Department III. During a period, 4,00,000 kg of raw material was processed in Department I at a total cost of Rs. 17,50,000, and the resultant 50% becomes A and 40% becomes B and 10% normally lost in processing. (2+1+2+2+1) Approach & Time-Saving Tips  Step 1 – Quantity Table: First, prepare a table with input, loss, output at each department for A and B. This avoids repeated calculations.  Step 2 – Apportion Joint Cost: Use split-off point sales value ratio (A:B = 16,00,000:6,40,000 → 5:2).  Step 3 – Cost per kg: Add further processing costs per kg to joint cost per kg.  Step 4 – Profit Calculation: Multiply sales quantity with selling price, add closing stock value at cost, subtract total costs.  Step 5 – Further Processing Decision: Compare profit before and after processing to decide.

Examiner Observations  Quantity Calculation Errors:

 Students often take 50% A, 40% B directly as final production, ignoring normal loss (10%) in Dept I.  In Dept II, 1/5th loss of A is sometimes ignored. Similarly, for B, forgetting to double the weight in Dept III leads to wrong cost per kg.  Joint Cost Apportionment Mistakes:

 Students sometimes use final output instead of sales value at split-off point. Using post-processing prices instead of split-off prices (Rs. 8 for A, Rs. 4 for B) is a frequent error.  Processing Cost Allocation:

 Some allocate Dept II and III costs incorrectly, or per kg wrongly due to miscalculated quantities after loss/additions.  Profit Statement Errors:

 Ignoring closing stock (kg × total cost) or using selling price for stock valuation is common.  Profitability analysis before and after further processing is skipped or misinterpreted.  Presentation / Stepwise Approach:

 Marks are lost if the solution is not structured stepwise: Quantity → Joint Cost → Cost/kg → Profit → © Catestseries.org® | Cost and Management Accounting Pg. 707

(4+4) Approach & Time-Saving Tips  Step 1 – Joint Cost Apportionment: Divide pre-separation cost in proportion to physical units. Use fractions for accuracy.  Step 2 – Profit/Loss Statement: Deduct apportioned joint cost and further processing cost from sales value after further processing.  Step 3 – Incremental Analysis: Compute incremental revenue = (Post-processing SP – Pre-separation SP) × Quantity. Deduct only further processing cost to decide profitability.  Step 4 – Management Decision: Compare incremental profit; process only if positive.

Examiner Observations  Joint Cost Apportionment:

 Students frequently misallocate joint costs using sales value at further processing instead of physical output (weight) as given in the question.  Rounding errors in fractions (0.4, 0.28, 0.32) sometimes lead to incorrect cost per product.  Further Processing Cost Deduction:

 Some incorrectly deduct pre-separation costs again under further processing, double counting costs.  Incremental Profit Calculation:

 A common mistake is to compare total sales after processing with total cost instead of focusing on incremental revenue vs further processing cost.  Students often fail to interpret the result for decision-making: for example, product Y shows negative incremental profit, so it should be sold at split-off point.  Presentation / Stepwise Approach:

 Marks are lost if apportionment, total cost, profit, and incremental analysis are not in clearly labeled tables.

(3+2) Approach & Time-Saving Tips  Step 1 – Adjust Joint Cost: Deduct by-product NRV from total joint cost to get net joint cost for main product.  Step 2 – Add Further Processing Cost: Include all costs necessary to make main product saleable.  Step 3 – Profit Calculation: Subtract net joint cost + processing cost from sales revenue to get profit/loss.  Step 4 – Selling Price for Desired Profit: Total cost + desired profit ÷ number of units.

Examiner Observations  Ignoring By-product Value: The most common error is treating the main product as absorbing full joint cost rather than reducing it by by-product NRV (200 units × Rs. 5 = Rs. 1,000). This inflates the cost and underestimates profit.  Further Processing Cost Errors: Some students fail to include further processing cost when computing total cost for profit or selling price calculation.  Profit/Selling Price Miscalculation: When calculating selling price for a desired profit, students sometimes divide only the joint cost by units instead of total cost (joint cost net of by-product + further processing) + desired profit, leading to incorrect price per unit.  Presentation Mistakes: Stepwise format is crucial: Deduct by-product value → Add further processing → Compute profit → Compute selling price. Skipping steps leads to loss of marks.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips  Step 1 – Compute NRV: Sales revenue after further processing – Further processing cost for each product.  Step 2 – Apportion Joint Costs: Joint cost × (NRV of product ÷ Total NRV).  Step 3 – Income Forecast (No Further Processing): Use split-off sales price, subtract apportioned joint cost, then fixed costs.  Step 4 – Income Forecast (All Processed): Use post-processing sales revenue, subtract apportioned joint cost + further processing cost, then fixed costs.  Step 5 – Suggested Plan: Compare incremental profit for each product (Revenue – Total Cost), process only those with positive incremental profit.  Step 6 – Tabulate Clearly: Present all 3 scenarios in tables to save time and avoid calculation errors.

Examiner Observations  Incorrect Joint Cost Apportionment:

 Students sometimes use sales revenue at split-off point for apportionment instead of NRV after deducting further processing costs.  Rounding errors in fractions may lead to slightly wrong apportioned costs.  Incremental Profit Errors:

 Many misinterpret further processing cost as part of joint cost rather than an additional cost.  Some fail to compare incremental revenue vs further processing cost for each product when deciding which products to process further.

 Profit Statement Mistakes:

 Confusion between total processing cost (apportioned joint cost + further processing cost) and separate calculations often leads to misstatement of profit.  Fixed costs are sometimes incorrectly allocated or ignored.  Presentation / Stepwise Approach:

 Marks are lost if income statements for “no further processing,” “all further processing,” and “suggested plan” are not clearly tabulated and labeled.

Conversion cost of Rs.1,00,000 were incurred up-to the split off point, where two saleable products were produced i.e. buttermilk and butter. Butter can be further processed into Ghee. The January production and sales information is as follows: Products Production (in Sales Quantity (in Selling price per Litre/Kg

Kilolitre/tonne) Kilolitre/tonne) (Rs.) Buttermilk 28 28 30 Butter 20 — — Ghee 16 16 480 All 20 tonne of butter were further processed at an incremental cost of Rs. 1, 20,000 to yield 16 Kilolitre of Ghee. There was no opening or closing inventories of buttermilk, butter or ghee in the month of January.

Required: (i) SHOW how joint cost would be apportioned between Buttermilk and Butter under Estimated Net Realizable Value method. (ii) ‘Healthy Bones’ offers to purchase 20 tonne of butter in February at Rs. 360 per kg. In case ‘Buttery Butter’ accepts this offer, no Ghee would be produced in February. SUGGEST whether ‘Buttery Butter’ shall accept the offer affecting its operating income or further process butter to make Ghee itself?

Answer 13

(i) Estimated Net Realisable Value Method:

Buttermilk Amount (Rs.) Butter Amount (Rs.) Sales Value 8,40,000 (Rs. 30 × 28 × 1000) 76, 80,000 (Rs. 480 × 16 × 1000)

Less: Post split-off cost (Further processing - (1,20,000) cost) Net Realisable Value 8,40,000 75,60,000 Apportionment of Joint Cost of Rs. 5,10,000 45,90,000 51,00,000\* in ratio of 1:9

The operating income of ‘Buttery Butter’ will be reduced by Rs. 3,60,000 in February if it sells 20 tonne of Butter to ‘Healthy Bones’, instead of further processing of Butter into Ghee for sale. Approach & Time-Saving Tips  Step 1 – Calculate NRV: For Butter, subtract further processing cost (Rs. 1,20,000) from post-processing sales revenue (Ghee).  Step 2 – Apportion Joint Cost: Joint cost × (NRV of product ÷ Total NRV). Do the same for Buttermilk.  Step 3 – Incremental Analysis: Compare incremental revenue from processing Butter into Ghee (Revenue from Ghee – Revenue from selling Butter) minus incremental cost.  Step 4 – Decision: Accept offer only if incremental operating income is positive; otherwise, process Butter into Ghee.

Examiner Observations  Incorrect Joint Cost Apportionment:  Common error is to apportion the joint cost of Butter and Buttermilk based on sales value at split-off, ignoring that Butter is further processed to Ghee, so NRV must deduct incremental processing cost.  Incremental Analysis Errors:  Many students calculate total sales from Butter vs Ghee, ignoring the incremental operating income from further processing.  Some miscalculate quantity conversion (20 tonnes Butter → 16 tonnes Ghee) or fail to multiply by 1,000 to convert kilolitres to litres.  Profit/Decision Confusion:  Students sometimes suggest selling Butter to ‘Healthy Bones’ without showing reduction in operating income, which is essential for ICAI exams.  Presentation / Stepwise Approach:  Marks are lost if NRV calculation, apportionment, and incremental analysis are not in tabular form with clear labeling of costs and revenues.

Approach & Time-Saving Tips  Step 1 – Apportion Joint Costs: Joint cost × (Sales value at split-off ÷ Total split-off sales). Keep this constant for all products.  Step 2 – Compute Profit at Split-off: Sales at split-off – Apportioned joint cost.  Step 3 – Compute Profit after Further Processing: Sales after further processing – Apportioned joint cost – Further processing cost.  Step 4 – Incremental Profit: Difference between profit after further processing and split-off profit.  Step 5 – Suggestion: Process only products with positive incremental profit (S), sell the rest at split-off.

Examiner Observations  Incorrect Apportionment of Joint Costs:

 Students sometimes apportion based on post-processing sales instead of split-off sales, inflating joint cost for products and distorting profit comparison.  Profit Comparison Errors:

 Many students calculate “profit if further processed” correctly but forget to subtract the profit at split-off to compute incremental profit, leading to wrong decision on which products to process further.  Ignoring Negative Incremental Profit:

 For Product N, further processing decreases profit, but students often overlook this and suggest processing it.  Presentation / Stepwise Approach:

 Marks are lost if split-off profit, post-processing profit, and incremental profit are not tabulated clearly.
